benchmarks.name: LoCoMo
benchmarks.title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
benchmarks.what: 10 very long two-speaker conversations (~300 turns, up to 35 sessions each) with QA in five categories.

versions.original: The released locomo10.json.
versions.refined: LoCoMo Refined (mem-eval-suite): cleaned answers plus a stricter judge prompt.
versions.secom-gpt4-generated-qa: version as reported by secom; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Category 5 (adversarial) is usually dropped, leaving about 1,540 of 1,986 questions; papers that keep it are not comparable with those that drop it.
The category ids in the released file are not in the order the paper lists them, and papers map ids to names differently. Check which mapping a paper used before comparing per-category scores.
'LLM-judge accuracy' depends heavily on the judge prompt: the Mem0-style lenient prompt and stricter prompts differ by many points on identical answers.
Some gold answers are wrong or ambiguous, which is what LoCoMo Refined fixes.

benchmarks.name: LoCoMo Refined
benchmarks.title: LoCoMo Refined: Recalibrating LoCoMo with Stricter LLM Judging and A Cleaned Dataset
benchmarks.what: LoCoMo with corrected gold answers and a stricter judge. Recorded as benchmark 'locomo', version 'refined', when a paper uses it.
pitfalls: Scores are not comparable with original-LoCoMo scores even for the same system and backbone.

benchmarks.name: LoCoMo-Plus
benchmarks.title: Locomo-Plus: Beyond-Factual Cognitive Memory Evaluation Framework for LLM Agents
benchmarks.what: Extends LoCoMo beyond factual recall.

benchmarks.name: LongMemEval
benchmarks.title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
benchmarks.what: 500 questions over user–assistant chat histories, testing extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention.
pitfalls: S, M and oracle are different difficulty levels; always record which one.
The official judge is GPT-4o with the benchmark's own prompt; papers that swap the judge are not directly comparable.
Some papers evaluate a subset of the 500 questions.

benchmarks.name: PersonaMem
benchmarks.title: Know Me, Respond to Me: Benchmarking LLMs for Dynamic User Profiling and Personalized Responses at Scale
benchmarks.what: Multiple-choice questions on evolving user personas across long histories.

versions.1m: version as reported by qumem; see that results file's notes
versions.all: version as reported by qumem; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Context length (32K / 128K / 1M) changes difficulty; record it as the version.
Multiple-choice accuracy; random baseline is not zero.

benchmarks.name: PersonaMem-v2
benchmarks.title: PersonaMem-v2
benchmarks.what: Second version of PersonaMem with implicit personas.

versions.32k: version as reported by evermemos; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Not comparable with PersonaMem v1 scores.

benchmarks.name: Multi-Session Chat (MSC)
benchmarks.title: Beyond Goldfish Memory: Long-Term Open-Domain Conversation
benchmarks.what: Multi-session open-domain dialogues; memory papers often use it for response generation or derived QA.

versions.dmr: version as reported by memgpt; see that results file's notes
versions.conversation-opener: version as reported by memgpt; see that results file's notes
versions.original: version as reported by theanine; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Papers derive different QA sets from MSC (e.g. MemGPT's deep memory retrieval task); record which one in 'subset'.

benchmarks.name: HaluMem
benchmarks.title: HaluMem: Evaluating Hallucinations in Memory Systems of Agents
benchmarks.what: Operation-level evaluation of memory extraction, updating and QA hallucination.

benchmarks.name: MemoryAgentBench
benchmarks.title: Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions
benchmarks.what: Accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding and conflict resolution.

versions.FactConsolidation: version as reported by mindmemos; see that results file's notes
versions.RULER-QA1 (Single-Doc): version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.RULER-QA2 (Multi-Doc): version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.LME(S*): version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.TREC-Coarse: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.NLU: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.TREC-Fine: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.Clinic150: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.Banking77: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.InfBench-Sum: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes
versions.average of 9: version as reported by mem; see that results file's notes

benchmarks.name: BEAM
benchmarks.title: Beyond a Million Tokens: Benchmarking and Enhancing Long-Term Memory in LLMs
benchmarks.what: Long-term memory QA over conversations of 100K to 10M tokens.
pitfalls: Scale (100K / 500K / 1M / 10M) is the version and changes difficulty sharply.

benchmarks.name: DialSim
benchmarks.title: DialSim
benchmarks.what: Real-time dialogue simulation benchmark used by A-Mem. Link not yet verified.

versions.v1.1: version as reported by higmem; see that results file's notes

benchmarks.name: GVD
benchmarks.title: GVD dialogue set (from MemoryBank)
benchmarks.what: Multi-day dialogue set introduced with MemoryBank; MemoryOS reports judge-based scores on it.

versions.original: version as reported by memoryos; see that results file's notes

benchmarks.name: REALTALK
benchmarks.title: REALTALK
benchmarks.what: Long-term real-world conversation dataset used by H-Mem. Link not yet verified.

versions.original: version as reported by h; see that results file's notes

benchmarks.name: Long-MT-Bench+
benchmarks.title: Long-MT-Bench+ (built by SeCom from MT-Bench+)
benchmarks.what: Long multi-session conversations assembled from MT-Bench+ with QA, introduced in the SeCom paper.

versions.original: version as reported by secom; see that results file's notes

benchmarks.name: ALFWorld
benchmarks.title: ALFWorld: Aligning Text and Embodied Environments for Interactive Learning
benchmarks.what: Text-based household environments where an agent follows instructions over many steps; six task types such as pick-and-place, clean, heat and cool (as described in AgeMem App. C.1).

versions.original: As released; AgeMem does not state which split or how many games it evaluates.

pitfalls: Scored by success rate; the split and the number of evaluated games vary between papers.
Not a memory benchmark by design: what an agent can store before the task depends on each paper's setup.

benchmarks.name: ScienceWorld
benchmarks.title: ScienceWorld: Is your Agent Smarter than a 5th Grader?
benchmarks.what: Interactive text simulator of science experiments (physics, chemistry, biology) requiring multi-step procedures (as described in AgeMem App. C.1).

versions.original: As released; AgeMem does not state the task subset.

pitfalls: Papers report either a success rate or a partial score; AgeMem reports success rate (SR).

benchmarks.name: PDDL (AgentBoard)
benchmarks.title: AgentBoard: An Analytical Evaluation Board of Multi-turn LLM Agents
benchmarks.what: Symbolic planning problems written in the Planning Domain Definition Language, from the AgentBoard suite; agents must produce action sequences that reach a goal state.

versions.original: AgentBoard PDDL tasks; AgeMem cites Chang et al. 2024 (AgentBoard).
versions.AgentBoard: version as reported by hiagent; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Scored by progress rate (PR), not success rate; not comparable with success-rate numbers.

benchmarks.name: BabyAI
benchmarks.title: BabyAI: A Platform to Study the Sample Efficiency of Grounded Language Learning
benchmarks.what: Grid-world navigation levels with compositional natural-language instructions (as described in AgeMem App. C.1).

versions.original: As released; AgeMem does not state which levels are used.

pitfalls: The levels and the text interface used by LLM-agent papers differ; check them before comparing.

benchmarks.name: HotpotQA
benchmarks.title: HotpotQA: A Dataset for Diverse, Explainable Multi-hop Question Answering
benchmarks.what: Multi-hop Wikipedia questions (about 90k training questions) annotated with supporting-fact sentences.

versions.original: As released (distractor and fullwiki settings); AgeMem's released config uses fullwiki, train split for RL and test split for evaluation.
versions.memagent-7k: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~7K tokens of context
versions.memagent-14k: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~14K tokens of context
versions.memagent-28k: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~28K tokens of context
versions.memagent-112k: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~112K tokens of context
versions.memagent-896k: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~896K tokens of context
versions.memagent-1.75m: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~1.75M tokens of context
versions.memagent-3.5m: MemAgent (arXiv 2507.02259) RULER-HQA set, ~3.5M tokens of context

pitfalls: Distractor and fullwiki settings are different tasks.
Scores differ by metric: EM/F1 vs an LLM judge (AgeMem uses a Qwen-Max judge on a 0-1 scale).
In memory papers the paragraphs are fed as pre-task context the agent may store, which is not the standard reading-comprehension setup.
The original HotpotQA and MemAgent's distractor-padded version are different tasks; check the context length.
F1/EM normalisation differs between evaluation scripts.
Settings (distractor vs full-wiki, subset size, agent tools) vary across papers and are often not reported.

benchmarks.name: NovelQA
benchmarks.title: NovelQA: Benchmarking Question Answering on Documents Exceeding 200K Tokens
benchmarks.what: Question answering over whole novels (on average more than 200K tokens each); CAM's split has 89 novels and 2,305 questions, annotated by complexity (single-hop, multi-hop, detail) and aspect.

versions.generative: Free-form answers scored with ROUGE and an LLM judge (as in CAM Table 2).
versions.multichoice: Four options A-D; the CAM code's default QA mode.

pitfalls: Full texts and gold answers are not public; access is by request to the authors.
Generative and multiple-choice settings are not comparable.

benchmarks.name: QMSum
benchmarks.title: QMSum: A New Benchmark for Query-based Multi-domain Meeting Summarization
benchmarks.what: Query-based summarization of meeting transcripts (around 10K words each); CAM uses 232 transcripts and 1,808 queries.

versions.original: version as reported by cam; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: ROUGE and LLM-judge accuracy can rank systems differently.

benchmarks.name: FABLES
benchmarks.title: FABLES: Evaluating Faithfulness and Content Selection in Book-Length Summarization
benchmarks.what: Claim verification against book-length documents (more than 120K tokens on average); CAM uses 26 documents and 3,158 claims, reporting F1 for the true and false labels separately.

versions.original: version as reported by cam; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: CAM removes unanswerable claims before evaluation.
Documents and labels are released only on request.

benchmarks.name: MultiHop-RAG
benchmarks.title: MultiHop-RAG: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-Hop Queries
benchmarks.what: Multi-hop questions over a corpus of 609 news articles (about 2K tokens each) in six categories; short answers scored by exact match and F1.

versions.original: version as reported by cam; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: CAM removes unanswerable questions (2,255 kept).

benchmarks.name: ODSum
benchmarks.title: ODSum: New Benchmarks for Open Domain Multi-Document Summarization
benchmarks.what: Open-domain query-based summarization over many documents.

versions.story: ODSum-Story: 1,190 story documents (~809 tokens each), 635 queries in CAM.
versions.meeting: ODSum-Meeting: 232 meeting documents (~7,176 tokens each), 436 queries in CAM.

pitfalls: Story and Meeting are separate subsets; always record which.

benchmarks.name: Multi-Agent Crafter
benchmarks.title: Multi-Agent Crafter (MAC), introduced in the DAMCS paper
benchmarks.what: Multi-agent extension of the Crafter survival game: n agents with separate observations and inventories can share items and must climb a 10-task crafting chain to obtain a diamond as fast as possible; scored by average steps to complete each task.

versions.diamond task (paper's environment): 1, 2 or 6 agents; average steps per task over ten runs (DAMCS Table 1)

pitfalls: Lower is better (steps, not accuracy).
Only the DAMCS authors report results; LLM rows use GPT-4o.

benchmarks.name: OVO-Bench
benchmarks.title: OVO-Bench: How Far is Your Video-LLMs from Real-World Online Video Understanding?
benchmarks.what: Online video QA where a model may use only the video before the question time; 12 tasks in three groups: Real-Time Visual Perception, Backward Tracing and Forward Active Responding.
pitfalls: EventMemAgent's overall score is the mean of the three group averages; check that other papers aggregate the same way.
Frame budgets differ widely across reported models (32 frames, 64 frames, 1-2 fps).
EventMemAgent cites it as CVPR 2025 without an arXiv id or code link; fill these from the benchmark paper.

benchmarks.name: StreamingBench
benchmarks.title: StreamingBench: Assessing the Gap for MLLMs to Achieve Streaming Video Understanding
benchmarks.what: Streaming video QA; EventMemAgent reports its real-time visual understanding part (10 task columns: OP, CR, CS, ATP, EU, TR, PR, SU, ACP, CT) plus an overall score.
pitfalls: Weighted accuracy and task-macro accuracy differ; EventMemAgent's overall column is weighted accuracy (its repo docs).

benchmarks.name: RULER
benchmarks.title: RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?
benchmarks.what: Synthetic long-context tasks at configurable lengths: retrieval (needle), multi-hop tracing of variable assignments, aggregation, and QA.

versions.niah-8k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~8K tokens, as run by MemAgent
versions.niah-16k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~16K tokens, as run by MemAgent
versions.niah-32k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~32K tokens, as run by MemAgent
versions.niah-64k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~64K tokens, as run by MemAgent
versions.niah-128k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~128K tokens, as run by MemAgent
versions.niah-256k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~256K tokens, as run by MemAgent
versions.niah-512k: needle-in-a-haystack tasks at ~512K tokens, as run by MemAgent

pitfalls: Papers report subsets of the task groups and different lengths; per-group accuracies are only comparable at the same length and task mix.

benchmarks.name: NarrativeQA
benchmarks.title: The NarrativeQA Reading Comprehension Challenge
benchmarks.what: Questions over whole books or movie scripts, answered from the full text.

versions.original: full-document setting (TACL 2018)

pitfalls: Memory papers often score a random subset (e.g. 300 questions in GAM) that is not released, so numbers across papers are not directly comparable.

benchmarks.name: BABILong
benchmarks.title: BABILong: Testing the Limits of LLMs with Long Context Reasoning-in-a-Haystack
benchmarks.what: bAbI reasoning tasks (qa1-qa20) whose supporting facts are scattered through long distractor text of a chosen length.

versions.10 cases per cell: ILM-TR paper: qa1-qa5, lengths 0k-128k, 10 test cases per task and length

pitfalls: Papers often evaluate a subset of tasks and lengths with few samples.

benchmarks.name: Multi-Needle In A Haystack
benchmarks.title: LLMTest_NeedleInAHaystack (multi-needle variant, Kamradt 2024)
benchmarks.what: Several related sentences (needles) are inserted into a long text at chosen depths; the question needs all of them.

versions.3 needles: ILM-TR paper: 3 pizza-ingredient needles, 150k-500k tokens, 5 depths; cell scored 1/3/7/10 by keywords found

pitfalls: Needles, haystack text and scoring vary between papers.

benchmarks.name: Memalpha dataset
benchmarks.title: Mem-α training and validation data (SQuAD, HotpotQA, PerLTQA, LongMemEval-train, NLU, TREC-Coarse, PubMed-RCT, BookSum rebuilt as chunked multi-turn inputs)
benchmarks.what: Instances of about 8-23 chunks (roughly 400-1,900 tokens per chunk, at most 30K tokens in total) followed by questions; covers accurate retrieval, test-time learning (classification from labelled examples) and long-range understanding (summary keyword hit).

versions.validation: 463 instances from 7 sources, same distribution as training (Mem-α Table 6-7).

pitfalls: Built by the Mem-α authors and matches their training distribution; results on it are in-distribution for Mem-α.
Each source uses a different metric (SubEM, EM, keyword hit), so the average mixes scales.

benchmarks.name: FEVER
benchmarks.title: FEVER: a large-scale dataset for Fact Extraction and VERification
benchmarks.what: Human-written claims about Wikipedia entities labelled Supported, Refuted or NotEnoughInfo; used as a fact-verification task for agents.

versions.original: version as reported by expel; see that results file's notes
versions.KILT dev: version as reported by knowledgeeditor; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Agent-memory papers evaluate their own subsets with their own agent loop; the number of claims and the retrieval tool are often not stated.

benchmarks.name: DeepResearch Bench
benchmarks.title: DeepResearch Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Deep Research Agents
benchmarks.what: 100 PhD-level research tasks from 22 fields. RACE scores report quality against a reference report (comprehensiveness, insight, instruction following, readability); FACT scores citation accuracy and effective citations per task.

versions.original: 100 tasks, official RACE/FACT with Gemini-2.5-pro judge

pitfalls: RACE is relative to a reference report and judged by an LLM; the judge model changes scores.
Leaderboard numbers for proprietary agents are copied, not rerun.

benchmarks.name: DeepConsult
benchmarks.title: Deep Consult (ydc-deep-research-evals)
benchmarks.what: Business and consulting research prompts; reports are judged pairwise against an OpenAI deep-research baseline (win/tie/lose rates plus an average quality score on a 0-10 scale).

versions.original: pairwise vs openai-deepresearch, GPT-4.1 judge

pitfalls: Scores are relative to one fixed baseline report set; the baseline itself scores 0/100/0 by construction.

benchmarks.name: DeepResearchGym
benchmarks.title: DeepResearchGym: A Free, Transparent, and Reproducible Evaluation Sandbox for Deep Research
benchmarks.what: Evaluation sandbox; 100 queries sampled from Researchy Questions, reports judged by an LLM on clarity, depth, balance, breadth, support and insightfulness.

versions.original: 100 Researchy Questions queries, GPT-4.1-mini judge

pitfalls: Several dimensions saturate near 100 for strong systems, so differences are small.

benchmarks.name: LatentNeeds-Bench
benchmarks.title: PASK: Toward Intent-Aware Proactive Agents with Long-Term Memory (benchmark introduced in the paper)
benchmarks.what: Turn-level proactive demand detection on real speech transcripts: 100 sessions (3,936 turns) across 10 subcategories of work, learning and daily life; at each turn a model must reply with help or output [NO_DEMAND]. 41.9% of turns carry an annotated demand (Requirement or Insight type).

versions.original: Evaluation split of 100 sessions, 10 per subcategory (§6.1.1).

pitfalls: Scores are balanced accuracy (mean of demand and non-demand accuracy), judged by an LLM; the paper names GPT-5.2 while the released config uses gpt-4.1-mini.
Each model is reported at its best of three prompt levels, so rows use different prompts.
A reply on a non-demand turn can still count as correct if the judge finds it valuable.
Long recordings are split into 60-turn parts; later parts get a short LLM summary of earlier parts as 'memory', the same for every model.
The benchmark data file is not in the repository at the checked commit (data/ is git-ignored); only per-model outputs and scores are released.

benchmarks.name: ZH-4O
benchmarks.title: MOOM: Maintenance, Organization and Optimization of Memory in Ultra-Long Role-Playing Dialogues
benchmarks.what: Chinese role-playing benchmark of 28 real human-LLM sessions (about 600 turns each) with 1,068 multiple-choice probing questions on memory (as described in TeleMem §4).

versions.original: As released with MOOM; TeleMem's repo ships a LoCoMo-format copy at data/zh4o/data.json (28 samples, 1,068 questions).

pitfalls: Multiple choice: chance accuracy is well above zero and answers are parsed as a single letter.
Chinese only; memory prompts written for English data may not transfer.

benchmarks.name: AppWorld
benchmarks.title: AppWorld: A Controllable World of Apps and People for Benchmarking Interactive Coding Agents
benchmarks.what: Tasks over nine simulated everyday apps (Spotify, Venmo, SimpleNote, Gmail, ...) with 457 APIs and about 100 simulated users; agents write API calls over many steps.

versions.test-normal: official test-normal split (168 tasks in ACON)
versions.test-challenge: version as reported by ace; see that results file's notes
versions.test-normal + test-challenge: version as reported by ace; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Scores are task goal completion; report which split (test-normal vs test-challenge) and the difficulty levels.

benchmarks.name: OfficeBench
benchmarks.title: OfficeBench: Benchmarking Language Agents across Multiple Applications for Office Automation
benchmarks.what: Office automation tasks that span one to three apps (Word, Excel, PDF, calendar, email, shell).

versions.text-only, authors' split: ACON: OCR tasks removed, random 1:1 train/test split (92/95), ambiguous tasks removed

pitfalls: No official split; ACON's split and task filtering are its own, so scores are not comparable across papers.

benchmarks.name: Multi-objective QA
benchmarks.title: MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents
benchmarks.what: Several NaturalQuestions questions bundled into one task; the agent searches Wikipedia and must answer all of them at the end.

versions.8-objective: 8 questions per task (ACON: 100 train / 100 test tasks, BM25 over 2018 Wikipedia)

pitfalls: Number of objectives per task changes difficulty; check it before comparing.

benchmarks.name: CounterFact
benchmarks.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
benchmarks.what: Counterfactual factual rewrites (subject, relation, new object) with paraphrase prompts, neighborhood prompts about related subjects, and generation prompts for fluency and consistency.

versions.mcf: MultiCounterFact as distributed with MEMIT and used by AlphaEdit (--ds_name=mcf), 2,000 random records edited in batches of 100.

pitfalls: Efficacy, generalization and specificity compare probabilities of the new vs original object, not generated answers.
Fluency is an n-gram entropy (~600 for fluent text), not a percentage.
Results depend strongly on the number of sequential edits and the batch size.

benchmarks.name: WebArena
benchmarks.title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
benchmarks.what: 812 tasks on self-hosted websites (shopping, shopping admin, Reddit-like forum, GitLab, map), scored by programmatic success checks.

versions.original: The 812-task release.

pitfalls: Tasks come from templates (up to five tasks per template), so learning methods can gain by reusing a template's solution; cross-template success is a stricter view.
Agents differ in observation space and harness (e.g. BrowserGym vs the original), which moves scores by several points.
Some papers report per-site splits only, and the 'Average' is sometimes a task-weighted mean, sometimes not.

benchmarks.name: VisualWebArena
benchmarks.title: VisualWebArena: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Realistic Visual Web Tasks
benchmarks.what: 910 multimodal web tasks on classifieds, shopping and forum sites, many needing images in the goal or page.

versions.original: The 910-task release.

pitfalls: Results depend on the observation format (Set-of-Marks screenshots, accessibility tree) and step limit.
Search-based methods spend far more tokens per task than single-trajectory agents.

benchmarks.name: ∞Bench (InfiniteBench)
benchmarks.title: ∞Bench: Extending Long Context Evaluation Beyond 100K Tokens
benchmarks.what: Long-context tasks averaging over 100k tokens; the novel QA tasks En.QA (free-form answers) and En.MC (multiple choice) are the ones memory and RAG papers use.

versions.original: As released; EM-LLM uses six tasks (Code.Debug, Math.Find, En.MC, Retrieve.KV, Retrieve.PassKey, Retrieve.Number) and also an extended passkey test up to 10.2M tokens.

pitfalls: En.QA and En.MC are separate tasks with different metrics (F1/EM vs accuracy); keep them apart via the subset field.
Averages depend on which tasks are included.
Passkey and number retrieval are near 100% for most methods, which lifts averages.

benchmarks.name: DetectiveQA
benchmarks.title: DetectiveQA: Evaluating Long-Context Reasoning on Detective Novels
benchmarks.what: Multiple-choice questions on detective novels averaging over 100k tokens, asking who did it, how and why.

versions.original: 2024 release

pitfalls: ComoRAG scores a random 20% of stories that is not released.

benchmarks.name: ToolBench
benchmarks.title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
benchmarks.what: Tasks over 16,000+ real RapidAPI tools in 49 categories; DeepAgent uses the G3 multi-tool subset with 100 test cases (App. A.2).

versions.original: As released; DeepAgent reports the G3 subset, with ground-truth tools or open-set retrieval over the full toolset.
versions.G3: I3-Instruction (G3) test queries: multi-tool requests across categories

pitfalls: Real APIs change or fail over time, so reruns are unstable.
Labeled-tool and open-set retrieval settings are different tasks.
Success and path metrics are defined per paper.
Live RapidAPI endpoints change or fail over time, so reruns of the same method drift.
Papers use different subsets (I1/I2/I3) and small samples of them; DRAFT uses 100 I3 queries.
Win rate is a ChatGPT pairwise judgement against a reference method and depends on the evaluator model.

benchmarks.name: API-Bank
benchmarks.title: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
benchmarks.what: Runnable tool-use benchmark with 73 APIs and 314 dialogues (753 calls), testing planning, retrieval and calling (DeepAgent §4.1).

versions.original: As released; level/subset used by DeepAgent not stated.

pitfalls: Levels (call, retrieve+call, plan+retrieve+call) are often mixed or unreported.

benchmarks.name: RestBench
benchmarks.title: RestGPT: Connecting Large Language Models with Real-World Applications via RESTful APIs
benchmarks.what: Real REST API scenarios: TMDB (100 questions, 54 tools, 2.3 calls each) and Spotify (57 questions, 40 tools, 2.6 calls each), per DeepAgent App. A.2.
pitfalls: TMDB and Spotify are separate scenarios with different sizes; Spotify needs a live account.
Correct Path Rate only checks that the gold APIs appear in order among the calls, not that the final answer is right.
Small test sets (about 100 TMDB and 57 Spotify queries), so single queries move scores by 1-2 points.

benchmarks.name: ToolHop
benchmarks.title: ToolHop: A Query-Driven Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Multi-Hop Tool Use
benchmarks.what: 995 multi-hop questions over 3,912 locally executable tools, needing 3-7 sequential calls (DeepAgent App. A.2).

versions.original: As released.

pitfalls: Answer correctness and path scores are reported separately.

benchmarks.name: WebShop
benchmarks.title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents
benchmarks.what: Simulated shopping site with 12,087 instructions over 1.18M products; the agent searches and clicks to buy a matching item.

versions.original: As released; ReAct, Reflexion and ExpeL evaluate the same 100 tasks.

pitfalls: Success rate and average score are different metrics.
Number of evaluated instructions is often unstated.
Success rate and mean reward are different metrics.
ExpeL fixes prices to the average value and shows 10 items per page instead of 3, so its numbers are on a modified environment.

benchmarks.name: GAIA
benchmarks.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
benchmarks.what: 466 real-world assistant questions needing web browsing, code, multimodal input and files; 300 held out as test (DeepAgent App. A.2).

versions.original: papers often use the text-only validation subset

pitfalls: Validation and test sets differ; many papers report a text-only subset.
Scores depend strongly on the search and browsing tools used.
Which split and subset is used is often unstated.

benchmarks.name: Humanity's Last Exam
benchmarks.title: Humanity's Last Exam
benchmarks.what: 2,500 very hard graduate-level multi-disciplinary questions, text and multimodal.

versions.original: full question set as used by the reporting paper; text-only subsets are common

pitfalls: Papers often evaluate subsets (text-only or sampled).
Tool access (search, code) changes what is measured.
Papers differ on text-only vs full set and on the grading model; IterResearch does not state which it used.

benchmarks.name: LongBench
benchmarks.title: LongBench: A Bilingual, Multitask Benchmark for Long Context Understanding
benchmarks.what: Long-context tasks grouped into single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, summarisation, few-shot learning, retrieval and code; EM-LLM reports 15 tasks.

versions.original: As released; EM-LLM reports 15 tasks and six grouped averages (average example length 12K ± 10K tokens with Mistral's tokenizer, App. D.3).
versions.v1: LongBench v1 (ACL 2024); MemAgent uses the five QA sets as LongBench-QA and GovReport + QMSum as LongBench-SUM

pitfalls: Each task has its own metric (F1, ROUGE-L, classification, retrieval, code similarity in the EM-LLM scorer), so averages mix scales.
Papers pick different task subsets; check which tasks enter an average.
Papers pick different subsets and metrics (MemAgent scores QA with sub-EM and summaries with ROUGE recall, not the LongBench F1 / ROUGE-L F defaults).
Question counts per subset are often not stated.

benchmarks.name: LongFact
benchmarks.title: Long-form factuality in large language models
benchmarks.what: GPT-4-generated prompts asking for detailed long-form answers about a specific object or concept across topics; EWE uses the 250 LongFact-Objects prompts.
pitfalls: Scored with claim-level factuality metrics (SAFE, VeriScore) whose recall cap and knowledge source differ across papers.

benchmarks.name: FAVA
benchmarks.title: Fine-grained Hallucination Detection and Editing for Language Models
benchmarks.what: Information-seeking queries that need long factual answers, drawn from Open Assistant, No Robots, WebNLG and author-written prompts; EWE uses 141 of them (selection from FLAME).
pitfalls: Papers use different subsets of the 200 queries.

benchmarks.name: AlpacaFact
benchmarks.title: FLAME: Factuality-Aware Alignment for Large Language Models (fact-seeking subset of AlpacaFarm)
benchmarks.what: 241 fact-seeking instructions selected from the 805 AlpacaFarm evaluation instructions.
pitfalls: A subset defined by FLAME; not a standalone release.

benchmarks.name: Biography (FActScore)
benchmarks.title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
benchmarks.what: 'Tell me a bio of <person>' prompts for people with Wikipedia pages, used to score factual precision of generated biographies.
pitfalls: Prompt counts vary by paper (EWE says 181 in §4.1 and 183 in App. A).
FActScore (Wikipedia) and VeriScore (Google snippets) scores are not comparable.

benchmarks.name: Jericho (AgentBoard)
benchmarks.title: Interactive Fiction Games: A Colossal Adventure
benchmarks.what: Text adventure games in which an agent navigates and interacts with a fictional world through typed commands; HiAgent uses the AgentBoard version, scored by progress rate over annotated subgoals and success rate.

versions.AgentBoard: AgentBoard's Jericho task (HiAgent's config lists 20 games); max 30 steps in HiAgent.

pitfalls: Progress rate and success rate depend on AgentBoard's subgoal annotations and the step limit; not comparable with game-score numbers from the original Jericho paper.

benchmarks.name: BrowseComp
benchmarks.title: BrowseComp: A Simple Yet Challenging Benchmark for Browsing Agents
benchmarks.what: 1,266 questions whose short answers require persistent web navigation to find entangled, hard-to-find facts.

versions.original: 1,266 questions
versions.200 subset: a 200-question subset used for scaling curves

pitfalls: Scores depend heavily on the search back-end and the turn budget.

benchmarks.name: BrowseComp-ZH
benchmarks.title: BrowseComp-ZH: Benchmarking Web Browsing Ability of Large Language Models in Chinese
benchmarks.what: 289 multi-hop questions over the Chinese web in 11 domains, each built backwards from a short verifiable answer.

versions.original: 289 questions

pitfalls: Search back-end and region settings change results.

benchmarks.name: xbench-DeepSearch
benchmarks.title: Xbench-DeepSearch
benchmarks.what: Deep-search agent benchmark from the xbench team (Chinese-language search tasks).

versions.original: as released by xbench

pitfalls: No paper; version and grading details are not stated by reporting papers.

benchmarks.name: SEAL-0
benchmarks.title: SealQA: Raising the Bar for Reasoning in Search-Augmented Language Models
benchmarks.what: Main SealQA split: fact-seeking questions where web search returns conflicting, noisy or unhelpful results and chat models score near zero.

versions.original: Seal-0 split

pitfalls: Small, adversarially filtered set, so a few questions move the score a lot.

benchmarks.name: zsRE (Zero-Shot Relation Extraction)
benchmarks.title: Zero-Shot Relation Extraction via Reading Comprehension
benchmarks.what: Relation questions about entities (e.g. 'What is the capital of X?') with human-written question paraphrases; used closed-book as a QA and knowledge-editing benchmark.

versions.re-split (paper): KnowledgeEditor re-splits zsRE so train and validation share relation types: 244,173 train and 27,644 validation instances with paraphrases (App. B.2).
versions.mend-split: The MEND train/test split (163,196 / 19,086) as packaged in EasyEdit (zsre_mend_edit.json), used by WISE; edit sets are random 1K or 3K samples of the test split.
versions.memit-eval: zsre_mend_eval.json as distributed with ROME/MEMIT (also the MEND split), used by AlphaEdit: 2,000 random records edited in batches of 100.

pitfalls: The original split is zero-shot over relations; the KnowledgeEditor re-split is not, so accuracies differ across splits.
Knowledge-editing papers report success, retain and paraphrase accuracy, not answer accuracy.
Scores are usually token-level top-1 accuracy with the gold prefix given, not exact match of a generated answer.
Editors are compared at a fixed number of sequential edits T and batch size; numbers at different T or batch size are not comparable.
Unedited models already score about 22-39% on edit prompts under token-level accuracy (WISE Table 3, AlphaEdit Table 1), so efficacy is not measured from zero.

benchmarks.name: Sorting (∞-former task)
benchmarks.title: ∞-former: Infinite Memory Transformer (sorting task)
benchmarks.what: Synthetic task: read a long sequence of symbols and output them sorted by how often each occurred; the frequencies change along the sequence, so early tokens must be remembered.

versions.infinite-former script: Memoria paper: data generated with the ∞-former generate_data.py script, 20 symbols, 1K-32K tokens (48K in the ablation)

pitfalls: Accuracy depends on both total length and segment length; compare only equal (segments × segment length) settings.

benchmarks.name: WikiText-103
benchmarks.title: Pointer Sentinel Mixture Models
benchmarks.what: Word-level language modeling benchmark; reported as test perplexity.

versions.raw: WikiText-103 (Raw), as used by Memoria with the GPT-2 tokenizer

pitfalls: Perplexities depend on tokenizer, model size and segment/memory length; papers train their own baselines.

benchmarks.name: PG-19
benchmarks.title: Compressive Transformers for Long-Range Sequence Modelling (PG-19 corpus)
benchmarks.what: Language modeling over long books; reported as perplexity.

versions.first 2,000 training books: Memoria and ∞-former train on only the first 2,000 books

pitfalls: Subsets of the training books and tokenizers differ across papers.

benchmarks.name: enwik8
benchmarks.title: Large Text Compression Benchmark (enwik8)
benchmarks.what: Character-level language modeling benchmark; reported in bits per character.

versions.original: as released

pitfalls: Lower BPC is better; papers usually report a single run.

benchmarks.name: Hyperpartisan
benchmarks.title: SemEval-2019 Task 4: Hyperpartisan News Detection
benchmarks.what: Long news articles labelled as hyperpartisan or not; binary document classification.

versions.original: Memoria reports validation and test splits separately because their distributions differ

pitfalls: Validation and test distributions differ (Memoria §5.3), so report both; Memoria averages five runs.

benchmarks.name: TravelPlanner
benchmarks.title: TravelPlanner: A Benchmark for Real-World Planning with Language Agents
benchmarks.what: Tool-use planning benchmark: an agent gathers flight, accommodation, restaurant, attraction and distance information with tools and writes a multi-day travel plan under commonsense and hard (user-stated) constraints (as described in Memp §4.1, App. C).

versions.original: As released; Memp evaluates on the test set in a two-stage mode (App. C).

pitfalls: Plans are converted to JSON by an LLM (GPT-4o in Memp) before rule-based checking, so the converter can affect scores.
Papers report different constraint pass rates (commonsense, hard constraint, delivery, final pass) and micro or macro variants; Memp does not say which variant #CS and #HC are.
Not a memory benchmark by design: what can be stored depends on each paper's use of training trajectories.

benchmarks.name: Natural Questions
benchmarks.title: Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research
benchmarks.what: Real anonymised Google queries with Wikipedia answers; used for open-domain QA with a retriever.

versions.original: As released; search-agent papers use the FlashRAG test split.

pitfalls: EM vs F1 and answer normalisation differ between papers.
Retriever and corpus (2018 Wikipedia dump) must match for comparison.

benchmarks.name: TriviaQA
benchmarks.title: TriviaQA: A Large Scale Distantly Supervised Challenge Dataset for Reading Comprehension
benchmarks.what: Trivia questions with evidence documents; used here as open-domain QA over Wikipedia.

versions.original: As released; FlashRAG test split in MemSearcher's released eval script.

pitfalls: Web and Wikipedia settings differ.
EM normalisation differs between papers.

benchmarks.name: PopQA
benchmarks.title: When Not to Trust Language Models: Investigating Effectiveness of Parametric and Non-Parametric Memories
benchmarks.what: 14k questions about long-tail entities.

versions.original: As released; FlashRAG test split in MemSearcher's released eval script.

pitfalls: Some papers use a sampled subset.

benchmarks.name: 2WikiMultiHopQA
benchmarks.title: Constructing A Multi-hop QA Dataset for Comprehensive Evaluation of Reasoning Steps
benchmarks.what: Multi-hop questions built from Wikipedia and Wikidata that require several reasoning steps.

versions.original: As released; dev split in MemSearcher's released eval script.

pitfalls: Dev split is used as test in most search-agent papers.
Subset sizes vary.

benchmarks.name: MuSiQue
benchmarks.title: MuSiQue: Multihop Questions via Single-hop Question Composition
benchmarks.what: 2-4 hop questions composed from single-hop ones so that shortcuts do not work.

versions.original: As released (answerable); dev split in MemSearcher's released eval script.

pitfalls: Answerable-only vs full versions differ.
Dev split used as test.

benchmarks.name: Bamboogle
benchmarks.title: Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models
benchmarks.what: 125 hand-written two-hop questions that a single search cannot answer.

versions.original: As released (125 questions).

pitfalls: Very small, so single-question differences move the score by 0.8 points.

benchmarks.name: ESConv
benchmarks.title: Towards Emotional Support Dialog Systems
benchmarks.what: Emotional-support conversations between a help-seeker and a supporter annotated with 8 support strategies; used in PRINCIPLES as seeds for LLM self-play where an agent tries to resolve a simulated patient's problem.

versions.original: PRINCIPLES: 130 test episodes seeded with the patient's situation; success judged by a gpt-4o critic (App. F.1).

pitfalls: Self-play scores depend on the user-simulator and critic models: PRINCIPLES reports Standard SR 91.54 with a gpt-3.5-turbo critic vs 55.83 with gpt-4o (Table 8).
Scores are success rate and average turns of simulated dialogues, not metrics on the human dialogues.

benchmarks.name: ExTES
benchmarks.title: Building Emotional Support Chatbots in the Era of LLMs
benchmarks.what: Extended emotional-support dialogue dataset with a larger strategy set (16 strategies as listed in PRINCIPLES Table 15); used for LLM self-play.

versions.original: PRINCIPLES: 130 test episodes; success judged by a gpt-4o critic (App. F.1).

pitfalls: Self-play success depends on the simulator and critic models (see ESConv).

benchmarks.name: PersuasionForGood (P4G)
benchmarks.title: Persuasion for Good: Towards a Personalized Persuasive Dialogue System for Social Good
benchmarks.what: Persuasion dialogues in which a persuader asks a persuadee to donate to Save the Children, annotated with persuasion strategies; used as seeds for LLM self-play.

versions.original: PRINCIPLES: 120 test episodes started from the first two utterances; success judged by a gpt-4o critic (App. F.1).

pitfalls: A single goal (one charity) lets a small fixed strategy set do well; top systems are within a few points (PRINCIPLES §4.2).
Self-play success depends on the simulator and critic models.

benchmarks.name: P4G+
benchmarks.title: PRINCIPLES: Synthetic Strategy Memory for Proactive Dialogue Agents (P4G+ introduced in the paper)
benchmarks.what: LLM-generated extension of P4G with varied organizations, personas, situations and donation barriers (e.g. financial limits); 10 original P4G strategies plus 6 from Cialdini's Influence (PRINCIPLES App. F.3).

versions.original: 120 test episodes in PRINCIPLES (App. F.1); the repository ships 78 training and 120 test cases.

pitfalls: Synthetic scenarios generated by an LLM; only evaluated by LLM self-play with a gpt-4o critic.

benchmarks.name: HumanEval
benchmarks.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
benchmarks.what: 164 hand-written Python programming problems (function signature and docstring) checked by hidden unit tests.

versions.rust: Translated to Rust with MultiPL-E; Reflexion uses the 50 hardest problems.

pitfalls: Pass@1 depends on whether the method may see hidden tests; Reflexion only uses self-written tests.
Rust numbers in Reflexion are on a 50-problem subset.

benchmarks.name: MBPP
benchmarks.title: Program Synthesis with Large Language Models
benchmarks.what: Crowd-sourced entry-level Python programming problems with test cases.
pitfalls: Reflexion does not state which MBPP subset or split it evaluates.

benchmarks.name: LeetcodeHardGym
benchmarks.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (benchmark introduced in the paper)
benchmarks.what: 40 LeetCode hard-rated problems released after 8 October 2022, as an interactive code-generation environment in 19 languages.

versions.python: Python version used in Reflexion Table 1.

pitfalls: Only 40 problems, so one problem is 2.5 points.

benchmarks.name: PinchBench
benchmarks.title: PinchBench: Real-world benchmarks for AI coding agents
benchmarks.what: Real-world agent tasks graded by task-specific checks on the delivered outputs; the TokenPilot snapshot has 123 tasks in 11 categories (productivity, research, writing, coding, analysis, CSV, log and meeting analysis, memory, skills, integrations).

versions.snapshot 0347a7f: frozen snapshot used by TokenPilot, 123 tasks

pitfalls: The upstream repo updates continuously; results need a pinned snapshot.
Some categories have 2-6 tasks, so category scores are noisy.

benchmarks.name: Claw-Eval
benchmarks.title: Claw-Eval: Towards Trustworthy Evaluation of Autonomous Agents
benchmarks.what: Containerized agent evaluation with 300 human-verified tasks in three groups, graded from execution traces, audit logs and environment snapshots on completion, safety and robustness.

versions.General group: 161 service-orchestration and analytical tasks (as used by TokenPilot)

pitfalls: Scores are rubric-based partial credit, with safety as a multiplicative gate.

benchmarks.name: SelfCheckGPT hallucination editing
benchmarks.title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
benchmarks.what: GPT-3 Wikipedia-style biographies with inaccurate sentences; editing replaces them with the real Wikipedia sentences (setup from GRACE). Reliability is perplexity on the corrected sentence; locality uses pretraining-style text.

versions.wise-600: WISE's version: prompts over 254 tokens dropped (906 of 1,392 kept), split 306 train / 600 test; locality text from RedPajama.

pitfalls: Reliability is perplexity (lower is better), not a success rate.
There is no paraphrase set, so no generalization metric.

benchmarks.name: Temporal (canonical-example editing)
benchmarks.title: Model Editing with Canonical Examples
benchmarks.what: Edits about entities that emerged after 2019: the model is edited with a GPT-4-written paragraph and tested on the entity's real Wikipedia continuation (out-of-distribution generalization); locality text from the Pile.

versions.hewitt-2024: As used by WISE with GPT-J-6B, T = 10 and 75 edits; success when the loss on the real continuation is below -log(0.8).

pitfalls: Uses GPT-J-6B because newer models may already know the entities.
Success is a loss threshold, not an exact match.

benchmarks.name: Hou et al. recall tasks
benchmarks.title: "My agent understands me better" (CHI EA '24), own evaluation set
benchmarks.what: 10 tasks built from the authors' own conversation logs; each has 4 timestamped candidate events tagged with topics and keywords, and the model's scores are compared with the one correct event by a softmax squared-error loss.

versions.original: as in the paper; not released

pitfalls: Not public, 10 items only.
Loss is on memory scores, not on generated answers; lower is better.

benchmarks.name: EMG-RAG assistant data (Huawei, proprietary)
benchmarks.title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
benchmarks.what: Proprietary smartphone-assistant data (chats and OCR'd screenshots, Mar-Jun 2024) turned into memories by GPT-4; GPT-4 also writes QA pairs with required memories. Tasks: question answering (ROUGE, BLEU), autofill forms and user services (reminder, travel; exact match). 2,000 training and 500 test users.

versions.original: Static evaluation (EMG-RAG Table 2).
versions.continuous edits, week 1-4: Memories edited over four weeks, scored per week (Table 3).
versions.continuous edits, week 1: version as reported by emg-rag; see that results file's notes
versions.continuous edits, week 2: version as reported by emg-rag; see that results file's notes
versions.continuous edits, week 3: version as reported by emg-rag; see that results file's notes
versions.continuous edits, week 4: version as reported by emg-rag; see that results file's notes

pitfalls: Not public; results cannot be reproduced or compared across papers.
References and required-memory labels are GPT-4 outputs.

benchmarks.name: Re-DocRED
benchmarks.title: Revisiting DocRED - Addressing the False Negative Problem in Relation Extraction
benchmarks.what: DocRED Wikipedia documents re-annotated with Wikidata-style entity mentions, coreference and 96 relation types, adding many relations DocRED missed. MemLLM uses it to build write/read training data and to measure language-modeling perplexity with a memory.

versions.memllm-ppl: MemLLM (arXiv 2404.11672) perplexity evaluation: OVERALL, TARGET (entities a memory read could supply) and ENTITY perplexity over Re-DocRED eval documents, with memory reads placed before target entities.

pitfalls: Perplexity, lower is better; not a 0-100 score.
MemLLM's numbers depend on what fills the memory (its own writes over Wikipedia vs gold triples); compare only rows with the same memory content.
MemLLM scores memory reads only at the evaluation data's read positions, so its PPL is an upper bound by the authors' own account.

benchmarks.name: MemoryBank probing questions
benchmarks.title: MemoryBank: Enhancing Large Language Models with Long-Term Memory
benchmarks.what: Simulated 10-day conversations of 15 ChatGPT-played users with set personalities and topics, in English and Chinese, plus hand-written probing questions about earlier days; answers scored by human annotators for retrieval accuracy, correctness, coherence and ranking (MemoryBank §4.2).

versions.en: English memory store and 97 probing questions (paper; the repo file has 100).
versions.cn: Chinese memory store and 97 probing questions (paper; the repo file has 100).

pitfalls: Scores are human labels from the authors' own annotation; no judge prompt or annotator count is given.
The ranking score (1/rank among three variants) only compares systems ranked together.
Later papers reuse the store with different questions or LLM judges.

benchmarks.name: CMV (PRIME)
benchmarks.title: PRIME: Large Language Model Personalization with Cognitive Dual-Memory and Personalized Thought Process (dataset in §3)
benchmarks.what: Personalization as ranking on Reddit r/ChangeMyView: given a user's new post and candidate replies, rank the reply that received the user's delta. 133 evaluation queries (2023-2024) from 41 active users, with 7,514 historical threads (2013-2022).

versions.original: The released evaluation_data.json (133 queries) with history_data.json and target_authors_collection.json.

pitfalls: Queries were filtered to those Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B get wrong without history (Hit@1 <= 0.3, Hit@3 <= 0.5), so non-personalized scores of those models are low by construction.
Metrics are Hit@1, Hit@3, DCG@3, MRR and their average; the number of negatives per query differs between the data (47.5 on average) and the 9 sampled negatives used in the paper's preliminary study.

benchmarks.name: LaMP
benchmarks.title: LaMP: When Large Language Models Meet Personalization
benchmarks.what: Seven personalization tasks (three classification, four generation) with per-user profiles. PRIME uses LaMP-1 to LaMP-5 (citation identification, movie tagging, product rating, news headline and scholarly title generation) and drops LaMP-6 (private data) and LaMP-7.
pitfalls: Papers use different splits (user-based vs time-based) and subsets; PRIME's query counts (Table A1) do not name the split.
MAE and RMSE are lower-is-better and not on a 0-100 scale.

benchmarks.name: BFCL-V3
benchmarks.title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
benchmarks.what: Function-calling benchmark; the multi-turn categories have an agent carry out multi-step API calls over several user turns, checked by AST matching and by executing the calls.

versions.base-multi-turn: the base multi-turn category; ReMe samples 50 tasks to build memory and evaluates on the remaining 150
versions.multi-turn-other: missing-parameter, missing-function and long-context multi-turn categories (200 tasks each in ReMe's Table 8)

pitfalls: There is no official train split; papers that build memory from BFCL carve their own split, so task subsets differ.
Scores depend on thinking mode and on how many trials are averaged (Avg@k vs Pass@k).

benchmarks.name: PersonaBench
benchmarks.title: PersonaBench: Evaluating AI Models on Understanding Personal Information through Accessing (Synthetic) Private User Data
benchmarks.what: Synthetic private user documents (conversations with friends, user-AI chats, purchase histories) with questions about each user's basic information, social ties and preferences; RF-Mem uses it to score retrieval of the relevant documents.

versions.original: As used by RF-Mem: 6 users, 263 queries, 527 corpus items, session-level memory (RF-Mem App. A Table 9).

pitfalls: RF-Mem reports only Recall@5/10 of relevant memories, not answer accuracy.
Categories: Basic Info, Social Info, Preference Easy, Preference Hard.
Findings of ACL 2025 (Tan et al., pp. 878-893, per RF-Mem's reference list); arXiv id not given there.

benchmarks.name: WebQSP
benchmarks.title: The Value of Semantic Parse Labeling for Knowledge Base Question Answering
benchmarks.what: 4,737 natural-language questions over Freebase, annotated with semantic parses; mostly one- or two-hop.

versions.original: Standard train/test split used by RoG and UniKGQA.

pitfalls: Hits@1 and F1 are both reported; methods that return one answer and methods that return answer sets are not comparable on F1.
Results depend on the Freebase subgraph used per question.

benchmarks.name: ComplexWebQuestions
benchmarks.title: The Web as a Knowledge-base for Answering Complex Questions
benchmarks.what: 34,699 complex questions built from WebQSP by composition, conjunction, comparatives and superlatives; multi-hop over Freebase.

versions.original: Standard train/dev/test split used by RoG and UniKGQA.

pitfalls: Hits@1 and F1 are both reported; compare like with like.

benchmarks.name: MetaQA
benchmarks.title: Variational Reasoning for Question Answering with Knowledge Graph
benchmarks.what: Movie-domain questions over the WikiMovies KG in 1-, 2- and 3-hop subsets.

versions.original: Vanilla questions; papers usually report the 1-hop, 2-hop and 3-hop subsets separately.

pitfalls: Always record which hop subset (MetaQA-1/2/3) a score is for.

benchmarks.name: TextArena Mastermind
benchmarks.title: TextArena
benchmarks.what: Single-player code-guessing game from the TextArena suite: the agent guesses a hidden digit code and gets black/white peg feedback, for up to 20 turns (as described in Skill-Pro §5.1, App. D.1). Scored by average episode return.

versions.v0: Mastermind-v0: 4 digits from 1-6, no duplicates (Skill-Pro App. D.1, code run.py).

pitfalls: Return is a partial-credit score in [0, 1], not a win rate.
Not a memory benchmark by design: what is stored depends on each paper's learning phase.

benchmarks.name: BFCL
benchmarks.title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
benchmarks.what: Function-calling benchmark covering single- and multi-turn calls, parallel calls and detecting irrelevant or uncallable requests (as described in Skill-Pro App. C.2; ICML 2025).

versions.v4: BFCL v4, as used by Skill-Pro; the subset is not stated.

pitfalls: Overall accuracy depends on which categories are included; Skill-Pro does not say.

benchmarks.name: MiniWoB++
benchmarks.title: Reinforcement Learning on Web Interfaces Using Workflow-Guided Exploration (MiniWoB++); World of Bits (MiniWoB)
benchmarks.what: Over 100 small synthetic web tasks (click, type, fill forms, book a flight) given as HTML; scored by per-task success rate.

versions.legacy: the legacy branch used by RCI and Synapse

pitfalls: Papers average over different task subsets (e.g. 54, 64 or 104 tasks), so mean success rates are not comparable across papers.
Some methods use self-correction or many retries; check the number of attempts.

benchmarks.name: Mind2Web
benchmarks.title: Mind2Web: Towards a Generalist Agent for the Web
benchmarks.what: Static dataset of 2,000+ human demonstrations on 137 real websites in 31 domains; agents predict the next action given gold history; metrics element accuracy, step success rate and task success rate on cross-task (252), cross-website (177) and cross-domain (912) test splits.

versions.original: offline evaluation with the released element-ranker candidates

pitfalls: Offline: history is gold, so step success is teacher-forced.
Results depend on how many ranked elements (k) are shown; a target missing from the top-k counts as a failure.

benchmarks.name: Conversation Chronicles (CC)
benchmarks.title: Conversation Chronicles: Towards Diverse Temporal and Relational Dynamics in Multi-Session Conversations
benchmarks.what: Multi-session (5-session) English dialogues in which the two speakers have a defined relationship (e.g. employee and boss); used for next-response generation (as described in THEANINE §3.1).

versions.original: As released; THEANINE samples 50 test episodes and scores sessions 3-5.

pitfalls: Papers sample different subsets of the 20,000+ test episodes; record the sample in 'subset'.
Response-generation metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, MAUVE, BERTScore) compare to one reference utterance and are not QA accuracy.

benchmarks.name: TeaFarm (TeaBag)
benchmarks.title: Towards Lifelong Dialogue Agents via Timeline-based Memory Management (TeaFarm evaluation)
benchmarks.what: Counterfactual memory test: after 5 sessions of MSC or CC, a GPT-4-synthesized session 6 leads to a question that assumes something false about the past; the agent passes if its answer is not misled (GPT-4 grades). TeaBag: 100 episodes, 200 questions.

versions.TeaBag: Released data: 50 MSC + 50 CC episodes, 2 counterfactual QAs and 2 synthesized session-6 dialogues each.

pitfalls: Questions target the newest state of each event, so memory update barely matters (THEANINE footnote 10).
Grading is by GPT-4 against a GPT-4-written answer.

benchmarks.name: TReMu temporal QA
benchmarks.title: TReMu: Towards Neuro-Symbolic Temporal Reasoning for LLM-Agents with Memory in Multi-Session Dialogues (benchmark in §2)
benchmarks.what: 600 multiple-choice temporal questions over LoCoMo dialogues (264 temporal anchoring, 102 precedence, 234 interval; 112 unanswerable), built with GPT-4o event extraction, linking and QA writing, then manual review.

versions.original: The 600-question set of Table 2 in the TReMu paper; release promised but no link given.

pitfalls: Multiple choice with 3 or 5 options including 'Unanswerable', so accuracy is not comparable with LoCoMo's free-form temporal category.
Built and evaluated by the same authors; questions were generated by GPT-4o, which is also one of the evaluated models.

benchmarks.name: FiNER
benchmarks.title: FiNER: Financial Numeric Entity Recognition for XBRL Tagging
benchmarks.what: Tag numeric tokens in financial filings with one of 139 fine-grained XBRL entity types (as described in ACE §4.1).

versions.original: the dataset's own split; ACE's released code evaluates a 441-question test subset

pitfalls: Papers evaluate subsets of the test split; check the number of questions before comparing accuracies.

benchmarks.name: Formula
benchmarks.title: FinLoRA: Benchmarking LoRA Methods for Fine-Tuning LLMs on Financial Datasets
benchmarks.what: XBRL-based financial numerical reasoning: apply financial concepts and compute the answer to a query (as described in ACE §4.1); comes from the FinLoRA benchmark suite.

versions.original: FinLoRA split; ACE's released code uses a 200-question test file

pitfalls: Accuracy is exact match of the final number, so answer formatting matters.

benchmarks.name: LV-Eval
benchmarks.title: LV-Eval: A Balanced Long-Context Benchmark with 5 Length Levels Up to 256k
benchmarks.what: Long-context QA at five length levels up to 256k tokens, with keyword and phrase replacement to reduce knowledge leakage.

versions.original: As released; HippoRAG 2 uses the hotpotwikiqa-mixup 256k subset (124 questions) split into passages for RAG.

pitfalls: Papers use single subsets and length levels; check which one.
In RAG papers the long context is segmented into a passage corpus, which is not the benchmark's long-context setting.

benchmarks.name: HyperGraphRAG domain QA
benchmarks.title: HyperGraphRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Hypergraph-Structured Knowledge Representation (evaluation sets)
benchmarks.what: Knowledge-intensive QA over five domain corpora: Medicine (2024 ESC hypertension guideline) and Agriculture, CS, Legal and Mix contexts from UltraDomain. 512 GPT-generated, human-checked questions per domain from 1-3 hop knowledge samples, split into binary-source and n-ary-source halves. Scored with F1, retrieval similarity (R-S) and an LLM-judge generation score (G-E).

versions.original: As released with HyperGraphRAG (data on Terabox, linked from evaluation/README.md).

pitfalls: Built by the HyperGraphRAG authors; the paper does not say which graph the multi-hop fact samples were drawn from.
G-E averages the judge score with F1, and R-S is 0 by construction for methods that retrieve nothing.
Different from the UltraDomain query-focused summarisation tasks used by LightRAG, even though the corpora are shared.

benchmarks.name: SWE-Bench Verified
benchmarks.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
benchmarks.what: 500 manually verified GitHub issues from Python repositories; the agent writes a patch and an issue counts as resolved when the repository's tests pass (as described in ReasoningBank App. B.2).

versions.original: the 500-instance Verified split

pitfalls: Resolve rate depends heavily on the agent scaffold (e.g. bash-only mini-SWE-agent vs tool-rich agents); compare only within one scaffold.

benchmarks.name: FinMem single-stock trading
benchmarks.title: FinMem: A Performance-Enhanced LLM Trading Agent with Layered Memory and Character Design
benchmarks.what: Daily buy / sell / hold trading of one share of a single US stock, with Benzinga news (Alpaca News API), SEC 10-Q and 10-K filings and Yahoo Finance prices from 2021-08-15 to 2023-04-25. Main test window 2022-10-06 to 2023-04-10 on TSLA, NFLX, AMZN, MSFT and COIN; scored by cumulative (log) return, Sharpe ratio, daily and annualized volatility and max drawdown (FinMem §4).
pitfalls: One test window of about six months; results are averages of 5 runs but from a single market period.
Cumulative return, volatility and drawdown are in percent; Sharpe ratio is a plain ratio; lower is better for volatility and drawdown.
Ablations in the same paper use a different TSLA window (2022-06-16 to 2022-12-28), so their numbers are not comparable with the main table.
Training periods differ by agent family (DRL agents trained from 2012).

benchmarks.name: GraphPlanner routing tasks
benchmarks.title: GraphPlanner: Graph Memory-Augmented Agentic Routing for Multi-Agent LLMs (evaluation suite)
benchmarks.what: LLM-routing evaluation over 11 in-domain tasks in five domains (Math: GSM8K, MATH; Code: MBPP, HumanEval; Commonsense: CommonsenseQA, ARC, OpenBookQA; World knowledge: NQ, TriviaQA; Popular: MMLU, GPQA) plus 3 held-out tasks (LogicGrid, MGSM, CommonGen). Routers pick among a pool of open LLMs; accuracy and a token-price cost are reported per domain.

versions.phase1-d1w3: Router picks the LLM for each agent of a fixed workflow, 1 planner, up to 3 sub-queries.
versions.phase1-d2w2: Same with 2 planner levels, up to 2 sub-queries each.
versions.phase2: Router builds the workflow: chooses roles and LLMs per step.
versions.phase2-unseen-tasks: Phase-2 routers tested zero-shot on LogicGrid, MGSM and CommonGen.

pitfalls: Domain scores average tasks with different metrics (accuracy, pass@1, CEM, coverage).
Test sets are 44-50 questions per task, so one point on a domain is about one question.
The Average column is not the plain mean of the domain columns.
Accuracy must be read together with the cost column: routers differ several-fold in cost and LLM calls.

benchmarks.name: AIME
benchmarks.title: American Invitational Mathematics Examination
benchmarks.what: Competition math problems with integer answers, 15 per exam; papers pick different year ranges.
pitfalls: Year ranges differ across papers (e.g. AIME 2024 only vs 2016-2025); always record them.

benchmarks.name: MultiTQ
benchmarks.title: Multi-granularity Temporal Question Answering over Knowledge Graphs
benchmarks.what: Temporal KGQA over ICEWS05-15 events: 500K+ generated questions (54,584 test) at day, month and year granularity; single-constraint (Equal, Before/After, First/Last) and multiple-constraint (Equal-Multi, After-First, Before-Last) questions.

versions.original: Test split as released with the ACL 2023 paper.

pitfalls: Scored as Hits@1 (exact match); papers differ in how leniently a predicted string is matched to the gold entity or time.
Many LLM-agent papers copy baseline numbers from earlier papers rather than rerunning them; backbones then differ across rows.

benchmarks.name: TimeQuestions
benchmarks.title: Complex Temporal Question Answering on Knowledge Graphs
benchmarks.what: About 16K manually curated temporal questions grounded in Wikidata (3,237 test) in four categories: explicit, implicit, temporal and ordinal; yearly granularity only.

versions.original: Train/dev/test split of the EXAQT paper (6,970 / 3,236 / 3,237 per MemoTime Table 8).

pitfalls: Scored as Hits@1; answer-matching rules differ between papers.
Category scores are sometimes grouped as question type (explicit, implicit) and answer type (temporal, ordinal); the four are the dataset's own categories.

benchmarks.name: Complex-TR
benchmarks.title: Towards Robust Temporal Reasoning of Large Language Models via a Multi-Hop QA Dataset and Pseudo-Instruction Tuning
benchmarks.what: Multi-answer, multi-hop temporal QA over Wikidata-derived facts; REMem splits it into time-to-event and event-to-event questions.

versions.original: As released; REMem samples 1,000 queries at random.

pitfalls: Papers evaluate random subsets; check the sample size.
Answers can be lists of entities, so partial answers affect F1 and judge scores differently.

benchmarks.name: Test of Time
benchmarks.title: Test of Time: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Temporal Reasoning
benchmarks.what: Synthetic temporal reasoning over anonymised entity facts; the semantic part has eight question types (before-after, event at time, first-last, duration, timeline, ...), scored by exact match.

versions.original: As released; REMem uses the semantic part (2,800 questions, 350 per type).

pitfalls: Semantic and arithmetic parts are different tasks; check which one is reported.
Entities are anonymous labels, so dense embeddings retrieve poorly and BM25 is a strong baseline.

benchmarks.name: GrailQA
benchmarks.title: Beyond I.I.D.: Three Levels of Generalization for Question Answering on Knowledge Bases
benchmarks.what: Freebase KBQA with test questions split by i.i.d., compositional and zero-shot generalization; answers are entities or numbers.

versions.original: Think-on-Graph uses 1,000 random questions of the test set (44,337 train).

pitfalls: Subsampled test sets (e.g. 1,000 random questions) are not comparable with full-test leaderboard numbers.
Exact match in LLM papers is often substring matching of the generated answer.

benchmarks.name: QALD-10
benchmarks.title: QALD-10 (QALD challenge over Wikidata); cited via QALD-9-plus (Perevalov et al., ICSC 2022)
benchmarks.what: Question answering over Wikidata; the English test set has 333 questions with entity or number answers.

versions.QALD-10 en: English test questions over Wikidata, as used by Think-on-Graph (333).

pitfalls: QALD-9, QALD-9-plus and QALD-10 are different sets over different KGs (DBpedia vs Wikidata).

benchmarks.name: SimpleQuestions
benchmarks.title: Large-scale Simple Question Answering with Memory Networks
benchmarks.what: Single-relation questions over Freebase: each is answered by one triple.

versions.original: Think-on-Graph uses 1,000 random test questions.

pitfalls: Subsampled test sets are not comparable with full-test results.

benchmarks.name: WebQuestions
benchmarks.title: Semantic Parsing on Freebase from Question-Answer Pairs
benchmarks.what: Questions from Google Suggest answered with Freebase entities; used as open-domain QA (2,032 test questions).

versions.original: Standard test split (2,032).

pitfalls: Open-domain QA systems answer from Wikipedia while KBQA systems use Freebase; the evidence source changes the task.

benchmarks.name: T-REx
benchmarks.title: T-REx: A Large Scale Alignment of Natural Language with Knowledge Base Triples (LREC 2018)
benchmarks.what: Slot filling: given a subject entity and a relation, produce the object entity; used through the KILT benchmark.

versions.KILT slot filling: KILT version as used by Think-on-Graph (5,000 test instances, 2,284,168 train).

pitfalls: KILT leaderboard numbers and self-evaluated subsets are not directly comparable.

benchmarks.name: CREAK
benchmarks.title: CREAK: A Dataset for Commonsense Reasoning over Entity Knowledge
benchmarks.what: True/false claims about entities that combine entity facts with commonsense; 1,371 test claims.

versions.original: Standard split (10,176 train, 1,371 test).

pitfalls: Binary labels: 50% is chance, so accuracies near 90% leave little room between methods.

benchmarks.name: Long-time Video
benchmarks.title: Video Object Segmentation with Adaptive Feature Bank and Uncertain-Region Refinement (AFB-URR)
benchmarks.what: Three long videos with more than 7,000 frames in total, for semi-supervised video object segmentation over long durations; scored by J&F.

versions.3x: each video played back and forth to three times its length (XMem §4.1)

pitfalls: Only three videos: results swing with memory-insertion offsets, so XMem reports mean ± sd over 5 offsets.
The n× variants repeat content, so they test memory growth, not new appearance changes.

benchmarks.name: YouTube-VOS
benchmarks.title: YouTube-VOS: A Large-Scale Video Object Segmentation Benchmark
benchmarks.what: Large video object segmentation benchmark with seen and unseen object classes in validation; score G averages J and F over both.
pitfalls: 2018 and 2019 validation sets differ; do not mix.
Some methods skip frames at test time; AOT had to be re-run with all frames for a fair comparison (XMem Table 2).

benchmarks.name: DAVIS 2017
benchmarks.title: The 2017 DAVIS Challenge on Video Object Segmentation
benchmarks.what: Multi-object semi-supervised video object segmentation on short videos; scored by region similarity J, contour accuracy F and their mean J&F.
pitfalls: Results at 600p or with multi-scale testing are not comparable with 480p single-scale results.
BL30K or other extra pretraining data changes results; XMem marks it with *.

benchmarks.name: DAVIS 2016
benchmarks.title: A Benchmark Dataset and Evaluation Methodology for Video Object Segmentation (CVPR 2016)
benchmarks.what: Single-object video object segmentation on short videos; scored by J, F and J&F.
pitfalls: Nearly saturated (above 90 J&F for recent methods), so differences are small.

benchmarks.name: PathQuestions (PQ)
benchmarks.title: An Interpretable Reasoning Network for Multi-Relation Question Answering
benchmarks.what: Path questions over a small Freebase-derived KG (2,215 entities, 14 relations): 1,908 2-hop and 5,198 3-hop queries with the topic entity written in the question.

versions.original: 2-hop and 3-hop subsets, all queries (as used by SimGRAG).

pitfalls: Report the hop subset; 2-hop and 3-hop scores differ widely.

benchmarks.name: WorldCup2014 (WC2014)
benchmarks.title: Gaussian Attention Model and its Application to Knowledge Base Embedding and Question Answering
benchmarks.what: Questions over a KG of football players at the 2014 FIFA World Cup (1,127 entities, 6 relations): 10,162 queries, mixing 6,482 single-relation, 1,472 two-hop path and 2,208 conjunctive questions.

versions.original: all 10,162 queries (as used by SimGRAG).

pitfalls: Papers may score only one question type; check whether conjunctive questions are included.

benchmarks.name: FactKG
benchmarks.title: FactKG: Fact Verification via Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs
benchmarks.what: Claims in colloquial and written style to verify as Supported or Refuted against DBpedia; five reasoning types (one-hop, conjunction, existence, multi-hop, negation); test set of 9,041 statements.

versions.original: full test set with the 2015 DBpedia KG released with the dataset.

pitfalls: Binary labels: accuracy near 70% is reachable without evidence (LLM-only rows in SimGRAG score about 68).

benchmarks.name: TruthfulQA
benchmarks.title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods
benchmarks.what: 817 questions written so that common misconceptions lead to false answers; used as free-form generation scored against reference answers.

versions.original: 817 questions (generation setting).

pitfalls: Generation vs multiple-choice settings and the metric (F1, ROUGE-L, judge models) differ between papers.

benchmarks.name: τ-bench
benchmarks.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains (Yao et al., ICLR 2025)
benchmarks.what: Customer-service tasks in which an agent talks with an LLM-simulated user, calls domain APIs over several turns and must follow a policy document; success is a final reward of 1 (as described in Early Experience App. B.2, C.4).

versions.retail: Retail domain; Early Experience uses 495 training and 115 evaluation tasks (App. C.4).

pitfalls: The user is simulated by an LLM, so scores depend on the user model.
Papers report different domains (retail, airline); Early Experience reports retail only.

benchmarks.name: SearchQA (Search-R1 suite)
benchmarks.title: Multi-hop QA with a search tool, in the Search-R1 setup (Jin et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.09516)
benchmarks.what: The agent issues search queries inside <search> tags, reads retrieved passages and answers multi-hop questions; Early Experience groups Musique, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA and Bamboogle under this name and scores F1 (App. C.5, Table 7).

versions.search-r1: Search-R1 retrieval setup; Early Experience trains on MuSiQue and treats the other datasets as out-of-domain.

pitfalls: 'SearchQA' here is not the 2017 SearchQA dataset.
Early Experience's Table 1 'SearchQA' column equals its Musique column only, while Figure 3 uses the four-dataset average.
How the OOD number in Table 2 is formed is not stated.

benchmarks.name: MinAtar
benchmarks.title: MinAtar: An Atari-inspired testbed for thorough and reproducible reinforcement learning experiments
benchmarks.what: Small 10x10 versions of Atari games; FAME builds continual-RL sequences of 7 tasks drawn from Breakout, Space Invaders and Freeway, 500k steps per task, with games allowed to repeat (App. F.1).

versions.cl-7task: FAME's 10 fixed random sequences of 7 tasks (App. F.1), following Anand & Precup (2023).

pitfalls: Average performance is a raw game return per game, so games are not on one scale.
Tasks repeat inside a sequence, which favours methods that can recognise an old task.
Forgetting is normalised by the standard deviation across the compared methods, so it changes if the method set changes.

benchmarks.name: Atari playing-mode sequences
benchmarks.title: Continual RL over the playing modes of ALE/SpaceInvaders-v5 and ALE/Freeway-v5 (setting of Malagon et al., ICML 2024)
benchmarks.what: Each task is one playing mode of the same Atari game (10 SpaceInvaders modes, 7 Freeway modes) seen in sequence, 1M steps per task (FAME App. F.1).
pitfalls: Modes share the game's dynamics and goal, so forward transfer is easy compared with switching games.
The scale of 'average performance' is not stated in FAME.

benchmarks.name: Meta-World continual sequences
benchmarks.title: Meta-World: A benchmark and evaluation for multi-task and meta reinforcement learning (Yu et al., CoRL 2020), used as task sequences
benchmarks.what: Robot-arm manipulation tasks (e.g. button-press, window-open, peg-unplug) trained one after another, 1M steps each, scored by success rate; includes the Continual World CW10 sequence (Wolczyk et al., 2021).

versions.3-random-sequences: Three random 10-task sequences from Chung et al. (2024), listed in FAME App. G.1.

pitfalls: Results depend on which task sequence is used; FAME's three sequences are its own random picks.
Methods that store past parameters (PackNet, ProgressiveNet, CompoNet) have zero forgetting by construction and need task identity.

benchmarks.name: Associative KV-retrieval (GradMem)
benchmarks.title: GradMem: Learning to Write Context into Memory with Test-Time Gradient Descent (synthetic task)
benchmarks.what: Synthetic key-value lists (!k:v!...) followed by a query ?!k:; the model must output the value from memory alone. Keys and values are 2 symbols from a 62-character vocabulary; 4 to 96 pairs.

versions.2-char keys/values, 62-symbol vocab: GradMem §3.1; datasets N{4..96}-K2V2-V62_1M in the repo's download script

pitfalls: Models are trained from scratch per number of pairs (with a curriculum), so scores measure what a memory can learn to store, not a pretrained model's ability.
Capacity depends on the memory size and number of update steps; compare only equal memory-state sizes.

benchmarks.name: bAbI
benchmarks.title: Towards AI-Complete Question Answering: A Set of Prerequisite Toy Tasks
benchmarks.what: 20 synthetic story-QA tasks; QA1-QA3 need one to three supporting facts, QA4-QA5 two- and three-argument relations.

versions.original (QA1-QA5): GradMem: tasks QA1-QA5, story as context, question as query; the released scripts load them as BABILong 'qa*_0k' (no added distractor text)

pitfalls: Short contexts (~20-300 tokens); near 100% for most models on QA1, QA4 and QA5.
Same stories as BABILong at 0k length; BABILong at longer lengths is a different task.

benchmarks.name: SQuAD
benchmarks.title: SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text
benchmarks.what: Extractive QA over Wikipedia paragraphs; the answer is a span of the paragraph.

versions.short (answer sentence only): GradMem: context cut to the sentence(s) containing the answer span (~40 tokens)

pitfalls: The short variant removes almost all distractor text; not comparable with full-paragraph SQuAD scores.

benchmarks.name: PwC (Prompt-with-Context)
benchmarks.title: In-context Autoencoder for Context Compression in a Large Language Model (App. C)
benchmarks.what: GPT-4-written (context, prompt, answer) triples over 20k Pile texts: 10 text-specific and 5 general prompts per text; 240k train and 18k test examples, contexts mostly over 500 tokens.

versions.original: 240k train / 18k test as released with ICAE.

pitfalls: Answers and the usual pairwise judge are both GPT-4, which favours longer responses.
Scores are win/lose/tie against a named opponent, so numbers only compare within one pairing.

benchmarks.name: ScreenSpot
benchmarks.title: SeeClick: Harnessing GUI Grounding for Advanced Visual GUI Agents
