benchmarks.what: GUI grounding: over 1,200 instructions on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and web screenshots; the model must point inside the target element's box; split into text and icon/widget elements.

versions.original: mobile, desktop and web, text and icon subsets

pitfalls: Single-screenshot grounding: it measures perception, not memory.

benchmarks.name: AndroidControl
benchmarks.title: On the Effects of Data Scale on Computer Control Agents
benchmarks.what: Over 15,000 human demonstrations across 833 Android apps; offline step-level evaluation with high-level goals (High) or step instructions (Low); action type accuracy, grounding accuracy and success rate.
pitfalls: Offline evaluation over recorded episodes; check whether a paper's success rate is per step or per episode.
Low and High are different difficulty levels; always record which.

benchmarks.name: GUIOdyssey
benchmarks.title: GUIOdyssey: A Comprehensive Dataset for Cross-App GUI Navigation on Mobile Devices
benchmarks.what: 7,735 cross-app navigation episodes over 201 apps and 6 devices, with random, task, device and app test splits; offline step-level type accuracy, grounding accuracy and step success rate.

versions.original: released splits

pitfalls: Papers often evaluate a random subset (e.g. 500 episodes); record which split and subset.
Offline, step-level metrics.

benchmarks.name: AndroidWorld
benchmarks.title: AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents
benchmarks.what: Online benchmark of 116 parameterised tasks across 20 apps on a live Android emulator, scored by task success.

versions.original: 116 tasks

pitfalls: Online evaluation on a live emulator; papers usually report a single success rate without variance.

benchmarks.name: Video-MME
benchmarks.title: Video-MME: The First-Ever Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark of Multi-modal LLMs in Video Analysis
benchmarks.what: Multiple-choice QA over real-world videos split into short, medium and long subsets (11 s to 1 h, per Video-RAG §4.1); scored with and without subtitles.

versions.original: Full benchmark, reported per length subset and overall, with or without subtitles.

pitfalls: Scores with subtitles and without subtitles are different settings and must not be compared across.
Frame count changes scores a lot; papers use each model's own frame setting (8-768 frames).

benchmarks.name: MLVU
benchmarks.title: MLVU: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multi-Task Long Video Understanding
benchmarks.what: Long-video benchmark with 9 tasks on videos of 3 min to 2 h (about 12 min on average), per Video-RAG §4.1.

versions.dev: Dev split, multiple-choice (M-avg) tasks, as used by Video-RAG Table 2.

pitfalls: Multiple-choice (M-avg) and generation (G-avg) scores are separate; check which one a paper reports.

benchmarks.name: LongVideoBench
benchmarks.title: LongVideoBench: A Benchmark for Long-context Interleaved Video-Language Understanding
benchmarks.what: 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions in 17 categories over long videos, per Video-RAG §4.1.

versions.val: Validation set, as used by Video-RAG Table 3.

pitfalls: The benchmark defines an interleaved video-subtitle input; Video-RAG drops it, so its runs are not in the standard input format (§4.3).

benchmarks.name: ShareGPT (serving trace)
benchmarks.title: ShareGPT: user-shared ChatGPT conversations
benchmarks.what: Used by vLLM as a serving workload: the input and output lengths of ShareGPT conversations define synthetic requests, with Poisson arrival times at a chosen request rate. Mean input 161.31 and output 337.99 tokens (vLLM Fig. 11).

versions.length trace: only token lengths are used; requests arrive by a Poisson process at the stated rate

pitfalls: Scores depend on the request rate and the trace length (1 hour, or 15 minutes for OPT-175B in vLLM).
Not a QA benchmark: metrics are latency, throughput, batch size or memory.

benchmarks.name: Alpaca (serving trace)
benchmarks.title: Stanford Alpaca: An Instruction-following LLaMA model
benchmarks.what: Used by vLLM as a serving workload: Alpaca instruction/response lengths define synthetic requests with Poisson arrivals. Mean input 19.31 and output 58.45 tokens (vLLM Fig. 11), much shorter than ShareGPT.

versions.length trace: only token lengths are used; requests arrive by a Poisson process at the stated rate

pitfalls: Short sequences make large configurations compute-bound, which shrinks memory-management gains (vLLM Fig. 12f).

systems.name: A-Mem

paper.title: A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents

construction.unit: note (one interaction + LLM attributes)
construction.kept_as: original content kept; keywords/tags/context LLM-generated
construction.processing: LLM writes keywords, tags, contextual description; note embedded
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 ...)

organization.structure: linked notes (Zettelkasten 'boxes')
organization.stores: one note store
organization.index: all-minilm-l6-v2 embeddings of content + attributes

management.operations: link generation; memory evolution rewrites neighbours' context/keywords/tags
management.conflicts: none (no contradiction handling described)

retrieval.query: query text embedded as is
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity over all notes, plus notes linked in same box
retrieval.selection: top-k (k=10 default; 10-50 per category, Table 8)
retrieval.budget: k notes

use.context: retrieved notes in the prompt
use.reasoning: single answer call

stages.ingestion: Each new interaction becomes one memory note with its original content and timestamp.
stages.construction: An LLM generates keywords, tags and a contextual description for the note; content plus attributes are embedded (all-minilm-l6-v2 in experiments).
stages.organization: Zettelkasten-style network of notes; links are stored on notes and a note can sit in several 'boxes'.
stages.update: Link generation: top-k nearest notes are retrieved and an LLM decides which links to create. Memory evolution: an LLM may rewrite the context/keywords/tags of those neighbouring notes.
stages.retrieval: Cosine top-k over note embeddings (k=10 default, 10-50 per category in Table 8); notes linked within the same box are also returned.
stages.answer: Retrieved notes are inserted into the prompt of the backbone LLM.

systems.summary: Agentic Zettelkasten memory: each interaction becomes an LLM-enriched note that is linked to related notes and can trigger rewriting ('evolution') of older notes' attributes.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: consistent with the seed taxonomy row; the original interaction content c_i is kept and only LLM-generated attributes are rewritten during evolution, hence fidelity tag verbatim+derived. Separate production code: https://github.com/WujiangXu/A-mem-sys.
DESIGN: Sec 3.1-3.4, Sec 4.2, App. A.5 (Table 8). Corrected: 'partly rewritten' clarified (content kept, attributes rewritten); links moved from processing to management.operations.

systems.name: ACE

paper.title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models

construction.unit: bullet: id, helpful/harmful counters, one short strategy, concept, formula, code snippet or failure mode, filed under a section
construction.kept_as: LLM-written lessons (Reflector diagnoses, Curator phrases the bullet)
construction.processing: Generator answers with the playbook; Reflector diagnoses the attempt against feedback and tags used bullets; Curator proposes new bullets as ADD operations
construction.writer: the same LLM in three roles (DeepSeek-V3.1 non-thinking by default)

organization.structure: one playbook of bullets grouped under fixed section headings
organization.stores: a single text playbook (the context) per task domain

management.operations: deterministic append of Curator ADDs under their section with fresh ids; helpful/harmful counters incremented from Reflector tags; optional embedding dedup with LLM merge (off by default in code)
management.conflicts: not resolved in code: UPDATE, MERGE and DELETE are listed as TODO
management.forgetting: paper: lazy pruning when the context window is exceeded; not in the released code

retrieval.candidates: none: the whole playbook is read
retrieval.selection: none; the Generator lists the ids of bullets it found useful
retrieval.budget: whole playbook (curator prompt states an 80k-token budget but nothing enforces it)

use.context: full playbook plus question and context (finance); playbook inside the first ReAct prompt, before the task (AppWorld)
use.reasoning: single JSON answer (finance) or ReAct loop up to 40 steps (AppWorld)

classify.note: Sections are headings inside one prompt, not separate stores. Counters change in place, but bullet text is only ever added in the released code; the paper's de-duplication is an optional flag.

stages.ingestion: Each training sample (offline, up to 5 epochs) or each test sample (online) is answered by the Generator with the current playbook; its reasoning, answer and the ids of bullets it used are kept.
stages.construction: The Reflector compares the attempt with feedback (ground-truth answer, or execution result / unit tests on AppWorld), explains the error, and tags used bullets helpful or harmful; if the answer was wrong it can refine over several rounds while the Generator retries. The Curator then writes only new bullets as ADD operations.
stages.organization: One playbook of bullets under fixed section headings (e.g. strategies, formulas, code snippets, common mistakes); each bullet has an id and helpful/harmful counters.
stages.update: Non-LLM merge: ADDs get fresh ids and are appended under their section; counters are incremented from the Reflector's tags. The paper adds embedding-based de-duplication and lazy pruning (grow-and-refine); in the code dedup is an optional flag and pruning is absent.
stages.retrieval: None. The whole playbook is placed in every Generator call; the Generator reports which bullet ids it relied on.
stages.answer: Generator answers with the full playbook, the question and its context (finance), or acts in AppWorld's ReAct loop with the playbook in its system prompt.

systems.summary: Treats the prompt as a growing playbook of itemised bullets: a Generator uses it, a Reflector diagnoses each attempt against feedback and scores bullets, and a Curator appends new bullets as small deltas merged without an LLM, avoiding the collapse that full LLM rewrites cause.
systems.notes:
Venue: ICLR 2026 main conference, poster (iclr.cc/virtual/2026/poster/10008343; ICLR 2026 proceedings; OpenReview forum eC4ygDs02R); arXiv comment 'ICLR 2026'; the v3 PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026'. PDF read: arXiv v3 (29 Mar 2026).
Code: ace-agent/ace at 4f679bef (committed 2026-03-11, the last commit before v3 of 29 Mar 2026; later commits add task-specific prompts and ComBEE batching) for the finance pipeline; its ace-appworld submodule pins ace-agent/ace-appworld at 9f3e9215 (2025-11-18) for AppWorld.
DESIGN: paper §3, §4.1-4.2, App. A.4-A.6, F; code ace/ace.py, playbook_utils.py, ace/core/*.py, ace/prompts/*.py, eval/finance/run.py; ace-appworld experiments/code/ace/adaptation_agent.py, adaptation_react.py, playbook.py, configs. trigger 'session-end' = after each sample/task. index null: nothing is embedded unless the optional dedup runs. control.retrieval 'none': there is no retrieval step.

sources.code_note: Finance/general pipeline: ace-agent/ace at 4f679bef (2026-03-11), the last commit before paper v3 (later ones add ComBEE batching). AppWorld runs live in the submodule ace-agent/ace-appworld, pinned by that commit to 9f3e9215 (2025-11-18): https://github.com/ace-agent/ace-appworld/tree/9f3e92155345a9159f3a8b25abc334eeca05b545/ . The two pipelines differ (see paper_vs_code).

headline: There is no retrieval: every bullet in the playbook goes into every call, so the context grows with experience (24.9k vs 10.9k input tokens per AppWorld call against GEPA).
The Curator only adds; the released code implements ADD alone, so bullets are never rewritten or deleted and de-duplication is an optional switch.

discussion.takeaway: Letting a context grow as an itemised playbook, written by reflection and merged in small deltas rather than rewritten, beats prompt optimisers and Dynamic Cheatsheet on AppWorld and financial tasks, at lower adaptation cost.

claims.claim: Large gains on agents.
claims.evidence: AppWorld average 59.4 offline and 59.5 online vs ReAct 42.4, GEPA 46.4, DC 51.9 (DeepSeek-V3.1). Table 1

claims.claim: Large gains on domain tasks.
claims.evidence: FiNER/Formula average 81.9 offline vs GEPA 72.5 and base 69.1. Table 2

claims.claim: Works without labels when execution feedback exists.
claims.evidence: AppWorld offline without labels 57.2 vs 59.4 with; but finance online without labels drops to 67.3 on FiNER (base 70.7). Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Full rewriting collapses contexts; deltas avoid it.
claims.evidence: DC context fell from 18,282 to 122 tokens and 66.7 → 57.1; removing incremental updates cuts test-normal TGC 76.2 → 67.3. §2.2, Table 18

claims.claim: Cheaper to adapt.
claims.evidence: −82.3% latency and −75.1% rollouts vs GEPA offline; −91.5% latency and −83.6% token cost vs DC online. Table 4

claims.claim: Holds across models.
claims.evidence: Gains with GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1 and Llama-3.3-70B. Tables 5-9

limits: Depends on a reasonably strong Reflector; poor insights make the context noisy or harmful.
Without reliable feedback (labels or execution signals) adaptation can hurt.
Not every task needs a long context; tasks like HotPotQA or Game of 24 gain little.
reading: There is no retrieval: every call carries the whole playbook, which on AppWorld more than doubles input tokens per call (Table 15); the paper argues KV-cache reuse offsets the cost.

The released code only appends bullets; UPDATE/MERGE/DELETE are TODO, dedup is off by default and pruning is not implemented, so the 'refine' half of grow-and-refine is not what the code runs by default.
Table 1's online ACE row (59.5) is the warm-started variant from Table 3; the plain online run is 56.1, still above DC (51.9), which gets no warm-up.
'Without labels' on finance still gives the Reflector a right/wrong signal in the released code; on AppWorld it means execution output instead of ground-truth code and unit tests.
The offline finance run keeps the playbook with the best validation accuracy, so validation labels steer the no-label rows too; the released test files are subsets (FiNER 441, Formula 200 questions).
All three roles use the same model, so gains are not from a stronger teacher (§4.2); Table 16 shows a weaker Reflector still helps.

abstract.text: ACE improves an LLM application by editing its context instead of its weights. The context is a playbook of small, itemised bullets that grows over time: a Generator attempts tasks, a Reflector turns successes and failures into lessons, and a Curator adds new bullets that are merged by simple code rather than rewritten by an LLM. The authors argue this avoids brevity bias and the 'context collapse' seen when an LLM repeatedly rewrites its whole context. On AppWorld and financial reasoning benchmarks it beats prompt optimisers and Dynamic Cheatsheet in both offline and online adaptation, with lower adaptation latency and cost.

paper.title: ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-horizon LLM Agents

construction.unit: one structured history summary (REASONING, VARS, TODO, COMPLETED, GUARDRAILS in the optimized AppWorld guideline); optionally a refined version of each long observation
construction.kept_as: LLM-compressed text that replaces the raw history; the last action-observation pair stays raw
construction.processing: compressor LLM follows a natural-language guideline optimized offline from contrasts between full-context and compressed runs
construction.writer: compressor LLM (gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, or a LoRA-distilled Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-8B or Phi-4)

organization.structure: single summary block in the prompt, followed by the kept and newer turns
organization.stores: none outside the agent's context

management.operations: when history passes the threshold, the compressor rewrites previous summary + older turns into a new summary that replaces the old one and a new session starts
management.conflicts: resolved implicitly by the rewrite
management.forgetting: raw turns are dropped after being summarized; long observations are replaced by their refined version

retrieval.candidates: none: the whole compressed context is in the prompt
retrieval.selection: none
retrieval.budget: history compressed above 4,096 tokens (AppWorld, OfficeBench) or 2,048 (QA); observations above 1,024 / 512 / 400 tokens

use.context: system prompt + task + <HISTORY_SUMMARY> + last kept turn and newer turns (+ refined observation in observation mode)
use.reasoning: ReAct agent: one thought and action per step

classify.note: Memory is one rolling summary inside the agent's prompt; each compression rewrites the previous summary together with the older turns. The contribution is how the compression instruction is learned, not how memory is searched.

stages.ingestion: Each agent step adds a thought/action and the tool's observation to the interaction history.
stages.construction: When the history passes a token threshold, a compressor LLM rewrites it into a structured summary; separately, any observation longer than its own threshold is rewritten into a shorter refined observation before it enters the history.
stages.organization: No store outside the prompt: a new session holds the system prompt, the task, the summary and the last raw action-observation pair.
stages.update: Each later compression reads the previous summary plus the turns since then and writes a summary that replaces it.
stages.answer: The ReAct agent reads its whole compressed context at every step.
stages.learning: The compressor's guideline is optimized offline: o3 reads trajectories where full context succeeded but compression failed, writes feedback, and proposes 5 revised guidelines, of which the best on training tasks is kept (UT); an optional second pass trims content that successful compressed runs never used (CO). The compressor can then be distilled into a small model with LoRA.

systems.summary: Compresses a long-horizon agent's history and long tool outputs with an LLM whose instruction is refined offline from failures caused by compression, then distils that compressor into small models.
systems.notes: Venue checked: ICML 2026 main-conference poster (icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/66270; PDF footer 'Proceedings of the 43rd ICML, PMLR 306'). Paper text from arXiv v3 (1 Jun 2026). Code: official repo microsoft/acon at d63f9ae (2025-10-14), the only commit after the initial one; it predates v3 by eight months. Two variants: history compression and observation compression, each after the UT step or UT+CO steps; they are run separately in the main tables (combined in App. Table 14).

headline: ACON is prompt optimization for a summarizer: the memory itself is one rolling summary that replaces the raw history once it passes 4,096 tokens.
The guideline is learned from contrast pairs: tasks the agent solves with full context but fails after compression.
On AppWorld with gpt-4.1, UTCO history compression keeps accuracy (56.5 vs 56.0) at 26% lower peak tokens (7.33k vs 9.93k).

discussion.takeaway: An agent's history can be replaced by an LLM summary without losing accuracy if the summarizer's instruction is tuned on the failures that compression causes; the tuned summarizer can run on a small model.

claims.claim: ACON cuts peak tokens by 26-54% while beating other compression baselines.
claims.evidence: AppWorld history UTCO 56.5 at 7.33k peak vs 56.0 at 9.93k with no compression and 43.5 for naive prompting (Table 1); 8-objective QA peak 10.35k → 4.65k (Table 2b).

claims.claim: Optimized compressors distil into small models with little loss.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-8B and Phi-4 compressors keep over 95% of the gpt-4.1 teacher's accuracy. Fig. 4

claims.claim: Compression helps small agents by removing distraction.
claims.evidence: Distilled Qwen3-14B agent: AppWorld 25.6 → 33.9 (+32%), 8-objective QA EM 0.158 → 0.230 (+46%). Fig. 5, §4.4

claims.claim: Contrastive feedback and a strong optimizer matter.
claims.evidence: o3 with contrast 51.2 vs 50.6 without contrast and 47.6 with gpt-4.1 as optimizer. Table 3

claims.claim: Moderate thresholds give the best trade-off.
claims.evidence: 4,096 for history and 1,024 for observations on AppWorld. Fig. 6

limits: Experiments mostly use GPT models; other model families are untested.
Benchmarks are controlled environments, not live deployments.
Natural-language guideline optimization has no convergence guarantee.
Distilled students still trail the teacher; training data is about 100 examples per domain.
Compression adds latency and invalidates the KV cache of the history.
reading: UT beats UTCO on OfficeBench (74.74 vs 72.63) and QA EM (0.373 vs 0.335) but loses on AppWorld (51.2 vs 56.5); the paper picks the variant per environment after seeing test results, so no single setting wins everywhere.
On AppWorld only UTCO history compression matches no compression (56.5 vs 56.0); UT history (51.2) and both observation variants (47.0, 53.6) stay below it.

The FIFO baseline keeps the last 5 turns and Retrieval keeps 4 retrieved turns plus the last one; these are not set to ACON's token budget, and FIFO scores 84.2 on easy AppWorld tasks, above ACON UT (77.2).
Latency per task rises with compression (73.2 s → 87.7 s history, 101.9 s observation) even though API cost falls (Table 4).
The public code predates the ICML version by eight months and does not include the optimized guidelines used for the tables.

abstract.text: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate an ever-growing log of actions and observations, which raises memory cost and distracts the model. ACON compresses both the interaction history and long observations with an LLM, and improves the compressor's instructions in natural language: on training tasks, it compares runs that succeed with full context against runs that fail after compression, and an optimizer LLM rewrites the guideline from that feedback. The optimized compressor can then be distilled into smaller models. On AppWorld, OfficeBench and multi-objective QA it lowers peak tokens by 26-54% while doing better than other compression methods, and it helps small models act as agents.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: AgeMem

paper.title: Agentic Memory: Learning Unified Long-Term and Short-Term Memory Management for Large Language Model Agents

construction.unit: LTM entry: free text the agent chooses to store, with an embedding, metadata and an id
construction.kept_as: agent-written text (whatever the policy puts in an Add_memory call)
construction.processing: no fixed extraction step: the policy decides in its own output whether to call Add / Update / Delete
construction.writer: the agent policy itself (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct or Qwen3-4B-Instruct, RL-trained)

organization.structure: flat long-term vector store + the agent's short-term context (message list)
organization.stores: LTM: in-memory vector store; STM: the running message context
organization.index: dense embeddings, cosine (text-embedding-v4, 256-d, in the released code)

management.operations: LTM: Add / Update / Delete by memory_id; STM: Summary (LLM rewrites a span as one message), Filter (drops messages similar to a criterion)
management.conflicts: the agent updates or deletes an entry whose id it saw in an earlier retrieval
management.forgetting: Delete tool (LTM); Filter removes context messages (STM)

retrieval.query: a query the agent writes in a Retrieve_memory call
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity against every LTM entry (optional metadata filter)
retrieval.selection: top-k, k chosen by the agent (default 3; paper: typically 3-5)
retrieval.budget: 8,192-token context, 2,048-token responses; up to 5 rounds per stage (released config)

use.context: the agent's own context: system prompt with the six tool schemas, messages, and retrieved entries appended as tool messages
use.reasoning: multi-round think / tool call / answer loop by the same policy

classify.note: The trained agent decides whether to search, what query to write and k; the store then returns the k most similar entries by cosine, with no reranking.

stages.ingestion: Pre-task information arrives as ordinary messages in the agent's context; for HotpotQA the code sends all context paragraphs (up to 10 sentences each) as one 'casual chat' message.
stages.construction: The agent writes long-term entries itself by calling Add_memory with content, metadata and a type; each entry is embedded and stored with a new id.
stages.organization: One flat vector store of entries (content, embedding, metadata, id) plus the short-term message context; no links or hierarchy.
stages.update: Update_memory rewrites and re-embeds an entry, Delete_memory removes one (both need an id seen in a retrieval); Summary_context replaces a span of messages with an LLM summary and Filter_context drops messages judged similar to a criterion (threshold 0.6).
stages.retrieval: Retrieve_memory embeds an agent-written query and appends the top-k entries by cosine (k default 3) to the context as a tool message with their ids.
stages.answer: The same policy answers from its context after up to 5 think/tool rounds; there is no separate reader.
stages.learning: Three-stage rollouts (store from context; manage context under distractors after a context reset; answer the question) are scored once at the end, and step-wise GRPO gives every step of the trajectory the same group-normalised advantage (K = 8 rollouts). Trained on HotpotQA only.

systems.summary: Memory operations on a vector store (add, update, delete, retrieve) and on the agent's own context (summarise, filter) become tool calls of the agent itself, trained end to end with a three-stage RL curriculum and step-wise GRPO.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: control is learned-rl at every stage because the RL-trained policy emits every memory tool call; the operations themselves are fixed code (cosine top-k) or an external Qwen-Max (Summary, Filter). Venue: the arXiv PDF (v3, 23 Jul 2026) names no venue; 'ACL 2026' comes from the authors' GitHub repo description ('ACL 2026 SAC Highlight'), and track 'main' is assumed from that label, not stated. Code: y1y5/AgeMem (owner matches the first author's handle, not linked from the PDF), pinned at 98f563f9 (2026-04-24). It covers only the HotpotQA workflow.

headline: Memory is not a pipeline around the model: the RL-trained agent itself decides when to store, update, delete, retrieve, summarise or filter.
Retrieval is plain cosine top-k over a flat store; what is learned is when to call it and what to store.
Summary and Filter are executed by an external Qwen-Max in the released code, not by the trained model.

discussion.takeaway: Give an agent tools for both a long-term store and its own context and train when to use them with RL. Trained only on HotpotQA, AgeMem beats LangMem, A-Mem and Mem0 on average over five agent benchmarks in its own paper.

claims.claim: Unified, learned memory management beats memory-augmented baselines.
claims.evidence: Average 41.96 (Qwen2.5-7B) and 54.31 (Qwen3-4B) vs best baselines 37.14 (Mem0) and 45.74 (A-Mem). Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: RL training is what makes the tools pay off.
claims.evidence: +8.53 and +8.72 points over AgeMem-noRL (33.43, 45.59). Table 2

claims.claim: The agent stores better long-term memories.
claims.evidence: Memory quality 0.533 and 0.605 vs 0.527 (Mem0) and 0.587 (A-Mem). Fig. 2

claims.claim: Learned context tools use fewer tokens than retrieval at every step.
claims.evidence: 2,117 vs 2,186 (−3.1%) and 2,191 vs 2,310 (−5.1%) prompt tokens on HotpotQA. Fig. 3

claims.claim: LTM tools, RL and STM tools each add accuracy.
Memory-aware reward terms help beyond the task reward.
claims.evidence: J 0.544 vs 0.509 and memory quality 0.533 vs 0.479 against an answer-only reward. Table 4

claims.claim: Gains are not only from adding STM tools and RL to an existing memory.
claims.evidence: LangMem, A-Mem and Mem0 with the same ST/RL additions average 41.56, 41.70 and 40.67 vs 43.69 for AgeMem on three benchmarks. Table 7, App. D.3

limits: The tool set is fixed; finer-grained control is left open.
The benchmarks are controlled; long real dialogues and real users are untested.
Training trajectories come only from HotpotQA.
reading: Only HotpotQA comes with pre-task context (its supporting facts). The paper does not say what the agent can store before the task on ALFWorld, SciWorld, PDDL or BabyAI, and the repo has no code for them, so how memory works on four of the five benchmarks is undocumented.
In the released HotpotQA evaluation the distractor stage is off and the context is wiped after Stage 1: the score measures storing and retrieving, not the distractor handling trained in Stage 2.

Summary, Filter, distractor generation and all judging call Qwen-Max through an API. The trained model makes the decisions, but the context operations depend on a larger external model, which the paper's point about avoiding auxiliary expert models does not mention.
The code's reward differs from the paper's: weights 0.5 / 0.2 / 0.15 / 0.15 with an extra tool-efficiency term instead of 1/3 each; Filter uses LLM-scored similarity instead of embedding cosine.
Token savings are small (3.1% and 5.1%) and every variant stays near 2.1-2.3k tokens under an 8,192-token budget, so context overflow is not what separates the configurations.
The per-bar gains in Fig. 4 (e.g. '+10.6') are percentage points, although the text calls them %.
Without RL the tools can hurt: AgeMem-noRL is below no memory on PDDL (8.87 vs 10.15) and BabyAI (46.34 vs 50.80) with Qwen2.5-7B.
Baselines run with default settings and untuned backbones, while AgeMem's backbone is RL-tuned on HotpotQA; Table 7 addresses this on three benchmarks only.

abstract.text: AgeMem treats both long-term memory and the agent's working context as things the agent manages itself through tools. It can add, update and delete entries in a long-term store and retrieve, summarise or filter what is in its context. A three-stage RL curriculum (store, handle distractors, answer) with a step-wise GRPO that passes the final reward to every step teaches it when to use each tool. Across ALFWorld, SciWorld, PDDL, BabyAI and HotpotQA, and two Qwen backbones, it outperforms LangMem, A-Mem and Mem0.

systems.name: AlphaEdit

paper.title: AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models

construction.unit: a batch of 100 factual rewrites (subject, relation, new object)
construction.kept_as: parametric: closed-form update to FFN output matrices
construction.processing: optimise a target hidden vector per fact (25 gradient steps), take the subject's FFN key, then solve a least-squares weight update projected onto the approximate null space of preserved-knowledge keys
construction.writer: closed-form solver (no LLM writes text)

organization.structure: the model's FFN output (down_proj) matrices of 5-6 consecutive layers (4-8 for LLaMA3)
organization.stores: edited weights; running sum KpKpᵀ of past edit keys; one fixed projection P per layer

management.operations: each batch adds its projected update to W and its keys to KpKpᵀ
management.conflicts: the update is penalised on keys of earlier edits (‖ΔP Kp‖²) and projected off the keys of preserved knowledge

retrieval.query: the prompt itself
retrieval.candidates: none: every forward pass uses the edited weights

use.context: no retrieved text; the edited weights produce the answer
use.reasoning: ordinary forward pass / generation

classify.note: Parametric: edits are folded into the FFN weights, so there is no store to search; every prompt passes through the edited matrices.

stages.ingestion: Edits arrive in batches of 100 factual rewrites (subject, relation, new object); 2,000 in the main experiments.
stages.construction: For each fact a target hidden vector at the last edited layer is found by 25 gradient steps; its key is the FFN input at the subject's last token, averaged over the bare prompt and 5 generated prefixes.
stages.organization: Knowledge stays in the FFN output matrices of layers 4-8 (LLaMA3; 3-8 GPT-J; 13-17 GPT2-XL). A projection P per layer, computed once from 100,000 Wikipedia samples, points away from directions that preserved knowledge uses.
stages.update: Per layer, Δ = R K1ᵀ P (Kp Kpᵀ P + K1 K1ᵀ P + αI)⁻¹ is added to W (the residual is spread over the edited layers), then the batch's keys are added to Kp Kpᵀ so later batches avoid them.
stages.answer: The model answers from its edited weights in an ordinary forward pass.

systems.summary: Locate-then-edit with one extra projection: each MEMIT-style weight update is projected onto the approximate null space of preserved-knowledge keys, so thousands of sequential edits barely move the model's other outputs.
systems.notes: VENUE: ICLR 2025 main conference, oral (OpenReview forum HvSytvg3Jh, venue 'ICLR 2025 Oral'; the PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025'). CODE: github.com/jianghoucheng/AlphaEdit pinned to aac456de (2025-04-22), the last code change, same day as arXiv v4; later commits touch only README and LICENSE. This is a model-editing paper: the memory is the model's own weights, so there is no retrieval stage and the Map placement is 'none / reads everything'. TAGS: write_time=learned because the target vectors are found by gradient steps before the closed-form write; learning=training-free because no editor network or policy is trained. Main results also include memory-based editors (SERAC, GRACE, MELO) in App. C.5 Table 2, and Gemma / phi-1.5 in Table 3 (not transcribed). KnowEdit, MQuAKE and LEME results (Tables 4-5) are appendix extras, not transcribed.

sources.code_note: Official repository named in the paper. Commit aac456de (2025-04-22) is the last code change and matches arXiv v4 (2025-04-22); the repo builds on the MEMIT codebase (rome/, memit/ folders).

headline: The memory is the model's own FFN weights; nothing is stored beside them except key statistics used for later writes.
The only change from sequential MEMIT is where the update may point: into directions that preserved-knowledge keys (almost) never use.
The null space is approximate (eigenvalues below a threshold), so preserved facts still move: Counterfact specificity 89.48 → 67.88 on LLaMA3 after 2,000 edits.

open_questions: How many directions P keeps per layer is not reported, so how much room the edits have, and how far from an exact null space it is, is unknown.
AlphaEdit changes three things relative to MEMIT (projection, dropping the K0 term, the ‖ΔP‖² term); Fig. 6 adds the projection to baselines, but no run separates the three.
P is computed once on the unedited model; edits to earlier layers change the keys later layers see, and the effect of not recomputing P is not studied.

glance.a: A batch of 100 facts folded into the FFN output matrices of 5 layers; there is no separate item.
No. Only weights change; the code also keeps the sum of past edit keys (KpKpᵀ) to protect them in later batches.
It is not: facts live in the weights. A fixed projection per layer limits where updates may point.
No retrieval of any kind.

glance.q: Is memory reconstructed at question time?
glance.a: No. The edited model is queried like any model.
Only the prompt.

ablation.src: paper Table 6 (App. C.8) and Table 1; LLaMA3, 2,000 edits in batches of 100. The MEMIT row differs from AlphaEdit in more than the projection.

discussion.takeaway: Project each locate-then-edit update onto the approximate null space of preserved-knowledge keys. In its experiments this single change lets 2,000 sequential edits land without collapsing the model, and it improves MEMIT-style editors by large margins.

claims.claim: Sequential locate-then-edit degrades because each update disturbs preserved key-value pairs and shifts hidden representations.
claims.evidence: Fig. 1, Fig. 5 (t-SNE of hidden states before and after 2,000 edits), §1.

claims.claim: Best editing results across three LLMs.
claims.evidence: Table 1, LLaMA3: Counterfact Eff./Gen. 98.90/94.22 vs 83.33/67.79 for the best baseline (FT); ZsRE Eff. 94.47 vs 86.05 (RECT). Average +12.54% Eff. and +16.78% Gen. over the best baseline (§4.2).

claims.claim: General abilities survive heavy editing.
claims.evidence: GLUE-style F1 on SST, MRPC, CoLA, RTE, MMLU, NLI stays near the unedited level up to 3,000 edits while baselines fall toward zero after 2,000. Fig. 4, §4.3.

claims.claim: The projection is a plug-in for other editors.
claims.evidence: Adding it to MEMIT, PRUNE and RECT improves them by 28.24% (editing) and 42.65% (general capability) on average. Fig. 6-7, §4.5.

claims.claim: Better than memory-based editors on efficacy and generalization.
claims.evidence: LLaMA3 ZsRE Gen. 91.13 vs GRACE 1.03, SERAC 33.96, MELO 24.14; GRACE keeps higher Counterfact specificity (72.23 vs 67.88). Table 2, App. C.5.

claims.claim: No extra runtime.
claims.evidence: 231.40 s vs 231.32 s per 100 ZsRE edits on LLaMA3. Table 7.

limits: Not tested on multimodal LLMs or large reasoning models.
Applying null-space projection to other capabilities (safety, math, biochemistry) is left open.
reading: The null space is approximate, so preserved facts still move: Counterfact specificity drops from 89.48 (unedited) to 67.88 on LLaMA3 after 2,000 edits (Table 1).
P is computed once from the unedited model and not recomputed as edits to layers 4-7 change the keys that later layers see (evaluate.py L206-L209).
App. A.3 lists λ = 15,000 / 20,000, but the AlphaEdit update never reads that setting; preserved knowledge enters only through P (AlphaEdit_main.py L130-L132).
The released configs use a 2e-2 eigenvalue threshold, while the paper's footnote says 1e-2.
The same full-data LLaMA3 numbers carry ±0.10 in Table 1 and ±1.21 in Table 6, so the spreads come from different runs or calculations.
PRUNE has no public code and was reimplemented from its paper (App. A.4); ZsRE efficacy is token-level top-1 accuracy, and the unedited LLaMA3 already scores 36.99.

abstract.text: AlphaEdit addresses sequential knowledge editing, where many factual updates are written into an LLM's FFN weights one batch after another. Locate-then-edit methods such as MEMIT balance fitting the new facts against keeping old ones, and over many edits the balance fails and the model forgets or collapses. AlphaEdit instead projects each weight update onto the null space of the keys of preserved knowledge, so the fit to new facts no longer competes with preservation. With one extra line of code over MEMIT it reports large gains on Counterfact and ZsRE for LLaMA3, GPT-J and GPT2-XL, and the projection also lifts other editors.

retrieval.candidates: cosine prizes on nodes and edges, top-15 each with rank-decayed prizes; Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree gives a connected subgraph (edge cost 0.5)

stages.ingestion: Only user-side turns are used; on LoCoMo two dialogue turns (four utterances) form one unit because single utterances carry little information.
stages.construction: An LLM (Qwen-Turbo) reads each timestamped unit and returns events with an inferred absolute time, a description and (subject, relation, object) triplets; entities cover objects, people, places, goals, interests, sentiments and more.
stages.organization: Events, times, entities, the user and the source utterances form one graph with six edge types (event-time, event-fact-utterance, event-entity, utterance-entity, user-asks-utterance, entity-relation-entity).
stages.update: Duplicate events, entities and relations are merged: incrementally with FAISS above a similarity threshold, and in batches with agglomerative clustering. Nothing is deleted.
stages.retrieval: Nodes and edges get cosine prizes against the question (top-15 each, decaying by rank); a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree extracts a connected subgraph. A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-3B reads the subgraph and names missing entities; each is appended to the question and searched again (max_iter 2). Personalized PageRank then ranks the nodes.
stages.answer: GPT-4o answers from the retrieved utterances; the paper gives no QA prompt or context size.
stages.learning: The deliberating model is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on CoQA-derived samples labeled with qwen-plus: output {} when the subgraph holds the gold cue, otherwise the missing entities.

systems.summary: Event-centric graph memory over a user's dialogue history, read by prize-collecting Steiner-tree subgraph search, a small fine-tuned model that asks for missing entities, and PageRank ranking of utterances.
systems.notes: Venue: Findings of ACL 2025, pages 17533-17547, verified on the ACL Anthology page and the PDF footer. No arXiv version found. CODE: the paper gives no code link and a GitHub search found no official repository, so the record follows the paper only. The in-text citation for MemoRAG points to Izacard et al. 2021 (Contriever), an error in the paper.

sources.code_note: No official code: the paper has no repository link, and a GitHub search for the method name and title found none. Everything below follows the paper; unstated settings (similarity thresholds, PageRank damping, QA context size) are left null.

headline: Utterances are kept verbatim; the LLM-extracted events, times and triplets act as a graph index pointing back to them.
Retrieval is a Steiner-tree subgraph over dense prizes, widened once by a fine-tuned 3B model that lists missing entities, then ranked by PageRank.
The gains are large on LongMemEval-S retrieval (R@5 0.87 vs 0.75 for BGE) but small on LoCoMo (0.74 vs 0.71) and on QA (0.81 vs 0.80).

discussion.takeaway: Index a user's dialogue history with an event-and-entity graph, pull a connected evidence subgraph instead of top-k passages, and let a small tuned model ask for what is missing. This gives clearly better evidence recall on LongMemEval and small gains on LoCoMo and QA.

claims.claim: Graph association plus deliberate recall retrieves evidence better than dense retrievers.
claims.evidence: LongMemEval-S R@5 0.87 vs 0.75 (BGE); LongMemEval-M 0.66 vs 0.56; LoCoMo 0.74 vs 0.71 (LongMemEval pipeline). Table 1

claims.claim: Better retrieval gives better answers.

limits: Temporal information is not modeled in retrieval.
Evaluated only on English datasets.
reading: Recall@N counts 1 only if all evidence is in the top N, so it is stricter than the per-item recall other papers report.
Associa uses only user-side turns and drops the few questions whose evidence is not in user turns (§5.2.1); the paper does not say whether the baselines were scored on the same reduced set.
Text says removing evidence ranking gives better recall@10, but Table 3 shows 0.85 vs 0.93 for the full model.
w/o DM equals Associa max_iter=1 on every metric, so 'deliberating module' and 'second round' are the same ablation.
The QA gain over the LongMemEval pipeline is 0.01 on LongMemEval-S and 0.02 on -M; only LoCoMo shows a clear margin (0.69 vs 0.62).
No code is released, and thresholds (dedup similarity, PageRank damping) and the QA context size are not given, so the system cannot be rebuilt from the paper alone.
LongMemEval (w UF and TF) is not run on LoCoMo because LoCoMo questions lack timestamps, and LightRAG is missing on LongMemEval-M.

abstract.text: Associa is a long-term memory for LLM personal assistants that indexes a user's past dialogue as an event-centric graph of events, times, entities and the original utterances. At question time it scores graph nodes and edges against the query and extracts a connected evidence subgraph with a prize-collecting Steiner tree. A small fine-tuned model then lists entities the subgraph still lacks, triggering further searches, and PageRank ranks the collected utterances. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo the authors report higher evidence recall and QA accuracy than dense retrievers and memory baselines.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on the ACL Anthology.

paper.title: CAM: A Constructivist View of Agentic Memory for LLM-Based Reading Comprehension

construction.unit: text chunk (256 or 512 tokens) as a graph node; LLM summary node per cluster at each higher level
construction.kept_as: raw chunks kept verbatim + LLM summaries of overlapping chunk clusters
construction.processing: link chunks by embedding similarity mixed with position; copy nodes that bridge separate neighbour groups; label propagation clusters; LLM summarises each cluster; recurse
construction.writer: GPT-4o-mini (summaries); text-embedding-3-small (edges)

organization.structure: multi-level graph: chunk graph at level 0, cluster-summary graphs above, a node may belong to several clusters
organization.stores: one composed graph of all levels + one embedding matrix
organization.index: dense embedding of every node at every level

management.operations: new batch: add edges for new chunks, redo replicas and labels only for affected nodes, re-summarise changed clusters, propagate upward (paper; not in released code)

retrieval.query: question as is
retrieval.candidates: cosine top-s over all nodes of all levels (s=5 in paper, 10 in code default), then same-level neighbours and child nodes of kept nodes
retrieval.selection: LLM keeps the helpful nodes each turn; repeat until the pool stops changing or 5 turns
retrieval.budget: no cap: every node kept in any turn

use.context: all kept nodes (summaries and raw chunks, adjacent chunks joined) as numbered passages
use.reasoning: up to 5 LLM selection calls, then one answer call

classify.note: Candidates start from a dense top-s over all levels, then grow along same-level edges and down to child nodes; an LLM picks which nodes to keep at every turn.

stages.ingestion: Documents are split into chunks of 256 or 512 tokens and each chunk is embedded (text-embedding-3-small).
stages.construction: Chunks form a level-0 graph: each chunk links to at most 10 others whose score (weighted cosine similarity plus a Gaussian bonus for nearby positions) passes a threshold. Each node is copied once per connected group of its neighbours, label propagation clusters the copies, and an LLM summarises every cluster into a node of the next level.
stages.organization: Summary nodes form their own graph (linked when clusters overlap or when their members are linked) and are clustered and summarised again, giving a hierarchy where one node can feed several parents.
stages.update: For a new batch of chunks the paper only recomputes the copies and labels of affected nodes and re-summarises clusters that changed, level by level. The released code builds the whole hierarchy in one pass.
stages.retrieval: Prune-and-Grow: cosine top-s over nodes of all levels, an LLM keeps the helpful ones, their same-level neighbours and children join the pool, and the LLM picks again, until the pool stops changing or 5 turns pass.
stages.answer: The answer model reads every node kept in any turn (summaries plus raw chunks, neighbouring chunks joined) as numbered passages.

systems.summary: Reading memory built by incremental overlapping clustering: chunks are linked by meaning and position, clustered with node copies so a chunk can feed several LLM summaries, stacked into levels, and read by an LLM that grows its selection along the graph.

headline: Memory is a stack of graphs: raw chunks at the bottom, LLM summaries of overlapping chunk clusters above; a chunk can feed several summaries.
Reading is Prune-and-Grow: an LLM keeps useful nodes from a dense top-s, the pool grows to their neighbours and children, and the LLM picks again for up to 5 turns.
The released code only builds offline, so the paper's batch-online results (Fig. 3) cannot be rerun from it.

abstract.text: CAM borrows Piaget's constructivist theory to state three properties a reading agent's memory should have: structured schemata, flexible assimilation and dynamic accommodation. It builds memory by incremental overlapping clustering: text chunks are linked by semantic similarity and position, nodes are copied so they can belong to several clusters, and each cluster is summarised by an LLM into a higher level, with new batches updating only the affected parts. At question time an LLM starts from the most similar nodes and grows its selection along the memory graph. The authors report gains over RAPTOR, GraphRAG, HippoRAG, MemTree and others on six long-text QA, summarisation and claim-verification sets, and faster batch insertion than rebuilding offline.

discussion.takeaway: Build reading memory as overlapping clusters stacked into summary levels, and let an LLM grow its evidence along that graph. In the paper this beats tree, graph and flat memories on six long-text tasks and lets new batches be added without a full rebuild.

claims.claim: Memory for reading agents should be structured, flexible (one unit feeds several abstractions) and dynamic (local updates).
claims.evidence: §3, Table 1

claims.claim: CAM is best on all six datasets.
claims.evidence: Average +3.0% over the best baselines (RAPTOR, GraphRAG), e.g. NovelQA ACC-L 52.3 vs 47.8, ODSum-Meeting 50.7 vs 45.8. Table 2, §5.2

claims.claim: Letting a node join several clusters matters.
claims.evidence: RAPTOR (soft clusters) beats MemTree (strict tree) by 2.1% on average; removing node copies drops QMSum ACC-L 57.6 → 51.5. §5.2, Table 3

claims.claim: Prune-and-Grow beats both tree traversal and flat global retrieval over the same memory.
claims.evidence: NovelQA ACC-L 52.3 vs 46.5 and 50.3. Table 3

claims.claim: Batch insertion is fast and stable.
claims.evidence: Under 0.3h per 500-chunk batch vs 1.2h (RAPTOR) and 1.8h (GraphRAG) rebuilds; ACC-L stays roughly flat across batch sizes. Fig. 3, §5.3

claims.claim: Knowledge-graph extraction is not worth it on narratives but helps entity-rich QA.
claims.evidence: Table 3 row 8 (> 3× cost, small change); Table 7: 2Wiki EM 61.4 → 65.8 with it. §5.4, App. G

limits: Only tested on long-text reading comprehension.
No self-questioning or reflection.
Summary hallucinations can propagate to higher levels.
Assumes source texts are internally consistent.
The clustering algorithm is one of several possible implementations.
Prompts and hyperparameters are fixed by hand; nothing is learned from feedback.
reading: The released code has no incremental path: it rebuilds all levels from all chunks, so the online-batch timing and stability results (Fig. 3) cannot be checked against it.

Code defaults differ from the paper: 10 seed nodes instead of 5, text-embedding-3-large instead of -small, and α = θ = 0.6, outside the reported grids. The per-dataset settings used for Table 2 are not given.

The answer context is every node kept in any of up to 5 turns, with no size cap, and no token counts are reported; the paper does not state the baselines' retrieval budgets, so context size is not controlled.
The paper names GPT-4o as ACC-L judge; the code's judge function uses the same client as the reader (gpt-4o-mini by default).
Clusters larger than 12 are cut into consecutive slices of the member list, not by structure.
The summarisation script reads the 'gist' field by default, which summary nodes do not have (their text is stored as 'text'); the flags behind the QMSum and ODSum runs are not stated.
All baselines were rerun by the authors with GPT-4o-mini and text-embedding-3-small; FullContext has no multi-document numbers.

stages.construction: For each question the top-1 passage is written as 'Question: q / Document: passage', cut to 180 tokens, and encoded by the context assessor (base LLM + LoRA) with 16 memory tokens; the last-layer states at those tokens (through an MLP projector in the code) are the soft context embeddings.

stages.answer: The frozen base LLM gets the instruction, the 16 embeddings in place of the background passage and the question, and generates up to 30 tokens greedily.
stages.learning: The assessor is pretrained to reconstruct 2M Wikipedia passages from its embeddings, then fine-tuned on NQ: questions the LLM answers closed-book get a hard-negative passage and a no-context teacher, the rest get a passage containing the answer and a teacher reading it; loss is LM plus λ-weighted KL to the teacher. The base LLM is never updated.

systems.summary: Encodes each retrieved passage with the question into 16 soft embeddings via a LoRA copy of the LLM, trained with helpful and hard-negative passages so the embeddings tell the frozen LLM how much to trust the passage.

headline: The memory is not a store: each retrieved passage is re-encoded with its question into 16 soft embeddings that take the passage's place in the prompt.
Conflict handling is learned, not decided: there is no gate; the embeddings are trained to be weak when the passage would mislead, and the frozen LLM then leans on what it knows.
All main tests use the single top-1 ColBERTv2 passage and short greedy answers (at most 30 tokens).

glance.a: Nothing persistent. A static Wikipedia corpus is searched with ColBERTv2; the passage found is turned into 16 soft embeddings for this question only.

glance.q: Does the question shape the encoding?
glance.a: Yes. The assessor reads 'Question: … Document: …', so the same passage is encoded differently for different questions.

glance.q: Who decides to ignore a bad passage?
glance.a: No explicit decision. The embeddings are trained to carry less influence for misleading passages; the frozen LLM does the rest.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: An instruction, 16 embeddings where the passage would be, and the question. Never the passage text.

discussion.takeaway: Instead of deciding whether to trust a retrieved passage, CARE compresses it into a few soft embeddings trained to carry that trust, so a frozen LLM can ignore misleading context yet still use helpful context. It beats RAG and other conflict methods on average without fine-tuning the LLM.

claims.claim: Best average among methods that leave the LLM unchanged.
claims.evidence: Average 0.458 vs 0.436 RAG and 0.435 Priori Judgment (Mistral); 0.467 vs 0.440 and 0.453 (LLaMA). Table 2, §5.1.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning the LLM itself hurts other tasks.
claims.evidence: Direct FT and RetRobust drop on TruthfulQA (Mistral F1 0.102 / 0.152 vs CARE 0.279) and Direct FT on FactKG with LLaMA (0.305). Table 2.

claims.claim: Soft reliance beats a hard retrieve-or-not decision.
claims.evidence: With Mistral, +5.29% over the best adaptive-retrieval baseline (Priori Judgment 0.435 vs 0.458); Adaptive-RAG averages 0.427. §5.1, Table 2.

claims.claim: Both kinds of supervision are needed, and pretraining is essential.
claims.evidence: Positives only: Resilience 0.696; negatives only: Boost 0.071; no pretraining: 0.347 vs 0.438 overall. Table 3.

claims.claim: Cheap at inference.
claims.evidence: 1.19 s per query vs 1.07 s RAG and 2.10 s Priori Judgment. Table 4.

claims.claim: Carries over to another LLM and to three passages.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B 0.454 vs 0.425 RAG (Table 7); top-3 NQ 0.504 vs 0.481 (Table 8).

limits: Only the top-1 passage and single-step answering are studied; conflicts among passages and within reasoning are left out (top-3 is a preliminary test).
A fixed budget of 16 embeddings suits short Wikipedia passages but may be too small for longer contexts.
Closed-book correctness is a noisy proxy for whether the LLM knows the answer.
reading: There is no persistent memory: the corpus is fixed and the soft context is rebuilt per question, so CARE is a way of reading retrieved evidence rather than of storing it.
The assessor sees the question with the passage (eq. 4; the released test file prefixes every passage with its question), so the same passage gets different embeddings for different questions.
Training uses NQ only. Gains are largest on the open-domain QA sets; with Mistral, CARE is 0.638 vs 0.639 for RAG on FactKG and 0.279 vs 0.277 F1 on TruthfulQA.
With LLaMA on WebQA the closed-book model (0.465) beats every retrieval method, CARE included (0.445).
All runs use a single seed (App. A.1), and several baselines were adapted (Adaptive-RAG relabelled to a binary retrieve decision, Priori Judgment used in its RAG setting; App. A.3).

abstract.text: When a retrieved passage contradicts what an LLM already knows correctly, standard RAG tends to follow the passage and get the answer wrong. CARE adds a context assessor, a LoRA-tuned copy of the base LLM that turns the question and passage into a few soft memory embeddings placed in the prompt instead of the passage. The assessor is first pretrained to reconstruct passages, then fine-tuned with helpful passages for questions the LLM cannot answer alone and hard negatives for questions it can, so the embeddings learn to signal how far to trust the passage. The base LLM is never fine-tuned, and CARE improves average results by about 5% over RAG across QA and fact-checking benchmarks.

construction.unit: experience: environment dynamics (page summary + URL) or skill (sub-goal workflow with steps)
construction.kept_as: LLM-distilled, abstracted with {variables}
construction.processing: two GPT-4o distillers read a whole trajectory and its goal: one summarizes visited pages with their URLs, one breaks the goal into sub-goal skills with step-by-step actions
construction.writer: GPT-4o

organization.structure: two flat lists in one buffer: dynamics and skills
organization.stores: experience buffer (dynamics list, skills list)

management.operations: append new dynamics and skills; distillers see existing ones and mark repeats 'Summarized before'

retrieval.query: task goal + website description
retrieval.candidates: the whole buffer (every dynamic, every skill) shown to two LLM selectors
retrieval.selection: LLM picks up to k_d = 5 pages and k_s = 5 skills

use.context: selected experiences turned into text by a fixed template and added to the agent's system prompt
use.reasoning: ReAct-format GPT-4o web agent (BrowserGym), multi-step

classify.note: Two typed lists (page dynamics, skills). There is no embedding or keyword index: an LLM reads the task goal and the whole list and names up to 5 entries of each type.

stages.ingestion: Input is a whole trajectory with its goal: in the online setting the agent's own trajectory after each task (success or failure, no reward), offline human-annotated demonstrations of 5-10 extra tasks per website, or both (hybrid).
stages.construction: A dynamics distiller writes one summary per useful page (name, description, possible usages) paired with its URL; a skills distiller splits the goal into sub-goals and writes each as a named skill with numbered steps, each step a sentence plus an example action, with specific values replaced by variables.
stages.organization: Dynamics and skills are kept as two separate lists in one experience buffer.
stages.update: New experiences are merged into the buffer after each task; the distillers see the existing entries and skip ones already summarized.
stages.retrieval: Two GPT-4o selectors each read the task goal, the website description and every dynamic or skill in the buffer, and return at most 5 of each.
stages.answer: The selected experiences are rendered by a fixed template into 'Environment dynamics' and 'Skills' sections of the agent's system prompt, and the agent acts step by step on the website.

systems.summary: Distills past web-agent trajectories into page summaries with URLs and reusable skills, and lets an LLM pick a few of them to replay in the agent's prompt on each new task, online, offline or both.
systems.notes:
Venue: ACL 2025 long paper (aclanthology 2025.acl-long.694, pp. 14179-14198); arXiv comment 'Accepted to ACL 2025'. The ACL PDF tables match arXiv v1. No official code found (no link in the arXiv or ACL PDF, no repo found on GitHub).
DESIGN: §3.1-3.4, §4.1 (GPT-4o-2024-05-13, temperature 0.1, k_d = k_s = 5), App. A.1 (prompts, Figs. 3-6), A.2 (replay format, Figs. 7-8). 'trigger' is 'other': online distillation runs after each task, offline on a fixed set of trajectories. Buffer scope (per website or shared) is not stated.

sources.code_note: No code: neither the arXiv nor the ACL PDF links a repository, and no official repo was found. Everything below comes from the paper text and its prompt figures (App. A.1-A.2).

headline: Memory is two lists written by GPT-4o from whole trajectories: page summaries with their URLs, and skills written as step lists with variables.
There is no vector search: an LLM reads the task goal and the whole buffer and picks up to 5 pages and 5 skills.
Online, CER learns from its own trajectories without any success signal; learning only from successful ones scores higher (33.5 vs 31.4).

LLM thinks, then writes one summary (name, description, usages) per unique URL, skipping pages already in the buffer
LLM breaks the goal into sub-goals and writes each as a skill with steps, replacing specific values with variable names, skipping skills already in the buffer
new entries are added to the buffer

open_questions: Online results depend on the order in which tasks are solved, which the paper does not state or vary.
The buffer grows with every task and the selector reads all of it; the paper gives no buffer size, so it is unclear how selection behaves as it grows.
The ablation removes dynamics or skills but not the URL field, which §7 names as a main reason dynamics help.

key_numbers.label: Offline data
key_numbers.value: 5-10 human-annotated tasks per website (~5% of the test set)

ablation.src: paper Table 8 (ablation), Table 9 (baseline and data sources)

components.model: GPT-4o (Llama-3.1-70B in one analysis), ReAct format, BrowserGym

discussion.takeaway: A web agent can improve without training by turning its own past trajectories into short page summaries and skills and replaying a few relevant ones in context; on WebArena this lifts GPT-4o from 24.3% to 36.7% success.

claims.claim: CER improves a GPT-4o BrowserGym agent substantially on both benchmarks.
claims.evidence: WebArena 24.3 → 36.7 (hybrid), relative +51.0%; VisualWebArena 26.2 → 31.9 (online), +21.8%. Tables 1-2, §4.2

claims.claim: It beats tree search on VisualWebArena at far lower cost.
claims.evidence: 31.9 vs 26.4; tree search samples 20 times per step. Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: Experiences cost few extra tokens.
claims.evidence: +5.8% to +17.3% input tokens. Table 3, §5.1

claims.claim: Gains come from fine-grained experiences, not memorizing tasks.
claims.evidence: Cross-template SR on Forum 44.7 → 60.0; stability 93%, plasticity 141%. Table 4, §5.2-5.3

claims.claim: Both dynamics and skills are needed.
claims.evidence: Forum 37.7 full, 33.3 without skills, 35.1 without dynamics. Table 8, §5.7

claims.claim: CER composes with other methods and weaker models.
claims.evidence: With sampling + reranking 52.6 vs 43.1 (Table 6); Llama-3.1-70B GitLab 17.3 → 22.0 (Table 5)

limits: Offline learning needs goal-oriented trajectories; trajectories from random exploration help little and can hurt.
Environment dynamics help partly because web pages can be reached by URL; use in other kinds of environments is untested.
The online setting has nothing to learn from at the start, and offline data depends on human annotators.
reading: The main rows are 'hybrid' on WebArena but 'online' on VisualWebArena; the hybrid setting adds human demonstrations of extra tasks that the baselines do not get.

Most baseline rows in Tables 1-2 are copied from their papers with different agents and setups; only the BrowserGym GPT-4o rows were rerun, so the like-for-like gains are 24.3 → 33.2 (online) on WebArena and 26.2 → 31.9 on VisualWebArena.
The relative gain for hybrid is 51.0% in the abstract and §4.2 but 52.5% in Table 3; (36.7 - 24.3) / 24.3 gives 51.0%.
Several analyses (Tables 4, 6, 8, 9) use only the Forum split, and the success-only comparison (Table 7) uses text observations, so its 31.4 differs from the 33.2 main online number.
Learning from failures is allowed but not filtered; using only successful trajectories (which needs the benchmark's evaluator) scores higher.

abstract.text: CER targets web agents that start every task without knowledge of the site. After tasks, it prompts an LLM to distill trajectories into two kinds of experience, summaries of useful pages with their URLs and reusable multi-step skills, and keeps them in a growing buffer. For a new task an LLM picks a few relevant experiences, which are written into the agent's prompt. It works with the agent's own trajectories, with human demonstrations, or both, and raises a GPT-4o agent to 36.7% success on WebArena and 31.9% on VisualWebArena.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: ComoRAG

paper.title: ComoRAG: A Cognitive-Inspired Memory-Organized RAG for Stateful Long Narrative Reasoning

construction.unit: three indexes over a book (raw chunks with KG triples, cluster summaries, window summaries) + per-question memory units (probe, evidence, cue)
construction.kept_as: verbatim 512-token chunks plus LLM summaries; memory units hold LLM-written cues
construction.processing: LLM extracts triples per chunk (HippoRAG 2 recipe); GMM clusters summarized recursively (RAPTOR recipe); non-overlapping windows of W chunks summarized in story order
construction.writer: GPT-4o-mini (triples, summaries, cues)

organization.structure: Veridical layer (chunk-entity graph), Semantic layer (summary tree), Episodic layer (timeline summaries); a per-question memory pool beside them
organization.stores: three BGE-M3 embedding stores + igraph KG; memory pool of units (probe, evidence, cue, embedding)
organization.index: BGE-M3 dense vectors; fact embeddings seed Personalized PageRank on the KG

management.operations: knowledge source is static; each failed cycle appends new memory units and one fused note to the per-question pool
management.forgetting: pool is discarded after each question

retrieval.query: question at step 0; afterwards up to 3 LLM-written probes per cycle
retrieval.candidates: Veridical: top-5 facts by similarity, LLM fact filter, PPR over KG; Semantic and Episodic: dense similarity; top 50 per layer, items already in the pool dropped
retrieval.selection: per-layer token budget; Mem-Fuse picks the top 50% of pool units by similarity to the question
retrieval.budget: answer context capped at 6k tokens, 8:2:2:1 across Veridical, Semantic, Episodic and fused history (paper); code caps each layer separately (3,000/1,000/1,000 default, 2,000 each in the example script)

use.context: step 0: raw retrieved chunks and summaries; later cycles: LLM cues of the new units plus fused notes
use.reasoning: answer LLM returns an answer or a failure signal ('*'); on failure another probe cycle runs, up to 5 cycles

classify.note: Three different indexes, of which the Veridical one (PPR over a KG) carries most of the gain in the ablation; Semantic and Episodic use plain dense search. The set is fixed by top-50 plus a token cap; the LLM only decides whether to run another probe cycle and what to probe.

stages.ingestion: The book is split into 512-token chunks.
stages.construction: Three indexes are built once: chunks with LLM-extracted triples linked into an entity graph (Veridical), recursive GMM-cluster summaries (Semantic), and summaries of consecutive chunk windows in story order (Episodic).
stages.organization: The three layers are separate embedding stores (BGE-M3); a question-specific memory pool holds units of (probe, retrieved evidence from one layer, LLM cue).
stages.update: When the answer LLM signals failure, new units from the probes are appended to the pool and an LLM fuses the most question-similar half of the pool into a background note.
stages.retrieval: Each query hits all three layers (PPR over the KG for Veridical, dense search for the others), keeps the top 50 per layer minus items already seen, then cuts to a per-layer token budget; after a failure an LLM writes up to 3 new probes that are searched the same way.
stages.answer: Step 0 answers from the raw evidence; later cycles answer from the new cues plus fused notes, with multiple-choice options shown only at this step.

systems.summary: Long-narrative RAG that, when a first answer fails, loops up to five times: an LLM writes new probes, evidence from three indexes (entity graph, summary tree, timeline summaries) is turned into query-focused cues, and past cues are fused before answering again.
systems.notes: Venue checked: AAAI 2026, Proceedings vol. 40 no. 39, 'AAAI Technical Track on Natural Language Processing IV', pp. 33557-33565 (ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/40644); the repo README calls it a poster. Paper text from arXiv v3 (12 Nov 2025). Code: official repo at commit a4f8433 (2025-08-28, latest). The paper describes memory units as holding the retrieved evidence, but the answer LLM only sees raw evidence at step 0.

sources.code_note: Official repository linked from the paper. Commit a4f8433 (2025-08-28) is the newest; it only has three commits, all from 2025-08-28, so it was released after the first arXiv version (2025-08-14). The repo ships an example on a toy corpus, not the evaluation scripts or configs for the four benchmarks, so the exact settings behind Table 1 cannot be checked.

headline: The answer LLM reads raw text only at step 0. After a failure it reads LLM-written cues (up to 5 'key findings' per layer per probe) and fused notes, never the chunks themselves.
Almost all of the gain comes from the loop: step 0 alone is within 1% of the best baseline on EN.MC (64.6), the full loop reaches 72.93.
The memory pool lives for one question; nothing is carried across questions.

Because the answer LLM reads cues instead of text after step 0, gains could come from LLM pre-reading (query-focused summarization) as much as from multi-step memory; no baseline gives IRCoT the same summarization.
The loop costs up to 5 cycles of 3 probes × (fact filter + 3 cue calls) per question; the paper reports no per-question tokens or latency for Table 1.

glance.a: A three-part index over the book (chunks in an entity graph, a tree of cluster summaries, window summaries in story order), plus a per-question pool of LLM-written cues.
No. The pool is created for each question and dropped afterwards; only the static index is shared.
Not of chunks. The Veridical path filters the top 5 triples with an LLM before PageRank; the other two layers are plain dense top-k.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: First the raw retrieved text; after a failure, only LLM cues and fused notes.

discussion.takeaway: For questions over whole novels, retrieving once is not enough: letting an LLM probe again after a failed answer, and carrying forward short cues from earlier probes, gives the best scores on four narrative benchmarks with a small retriever.

claims.claim: Best results on all four long-narrative benchmarks.
claims.evidence: EN.MC 72.93 vs 64.19 (HippoRAGv2+IRCoT), EN.QA F1 34.52 vs 34.34 (NV-Embed-v2 RAG), DetectiveQA 68.18 vs 64.77 (RAPTOR+IRCoT). Table 1

claims.claim: The gain comes from the iterative loop, converging in 2-3 cycles.
claims.evidence: Step 0 is within 1% of the best baseline; EN.MC rises from 64.6 to 72.93. Fig. 4, §4.3

claims.claim: The Veridical layer matters most among the indexes.
claims.evidence: Without it EN.MC falls to 51.97 (about -30% relative). Table 2

claims.claim: The loop plugs into other indexes.
claims.evidence: EN.MC 60.26 → 68.56 on HippoRAGv2 and 57.21 → 69.00 on RAPTOR. Table 3

claims.claim: Largest advantage on narrative questions.
claims.evidence: 19% relative F1 on EN.QA and 16% accuracy on EN.MC over the strongest baselines for narrative queries. Fig. 6, §4.4

limits: The paper has no limitations section. It notes that the remaining unsolved queries reflect the base LLM's reasoning limits (§4.3).
reading: Baselines and ComoRAG share GPT-4o-mini and BGE-M3 and a 6k context, but ComoRAG makes many more LLM calls per question (probes, cues, fusion, up to 6 answer attempts); cost per question is not reported for Table 1.
In the released code the answer model reads raw text only at step 0; later answers rest on LLM cues, so wrong cues cannot be checked against the source.
Chunks are re-sorted into book order before the token cut, so the kept chunks are the earliest among the top 50 rather than the highest scored; the paper does not mention this.
The query-type analysis (factoid, narrative, inferential) uses the authors' own manual labels (Table 7).
NarrativeQA uses a random 500-question sample and DetectiveQA a random 20% of stories; the samples are not released, so other papers' numbers on these sets are not directly comparable.
The repo has no evaluation scripts or configs for the paper's datasets, so the settings behind Table 1 could not be checked in code.

abstract.text: ComoRAG targets question answering over whole novels, where one-shot retrieval misses how plot and motives change over hundreds of thousands of tokens. It indexes a book three ways (raw chunks linked through an entity graph, recursive cluster summaries, and summaries of consecutive passages). When the model cannot answer, a loop writes new probing queries, turns what each probe finds into short cues in a per-question memory pool, fuses relevant past cues, and tries again. On NarrativeQA, InfiniteBench EN.QA and EN.MC, and DetectiveQA it beats single-step, graph-based and multi-step RAG baselines, with the clearest gains on questions that need the whole storyline.

abstract.text: DAMCS puts several GPT-4o agents into a multi-agent version of the Crafter survival game, where the team must climb a crafting tree and obtain a diamond as fast as possible. Each agent keeps its own memory: a pool of its past decision steps organized into a graph of long-term goals, goals and steps, which is read back into a short working memory together with a recipe check. A structured communication scheme orders the agents so that each helps its predecessor and shares tools. On the new environment, two and six communicating agents reach the diamond in 63% and 74% fewer steps than a basic LLM agent, and 13.6% and 39% fewer than one agent with memory.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Memory is read by position, not by search: every decision sees the latest goal node, its chain of earlier goals, the previous step's summary and the last 7 actions.
The graph is built by fixed rules from the LLM's own structured outputs and rebuilt from scratch at every step; a new goal node starts whenever the inventory changes.
The 'messages' between agents are code-generated: agent i reads agent i−1's recipe check and a fixed role policy.

ablation.src: paper Table 1 (average steps, lower is better)

discussion.takeaway: Give each LLM agent a goal-organized record of its own steps and a fixed cooperation protocol, and a team finishes a long crafting chain in far fewer steps; the memory helps one agent, the protocol helps teams.

claims.claim: Goal-oriented memory lets one agent follow the crafting hierarchy much faster than a basic LLM agent.
claims.evidence: Diamond in 140.0 vs 334.67 steps (about 3x faster); the basic agent succeeds on the last three tasks in only 60% of episodes. §6.2, Table 1

claims.claim: Memory without communication does not help teams.
claims.evidence: Two Mem agents: 150.4 steps; six Mem agents: 140.6, vs 140.0 for one agent. §6.2, Table 1

claims.claim: Structured communication lets agents split work.
claims.evidence: 121.0 steps with two agents (13.6% fewer than one agent, 63% fewer than basic); 85.4 with six (39% and 74% fewer). §6.2, Table 1

claims.claim: RL baselines do not reach the diamond in the same environment.
claims.evidence: PPO and MADDPG rewards plateau after 1,000 training episodes. §6.2, Fig. 5 (no step numbers given)

limits: Memory quality and adaptability of LLM agents are hard to measure directly.
No standard metric exists for LLM-agent cooperation, so cooperation is measured indirectly through steps.
LLM agents are sensitive to the prompt and environment description.
reading: The released code reads memory by position only: the latest goal node, its chain, one summary and 7 actions. The similarity-retrieval function is commented out, so 'retrieving relevant experiences' amounts to a fixed recency window plus the goal chain.

Mem+Comm also adds a hard-coded division of labour (agent 0 crafts, agent 1 feeds stone, the last agent goes for the diamond), and messages are templates over the previous agent's recipe check rather than LLM-written text.
Table 1's caption says five environments and ten runs; the released run.py fixes seed 4, and the code has no switch to reproduce the Mem-only or basic settings.

The reflection text and the collaboration block are generated at each step but not copied into the graph nodes (only the last action and its result are), so they return to the prompt only through the one-step summary.
RL/MARL baselines are reported only as training reward curves, not as steps, so they cannot be compared with the LLM rows.
