classify.note: Memory is working context for one task: when to fold is a policy decision (trained with ToolPO), the content is written by a prompted auxiliary LLM, and the result is always read in full.

stages.ingestion: The agent's own interaction trace (thoughts, tool searches, tool calls and their results) grows inside one reasoning stream; long tool results (over 5,000 characters) are condensed by the auxiliary LLM before they enter it.
stages.construction: When the agent emits <fold_thought>, the auxiliary LLM reads the whole trace (and the tool-call history) and writes episodic, working and tool memory as three JSON objects in parallel.
stages.organization: Three typed blocks with fixed JSON schemas: episodic (task description, key events with step/outcome, progress), working (immediate goal, challenges, next actions), tool (per-tool success rate, effective parameters, errors, derived rules).
stages.update: Each fold rebuilds all three blocks from the full trace so far and replaces the previous memory in the prompt; the code allows 3 folds per task.
stages.retrieval: No memory retrieval: the folded memory is inserted in full before the question. Separate from memory, tools are found by dense search over tool documentation (bge-large-en-v1.5, top-10 in the code).
stages.answer: The main reasoning model (QwQ-32B) continues from the original instructions plus the folded memory and answers when done or at the action limit.
stages.learning: ToolPO (RL) trains the main model end-to-end with LLM-simulated APIs; the action-level reward includes a term for efficient folding, and its advantage is credited only to tool-call and fold tokens. The auxiliary memory writer is not trained.

systems.summary: A reasoning model that finds and calls tools inside one thought stream and can choose to 'fold' its history: an auxiliary LLM compresses the trace into episodic, working and tool memory, and reasoning restarts from that memory.
systems.notes: Venue: the paper's own ACM reference block and footers give WWW '26 (Dubai, April 13-17 2026), DOI 10.1145/3774904.3792460; arXiv comment 'Accepted by WWW 2026'. Text read from arXiv v3 (5 Feb 2026). Memory here is within-task context management, not memory across tasks or sessions: nothing persists between questions. The ToolPO training code is not in the repository, so the RL side (fold reward, tool simulator) is from the paper only.

sources.code_note: Commit 7febc95 (2025-10-26) is the first code release, days after arXiv v1; the folding, memory prompts and tool search are unchanged at the current HEAD (2e25aba, 2026-04-13), which only adds an Exa search option. The repository holds inference and evaluation code only; ToolPO training and the tool simulator loop are not released.

headline: The 'memory' is a compressed restart point inside one task: nothing is kept across questions.
Folding is the agent's choice (a special token); the summary itself is written by a separate, untrained auxiliary LLM.
Each fold summarises the whole trace from the start, including text already folded, and replaces the previous memory.

discussion.takeaway: Letting a reasoning model search for tools on demand and fold its own history into structured memory beats fixed ReAct-style workflows, most clearly when tools must be found in large open sets.

claims.claim: End-to-end reasoning with on-demand tool discovery beats workflow agents.
claims.evidence: Open-set ToolBench 64.0 and ToolHop 40.6 vs best baselines 54.0 and 29.0 (Table 1, §5.1).

claims.claim: Autonomous tool retrieval during reasoning is better than retrieving tools up front.
claims.evidence: Average 52.6 vs 28.5 for the best workflow method (Table 4, §5.5).

claims.claim: Memory folding matters for long-horizon tasks.
claims.evidence: Without folding the 4-task average drops 48.1 to 44.2 and GAIA 53.3 to 44.7 (Table 3, §5.4).

claims.claim: ToolPO improves over the untrained agent and over GRPO.
claims.evidence: GAIA 46.7 to 53.3, ALFWorld 88.1 to 91.8 (Table 2); higher, steadier reward curves than GRPO (Fig. 4).

discussion.limits_src: The paper has no limitations section.
reading: Memory here is per task and is rebuilt at each fold; nothing carries over between questions, so it is context compression rather than long-term memory.
The folding ablation is on the RL model and moves GAIA most (-8.6) while ToolBench moves 1 point; the paper does not report fold frequency or memory size, so how often folding fires is unknown.
In the code the tool list meant for the memory prompts is overwritten with an empty string, and every later fold re-summarises the full trace from the start.
The auxiliary LLM also condenses long tool outputs for all baselines (App. B), so the comparison with ReAct differs mainly in the reasoning model's control loop, folding and tool search.
Baseline numbers carry no statement of who ran them; OpenAI Deep Research and AgentLM rows have gaps that suggest reported numbers.

abstract.text: DeepAgent is a single-stream reasoning agent: a large reasoning model thinks, searches a tool index when it needs a tool, and calls tools without a fixed workflow. For long tasks it can fold its history: an auxiliary LLM compresses the trace into episodic, working and tool memory in JSON, and reasoning restarts from that. The model is trained with ToolPO, an RL method that uses LLM-simulated APIs and gives extra credit to the tokens of correct tool calls. Across ToolBench, API-Bank, RestBench, ToolHop, ALFWorld, WebShop, GAIA and HLE it outperforms workflow-based baselines, most in open-set tool retrieval.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

paper.title: From Exploration to Mastery: Enabling LLMs to Master Tools via Self-Driven Interactions

construction.unit: tool documentation of one API (its description text)
construction.kept_as: LLM-rewritten description, revised from real calls to the tool
construction.processing: per API, up to 5 rounds: Explorer writes a query + parameters and calls the tool; Analyzer suggests edits; Rewriter rewrites the doc and proposes the next exploration direction
construction.writer: GPT-4o (all three roles)

organization.structure: one document per API (plus one summary per tool in the code), keyed by tool and API name
organization.stores: documentation set; per-API history of explored queries and doc versions used during refinement
organization.index: none (docs are looked up by tool/API id); text-embedding-ada-002 only for the query-diversity and stop checks

management.operations: rewrite the doc in place each round; stop when two consecutive versions barely differ (avg of cosine and BLEU > 0.75)
management.conflicts: Analyzer checks the doc against the actual tool output and flags inconsistencies

retrieval.query: the user task (split into subtasks in the released inference script)
retrieval.candidates: the benchmark's candidate tools for the query; their docs are in the prompt
retrieval.selection: the agent LLM picks a tool, then APIs, then parameters from the docs

use.context: revised tool and API documentation in place of the original docs
use.reasoning: tool-use agent (ReAct/DFSDT-style); the paper does not name the agent loop used for DRAFT rows

classify.note: The memory is the documentation itself. At use time the agent reads the docs of every candidate tool the benchmark gives for the query and picks among them; there is no similarity search over docs (Table 3 tests BM25/Contriever only as an extra analysis).

stages.ingestion: For each API, an Explorer LLM invents a natural user query and parameters from the current doc and actually calls the tool; a new query whose ada-002 embedding is too close (cosine >= 0.9) to an earlier one is rejected and regenerated.
stages.construction: An Analyzer LLM compares the doc with the observed call and result and writes edit suggestions; a Rewriter LLM rewrites the doc from the example, the suggestions and the revision history, and proposes where to explore next.
stages.organization: One revised description per API kept in the tool's documentation file; the code also writes a new tool-level summary after all its APIs are revised.
stages.update: The loop repeats up to 5 rounds per API and stops early when the average of embedding cosine and BLEU between consecutive versions exceeds 0.75.
stages.retrieval: No memory search: the agent receives the documentation of the candidate tools; in the released script an LLM picks a tool from tool summaries, then APIs from the tool doc, then parameters from the API doc.
stages.answer: The tool-use agent calls APIs and answers from their responses; the docs only change how it understands the tools.

systems.summary: Rewrites human-written tool documentation into LLM-oriented documentation through an explore, analyze, rewrite loop driven by real tool calls, with a query-diversity check and a similarity-based stopping rule.
systems.notes:
Venue: PDF header 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025'; arXiv comment and repo README say ICLR 2025 Oral (OpenReview QKBu1BOAwd, page not reachable from here). Memory here is procedural: the stored item is the tool's documentation, refined offline before any test task; it is not per-user or per-episode memory.

headline: The memory is tool documentation: each API's description is rewritten by GPT-4o after it has actually called the tool, then frozen before testing.
Refinement stops per API when two consecutive versions are nearly the same (avg of cosine and BLEU > 0.75), at most 5 rounds.
The revised docs are longer: ToolBench API descriptions grow from 14 to 31 words on average, RestBench ones 3.6x (TMDB) to 6.9x (Spotify).

paper_vs_code.paper: not described

paper_vs_code.paper: not described
paper_vs_code.code: every API in the released DRAFT docs carries a 'User Query' + 'Parameters' example that DRAFT.py does not produce; the parameter prompt tells the agent to use it

paper_vs_code.paper: Table 1 compares DRAFT with ReAct, DFSDT and EasyTool without naming the agent loop DRAFT runs in

open_questions: Released DRAFT docs add a worked example per API that the original docs lack; no ablation separates the effect of the example from the rewritten description.
Table 1 does not say which agent loop the DRAFT rows use; if it is the released decompose-and-retry script, part of the gain over ReAct and DFSDT may come from the loop rather than the documentation.
The docs are refined with GPT-4o calling the same APIs that the test queries use, and no held-out-tool split is reported.

discussion.takeaway: Tool documentation can be treated as a memory the model writes for itself: letting GPT-4o call each API, critique the doc and rewrite it gives better tool use than the original or a one-shot rewrite (EasyTool), and the rewritten docs help other models too.

claims.claim: DRAFT docs beat ReAct, DFSDT and EasyTool on all three datasets and three agent models.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o CP%: TMDB 88 vs 79 (EasyTool), Spotify 70.17 vs 64.91 (DFSDT), ToolBench 51 vs 45. Table 1, §3.2

claims.claim: Docs refined by one model help other models (cross-model generalization).
claims.evidence: GPT-4o-refined docs lift GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3-70B; Llama-3-70B-refined docs also help on TMDB. Table 1, Fig. 7, §3.3

claims.claim: More rounds help up to a point, then docs get redundant and scores drop.
claims.evidence: Fig. 6 curves over rounds 1-5; App. E trajectory rounds 4-5

claims.claim: Both the diversity check and the adaptive stop matter.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o TMDB CP 88 → 84 without diversity, → 80 without adaptive stop. Table 2, Table 5

claims.claim: Revised docs also improve tool retrieval and read better to humans.
claims.evidence: BM25 NDCG@1 on TMDB 24.0 → 29.0 (Table 3); human raters prefer DRAFT docs for completeness 68% vs 4% on ToolBench (Table 4)

discussion.limits_src: The paper has no limitations section.
reading: The memory is built offline, once per API, before testing; there is no update from test episodes, so this is documentation refinement rather than memory that grows with use.
The released DRAFT docs contain a per-API usage example absent from the original docs and not produced by DRAFT.py; its contribution is not measured.
Win% is a ChatGPT pairwise judgement against ReAct, so ReAct is 50 by construction; CP% only checks that the gold API path appears as a subsequence of the calls made.
Test sets are small: the released files hold 100 ToolBench G3 queries, 100 TMDB and 57 Spotify queries, so one query moves CP by 1 to 1.75 points.
Refinement uses GPT-4o, and GPT-4o also scores best as the agent; the gains for the other two models test transfer of GPT-4o-written docs.

abstract.text: DRAFT argues that human-written tool documentation is often incomplete, redundant or wrong for LLMs, and that an LLM can fix it by using the tool. For each API it runs a loop in which an explorer invents a query and calls the tool, an analyzer points out where the doc disagrees with what happened, and a rewriter produces a new doc. A similarity check keeps the explored queries diverse, and a stopping rule ends the loop when the doc stops changing. On ToolBench and RestBench the revised docs raise tool-use accuracy for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3-70B.

paper.title: "My agent understands me better": Integrating Dynamic Human-like Memory Recall and Consolidation in LLM-Based Agents

construction.unit: event: a short statement about the user (e.g. "User stayed at home") with its time
construction.kept_as: short event sentences derived from the chat history; how they are generated is not described

management.operations: on each recall the event's decay slows: g_n = g_(n-1) + S(t), S(t) = (1 - e^-t)/(1 + e^-t)
management.forgetting: none by design: recall probability decays with time but never reaches zero

retrieval.query: the user's current message
retrieval.candidates: Qdrant vector search over events
retrieval.selection: recall probability p_n(t) from cosine relevance r, elapsed time t and strength g_n; recall when p exceeds k = 0.86
retrieval.budget: one past dialogue history / event added to the prompt

use.reasoning: single GPT-4-0613 reply

classify.note: Selection is a fixed formula plus a threshold (p > 0.86), with one event passed on; the only update is the recall-strength counter g of a recalled event. How events are written is not described.

stages.ingestion: Chat turns are kept in a Firestore chat history; an EventHandler builds chat events from past dialogue (the paper gives no prompt or rule for this).
stages.construction: Each event is a short sentence about the user (e.g. "User went to the university today") stored in Qdrant with its time and a recall strength g that starts at 1.
stages.organization: One flat vector collection of events alongside the raw chat history.
stages.update: When an event is recalled, its g grows by S(t) = (1 - e^-t)/(1 + e^-t), which is larger for longer gaps since the last recall, so the event decays more slowly afterwards; nothing is deleted.
stages.retrieval: The user's message is embedded; each candidate event gets p_n(t) = (1 - exp(-r e^(-t/g_n)))/(1 - e^-1) with r the cosine similarity and t the elapsed time, and is recalled when p exceeds 0.86.
stages.answer: GPT-4-0613 answers with a persona prompt, a system prompt holding the current time and the user's schedule, and a single recalled past dialogue.

systems.summary: Dialogue-agent memory that recalls a past event only when a cognitive-psychology recall probability (relevance x time decay, slowed by each spaced recall) passes a threshold, instead of summing recency, importance and relevance scores.
systems.notes: Venue: CHI 2024 Late-Breaking Work, published in the Extended Abstracts (CHI EA '24, Honolulu, 7 pages, DOI 10.1145/3613905.3650839; ACM reference in the PDF and dx.doi.org page). Track set to 'short' (extended abstract), not 'main'. Text read from arXiv v1. No code link in the paper and none found by web search; everything here is from the 7-page paper. Construction details (how events are generated, embedding model, time units) are not given, so those design fields are null. The per-task losses come from the bar labels of Fig. 3-A.

sources.code_note: No official code: the paper gives no repository link, and a web search found only unrelated projects. Everything is taken from the paper; the implementation of event generation, the embedding model and the time units of t cannot be checked.

headline: The recall score is a formula, not a learned or prompted choice: cosine relevance decayed by elapsed time, with slower decay for events recalled at long intervals.
Only one past event or dialogue enters the prompt, and only when its recall probability passes 0.86.
The evaluation is 10 hand-built recall tasks with 4 candidate events each, scored against Generative Agents' scoring rule; no public benchmark is used.

components.model: Qdrant vector search (embedding model not stated)

discussion.takeaway: Replacing a weighted recency/importance/relevance score with a recall-probability model in which spaced recalls slow forgetting picks the expected event in 9 of 10 small hand-built tasks where Generative Agents' scoring picks 1.

claims.claim: Lower recall loss than Generative Agents' scoring.
claims.evidence: Loss lower on all 10 tasks (e.g. 0.200 vs 0.500 on task 1); paired t = -5.687, p = 0.000299, 95% CI of the difference [-0.27, -0.12]. Fig. 3, §4.2

claims.claim: The agent's replies reflect recalled user habits and preferences.
claims.evidence: Two dialogue examples from the user study (ice cream reward, Hawaii paper deadline). Tables 3-4, §4.3.1

claims.claim: Keeps prompts short.
claims.evidence: Only one past dialogue is added to the prompt. §5

limits: Relies on long-term behaviour patterns, so it adapts poorly when the user's habits change (e.g. Task 0, where both models fail).
Needs a larger, high-quality dataset; the combination of relevance, time and frequency is not tuned.
Storage and compute costs of the database interaction are not studied.
Evaluated on specific domains and tasks only.
reading: The quantitative test is 10 tasks built from the authors' own conversation logs, each asking which of 4 events should be recalled; the loss compares softmax-normalised scores with a one-hot label, not answer quality.
The comparison changes only the scoring rule: Generative Agents' recency, importance and relevance scores are recomputed on the same events, with importance values (2-7) whose source is not stated.
The threshold 0.86 is set by trial, and scores below it are still counted as recalls in the examples, so the trigger itself is not evaluated.
The time unit inside Eq. 8 is not stated, and the reported scores do not follow Eq. 8 with t in any single unit we tried.
No code, embedding model or event-generation prompt is given, and the user study reports two example dialogues and no measured outcome.

abstract.text: The paper gives an LLM dialogue agent a memory modelled on human cued recall and consolidation. Past events about the user are kept in a vector database with their time, and a recall probability built from cosine relevance and elapsed time decides whether an event is brought back. Each recall slows the event's future decay, more so when recalls are spaced out, and memories never fully disappear. On 10 small recall tasks the model has lower loss than Generative Agents' scoring, and a short user study shows replies that use recalled preferences.

systems.name: Early Experience

paper.title: Agent Learning via Early Experience

construction.unit: one training example built from the agent's own step off an expert state: (state, alternative action) → observed next state (IWM), or state → reflection + expert action (SR)
construction.kept_as: IWM: next-state text as observed (summarised by the model on WebShop, SearchQA and WebArena); SR: LLM-written reflection plus the expert action
construction.processing: at each expert state the initial policy proposes K non-expert actions (or they are sampled from the admissible list); each is executed and its next state recorded; for SR an LLM compares expert and alternative outcomes and explains the expert choice
construction.writer: SFT of the policy LLM (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B; LoRA for 70B); reflections written by the same policy model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for all models on TravelPlanner)

organization.structure: parametric: everything is trained into the policy's weights; no external store
organization.stores: rollout set D_rollout and reflection set D_refl exist only as training data

management.operations: IWM: one epoch of next-state prediction, then imitation on expert data with the remaining step budget; SR: reflection data mixed with expert data in one SFT run
management.conflicts: SR drops reflections whose concluded action is not the expert action (BFCLv3, WebArena); Tau-Bench drops a few 'low-quality' reflections without saying by what test

retrieval.candidates: no retrieval: the policy reads only the current state

use.context: current task and state only; learned dynamics and reflections act through the weights
use.reasoning: one action per step; SR-trained models write a reflection before the action

classify.note: Parametric memory: the agent's own off-expert experience is distilled into the policy by SFT before deployment, and nothing is stored or looked up at test time. 'Consolidate' stands for this offline distillation.

stages.ingestion: Starts from expert demonstrations split into (state, expert action) pairs, 1,395 to 21,031 per environment (App. C).
stages.construction: At each expert state the initial policy proposes K alternative actions (or they are drawn from the admissible list); each is executed and the resulting next state is recorded as (state, action, next state). For SR, an LLM is shown the expert action, its outcome and the alternatives with their outcomes, and writes a reflection explaining the expert choice.
stages.answer: The fine-tuned policy acts from the current state alone; an SR-trained policy writes its reasoning, then the action.
stages.learning: IWM trains next-state prediction for one epoch, then imitation on expert data within the same step budget as the IL baseline; SR trains on reflection + expert action mixed with expert data. Checkpoints can then start GRPO where a reward exists.

systems.summary: Turns the agent's own non-expert actions at expert states into reward-free supervision (predicting the next state, or reflecting on why the expert action was better) and trains it into the policy, as a bridge between imitation learning and RL.
systems.notes: VENUE: ICML 2026 main (the PDF v3 carries the PMLR 306 ICML header; OpenReview N3dXUHY5dD lists 'ICML 2026 regular'). CODE: the paper links no code. OSU-NLP-Group/EarlyExperience (author group, created 2026-06, after the paper) ships only method notes, per-env READMEs and a Hugging Face dataset, with a unified training setup and different numbers; it is recorded as a data/notes release, not the evaluation code. MEMORY FRAMING: there is no retrieval-time memory; the 'memory' is the agent's own interaction experience written into the weights. RESULTS: Table 1 'SearchQA (F1)' equals the Musique column of Table 7, so those rows are stored under musique. Table 7 also covers Gemma-3-4B, which is absent from Table 1.

sources.code_note: No code is linked in the paper. The authors' group later released method notes, per-environment READMEs and SFT data (commit 3810f05e, 2026-07-08). The repo contains no training or evaluation code, uses a unified training setup, and its README reports numbers that differ from the paper, so every mechanism detail below comes from the paper.

headline: No reward is used: the only new signal is the next state the environment returns after the agent's own non-expert action.
Nothing is retrieved at test time. The experience reaches the agent only through SFT of its weights.
IWM does not add training steps: one epoch of next-state prediction comes out of the imitation budget.

discussion.takeaway: An agent can learn from the outcomes of its own non-expert actions without any reward, either by predicting those outcomes or by explaining why the expert's choice was better. Both beat imitation learning in all eight environments and give a better starting point for RL.

claims.claim: Early experience improves over imitation learning in every setting.
claims.evidence: Table 1: 8 benchmarks × 3 models; IWM +0.9 to +18.4, SR +0.6 to +15.0 points over IL (§5.2).

claims.claim: It helps out of domain.
claims.evidence: Table 2: ALFWorld OOD IWM +14.8 (Llama-3.1-8B); BFCLv3 OOD SR +8.5 (3B); SearchQA OOD +2.2 to +4.9 (§5.3).

claims.claim: It is a better starting point for RL.
claims.evidence: Fig. 3, Tables 4, 5, 7: after identical GRPO, e.g. ALFWorld 99.2 (SR) vs 92.2 (IL) for 3B; WebShop 92.2 (IWM) vs 82.0 (IL) (§5.4).

claims.claim: It saves demonstrations.
claims.evidence: WebShop with 1/8 and ALFWorld with 1/2 of the demonstrations already beat IL on all of them (Fig. 4a, §6.1).

claims.claim: Grounded reflections beat ungrounded ones and preference training.
claims.evidence: Table 3: STaR-style rationales drop WebShop from 47.3 to 25.0; DPO reaches 53.1 but collapses; IWM 58.6, SR 58.2 (§6.3).

limits: The paper has no limitations section; the impact statement notes that needing less data also lowers the barrier to training agents for malicious use.
Open action spaces (free-form search queries in SearchQA, fine-grained web actions in WebArena) are named the hardest regime (§5.2).
reading: Table 1's 'SearchQA (F1)' numbers are the Musique column of Table 7, while Figure 3 uses the four-dataset average; the two are different measures under one name.
Table 2's SearchQA OOD values are not the mean of the other three Table 7 columns, and the paper does not say how they are formed.

Expert data differ by environment: optimal walkthroughs (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), human or leaderboard-agent trajectories (WebShop, WebArena), and LLM-synthesised trajectories filtered by success (Tau-Bench, SearchQA, BFCLv3, TravelPlanner).

The number of alternatives, how they are drawn (policy samples vs uniform from the admissible list) and whether next states are summarised all change per environment, so the effect of each choice is only tested for K (Fig. 4b, two environments).
SR on TravelPlanner uses reflections written by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for all three trained models, so the 3B and Qwen results there are partly distillation from a different model.
Absolute scores stay low on WebArena-Lite: at most 8.5% success for the 3B-8B models, so gains of 1.2-3.6 points there rest on a 165-task set.

abstract.text: Most language agents are trained by imitating expert demonstrations, which cover few situations, while RL needs rewards that many environments do not provide. This paper proposes 'early experience': at states from expert trajectories the agent tries its own alternative actions and records what happens, using those future states as supervision with no reward. Two methods use this data: implicit world modeling, which trains the policy to predict next states, and self-reflection, which trains it to explain why the expert action beats the alternatives before acting. Across eight environments and several model families both improve over imitation learning, generalise better out of domain, and give stronger starting points for later RL.

paper.title: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs

construction.unit: event: the per-layer KV cache of 8-128 consecutive tokens plus one representative key
construction.kept_as: the model's own key-value pairs for the tokens; nothing is rewritten
construction.processing: a token whose surprise (-log p) exceeds mean + γ·std of the preceding 4,096 tokens opens a new event; optional refinement moves each boundary to maximise modularity (or minimise conductance) of the key-similarity graph
construction.writer: fixed rule over the base LLM's own token probabilities and attention keys (no extra model)

organization.structure: flat, time-ordered list of events, one store per layer
organization.stores: 128 initial tokens and a 4,096-token local window stay in context; events live in a KV store offloaded to CPU memory or disk, with representative keys kept for search
organization.index: one representative key per event and layer: mean of the keys of the 4 tokens with the highest accumulated attention

management.operations: append only; least-recently-used events are offloaded between GPU, CPU and disk

retrieval.query: mean attention query of the current 512-token chunk, per layer
retrieval.candidates: every event, ranked by dot product between the query and its representative key
retrieval.selection: take events in rank order until the token budget is filled (similarity buffer); +C variants reserve 30% for the ±1 neighbours of retrieved events, kept in a queue (contiguity buffer)
retrieval.budget: n_mem retrieved tokens: 2K (Mistral), 4K (LLaMA-3/3.1), 3K (Phi-3/3.5)

use.context: each layer attends to 128 initial tokens + its retrieved events (original order, one fixed position) + the local window
use.reasoning: ordinary decoding; retrieval is repeated for every 512-token chunk and every layer

classify.note: Events are a flat, time-ordered list; the contiguity buffer only adds temporal neighbours of what similarity already picked.

stages.ingestion: The input is fed in 512-token chunks; the first 128 tokens and the latest 4,096 tokens (1,024 for Phi) always stay in context, and older tokens become memory.
stages.construction: Tokens whose surprise exceeds a moving threshold (mean + γ·std over the preceding window) start a new event; events are clipped to 8-128 tokens, and an optional refinement shifts each boundary to improve modularity or conductance of the key-similarity graph.
stages.organization: Each layer keeps the events' key-value cache plus one representative key per event (mean of the 4 most-attended keys); boundaries are shared by all layers.
stages.update: Events are only appended; the KV cache is moved between GPU, CPU and disk by least-recent use.
stages.retrieval: For each chunk and layer, the mean query is compared by dot product with every representative key, and top events fill the token budget; +C variants also enqueue the neighbouring event on each side of retrieved ones (contiguity buffer, 30% of the budget).
stages.answer: The layer's softmax attention runs over initial tokens, retrieved events in original order at one fixed position, and the local window.

systems.summary: Training-free KV-cache memory that cuts the token stream into events at points of high LLM surprise (optionally refined by graph modularity) and retrieves whole events per layer by similarity plus their temporal neighbours.
systems.notes:
Long-context architecture, not an agent memory: memory is the base LLM's own KV cache grouped into events; evaluated on LongBench, ∞-Bench and extended passkey retrieval, extending InfLLM (fixed-size blocks) with surprise-based event boundaries.

abstract.text: EM-LLM gives a pretrained LLM an episodic memory without any fine-tuning. It splits the past token stream into events where the model is most surprised by the next token, can refine those boundaries with graph-clustering scores on attention keys, and at every step retrieves whole events per layer by similarity together with their temporal neighbours. On LongBench and ∞-Bench it improves on InfLLM across five base models, beats RAG and, on most tasks, full-context attention, and retrieves a passkey from 10M tokens. Its event boundaries also align with those that people report in podcast transcripts.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Memory is the model's own KV cache: nothing is summarised or rewritten, only grouped into events and fetched back.
Event boundaries come from the LLM's surprise; retrieval is per layer and per 512-token chunk, not once per question.
The released configs run the surprise-only variant; refinement and the contiguity buffer are flags.

key_numbers.label: Boundary threshold
key_numbers.value: mean + γ·std of surprise, γ = 1 (2 for LLaMA-3)

components.model: the base LLM's own next-token probabilities (surprise)
modularity or conductance over key dot products
dot product of mean chunk query with representative keys, per layer

discussion.takeaway: Grouping a frozen LLM's KV cache into surprise-defined events and fetching whole events per layer is a cheap, training-free way to extend context. It beats fixed-size blocks (InfLLM) on most tasks and, with LLaMA-3.1-8B, beats both RAG and full-context attention on LongBench.

claims.claim: EM-LLM improves on InfLLM across base models.
claims.evidence: LongBench avg 43.7 vs 41.9 (Mistral), 51.3 vs 51.1 (LLaMA-3.1), 35.4 vs 34.5 (Phi-3); significant at benchmark level except Phi-3.5 (p = 0.23). Table 1, App. A.1

claims.claim: It beats RAG and full context.
claims.evidence: LLaMA-3.1-8B LongBench 51.58 vs 39.30 full context and 36.44 RAG (NV-Embed-v2); ∞-Bench 66.66 vs 66.33 and 58.97. Table 9, Fig. 1

claims.claim: It scales to 10M tokens.
claims.evidence: 100% on extended Passkey.Retrieval up to 10.2M tokens. §4.1, Fig. 1

claims.claim: Surprise-based events match human event boundaries and group similar keys.
claims.evidence: Surprise methods are closest to human podcast annotations (Fig. 4B) and score higher modularity and intra/inter similarity than fixed blocks on PG-19 (Table 2).

claims.claim: Refinement and contiguity each help.
claims.evidence: Refinement is best in 60% of tasks, the contiguity buffer in 44%. §4.4, Tables 3-7

limits: Memory is non-parametric storage of key-value pairs, unlike synaptic change in the brain.
No nested, hierarchical event structure.
Text only in the current implementation; no multi-modal episodes.
No consolidation of memories over time.
The authors claim an episodic-memory-inspired method, not evidence that the model uses it like human episodic memory.
reading: Gains over InfLLM are small on LongBench for LLaMA-3 and LLaMA-3.1 (+0.2 each in Table 1), and for LLaMA-3 the ∞-Bench average is lower than InfLLM's (48.81-49.00 vs 50.31 across variants, Table 4).
Table 1 shows a different best variant per model, and no variant wins everywhere (Tables 3-7), so which component helps depends on model and task.

Full context scores 100 on PassageRetrieval and leads on several QA tasks, but gets 4.5 on TREC, 8.68 on SAMSum, 19.30 on LCC and 18.33 on RepoBench-P (Table 9); the 12-point LongBench average gap comes mostly from these few tasks.
In the released code the refinement graph is one matrix summed over layers ≥ 20 and all heads, and the same boundaries serve every layer, while the paper describes per-head key similarity.
Retrieval is per layer and per 512-token chunk, so it is not comparable to question-time retrieval in agent memory systems.

systems.name: EMG-RAG

paper.title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs

construction.unit: first-person memory sentence, attached to the entity nodes it mentions
construction.kept_as: LLM-standardized statements from assistant chats and OCR'd app screenshots
construction.processing: assistant filters raw data (auto-classification or user asks to remember); GPT-4 rewrites it as memory sentences with absolute dates and resolved coreference; entity recognition and relation extraction add graph nodes and edges
construction.writer: GPT-4

organization.structure: three layers: 4 memory types -> subclasses (tree) -> entity-relation memory graph
organization.stores: one Editable Memory Graph per user, kept on the device
organization.index: CPT-Text embeddings of memories and questions (Faiss); TransE embeddings of entities, relations and subclasses

management.operations: insert, delete (time-limited memories) or replace, chosen by comparing a new memory with the top-1 memory in its nearest subclass
management.conflicts: replacement rewrites the entity nodes of an existing relation (e.g. a changed departure time)
management.forgetting: deletion of memories valid only until a date (e.g. an expiring voucher)

retrieval.query: question; its entity and relation are extracted for the policy state (method not stated)
retrieval.candidates: top-K=3 memories by embedding similarity activate graph nodes; depth-first walk from each
retrieval.selection: RL policy (2-layer MLP) decides per visited memory: include and go deeper, or stop the branch
retrieval.budget: no fixed number of memories; K=3 start nodes

use.context: question concatenated with the selected memories
use.reasoning: single call to a frozen LLM

classify.note: Structure is a type/subclass tree over an entity graph; retrieval walks the graph, so 'graph'. The set is fixed by a small learned policy (not an LLM, not top-k); 'reranker' is the closest option.

stages.ingestion: Chats with a phone assistant and OCR text of app screenshots; the assistant keeps items it classifies as memorable or that the user asks it to remember.
stages.construction: GPT-4 turns the filtered raw data into standardized first-person memory sentences, with absolute dates and coreference resolved.
stages.organization: Each user gets an Editable Memory Graph: 4 memory types, their subclasses as a tree, and below them an entity graph built by entity and relation extraction; TransE places each entity under its nearest subclass.
stages.update: A new memory is placed in its nearest subclass and compared with the top-1 memory there, then inserted, deleted (time-limited) or used to replace entity nodes.
stages.retrieval: The top-3 memories for the question activate graph nodes; a depth-first walk starts from each, and an RL policy decides at every node whether to include its memory and continue or stop.
stages.answer: A frozen LLM (GPT-4, ChatGLM3-6B or PanGu-38B) answers from the question plus the selected memories.
stages.learning: Only the selection policy is trained: supervised warm start on GPT-4-labelled required memories, then REINFORCE with the change in ROUGE/BLEU of the answer as reward; online fine-tuning on real user questions after deployment.

systems.summary: Organizes a phone user's memories as an editable type/subclass tree over an entity graph and trains a small RL policy to walk the graph and choose which memories to give a frozen LLM, instead of a fixed top-K.
systems.notes:
Venue verified: EMNLP 2024 main, ACL Anthology 2024.emnlp-main.281; arXiv comment 'accepted by EMNLP 2024'. No code: the paper gives no repository and the anthology page lists none; the dataset is a proprietary Huawei assistant dataset. Paper read from arXiv v1 PDF.
DESIGN: §4.1-4.4, §5.1, App. A. control.management = fixed-rule is a best reading: the paper says edits follow from comparing relations of the new and top-1 memories but not who makes the comparison. learning = mixed (supervised warm start + REINFORCE).

sources.code_note: No official code found: none linked in the paper or on the ACL Anthology page, and a GitHub search for EMG-RAG finds only unrelated projects. Everything here is from the paper.

headline: The memory set is chosen by a tiny RL policy walking a user's memory graph, not by top-K; the LLM stays frozen.
Evaluation data, questions and reference answers are all generated by GPT-4 from a proprietary Huawei dataset, and there is no code.

units.name: Memory
units.role: one standardized fact or event about the user
units.made_by: GPT-4 from filtered chats and screenshots

fields.name: memory sentence
fields.what: first-person statement, dates made absolute, coreference resolved

fields.name: embedding
fields.what: CPT-Text vector; also used for subclass partition centres (mean of memory embeddings)

units.name: Entity node and relation edge
units.role: memory graph layer; each in-degree node carries its memory
units.made_by: entity recognition and relation extraction (models not named)

fields.name: entity / relation
fields.what: e.g. Boss -BookFlight-> EK349 -DepartAt-> 01:40; TransE embeddings

units.name: Type and subclass
units.role: tree over the graph: Relationship, Preference, Event, Attribute and their subclasses
units.made_by: fixed by the designers (Table 8)

fields.name: subclass
fields.what: e.g. Colleague, Arrangement, Diet preference; entities assigned by TransE nearness

write.how: assistant keeps chat items it classifies as memorable (Active Remember) or that the user asks to keep (Passive Remember); screenshots go through OCR
GPT-4 rewrites raw data into memory sentences; date conversion, anaphora and event coreference resolution
write.out: ~11.35B raw texts -> ~0.35B memories

write.how: entity recognition for nodes, relation extraction for edges; TransE assigns entities to the closest subclass
embed new memory, find nearest subclass, retrieve top-1 memory in it, then insert, delete or replace by comparing relations

read.how: CPT-Text similarity; nodes of the top memories are activated

depth-first search from each activated node; at each node the policy sees 3 cosine similarities (question entity vs node, question relation vs edge, question vs memory) and outputs include-and-continue or stop
frozen LLM generates the answer

answer_context.sees: the question and the memory sentences the policy selected
answer_context.format: not given beyond concatenation Q ⊕ M

compression.what: answer context vs all user memories
compression.basis: Not reported: the paper gives no counts of selected memories or tokens. Users hold roughly 72-296 new memories per day (App. A.3).

open_questions: Reference answers and 'required memories' come from GPT-4, and GPT-4 is also the answer model; the reward and the metric both favour matching GPT-4's wording.
No run separates the graph (editing, structure) from the learned selector: M-RAG differs in both.

glance.a: A first-person sentence GPT-4 writes from chats or screenshots, tied to entity nodes in a graph.
4 types -> subclasses (a tree) -> an entity-relation graph, one per user.
Yes: insert, delete time-limited memories, or replace entity nodes of an existing relation.
No reranker; a learned RL policy walks the graph from the top-3 matches and decides which memories to include.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: The question plus the selected memory sentences; the LLM is frozen.

text: The question's 3 closest memories activate graph nodes, and a depth-first walk starts from each; at every node an RL policy decides to include the memory and go on, or stop.
The selected memories go with the question to a frozen LLM; only the small policy is trained, with answer ROUGE/BLEU gains as reward.

discussion.takeaway: Personal-assistant memory needs editing and multi-memory selection; an editable type/subclass/entity graph plus a small RL selector beats fixed top-K RAG on the authors' own assistant data.

claims.claim: EMG-RAG beats all baselines on question answering.
It also helps autofill and user services.
claims.evidence: EM 92.86 autofill, 96.43 reminder, 91.46 travel vs M-RAG 90.87, 93.75, 86.67. Table 2

claims.claim: Editability keeps it ahead as memories change.
claims.evidence: About 10.6% (QA), 9.5% (AF), 9.7% (US) over M-RAG across 4 weeks of edits. Table 3

claims.claim: The policy gradient stage matters most.
claims.evidence: R-1 93.46 -> 90.59 without PG, 92.95 without WS. Table 4

claims.claim: Online fine-tuning on real questions fixes the cold start.
claims.evidence: One-month A/B test: QA 88.06 -> 91.99 (+4.5%). Table 6

limits: Training is no cheaper than naive RAG because the LLM must be queried during training to obtain rewards.
reading: The ~10% headline comes from the continuous-edit test (Table 3); in the main QA table the ROUGE-L gain over M-RAG is 3.9% (88.06 vs 84.74).
Questions, reference answers and required-memory labels are generated by GPT-4, and GPT-4 is the main answer model, so scores partly measure agreement with GPT-4.
The data is proprietary and there is no code, so no number can be reproduced.
M-RAG is run without its Agent-R, and all baselines are the authors' reimplementations.
The policy sees only three cosine similarities per node, not the memory text; §5.1 sets a 0.99 discount while Eq. 4 assumes no discounting.
The paper does not report how many memories are selected per question or the answer context size.

abstract.text: The paper defines the task of building personalized agents from the memories a user leaves on a smartphone assistant. EMG-RAG turns chats and screenshot text into memory sentences with GPT-4 and stores them in an Editable Memory Graph: a tree of memory types and subclasses over an entity graph that supports insertion, deletion and replacement. To answer, a reinforcement-learning policy walks the graph from the question's best matches and chooses which memories a frozen LLM receives. On the authors' real-world assistant data it improves question answering, form autofill and user services over existing RAG methods by about 10%, and it was deployed in a product assistant.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: EventMemAgent

paper.title: EventMemAgent: Hierarchical Event-Centric Memory for Online Video Understanding with Adaptive Tool Use

construction.unit: video event: frames in short-term memory; first frame + caption + embedding + change log in long-term memory
construction.kept_as: raw frames (STM, reservoir-sampled) and an MLLM caption of each archived event
construction.processing: 1 fps frames; cut an event when the gray-histogram correlation with the event falls below 0.2 (after 8 frames); on eviction a 4B VLM captions the event and describes the change from the previous event
construction.writer: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (frozen captioner); Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B

organization.structure: two tiers: short-term buffer of up to 32 frames grouped into events; long-term list of event records linked by change logs
organization.stores: STM frame buffer; LTM event list
organization.index: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B vectors of captions; event time ranges

management.operations: FIFO: when STM exceeds 32 frames the oldest event moves to LTM; a single event filling STM is thinned by reservoir sampling
management.forgetting: reservoir sampling drops frames of a long event before captioning; LTM keeps every archived event

retrieval.query: agent-written text query or time range, via tool calls
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity of query to caption embeddings (text mode) or overlap with a time range (time mode)
retrieval.selection: top 3 events, similarity ≥ 0.3 (text mode); agent decides whether and how often to search
retrieval.budget: 3 events per search; up to 10 agent turns in the evaluation scripts

use.context: all STM frames (≤ 32, labelled with frame number and time) + returned event captions, change logs and first frames + OCR/detection outputs
use.reasoning: ReAct loop of the RL-trained agent; answer in \boxed{}

classify.note: The agent chooses when and what to search, but each search returns a fixed top 3 by similarity (or time overlap).

stages.ingestion: The stream is sampled at 1 fps; each frame is compared with the current event by the Pearson correlation of gray-level histograms and starts a new event when it falls below 0.2, once the event has at least 8 frames.
stages.construction: When an event leaves short-term memory, Qwen3-VL-4B writes a one-paragraph caption from up to 32 of its frames, the caption is embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, and a change log sentence is generated from the first frames of this and the previous event.
stages.organization: Short-term memory holds at most 32 frames grouped into events and is shown to the agent in full; long-term memory is an ordered list of event records (first frame, time range, caption, embedding, change from previous / to next).
stages.update: When the buffer is full the oldest event moves to long-term memory (FIFO); if one event alone fills it, new frames replace random ones with probability 32/n (reservoir sampling).
stages.retrieval: The agent calls search_memory with a text query (cosine to caption embeddings, top 3 with similarity ≥ 0.3) or a time range (top 3 by overlap); it can also run OCR or object detection on an event's first frame or an STM frame.
stages.answer: Qwen3-VL-8B reasons over the STM frames and tool observations in a ReAct loop and answers in \boxed{}.
stages.learning: The agent's reasoning and tool use are trained end to end with GRPO (group size 8, KL 0) on 10K MovieChat samples with a 0/1 answer-correctness reward; memory construction is not trained.

systems.summary: Online video agent whose memory has two tiers: a 32-frame buffer segmented into events by histogram change (with reservoir sampling), and a long-term list of captioned events with change logs that an RL-trained MLLM agent searches and inspects with OCR and detection tools.
systems.notes: Video memory, not dialogue: the 'turns' are 1 fps frames. Paper v2 (11 Sep 2026) read from the arXiv PDF; LNCS-style template, no venue stated, so recorded as a preprint. Code checked at commit 203e635b (8 Sep 2026), the release of training, inference and evaluation code. Benchmark scoring: OVO-Bench overall = mean of the three category averages (e.g. (68.29+58.03+55.92)/3 = 60.75); StreamingBench ALL is weighted accuracy per docs/EVALUATION.md.

discussion.takeaway: Keep a small event-segmented frame buffer, archive older events as captioned records, and train the MLLM with RL to decide when to search them or zoom in with OCR and detection. With at most 32 frames in context it beats the other open-source models on OVO-Bench and is competitive on StreamingBench.

claims.claim: Best open-source result on OVO-Bench, above GPT-4o.
claims.evidence: 60.75 overall vs 59.54 GPT-4o and 55.81 Qwen3-VL-8B with 64 frames. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Competitive on StreamingBench real-time tasks with ≤ 32 frames.
claims.evidence: 77.00 vs 77.26 StreamForest and 75.69 Gemini 1.5 Pro. Table 2

claims.claim: Event memory beats fixed-length memory.
claims.evidence: 58.27 → 60.75 on OVO-Bench and 75.09 → 77.00 on StreamingBench. Table 3

claims.claim: Perception tools add fine-grained evidence.
claims.evidence: Without detection 57.80, without OCR 58.98, vs 60.75. Table 4

claims.claim: Agentic RL is needed to use memory and tools.
claims.evidence: Untrained agent 56.16 / 68.44 vs 60.75 / 77.00; Backward Tracing 46.18 (base) → 56.33 (untrained) → 58.03. Table 6, App. C

claims.claim: Latency stays flat as the video grows.
claims.evidence: Median 1.78 s up to 30 min; tools 1.6% of latency. Fig. 4, §4.3

limits: StreamingBench mostly rewards perception of current frames, so the long-term memory is not fully exercised there (stated as a caveat, §4.2).
reading: Only captions are embedded; change logs and first frames come back with a hit but never decide which events are found.
A long event is captioned from at most 32 frames that survived reservoir sampling (e.g. Event 11 in Fig. 9 spans 228-431 s from 32 frames).
The change log is written from two first frames, so it describes how the openings of consecutive events differ, not what happened within them.
Baselines use different frame budgets (64 frames or 1 fps) and the paper does not say whether their numbers were rerun or taken from earlier reports.
No row removes long-term memory while keeping the trained agent, so memory's own contribution is not isolated; the fixed-length ablation keeps a long-term memory.
Base and fine-tuned models differ in training as well as memory: EventMemAgent is Qwen3-VL-8B after GRPO on MovieChat, while the Qwen3-VL row is the untrained model.

abstract.text: EventMemAgent targets online video question answering, where an unbounded stream must fit a fixed MLLM context. It keeps a short-term buffer of recent frames split into events by visual change and thinned by reservoir sampling, and moves older events into a long-term store as captioned, searchable records with change logs. An MLLM agent searches that store and applies OCR and object detection, and its reasoning and tool use are trained end to end with GRPO. The authors report strong results on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench with at most 32 input frames.

stages.ingestion: An LLM-prompted Semantic Boundary Detector runs over a sliding window of the dialogue stream and cuts it into episode histories at topic shifts.
stages.construction: Each episode history is rewritten into a third-person Episode narrative (coreferences resolved), from which the LLM derives Atomic Facts and time-bounded Foresight signals with validity intervals; these plus metadata form a MemCell.
stages.organization: MemCells are incrementally clustered into thematic MemScenes (embedding similarity to scene centroid above threshold tau, with a max time-gap constraint); a user profile of explicit facts and implicit traits sits alongside.
stages.update: When a MemCell joins a MemScene the scene summary is updated and the user profile is refreshed from scene summaries with recency-aware updates and conflict tracking.
stages.retrieval: Dense (Qwen3-Embedding-4B) + BM25 over Atomic Facts fused by RRF; MemScenes scored by max member relevance (top N=10), Episodes pooled and re-ranked (Qwen3-Reranker-4B, K=10); an LLM sufficiency check triggers query rewriting (2-3 follow-up queries) when context is insufficient.
stages.answer: Reasoning mode answers from retrieved Episodes only; Chat mode additionally adds the User Profile and time-valid Foresight.

systems.summary: Engram-inspired memory lifecycle: dialogue is segmented into MemCells (episode narrative, atomic facts, time-bounded foresight), clustered online into MemScenes with a user profile, and recalled via scene-guided agentic retrieval with a sufficiency check.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: selection is broader than 'Emb-4B + BM25 + Reranker-4B' - retrieval is scene-guided (MemScene scored by max MemCell relevance) and includes an LLM sufficiency verifier with query rewriting (second round triggered for 31.0% of LoCoMo questions, App. A.1). Dense+BM25 run over Atomic Facts, reranker over Episodes. Venue: ACL 2026 long paper (aclanthology 2026.acl-long.2125); ACL version gives code URL https://github.com/EverMind-AI/EverOS. Text read from the HF paper.md mirror of the arXiv paper (matches the ACL abstract).
DESIGN: Sec 3.2-3.5, 4.1, App. A.1, A.3, C.1. Corrected prefill: 'MemScene consolidation' moved from construction.processing to management.operations; retrieval selection split into candidates (Emb-4B+BM25) and selection (Reranker-4B + sufficiency check). Foresight expiry is a retrieval-time filter, not deletion, so forgetting=null. control.management=fixed-rule for threshold clustering (profile refresh itself is a prompted LLM).

flow.title: Find matching MemCells
flow.out: up to 100 MemCells, one ranked list

text: The question is matched against MemCells; the 10 scenes holding the best matches are opened and a cross-encoder reranker keeps 10 episodes.
If an LLM judges them not enough (31% of LoCoMo questions), it writes new queries, searches all MemCells and reranks again. The answer model always reads 10 episodes.

discussion.takeaway: Store memory as rewritten episodes grouped by theme, and read it with a rerank-then-check loop. In its own paper this gives the best LoCoMo and LongMemEval scores, with the largest gains on multi-hop and temporal questions.

claims.claim: Memory should be a lifecycle (form episodes, consolidate them into themes and a profile, reconstruct at question time), not a store of isolated records.
claims.evidence: §1, Conclusion

claims.claim: State of the art on memory-augmented reasoning.
claims.evidence: LoCoMo +9.2% (GPT-4.1-mini) and +7.0% (GPT-4o-mini) over Zep; LongMemEval +6.7% over MemOS. Table 1-2, §4.2

claims.claim: Grouping MemCells into scenes helps questions that need scattered evidence.
claims.evidence: LoCoMo multi-hop +19.7%, temporal +10.0%; LongMemEval knowledge update +20.6%. §4.2

claims.claim: Every part contributes.
claims.evidence: Without MemScene 89.16, without MemCell 81.82, full 93.05 on LoCoMo. Fig. 4

claims.claim: The consolidated user profile adds signal beyond episodes.
claims.evidence: PersonaMem-v2: 53.25 with profile vs 43.93 episodes only. Table 4, §4.5

limits: Tested on text conversations only.
LLM calls in construction and retrieval add latency and cost over single-pass baselines.
Current benchmarks cannot stress-test very long timelines.
reading: Scene summaries and the profile never reach the answer model in the scored runs, so the MemScene gain may come from widening the rerank pool rather than from narrative grouping; the ablation cannot tell these apart.
Round 2 (31% of questions) searches without scenes, and the paper's own trace example finds its answer there.
On LongMemEval a scene holds 1.36 MemCells on average, so the hierarchy is nearly flat.
Scene thresholds are set per dataset (0.70 and 7 days on LoCoMo, 0.50 and 30 days on LongMemEval).
Other papers report 85.5 to 94.5 for EverMemOS on LoCoMo; the answer model and judge differ, so the headline 93.05 is one setting.

abstract.text: EverMemOS treats long-term memory for LLM agents as a lifecycle rather than a pile of stored snippets. Dialogue is cut into topic segments and rewritten as MemCells (an episode, atomic facts and time-bounded plans), which are grouped into thematic MemScenes that also update a user profile. At question time the system opens the scenes that hold the best-matching MemCells, reranks their episodes, and searches again when an LLM judges the evidence insufficient. The authors report state-of-the-art results on LoCoMo, LongMemEval and PersonaMem-v2.

systems.name: EvolveR

paper.title: EvolveR: Self-Evolving LLM Agents through an Experience-Driven Lifecycle

construction.unit: principle: one-sentence guiding or cautionary advice + (subject, predicate, object) triples, with usage/success counts and links to up to 3 successful and 2 failed source trajectories
construction.kept_as: LLM-distilled advice; source trajectories kept verbatim in a separate store
construction.processing: the agent's own policy model distils each stored RL trajectory (question, golden answer and dialogue, cut at 4,096 characters) into a principle, with separate prompts for successes and failures
construction.writer: the policy model being trained (Qwen2.5-0.5B to 7B); GPT-4o-mini in the teacher-distill ablation

organization.structure: flat pool of principles
organization.stores: Milvus collections: principles (embedded) and trajectories (by id)
organization.index: BGE-M3 dense embedding of the principle description, cosine, FLAT index

management.operations: LLM pairwise dedup among new principles from the same question; match against top-3 existing (cosine >= 0.85, then LLM yes/no): link the trajectory to the match or add a new principle
management.forgetting: score = (successes+1)/(uses+2); principles below 0.3 deleted every 10 RL steps

retrieval.query: a query the agent writes inside <search_experience>, not the question itself
retrieval.candidates: dense cosine over principle descriptions
retrieval.selection: top-3 by similarity; duplicates and malformed principles dropped
retrieval.budget: 3 principles per call, character budget of 2,048 (max_obs_length)

use.context: type, metric score, description and triples of each principle, inside <experience> tags in the agent's own reasoning trace
use.reasoning: multi-turn think / search_experience / search_knowledge / answer loop, up to 10 turns; policy trained with GRPO to use it

classify.note: Consolidate (merge a new principle into a matching one) was chosen over evict; score-based pruning also runs. The agent decides when and with what text to search, but a fixed top-3 rule decides what comes back.

stages.ingestion: During GRPO training (8 rollouts per question), 2 of the 8 trajectories per question (1 success and 1 failure when possible) are buffered after each step.
stages.construction: After each RL step the frozen policy model distils each buffered trajectory into a principle: a one-sentence description plus structured triples, typed guiding (success) or cautionary (failure).
stages.organization: Principles form a flat pool in Milvus, indexed by a BGE-M3 embedding of the description; each keeps counters and links to up to 3 successful and 2 failed trajectory ids.
stages.update: New principles from the same question are deduplicated by pairwise LLM judgement; each survivor is compared with its top-3 neighbours (cosine >= 0.85, then LLM yes/no) and either linked to the match or added with score 0.5. Scores (successes+1)/(uses+2) are refreshed from trajectory outcomes, and principles under 0.3 are pruned every 10 steps.
stages.retrieval: The agent may emit <search_experience> with its own query at any turn; the top-3 principles by cosine are returned.
stages.answer: The agent reads the returned principles (type, score, description, triples) in <experience> tags, may also search Wikipedia, and answers in <answer> tags.
stages.learning: The policy is trained with GRPO on outcome (exact match) plus a 0.1-weighted format reward, after a cold-start SFT; retrieved experience and document tokens are masked from the loss.

systems.summary: The agent's own policy distils its RL trajectories into scored principles that it can search as a tool during rollouts, and GRPO trains it to use them; the principle pool is deduplicated, merged and pruned by success rate.
systems.notes: VENUE: ICML 2026 poster (icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/65641), listed there under the title 'From Interactions to Principles: Experience-Driven Self-Distillation for Evolving LLM Agents'; same authors, arXiv comment 'Accepted by ICML 2026'. Paper read: arXiv v3 (16 May 2026). CODE: the paper links github.com/Edaizi/EvolveR, which redirects to KnowledgeXLab/EvolveR; both give the same HEAD. RESULTS: all baseline numbers in Table 1 equal Search-R1 (2503.09516v5) Table 2; run_by left null because the paper does not say they were copied. DESIGN: 'offline' here means between RL steps; test-time evaluation in the code does not add trajectories, so the pool is frozen at test time.

open_questions: How much of the gain is RL versus memory? RL alone gives 0.325 and the full system 0.382 on 3B, but the memory-only (no RL) run is still 0.357 (Table 4); the baselines are not retrained with the same cold start.
The experience base is built from the NQ and HotpotQA training questions that are also in-domain test sets; the paper does not measure overlap between principles and test questions.
Scores rise with pool size up to 45k principles and then drop (Table 7), measured on a 10% validation subset while training continues, so pool size and training step are confounded.

discussion.takeaway: An agent can distil its own RL trajectories into short scored principles and learn, through RL, to search them; on seven QA benchmarks this beats the Search-R1 numbers it compares against at 3B and 7B.

claims.claim: EvolveR outperforms prompting, SFT and RL search-agent baselines.
claims.evidence: Average EM 0.382 (3B) vs 0.325 for Search-R1-instruct and 0.303 for Search-R1-base; 0.417 (7B) vs 0.385 for Search-R1-instruct. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Access to the experience base at test time matters.
claims.evidence: 3B drops from 0.382 to 0.340 without experience search; 1.5B from 0.270 to 0.123. Table 3, §5.2.2

claims.claim: Self-distillation beats a stronger external distiller at 3B.
claims.evidence: 0.382 self vs 0.370 with GPT-4o-mini at 3B, but GPT-4o-mini wins at 0.5B (0.220 vs 0.150) and 1.5B (0.290 vs 0.270). Table 2, §5.2.1

claims.claim: Scoring and pruning keep useful principles.
claims.evidence: In 100 hand-labelled principles, 82% of high-score ones are ideal vs 26% of low-score ones. Table 6, §5.3

claims.claim: The pool scales without collapse.
claims.evidence: Latency 0.20 s and EM 0.387 at 49,934 principles. Table 7

limits: Principle quality is bounded by the base model's ability to distil.
Only QA tasks were tested; embodied or creative tasks remain open.
Keeping a growing experience base efficient for lifelong agents is unsolved.
A self-evolving agent could learn undesirable strategies without a value-aligned reward.
reading: Every baseline number equals Search-R1's Table 2; the 7B block drops Search-R1-base (0.431 average), which is higher than EvolveR 7B (0.417) and higher on 5 of the 7 datasets.
The retrieval query is text the agent writes, not the question; in the paper's example it is a list of guessed triples.
Past trajectories are linked to principles but never shown to the agent in the released scripts; only the one-line principle, its triples, type and score are.
The agent sees each principle's success score, so the score acts both as a pruning rule and as a signal inside the prompt.
Only 2 of 8 rollouts per question are distilled, usually one success and one failure; since in-batch dedup compares principles from the same question and same type, it has few pairs to check.
The pruning threshold barely matters (0.265 to 0.276 average over 0.1 to 0.9 on 1.5B, Table 9), so the reported score-tier quality difference (Table 6) does not translate into accuracy there.
The code gives the distiller the golden answer along with the trajectory, which the paper does not mention.

abstract.text: EvolveR lets an LLM agent improve from its own experience in a closed loop. Between RL steps, the agent's own model turns its recent trajectories into short guiding or cautionary principles, which are deduplicated, merged with near-identical ones and scored by how often they led to correct answers. During rollouts the agent can search this pool as a tool alongside a Wikipedia search, and GRPO trains it to make use of what it retrieves. On seven question-answering benchmarks with Qwen2.5 models, the authors report higher exact match than prompting, SFT and RL search-agent baselines.

paper.title: Improving Factuality with Explicit Working Memory

construction.unit: memory unit: the KV cache of one M-token text chunk (a retrieved passage or fact-check evidence)
construction.kept_as: verbatim passages, stored as KV caches rather than text
construction.processing: at pauses, retrieved passages above a score threshold and evidence for unsupported claims are each encoded separately by the generator into KV caches with shared position ids
construction.writer: the generator LLM (Llama-3.1 70B/8B) encodes; Contriever retrieves; VeriScore's claim extractor and verifier supply evidence

organization.structure: k parallel memory units, kept separately for retrieval feedback and fact-check feedback
organization.stores: working memory of KV caches outside the prompt, prepended per layer
organization.index: none inside memory; external datastore searched with Contriever (C4 + Wikipedia, MassiveDS)

management.operations: new units replace old ones first in, first out; a sentence with unsupported claims is deleted and regenerated
management.conflicts: fact-check evidence for refuted claims enters memory before the sentence is rewritten
management.forgetting: FIFO eviction when a pool is full

retrieval.query: input question + the sentence being checked
retrieval.candidates: Contriever dense search over C4 + Wikipedia; Google snippets inside the fact-checker
retrieval.selection: passages whose retrieval score passes a threshold
retrieval.budget: k units × M tokens; the values used for the main table are not stated (sweeps: 1-50 units, 128-6,400 tokens)

use.context: each memory unit is concatenated with the context in a separate attention pass per layer, plus one context-only pass; outputs are averaged with weights from the attention normalisers
use.reasoning: sentence-by-sentence decoding with pauses, checks and backtracking

classify.note: Two FIFO pools (retrieval feedback, fact-check feedback) of KV-cache units; admission is a retrieval-score threshold rather than a fixed k.

stages.ingestion: Decoding pauses periodically (retrieval every Tr=1 and verification every Tv=8 timesteps in the main runs); a pause does nothing unless a new sentence is complete.
stages.construction: Passages retrieved with the question and the new sentence as query (score above a threshold) and, when VeriScore finds unsupported claims, the evidence passages are each encoded by the generator into a separate KV-cache unit of M tokens.
stages.organization: Units sit in a working memory outside the prompt, with retrieval feedback and fact-check feedback kept apart; all units share the same position ids.
stages.update: Pools are refreshed first in, first out; a sentence with false claims is removed and generation backs up to regenerate it with the new units.
stages.retrieval: Contriever over C4 + Wikipedia (MassiveDS), query = question + current sentence, filtered by a score threshold.
stages.answer: At every layer each unit is attended together with the context in parallel, plus a context-only pass, and the hidden vectors are averaged using the attention normalisers (Eq. 1).

systems.summary: Long-form generation with a working memory of KV-cached passages that is refreshed during decoding from retrieval and online fact-checking, with backtracking when a sentence is found false.

discussion.takeaway: Giving the generator a refreshable working memory of cached passages, fed by retrieval and an online fact-checker, raises factuality of long answers over RAG and iterative-retrieval baselines without making them less helpful.

claims.claim: Best factuality on all four datasets.
claims.evidence: VeriScore F1 with Llama-3.1-70B: 75.9 / 61.0 / 66.9 / 49.7 on LongFact / Fava / AlpacaFact / Biography vs best baseline 72.7 / 57.2 / 66.0 / 43.8. Table 1

claims.claim: Helpfulness is kept.
claims.evidence: AlpacaEval win rate vs the 70B base: 49.9-50.2 for EWE-70B, all other 70B methods 9.1-49.4. Table 1

claims.claim: Gains are smaller with the 8B model.
Too many or too short units hurt; unit length trades precision for recall.
claims.evidence: Fig. 3-4 on 50 LongFact prompts, §5.1

claims.claim: Passage feedback beats instruction-style feedback.
claims.evidence: F1 74.8 with both passage types vs 72.5 with instructions only. Table 4

claims.claim: The datastore matters and preferences differ by dataset.
claims.evidence: LongFact 67.9 Wiki / 70.8 C4 / 74.8 both; Biography 46.1 / 44.6 / 48.4. Table 3

limits: Only English fact-seeking prompts were tested.
Only textual feedback; multimodal feedback not explored.
Human evaluation is small.
reading: The fact-checker used during generation is VeriScore's own claim extractor and verifier, and the metric is VeriScore F1, so part of the gain may come from optimising against the evaluator; the human study (κ 0.65 vs 0.61 on 100 samples each) only checks that VeriScore still agrees with people.
Over plain RA the 70B gains are 3.2 / 4.2 / 0.9 / 5.9 F1; on AlpacaFact the gain is under one point.
Memory size (units, unit length) and the retrieval threshold for the main table are not reported; all sweeps use 50 LongFact prompts with the 70B model.
Even with no feedback text, pausing and regenerating flagged sentences reaches 73.0 F1 vs 72.5 for RA (Table 4), so the checker's trigger alone accounts for part of the effect.
Baselines use the same retriever and datastore, but Nest uses 100 candidate passages and RA 10; CoVe was adapted from a third-party implementation.
Biography has 181 prompts in §4.1 but 183 names in App. A.

abstract.text: EWE adds an explicit working memory to an LLM that writes long factual answers. The memory holds KV caches of passages; while generating, the model pauses, retrieves passages for the latest sentence, and runs a fact-checker whose evidence also enters memory. Sentences found false are deleted and rewritten with the refreshed memory. On four fact-seeking long-form datasets the method raises VeriScore by 2-6 points with Llama-3.1 without lowering AlpacaEval helpfulness, and the analysis points to memory update rules, unit configuration and datastore quality as the key factors.

systems.name: ExpeL

paper.title: ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners

construction.unit: two kinds: successful trajectories from training tasks, and short natural-language insights
construction.kept_as: trajectories stored as they ran; insights written by an LLM from many trajectories
construction.processing: ReAct + Reflexion (up to 3 retries) on training tasks fills an experience pool; GPT-4 then compares failed and successful attempts of the same task and groups of L successes, editing a list of insights
construction.writer: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 gathers trajectories; gpt-4-0613 writes insights

organization.structure: experience pool of trajectories + a ranked flat list of insights with importance counts
organization.stores: Faiss vector store of successful trajectories (keyed by task text); insight list
organization.index: all-mpnet-base-v2 embedding of the task text, kNN in Faiss

management.operations: insights: ADD / EDIT / UPVOTE / DOWNVOTE by the insight LLM (AGREE / REMOVE in code), with importance counts
management.conflicts: the LLM can edit or downvote an insight a new comparison contradicts; an insight whose count reaches 0 is deleted
management.forgetting: insight deleted at count 0; no forgetting of trajectories

retrieval.query: the evaluation task's text (question, instruction or goal)
retrieval.candidates: kNN by inner product on task embeddings over successful training trajectories (code: same ALFWorld task type, k × 4 candidates)
retrieval.selection: top-k by task similarity; code skips trajectories longer than the longest hand-written example, the same task and duplicates
retrieval.budget: k = 6 HotpotQA, 2 ALFWorld, 2 WebShop few-shot trajectories; all insights

use.context: task instruction + k retrieved successful trajectories as few-shot + full insight list + task + current trajectory
use.reasoning: ReAct actor (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), one attempt per evaluation task

classify.note: Two stores: trajectories are retrieved by embedding kNN on the task text; the insight list is always read in full. Consolidation is the LLM editing the insight list offline.

stages.ingestion: On training tasks a ReAct agent with Reflexion retries each failed task up to 3 times; every trajectory, successful or failed, enters the experience pool.
stages.construction: Successful trajectories are kept as they ran. An insight LLM (gpt-4-0613) reads fail/success pairs of the same task and chunks of L successful trajectories (L = 8, or 4 on WebShop) and proposes operations on the insight list.
stages.organization: Successes are indexed in Faiss by an all-mpnet-base-v2 embedding of their task text; insights form one list ordered by importance count.
stages.update: ADD starts an insight at count 2; UPVOTE and EDIT add 1; DOWNVOTE subtracts 1 (code: 3 when the list is over its cap); an insight at 0 is removed.
stages.retrieval: For a new task, the top-k successful trajectories by task-text similarity become the few-shot examples (k = 6 HotpotQA, 2 ALFWorld and WebShop); the whole insight list is added without search.
stages.answer: A ReAct actor (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) solves the evaluation task in one attempt with these examples and insights in its prompt.
stages.learning: No weight updates: learning is the offline insight extraction plus the growing pool of retrievable successes. Insights can be carried from HotpotQA to FEVER by rewriting them with GPT-4 and target-task examples.

systems.summary: An agent gathers trial-and-error experience on training tasks, has GPT-4 distil it into a vote-weighted list of insights, and at test time solves new tasks in one try using all insights plus its most similar past successes as few-shot examples.

headline: Two memories: raw successful trajectories, retrieved by task similarity as few-shot examples, and a short list of GPT-4-written insights that is always read in full.
Everything is built offline from one half of the benchmark tasks and tested on the other half with a single attempt.

units.role: a solved training task, reused as an in-context example
units.made_by: ReAct + Reflexion agent during experience gathering

fields.name: task text
fields.what: the question or instruction; the only text that is embedded for retrieval

fields.name: trajectory
fields.what: thoughts, actions and observations as run; the shortest success of a task is the one shown

units.name: Failed trajectory
units.role: a failed attempt at a training task
units.made_by: ReAct + Reflexion agent

fields.name: trajectory
fields.what: compared with a success of the same task during insight extraction; never retrieved

units.name: Insight
units.role: one general rule for the task family
units.made_by: insight LLM (gpt-4-0613)

fields.name: rule text
fields.what: one sentence of advice, e.g. to reassess or to try other search terms
fields.src: paper §4.2, App. G; code agent/expel.py L404-L412

fields.name: importance count
fields.what: starts at 2; orders the list and deletes the rule at 0; not shown to the actor

write.how: ReAct on each training task; on failure Reflexion reflects and retries, reflections concatenated
for each training task with a success, GPT-4 sees the success and each failed attempt plus the current insight list and outputs operations
successful trajectories are split randomly into chunks of L and GPT-4 edits the insight list from each chunk
parse ADD / EDIT / AGREE / REMOVE; ADD = 2, AGREE and EDIT +1, REMOVE −1 (−3 when the list is 5 over the cap); drop at 0; sort by count
embed the task text of every successful trajectory (and of the hand-written few-shots) with all-mpnet-base-v2 into Faiss

read.how: Faiss kNN on all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings; ALFWorld restricted to the same task type
walk candidates in order; skip the same task, duplicates and trajectories longer than the longest hand-written example; stop at k
the whole numbered insight list is inserted before the task, with a benchmark-specific header

answer_context.sees: k successful past trajectories as few-shot, all insights, the task and the current trajectory
answer_context.format: instruction with the k trajectories as examples, then e.g. "The following are some experience you gather on a similar task..." and the numbered insights, then the task

compression.what: insights vs the experience they summarise
compression.basis: Not reported. The list is capped by prompt (10 or 8 rules in the README runs) whatever the number of trajectories.

paper_vs_code.paper: 'four-fold validation' (§5.1), described as training on one half and evaluating on the other, and vice versa (App. D.1)
paper_vs_code.code: k_folds: 2 in every benchmark config

paper_vs_code.paper: DOWNVOTE subtracts 1
paper_vs_code.code: REMOVE subtracts 1, or 3 once the list holds 5 more rules than the cap; the prompt also discourages ADD when the list is full

paper_vs_code.paper: top-k successful trajectories by task similarity
paper_vs_code.code: only the same ALFWorld task type; hand-written few-shots are in the pool; trajectories longer than the longest hand-written example are skipped; WebShop drops ones with invalid actions
default agent.llm is gpt-3.5-turbo; the README runs set agent.llm=gpt-4

open_questions: Training and evaluation tasks are two halves of the same small sets (100 HotpotQA, 134 ALFWorld, 100 WebShop), so retrieved successes are near neighbours by construction; how this transfers to a different task distribution is only probed by the HotpotQA → FEVER insight transfer.
ExpeL reads more context than ReAct (4,310 vs 1,320 tokens per HotpotQA trajectory, Table 6); no baseline gets the same budget of hand-picked examples.
