discussion.takeaway: Letting an agent practise on training tasks and then reuse both distilled insights and its own most similar successes improves single-attempt success on unseen tasks without any fine-tuning. The two parts help different domains: insights matter more on HotpotQA, retrieved examples on ALFWorld.

claims.claim: Learning from experience beats the ReAct and Act baselines.
claims.evidence: Success rate: HotpotQA 39 vs 28 (ReAct), ALFWorld 59 vs 40, WebShop 41 vs 35 (Fig. 5).

claims.claim: Insights and retrieval are complementary.
claims.evidence: Insights-only / retrieve-only: 36 / 31 on HotpotQA, 50 / 55 on ALFWorld, 37 / 38 on WebShop; both together are best (Fig. 5, §5.2).

claims.claim: Cross-task learning without retries can match Reflexion's retries.
claims.evidence: HotpotQA 39 vs Reflexion 40 at R3; ALFWorld 59 vs 54 at R3; WebShop 41 is below Reflexion's 43-48 (Fig. 5, §5.2).

claims.claim: More and more diverse experience helps.
claims.evidence: Insights from the few-shots alone give no gain over ReAct; gathering with Reflexion beats gathering with ReAct only (Fig. 6, §5.6).

claims.claim: Insights transfer across tasks.
claims.evidence: HotpotQA insights adapted to FEVER: 70 vs 63 (ReAct) and 65 without target examples (Table 1).

claims.claim: Design choices matter.
claims.evidence: Learned insights 39.0 beat hand-crafted 32.0; adding reflections drops to 29.0; gpt-3.5 insights 32.0; task-similarity retrieval 59.0 vs 48.5 reasoning similarity and 42.5 random on ALFWorld (Table 3).

limits: Only textual observations; images would need a VLM or captioner.
Only closed-source API LLMs were tested.
All insights fit in the context window here; lifelong use would need insight retrieval.
Prompting methods lack the theory behind RL, which may affect how good the resulting policy is.
reading: Insights are never retrieved: the whole list goes into every prompt, and the README caps it at 10 (8 on WebShop) through the extraction prompt, so the insight memory is small by design.
Retrieval matches only the task text; the trajectory, thoughts and outcomes are not compared with the new task.

Evaluation uses gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 while the insights come from gpt-4-0613, so part of the gain may be distilled GPT-4 advice; the gpt-3.5 insights ablation (32 vs 39 on HotpotQA) shows the size of that effect on one benchmark.
Reflexion baselines (R1-R3) retry the same test task with a correctness signal; ExpeL gets one attempt, so the comparison favours Reflexion's access to test feedback rather than ExpeL.
Main results are only given as bar labels (integers) and standard-error arrows in Fig. 5; Tables 2-3 and 5 give finer numbers for some settings.

abstract.text: ExpeL is an LLM agent that learns from its own experience without changing model weights. It first attempts a set of training tasks, retrying failures with self-reflection, and stores the resulting trajectories. An LLM then distils insights from contrasts between failures and successes and from groups of successes. At test time the agent solves each new task once, prompted with these insights and with its most similar past successes; the authors report consistent gains over ReAct on HotpotQA, ALFWorld and WebShop and positive transfer to FEVER.

systems.name: FAME

paper.title: Principled Fast and Meta Knowledge Learners for Continual Reinforcement Learning

construction.unit: a (state, action) pair from the last N steps of training on a task (MinAtar N = 12,000, 2.4% of the task's steps)
construction.kept_as: raw states with the actions the fast learner took (states only for FAME-WD); no rewards
construction.processing: a fast learner (DQN, PPO or SAC) trains on the current task; its final N steps are copied into the meta buffer; after the task a meta learner is refit to all stored pairs by maximum likelihood (FAME-KL) or a Wasserstein loss (FAME-WD)
construction.writer: rule: store the last N steps; supervised refit of the meta network

organization.structure: two learners: a fast learner for the current task (own replay buffer F, cleared per task) and a meta learner that holds all past tasks, fed by a fixed-size meta buffer M
organization.stores: meta buffer M (100k pairs MinAtar, 200k Atari); fast buffer F; fast and meta network weights

management.operations: after each task: refit the meta learner on old pairs plus the new task's pairs (new pairs sampled every k-th batch so each task weighs the same), then append the new pairs to M
management.conflicts: the refit minimises the policy divergence to every past task at once (forgetting as KL or W2 between policies)
management.forgetting: M is a FIFO deque; with 7 tasks × 12,000 pairs it never fills on MinAtar

retrieval.query: the first steps of a new task
retrieval.candidates: three initialisations: previous fast learner, meta learner, random network
retrieval.selection: run fast and meta greedily for n steps each and keep the higher mean return (or a one-sided t-test); a random network is compared by its Q-value at the start state in the code
retrieval.budget: n = 600 steps per candidate on MinAtar, 1,200 on Atari, 10 episodes on Meta-World

use.context: no text context: the chosen learner initialises or regularises the new fast learner
use.reasoning: meta chosen: BC regulariser KL(meta ‖ fast) for the first L = 50k steps (λ = 1); fast chosen: keep fine-tuning; random: reset

classify.note: Fast learner (current task) and meta learner (all tasks) are two tiers; a small buffer of past (state, action) pairs is consolidated into the meta network after each task. At a new task all candidate learners are evaluated and the best by mean return (top-1) is used.

stages.ingestion: Tasks arrive one at a time with known boundaries and a fixed step budget (500k steps per MinAtar task, 1M on Atari and Meta-World).
stages.construction: During the last N steps of a task the fast learner's (state, action) pairs are copied to the meta buffer (N = 12,000 on MinAtar, 20,000 on Atari).
stages.organization: Two learners of the same architecture: a fast learner trained by RL on the current task, and a meta learner meant to hold every past task, fed by one fixed-size meta buffer.
stages.update: After each task the meta learner is refit by supervised learning on all stored pairs (MLE on softmax policies for FAME-KL, a Gaussian W2 loss against the previous meta and current fast policies for FAME-WD).
stages.retrieval: When a new task starts, the previous fast learner and the meta learner are each run for n steps and compared with a random network; the best becomes the warm start.
stages.answer: If the meta learner wins, the fast learner is trained with a KL behaviour-cloning term toward the meta policy for the first L steps; the final evaluation uses the meta learner.
stages.learning: Fast learner: DQN, PPO or SAC. Meta learner: supervised (NLL or W2) on the meta buffer, 200 epochs on MinAtar and Atari, 5,000 × k mini-batches on Meta-World.

systems.summary: A hippocampus/neocortex-style pair for continual RL: a fast learner trains on each task, a meta learner is refit on a small buffer of every task's state-action pairs to minimise a policy-based forgetting measure, and each new task starts from whichever of fast, meta or random scores best in a short evaluation.

Figures follow the MinAtar code (the value-based algorithm of Alg. 1). MEMORY FRAMING: not an LLM memory; included as a parametric, two-tier procedural memory for RL agents. RESULTS: MinAtar and Atari scores are stored raw (return / unstated scale); Meta-World success, FT and forgetting are ×100.

headline: What is kept per task is only the (state, action) pairs of its last N steps, 2.4% of training on MinAtar; rewards are not stored.
The meta learner is a behaviour-cloned policy of all past fast learners, refit after every task; it is also the network that is scored at the end.
At a new task, stored knowledge is used only if the meta learner wins a short evaluation against the previous fast learner and a random network.

discussion.takeaway: Split continual RL into a fast learner for the current task and a meta learner that is refit, after each task, to imitate all past tasks from a small buffer; start each task from whichever learner does best in a short test. On MinAtar, Atari modes and Meta-World this gives the highest average performance with little forgetting.

claims.claim: Minimising a policy-based forgetting measure gives a simple incremental rule: maximum likelihood on a mixture of past tasks' state-action distributions.
claims.evidence: Prop. 1 and Eq. 5 (value-based), Eq. 7 (KL), Prop. 2 / Eq. 8 (Wasserstein) (§3).

claims.claim: FAME beats all baselines on MinAtar.
claims.evidence: Table 1: average return 14.54 / 18.72 / 1.69 vs best baseline 10.71 / 4.95 / 1.16; forgetting 0.72 vs ≥ 1.25; FT 0.16 ties LargeBuffer.

claims.claim: The warm-up test picks the right prior knowledge.
claims.evidence: Fig. 2 right: meta chosen 95.1% on a seen game; random chosen 70.2% on a new one.

claims.claim: It works with continuous control.
claims.evidence: Table 3: Meta-World average success 0.767 (WD) and 0.733 (KL) vs 0.491 PackNet, forgetting 0.023 / 0.073.

claims.claim: It scales in memory.
claims.evidence: Meta buffer ~1-2% of each task's data, same size as a standard replay buffer; meta refit takes minutes (App. E).

limits: One meta learner holds all knowledge; a learned latent representation might distil and reason better.
Other transfer techniques (e.g. context embeddings) are not explored.
Task boundaries must be known and all tasks must share state and action spaces.
reading: On Atari SpaceInvader modes, Finetune's forward transfer (0.65) is higher than FAME's (0.63), although the text says FAME beats all baselines on both metrics.

Baselines other than Finetune are reset at every task and have no access to past data except LargeBuffer, while FAME keeps a meta buffer and a second network; the paper argues the buffer matches the standard replay size, but Table 6 shows scores drop as N shrinks (Space Invaders 18.72 → 14.69 at N = 4,000).
MinAtar forgetting is normalised by each game's standard deviation across the compared methods, so the number depends on which baselines are in the table.
In the MinAtar code the random candidate is scored by an untrained network's Q-value, not by a return, so the three-way test compares returns with a Q estimate.
In the Meta-World code the warm start chooses only between a fresh agent and the meta actor; the previous fast policy is never a candidate, unlike the paper's description.
FAME-KL and FAME-WD are close on Meta-World (0.733 vs 0.767) and swap order on CW10 (0.370 vs 0.340), so neither divergence is clearly better.

abstract.text: The paper frames continual reinforcement learning after the brain's hippocampus-neocortex split. It defines a distance between MDPs and a measure of catastrophic forgetting, and builds FAME from two learners: a fast learner that learns the current task and a meta learner that, after each task, is refit on stored state-action pairs to minimise forgetting across all tasks seen so far. A new task starts from the previous fast learner, the meta learner or a random network, whichever wins a short evaluation, with a behaviour-cloning term when the meta learner is chosen. Experiments on MinAtar, Atari playing modes and Meta-World report better average performance and less forgetting than continual-RL baselines.

construction.unit: memory event: an LLM summary of one news item, 10-Q or 10-K, or one daily reflection
construction.kept_as: LLM summaries (news summarized to about 200 tokens in the released pipeline); reflections written by the backbone
construction.processing: summarize each source document; route it to a layer by source type (news, 10-Q, 10-K); each trading day the backbone writes a reflection that is stored too
construction.writer: summaries: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k in the released data pipeline (paper does not name it); reflections: backbone LLM (GPT-4-Turbo in the main runs)

organization.structure: layered long-term memory per ticker: shallow (news), intermediate (10-Q), deep (10-K); the code adds a fourth reflection layer
organization.stores: one FAISS index plus score list per layer and ticker
organization.index: text-embedding-ada-002 dense vectors (inner product on normalized vectors = cosine)

management.operations: every day recency and importance decay per layer; items move deeper when importance crosses 60 / 80 and back when it falls below (code); trading feedback adds importance to the memories the LLM cited
management.forgetting: purge an item when recency < 0.05 or importance < 5

retrieval.query: paper: trading inquiry plus character text; code: the fixed character text of the ticker
retrieval.candidates: per layer: top K by cosine plus K by stored recency+importance (the code takes the K lowest)
retrieval.selection: score = cosine + recency + importance/100, keep top K unique IDs per layer
retrieval.budget: K = 5 per layer (paper §5.1): 3K = 15 in the paper, up to 4K = 20 with the code's reflection layer

use.context: retrieved memories grouped by layer with their IDs, character text, and (testing) a momentum sentence or (training) the next-day price move
use.reasoning: one LLM call per day returning buy / sell / hold, a reason and the IDs of the memories used

classify.note: Layer moves and deletion are driven by decaying scores and trading feedback, so 'evict' rather than 'update in place'; nothing is rewritten after it is stored.

stages.ingestion: Each trading day the agent receives the day's news, any new 10-Q or 10-K filing and the price for one ticker; texts were summarized beforehand by an LLM.
stages.construction: News summaries go to the shallow layer, 10-Q summaries to the intermediate layer and 10-K summaries to the deep layer; each gets a sampled importance score and recency 1. The daily reflection from the backbone is stored as well (a separate reflection layer in the code).
stages.organization: Three long-term layers with different decay speeds (paper: stability 14 / 90 / 365 days and importance bases 0.9 / 0.967 / 0.988) plus a working-memory step that merges what is retrieved from each layer.
stages.update: Every day scores decay; items whose recency falls below 0.05 or importance below 5 are deleted. Memories the LLM cited get +5 importance per access-counter step, set from the sign of the 7-day trading result (code), and cross into deeper layers at importance 60 and 80.
stages.retrieval: Per layer, candidates from cosine similarity (ada-002, FAISS) and from the stored recency+importance ranking are scored by the sum of cosine, recency and importance, and the top K = 5 are kept.
stages.answer: The backbone LLM reads the memories of all layers with their IDs plus a momentum signal and returns buy, sell or hold with the supporting IDs; in training it instead explains the known next-day move.
stages.learning: No weights are trained. The 'training phase' fills and reshapes memory using the true next-day price moves.

abstract.text: FinMem is an LLM agent that trades a single stock day by day. A profiling module gives it sector knowledge and a risk attitude (risk-seeking, risk-averse, or one that switches with recent returns). Its memory keeps summarized news, quarterly and annual reports in three layers that forget at different speeds, and each day it retrieves the top-ranked items of every layer to decide whether to buy, sell or hold. On five US stocks it reports higher cumulative return and Sharpe ratio than buy-and-hold, three deep-RL agents, a Generative-Agents port and FinGPT, with less than a year of training data.

headline: Memory is scored like Generative Agents (recency + relevance + importance), but each source type has its own layer with its own decay speed.
In the code the retrieval query is the fixed character text of the ticker, not the day's question, so similarity ranks the same way every day.
The reported FinMem row per stock is the best of three risk settings, picked on the test period.

ablation.src: paper Table 5 (TSLA, test 2022-06-16 to 2022-12-28, GPT-4-Turbo, self-adaptive risk)

discussion.takeaway: Giving each kind of financial text its own memory layer with its own forgetting speed, and feeding the retrieved top items to a GPT-4-class model, produced the best return and Sharpe ratio among the compared agents on five stocks over one six-month test window.

claims.claim: FinMem beats every compared agent on cumulative return and Sharpe ratio on all five stocks.
claims.evidence: TSLA 61.78% vs 33.34% (DQN) and Sharpe 2.68 vs 0.97; COIN 34.98% vs 3.46% (Generative Agents); Wilcoxon test significant vs the second best. Table 2, §5.2

claims.claim: Less than a year of training data is enough.
claims.evidence: Trained on under six months of TSLA data it ranks near the top and leads after late December 2022; DRL agents got about 10 years. Fig. 7, §5.1-5.2

claims.claim: GPT-4-Turbo is the best backbone.
claims.evidence: Sharpe 2.50 (GPT-4-Turbo) vs 2.23 (GPT-4, which has the higher return 62.62%) vs -2.85 (Llama2-70b-chat). Table 3

claims.claim: The self-adaptive risk character is the best setting.
claims.evidence: 54.70% vs -19.41% (risk-seeking) and -12.47% (risk-averse) on TSLA. Table 4

claims.claim: Retrieval width matters; K = 5 is the best trade-off.
claims.evidence: K = 10 gives 79.44% but loses in calm markets; K = 5 has the lowest volatility and drawdown. Table 5, Fig. 11

limits: Uses a limited range and quality of news and reports.
Uses general-purpose LLMs; finance-tuned models are left to future work.
Llama2-70b-chat needed shortened prompts and memories because of its context window.
Ablations use a shorter TSLA period for budget reasons.
reading: The FinMem row for each stock is the best of three risk settings chosen by test-period cumulative return (§5.1); baselines were run with one setting, so part of the margin is selection on the test set.
No ablation replaces the layered memory with a single store while keeping everything else; the Generative Agents baseline also lacks the risk switch, so the effect of layering alone is not isolated.
In the code the retrieval query is the ticker's fixed character text, so cosine relevance does not depend on the day; day-to-day changes come from new items, decay and feedback.
The code's second candidate set takes the lowest recency+importance items (ascending sorted list), which the final top-K usually discards; the paper describes a plain combined ranking.
Daily reflections fill a fourth layer that is also retrieved, so the answer model sees up to 20 memories, not the 3 × K = 15 the paper describes.
The Top-K ablation is not monotone (Top 3: 29.44% below Top 1: 52.09%), from one ticker and one period averaged over 5 runs.
In Table 4 the 'Annualized Volatility' values of buy-and-hold and self-adaptive (3.8050, 2.5960) equal the daily volatility values in Table 3, so that row looks mislabeled.
One share is traded per day on 5 tickers in one test window; no transaction costs are mentioned.

retrieval.candidates: BM25 top 5 (all keywords in one query), dense top 5 (scores summed over queries), up to 5 page ids
retrieval.selection: LLM integrates the pooled pages into notes; LLM checks sufficiency and writes follow-up requests
retrieval.budget: ≤15 pages per round, at most 3 rounds (max reflection depth 3)

classify.note: The memo list is not searched; it only steers the planner, which chooses queries for BM25, dense and page-id tools.

stages.ingestion: History arrives as a stream of sessions; in the experiments a LoCoMo session is one page and long documents are cut into 2,048-token pages.
stages.construction: For each new page the memorizer LLM writes one concise memo paragraph, reading all earlier memos for consistency; the page is stored verbatim with the memo as its header.
stages.organization: Two flat stores: the list of memos (the 'memory') and the page-store. BM25 and BGE-M3 indexes are built over the raw page content.
stages.update: Append-only: memos and pages are added, never revised or deleted.
stages.retrieval: A researcher LLM plans from the question and the full memo list, calls BM25, dense and page-id tools (5 pages each), integrates the pages into notes, and repeats with LLM-written follow-up requests until an LLM check says enough (max 3 rounds).
stages.answer: The answer model reads only the researcher's integrated notes (Table 4 default); adding source pages is an ablation.
stages.learning: An RL objective for memorizer and researcher is written down (Eq. 6-7), but all reported runs use off-the-shelf models.

systems.summary: Just-in-time memory: keep every page verbatim with a short LLM memo, and build the answer context at question time with an iterative plan-search-integrate-reflect research loop over BM25, dense and page-id tools.
systems.notes: DESIGN: paper §2.2, §3.1, Tables 3-5, appendix prompts; code at commit 1af6bba1 (2025-12-01), research/ subfolder in later commits. Venue: only arXiv v1 (2025-11-23) is known from the arXiv page. control.management=fixed-rule because storage is a plain append; the RL formulation (§2.2.3) is not used in experiments, so learning=training-free. classify.decides='LLM decides' because the integrate LLM chooses what reaches the answer model.

sources.code_note: Commit 1af6bba1 (2025-12-01, merge of the gam_update branch with the evaluation scripts) is the earliest commit with the released eval scripts for LoCoMo, HotpotQA, RULER and NarrativeQA, eight days after arXiv v1. The same code was later moved to research/ (2026-02-28) when the repo was rebuilt as a general SDK. Exact identity with the paper's runs is not guaranteed.

headline: The stored memo is only a guide for the planner: search runs over the raw pages, and the memo is not even in the search index.
The answer model reads only the researcher's notes (about 106 tokens), not the pages it found.
Every question costs a multi-call research loop (plan, search, integrate, check, rewrite), about 12-18 s per question on HotpotQA.

An LLM check decides whether to stop or write a follow-up request (at most 3 rounds). The answer model reads only the notes.

discussion.takeaway: Do not bet on a pre-built compressed memory: keep all pages verbatim with light memos, and spend compute at question time on an agentic search-and-integrate loop. In its own paper this beats Mem0, A-Mem, MemoryOS, LightMem, RAG and long-context LLMs on LoCoMo, HotpotQA, RULER and NarrativeQA.

claims.claim: GAM beats memory-based and memory-free baselines on every benchmark.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o-mini: LoCoMo single-hop F1 57.75 vs 52.45 (RAG); HotpotQA-448K F1 59.81 vs 54.01 (RAG); RULER MT 93.20 vs 60.60 (long-LLM). Table 1

claims.claim: Pre-built memory alone loses information; search over full pages is needed.
claims.evidence: Memory without research 27.50 avg vs 53.18 full; research without memory 48.27. Table 3

claims.claim: The researcher needs a larger model than the memorizer.
claims.evidence: 0.5B memorizer still averages 48.83; 0.5B researcher drops to 9.08 (14B: 53.18). Table 2

claims.claim: More test-time compute helps.
claims.evidence: Scores rise with reflection depth 1→5 and retrieved pages 3→20, with diminishing gains. Fig. 2, §3.4

claims.claim: Cost is comparable to Mem0 and MemoryOS.
claims.evidence: HotpotQA-56K total 69.3 s vs Mem0 37.6 s, MemoryOS 80.8 s, A-Mem 210.3 s; but online 12.4 s vs ≤0.52 s. Table 5

discussion.limits_src: The paper has no limitations section.
reading: The memo is not indexed: BM25 and dense search run over raw page content, and the memo list only helps the planner choose queries and page ids.
The answer model reads about 106 tokens of LLM notes; the long-LLM baseline instead reads up to 128K tokens and takes the max score over chunks, so the settings differ in more than memory.
No baseline gets the same multi-round search budget; research-without-memory (48.27 avg) already beats every Table 1 baseline on HotpotQA, so much of the gain is the loop, not the memory.
LoCoMo is scored with F1 and BLEU-1 only (no LLM judge), and the paper says it re-mapped LoCoMo categories for A-Mem, Mem0 and MemoryOS, so per-category numbers differ from those papers.
The RL training in §2.2.3 is not used in any experiment and no training code is in the repo at the pinned commit.
Online serving is 60-100x slower than Mem0 or MemoryOS per question (Table 5).

abstract.text: GAM argues that memories compressed ahead of time inevitably lose details, and instead builds the context for each request at run time. A memorizer keeps every session or chunk verbatim in a page-store and adds a short LLM memo per page. A researcher agent reads the memos, plans keyword, dense and page-id searches over the page-store, integrates what it finds and reflects until the information is enough. On LoCoMo, HotpotQA, RULER and NarrativeQA it outperforms memory systems such as Mem0 and A-Mem as well as RAG and long-context baselines.

systems.name: GraphPlanner

paper.title: GraphPlanner: Graph Memory-Augmented Agentic Routing for Multi-Agent LLMs

construction.unit: interaction row: input node, (role, LLM) hub, output node, with task score and cost
construction.kept_as: Longformer embeddings of the step's input and output text; the text itself is not kept in memory
construction.processing: every routing step logs one row; no LLM processing of memory
construction.writer: environment logging rule (no LLM)

organization.structure: heterogeneous graph: query and response nodes linked to one shared hub node per (role, LLM) pair
organization.stores: workflow memory (rows of the current query) and historical memory (rows of all training episodes)
organization.index: none; the whole graph is encoded by GARNet at every step

management.operations: append a finished training episode's workflow rows to the historical memory

retrieval.query: current node embedding fused with root-query and task-type embeddings
retrieval.candidates: all history rows, averaged per hub (no search or top-k)
retrieval.selection: policy score state · hub, masked to valid roles; sampled in training, argmax at test
retrieval.budget: entire history, every step

use.context: memory only chooses the next (role, LLM); the LLM agents read text: original query, parent queries, sibling answers, summary
use.reasoning: multi-step planner / executor / summarizer workflow, 8.1 LLM calls per query on average in Phase 2

classify.note: Memory is read by a learned policy network, not searched: every history row is mean-pooled into its (role, LLM) hub at every decision. The output is an action (which role and LLM act next), not retrieved content.

stages.ingestion: Each step of a query's workflow (plan, answer or summarize, run by one LLM) produces a row: the embedding of the node being processed, the embedding of the LLM's output, the task score and the cost.
stages.construction: Rows are stored only as Longformer vectors plus two scalars; query and response nodes connect to a fixed hub node per (role, LLM) pair, whose feature is the role description embedding joined with the LLM description embedding.
stages.organization: Two graphs share the hubs: the workflow memory graph of the current query and the historical memory graph of past episodes; rounds are linked only through the shared hubs, not by temporal edges.
stages.update: During training the finished episode's rows are appended to the historical memory; nothing is merged or deleted. At test time the history is fixed and only the current query's rows grow.
stages.retrieval: At every step GARNet encodes the whole history (a scatter-mean per hub in the released code), injects the resulting hub vectors into the workflow graph encoder, and scores each hub against a fused state (node, root query, task type); invalid roles are masked.
stages.answer: The chosen LLM runs its role with a text prompt (original query, parent queries, sibling answers, summary); a final executor writes the answer. Memory vectors never enter a prompt.
stages.learning: The policy and value networks (GARNet) are trained with PPO on task score; the paper's reward also subtracts alpha times cost, the released code rewards only the final score.

systems.summary: An RL-trained router that decides, step by step, which agent role and which LLM act next, reading a heterogeneous graph memory of past and current (query, role-LLM, response) interactions.
systems.notes:
Venue: ICLR 2026 main conference, verified on the PDF header ('Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026') and the arXiv journal reference. Scope: memory here is interaction history for routing decisions, not user or task content; nothing from memory reaches an LLM prompt.
CODE: released dynamic_router at commit 56010b1 (2026-04-26) read in full for the memory path; static_router is the Phase-1 fixed-workflow variant and was not traced. Paper and code differ on the LLM pool (5 vs 10), the reward (no cost term in code) and PPO settings; see mechanism.paper_vs_code.

sources.code_note: Commit 56010b1 (2026-04-26) is the head of the repository and was pushed the same day as arXiv v1; the history has three commits, all on that day, so this is the only released version. The Phase-2 (dynamic) router is traced; the Phase-1 static router shares the design.

headline: Memory stores no text: each step is two Longformer vectors plus a score and a cost, attached to a (role, LLM) hub.
History is not searched. Every row is averaged into its hub at every step, so the history signal for an action is the same for every query.
The graph only decides who acts next; the LLM agents themselves read plain-text context (parent queries, sibling answers, summary).

open_questions: Does the history help because it describes past interactions, or because it gives each hub a learned per-action prior? In the code each hub gets one mean over all its rows, the same for every query, and no ablation separates the two.
The w/o History, Homo-Graph and Hetero-Graph ablation (Fig. 5b) and the inductive vs transductive comparison (Fig. 5c) are shown only as radar plots, without numbers.

discussion.takeaway: Routing across LLMs can be framed as building a multi-agent workflow, with a small RL policy reading a graph of past and current (query, role-LLM, response) interactions. In its own tests this beats single- and multi-round routers on accuracy with far less training compute.

claims.claim: Beats single- and multi-round routers.
claims.evidence: Phase 2 average 63.6 vs 54.3 (RouterDC) and 51.8 (Router-R1); Phase 1 58.60 vs 54.80 (d1w3) and 60.40 vs 56.20 (d2w2). Tables 2-3

claims.claim: Much cheaper to train.
claims.evidence: 1.04 GiB GPU memory vs 186.26 GiB for Router-R1; 120 min total training vs 300. Tables 4, 15

claims.claim: Generalizes to unseen tasks and LLMs.
claims.evidence: LogicGrid / MGSM / CommonGen average 78 vs 58 (RouterDC); AIME 14.7 vs 7.56. Tables 5, 14; unseen LLMs only in Fig. 5a

claims.claim: Historical memory is essential, and GARNet uses it better than generic GNNs or LLM-read history.
claims.evidence: Fig. 5b (radar, w/o History drops most); Table 12 (GAT, GraphTransformer lower); Table 13 (Router-R1 with retrieved or summarized history 0.12-0.62 vs 0.38-0.78)

claims.claim: Transductive inference (keep training history) is slightly better than inductive but costlier.
claims.evidence: Fig. 5c, radar only

limits: Only three agent roles (planner, executor, summarizer); richer roles are left to future work.
reading: Memory holds no user or task content: it is a log of routing outcomes stored as vectors, and nothing from it reaches an LLM prompt.

In the released code the history is not matched to the query: each hub receives the mean of all its rows, identical for every question, so its effect is closer to a learned per-action prior than to retrieval.

Costs are not comparable across the result tables: GraphPlanner averages 605.0 cost units and 8.1 calls per query in Phase 2, against 76.3 and 1.8 for Router-R1; the Pareto claim rests on Fig. 4 only.
The printed Average column is not the mean of the five domain columns (GraphPlanner 63.6 vs 62.2 by hand; Router-R1 51.8 vs 48.9), so it is presumably weighted by test items; the paper does not say.
Test sets are small (44-50 questions per task, Table 8), and one percentage point on a domain is about one question.
Released code differs from the paper in the LLM pool (5 vs 10), the reward (no cost term) and PPO settings, so the code as released does not reproduce the reported configuration.
The three memory ablations are radar plots without numbers; the only numeric memory ablation (Table 13) compares against Router-R1 variants, not GraphPlanner without history.

abstract.text: GraphPlanner treats LLM routing as building a small multi-agent workflow per query: at each step it chooses both an agent role (planner, executor or summarizer) and which LLM plays it. The choice is made by a graph neural policy, GARNet, that reads a heterogeneous graph of the current workflow and of past interactions, linking queries and responses to shared role-LLM nodes. The whole router is trained with PPO for accuracy and cost. Across 14 tasks the authors report higher accuracy than single- and multi-round routers, far lower training GPU memory, and zero-shot transfer to unseen tasks and LLMs.

systems.name: H-Mem

paper.title: H-Mem: A Novel Memory Mechanism for Evolving and Retrieving Agent Memory via a Hybrid Structure

construction.unit: memory event extracted per fragment; fragments and summaries also stored
construction.kept_as: extracted events + verbatim fragments + LLM summaries
construction.processing: LLM event extraction; LLM entity/relation extraction (spaCy NER fallback); parent summaries
construction.writer: LLM via extraction/consolidation prompts (App. C.1); backbones GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini

organization.structure: 4-level temporal-semantic tree + entity knowledge graph
organization.stores: tree (day/week/month/year levels); entity graph with salient-entity profiles
organization.index: Qwen3-Embedding-4B vectors for fragments/events/summaries; lexical entity matching

management.operations: join similar cluster in time window, regenerate parent summary; merge entities/relations
management.forgetting: no deletion described; Ebbinghaus decay (tau 365 days) only as ranking prior

retrieval.query: LLM decomposes into dependent sub-queries with Short/Long/Mixed scope, time hints
retrieval.candidates: lexical+vector entity seeds, multi-hop graph expansion, bottom-up tree search
retrieval.selection: 0.70 similarity + 0.15 time + 0.15 robustness; Qwen3-Reranker-4B; dedup
retrieval.budget: top-k candidates; default k not stated (k 5-50 tested, k=30 variant)

use.context: ranked evidence chain per sub-query plus prerequisite sub-answers
use.reasoning: sub-answer per sub-query, LLM synthesis; missing-info follow-up query

classify.note: Tree plus entity graph; the tree is the main structure.

stages.ingestion: Original memory fragments (speaker, timestamp, conversation text) are kept; an LLM extracts one or more fine-grained memory events from each fragment.
stages.construction: Each event becomes a leaf of a temporal-semantic tree; in parallel an LLM extracts entities and relations per fragment, which are normalised/disambiguated (lemmatisation, token overlap, fuzzy match; spaCy NER fallback) into a knowledge graph whose entity nodes link back to source fragments.
stages.organization: Hybrid structure: a 4-level tree (day/week/month/year windows) whose upper nodes hold LLM summaries of semantically similar children within the same time window (thresholds 0.8/0.7/0.6), plus an entity-relation knowledge graph with profiles for salient entities; embeddings kept for fragments, events and summaries.
stages.update: Incremental bottom-up insertion: a new node joins a similar cluster in its time window (parent summary regenerated) or gets a new parent; graph entities merge on exact/fuzzy match and duplicate relations merge evidence. A consolidation count and last-consolidation time feed an Ebbinghaus-style robustness score.
stages.retrieval: An LLM decomposes the query into dependent sub-queries, each labelled Short/Long/Mixed scope with temporal hints; seed entities are found by lexical + vector matching, expanded multi-hop in the graph, mapped to fragments/events, then the tree is searched bottom-up; evidence is ranked by 0.70*semantic + 0.15*temporal + 0.15*robustness and reranked (Qwen3-Reranker-4B); a missing-information follow-up query fires when first-pass evidence is insufficient.
stages.answer: A sub-answer is generated per sub-query (using prerequisite sub-answers as context) and an LLM synthesises the final answer.

systems.summary: Couples a temporal-semantic summary tree (short-term events consolidating into long-term summaries by time window) with an entity knowledge graph, and retrieves over both with LLM query decomposition and a time/robustness-aware evidence score.
systems.notes:
AXES CORRECTED from the paper; earlier taxonomy row was: turn | verbatim | write-time filter | dual tree | FAISS + LCA expansion (vector). AXES-CHECK: the seed taxonomy row (turn / verbatim / write-time filter / dual tree / FAISS + LCA expansion) does not match arXiv 2605.15701 and may describe a different H-Mem paper (e.g. 2507.22925). In 2605.15701: leaf unit is an LLM-extracted memory event (original fragments are also kept and retrievable); no write-time filter is described; organisation is one temporal-semantic tree plus an entity knowledge graph (not a dual tree); selection is LLM sub-query planning + lexical/vector entity seeding + multi-hop graph expansion + bottom-up tree search + reranking, with no FAISS or LCA mention. No code URL is given in the paper. Backbones in experiments: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1-mini; embedding Qwen3-Embedding-4B, reranker Qwen3-Reranker-4B (Appendix A.2).

management.operations: replace a finished chunk's pairs by its summary in the prompt; retrieve(id) shows the pairs again until the next subgoal
management.forgetting: nothing deleted; code drops the oldest entries when the prompt exceeds the 8,192-token window

classify.note: Memory is the in-trial context only. A finished subgoal's pairs are folded into a summary in the prompt; the agent re-expands a subgoal by id, so the lookup is by number, not by similarity.

stages.ingestion: Every environment observation is appended, with the action that caused it, to the chunk of the current subgoal.
stages.construction: Before acting, the LLM writes a subgoal; its actions and observations form one chunk. When the LLM judges the subgoal done it writes the next subgoal together with its first action.
stages.organization: Working memory is a two-level list: numbered past subgoals, each shown with a summarized observation, then the current subgoal with all of its pairs.
stages.update: A finished chunk's pairs are replaced in the prompt by an LLM summary that also states whether the subgoal was met; the raw pairs stay in the history.
stages.retrieval: When the LLM outputs retrieve(id), the pairs of that past subgoal are put back into the prompt in place of its summary, until a new subgoal is written.
stages.answer: Each step one LLM call reads the instruction, one in-context example and the working memory and outputs the next action.

systems.summary: Working-memory manager for long agent tasks: the LLM writes subgoals as memory chunks, finished chunks are shown only as subgoal + summary, and the agent can re-expand a past chunk by id.

headline: The memory lives only inside one trial: it is the agent's own prompt, reorganized by subgoal.
A finished subgoal's action-observation pairs leave the prompt and are replaced by a short summary; the raw pairs are kept and can be re-expanded by id.
In the released code Blocksworld and Gripper never call the summarizer: a finished subgoal shows only its last observation.

abstract.text: HiAgent targets the in-trial (working) memory of LLM agents on long tasks, where the usual practice feeds every past action and observation back into the prompt. The agent is prompted to write a subgoal before acting and to treat each subgoal as a memory chunk. When it moves to a new subgoal, the finished chunk is shown only as the subgoal and a summarized observation, and the agent can ask to see a past chunk's full trajectory again. On five long-horizon AgentBoard tasks with GPT-4 the authors report twice the success rate of the standard full-history prompt, 3.8 fewer steps and about a third less context.

key_numbers.value: gpt-4-turbo, same as the agent; off for Blocksworld and Gripper in code

ablation.src: paper Table 2 and Table 3, Tyreworld only (gpt-4-turbo). *Table 3 gives Context and Time relative to STANDARD, Table 2 relative to HiAgent.

discussion.takeaway: Treating subgoals as memory chunks, and showing only a summary of each finished one, lets a GPT-4 agent finish long planning tasks more often, in fewer steps and with less context, than feeding it the full history.

claims.claim: HiAgent doubles the success rate of the full-history STANDARD prompt.
claims.evidence: Average success 42.00 vs 21.00 and progress 62.55 vs 38.61 over five tasks; Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: It is also more efficient.
claims.evidence: 3.80 fewer steps, context 64.98% and run time 80.58% of STANDARD; Table 1

claims.claim: Both summarization and retrieval help.
claims.evidence: Tyreworld success 60.0 vs 30.0 without summarization and 50.0 without retrieval; Table 2, §5.1

claims.claim: The gain is not only from task decomposition.
claims.evidence: Subgoals without hiding past pairs reach 40.0 success on Tyreworld vs 60.0 for HiAgent, with 112.8% context; Table 3, §5.3

claims.claim: The improvement is statistically significant.
claims.evidence: Wilcoxon signed-rank: progress rate p = 2.38e-5, steps p = 0.0016; §5.5

limits: Very long tasks may still exceed memory limits despite the shorter context.
Better retrieval strategies are left to future work.
Experiments cover benchmark tasks only, not real-world applications.
reading: Only one backbone (gpt-4-turbo) and one baseline family are tested; the only other memory-style comparison is STANDARD, which keeps everything.
All ablations are on Tyreworld alone, and §5.1 says removing both modules cuts success by 20 while Table 2 shows 30.0 (-30.0).
In the released code Blocksworld and Gripper skip the summarizer and show the last observation, which is the paper's 'w/o OS' heuristic; the paper does not mention this.
In code, a retrieve(...) output is itself sent to the environment as that step's action, so it uses one of the step budget and the follow-up LLM action is discarded.
The number of problems per task is not stated in the paper; the released configs list 20 Jericho games, up to 20 Gripper and Barman problems, and Tyreworld problem indices 2-9 (8 of 10).
Context and time are reported only as percentages of STANDARD, so absolute token or summarizer cost is not given.

systems.name: HiGMem

paper.title: HiGMem: A Hierarchical and LLM-Guided Memory System for Long-Term Conversational Agents

construction.unit: Turn node (raw turn + LLM metadata), grouped under Event nodes
construction.kept_as: verbatim turn text + LLM context sentence, keywords, tags; event summary written by the LLM
construction.processing: LLM annotates each turn; LLM assigns it to one or more of the 10 most similar events or opens a new event; small events get their summary rewritten
construction.writer: GPT-4o-mini

organization.structure: two levels: events over turns (a turn may join several events)
organization.stores: turn store + event store (character profiles exist in code but are off in the paper setting)
organization.index: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 dense over turn text (with speaker, date) and over event keywords + tags + summary

management.operations: join existing events or NEW_EVENT; refresh event summary, keywords, tags and facts while the event has < 10 turns, then keywords/tags only

retrieval.query: LLM keyword rewrite of the question for both searches; the original question for the LLM steps
retrieval.candidates: top-10 turns + top-10 events by cosine similarity
retrieval.selection: one LLM call per event picks its turns; the union is filtered by an LLM in chunks of 10
retrieval.budget: no fixed cap; 8.09 turns per question on average (LoCoMo10)

use.context: selected turns with date, speaker, text and the LLM context sentence, sorted by date string
use.reasoning: single answer call with a LoCoMo-category-specific prompt

classify.note: Dense search only proposes candidates; LLM calls pick turns inside events and filter the union, so the LLM fixes the final set.

stages.ingestion: Each LoCoMo turn is added in order, with its speaker and session date.
stages.construction: An LLM writes keywords, tags and a one-sentence context for the turn; the raw text is kept as the Turn node's content.
stages.organization: The turn is embedded, the 10 most similar events are shown to an LLM (by title), and the LLM joins the turn to one or more of them or opens a new event.
stages.update: While an event has fewer than 10 turns the LLM rewrites its 2-3 sentence summary, keywords and tags and appends facts; after that only keywords and tags can change.
stages.retrieval: An LLM rewrites the question as keywords; dense search returns 10 turns and 10 events; an LLM reads each event's summary and turns and picks the useful turns; an LLM filter keeps the relevant ones from the union.
stages.answer: The kept turns (8.09 on average) are given to GPT-4o-mini with date, speaker, text and context sentence, under a category-specific short-answer prompt.

systems.summary: Two-level event-turn memory where event summaries act as anchors: an LLM reads each retrieved event and picks which of its raw turns to pass on, giving a much smaller evidence set than vector top-k.

glance.a: A Turn node: the raw dialogue turn with speaker and date, plus an LLM context sentence, keywords and tags.
The turns are kept verbatim. Events hold a 2-3 sentence LLM summary, which steers retrieval but never reaches the answer model.
Two levels: an LLM joins each new turn to one or more of the 10 most similar events, or opens a new one.
No cross-encoder. GPT-4o-mini picks turns inside each retrieved event and then filters the union, 10 candidates per call.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: About 8 raw turns per question, each with date, speaker and the one-sentence context; no event summaries.

An LLM filter then trims the union, so the answer model sees about 8 raw turns instead of a fixed top-k.

components.role: Turn annotation, event joining and updates

discussion.takeaway: Let an LLM use short event summaries to decide which raw turns to read. On LoCoMo10 this keeps recall close to A-Mem while passing about 12 times fewer turns to the answer model.

claims.claim: Best F1 on four of five LoCoMo10 categories.
claims.evidence: Multi-hop 0.31, open-domain 0.15, single-hop 0.49, adversarial 0.78; temporal 0.34 is below A-Mem's 0.39. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: A compact, precise evidence set rather than a bigger one.
claims.evidence: Avg K 8.09 vs 99.84, Precision@K 0.1909 vs 0.0101, Recall@K 0.7241 vs 0.7502. Table 2

claims.claim: The event layer matters, not only the LLM filter.
claims.evidence: Without events F1 0.39 / Recall 0.55 (Table 5); flat top-100 + same filter F1 0.46, Precision 0.065, K 22.7 (Tables 6-7)

claims.claim: Cheaper when a small model builds memory and a large model answers.
claims.evidence: GPT-5 answer tokens 25.38M → 1.62M; total $17.43 → $6.43. Table 3, App. B.3

limits: Extra LLM calls for construction and evidence selection; the benefit depends on using a cheap model for memory and an expensive one for answers.
Relies on the LLM judging relevance from event summaries and candidate turns.
On multi-party DialSim it scores lower F1 than A-Mem (0.42 vs 0.49) despite far fewer turns; broader tests on noisy, multi-party conversations are needed.
reading: The paper setting in code annotates each turn in isolation, keeps event summaries only as routing text, and never reads the event fact sheet or turn keywords/tags, so the answer depends on raw turns plus the one-sentence context.

Construction costs more than A-Mem (21.2M vs 9.2M tokens, 15.59 vs 6.38 s per turn), and QA-stage tokens are also higher (29.3M vs 25.5M, Table 9); the saving appears only when the answer model is priced far above the memory model.
Adversarial questions are answered by choosing between the distractor and 'Not mentioned in the conversation', so that category's F1 behaves like a two-way accuracy.
Turn keywords and tags are generated for every turn but never indexed: the turn index text is speaker, date and raw content only.
The final context is sorted by the session date string as text, so turn order is not guaranteed to be chronological.
ReadAgent and MemoryBank rows equal A-Mem's published GPT-4o-mini numbers rounded; Base LLM and A-Mem differ from A-Mem's paper, so they appear to be reruns.

abstract.text: HiGMem targets a trade-off in conversational memory: vector search finds relevant turns but also returns many look-alike turns that inflate the answer context. It stores every dialogue turn with light LLM metadata and groups turns into events that carry a short summary. At question time an LLM reads the retrieved events' summaries and turns, predicts which turns are worth passing on, and filters the result. On LoCoMo10 with GPT-4o-mini it has the best F1 on four of five categories and passes about 8 turns per question instead of about 100.

stages.ingestion: The corpus is a fixed set of passages (e.g. 11,656 for MuSiQue); each passage becomes a node as is.
stages.construction: An LLM runs NER on each passage and then extracts schema-free (subject, predicate, object) triples conditioned on those entities; subjects and objects become phrase nodes.
stages.organization: Phrase nodes are joined by relation edges (same triple) and synonym edges (embedding similarity >= 0.8); each passage node gets a 'contains' edge to every phrase from its triples.
stages.update: New passages are indexed into the same graph (the paper grows the corpus in four segments, §6.3); nothing is edited or merged beyond synonym links.
stages.retrieval: The question is matched to triple embeddings (top 5), an LLM keeps the relevant ones (at most 4), and their phrases (up to 5) plus every passage (dense score x 0.05) seed Personalized PageRank; passages are ranked by PageRank. With no triples left, plain dense retrieval is used.
stages.answer: The reader LLM gets the top 5 passages and answers after a short chain of thought.

systems.summary: Adds passages as nodes to HippoRAG's LLM-built phrase graph, links the question to whole triples, and filters those triples with an LLM before Personalized PageRank ranks passages.

headline: The reader only ever sees 5 raw passages; triples and phrases decide the ranking but never reach the answer model.
Every passage is a PageRank seed weighted by its dense score (x 0.05), so the dense retriever still anchors the result; phrase seeds come from at most 5 phrases in LLM-kept triples.
If the LLM filter keeps no triple, the graph is skipped and plain dense retrieval answers (18 of 100 failure cases in App. E).

No. Passages are stored and read verbatim; triples are only an index for linking the question to the graph.
One open knowledge graph: phrase nodes joined by triple edges and synonym edges (similarity >= 0.8), and a 'contains' edge from each passage to its phrases.
An LLM filters the 5 best-matching triples down to at most 4, and Personalized PageRank then re-orders all passages. There is no cross-encoder.

discussion.takeaway: Putting passages into HippoRAG's graph and linking the question to whole triples lets a PageRank retriever keep its multi-hop gains without losing to a strong 7B dense retriever on simple QA: 59.8 vs 57.0 average F1.

claims.claim: Earlier structure-augmented RAG falls below strong dense retrieval once simple factual QA is included; HippoRAG 2 does not.
claims.evidence: Average F1: NV-Embed-v2 57.0, RAPTOR 48.8, GraphRAG 49.6, LightRAG 6.6, HippoRAG 53.1, HippoRAG 2 59.8; NQ 63.3 vs 61.9. Table 2, §5

claims.claim: The largest gains are on associative (multi-hop) tasks.
claims.evidence: 2Wiki F1 71.0 vs 61.5, LV-Eval 12.9 vs 9.8; recall@5 MuSiQue 74.7 vs 69.7, 2Wiki 90.4 vs 76.5. Tables 2-3

claims.claim: Each design change helps, linking the question to triples most of all.
claims.evidence: Recall@5 average 87.1 vs 74.6 with NER-to-node, 59.6 with query-to-node, 81.0 without passage nodes, 86.4 without the filter. Table 4, §6.1

claims.claim: The gain holds with other dense retrievers.
claims.evidence: MuSiQue recall@5 +5.2 (GTE-Qwen2-7B), +5.6 (GritLM-7B), +5.0 (NV-Embed-v2). Table 7, §6.4

claims.claim: Indexing is far cheaper than GraphRAG or LightRAG.
claims.evidence: MuSiQue: 9.2M input tokens vs 115.5M (GraphRAG) and 68.5M (LightRAG); 1.2 s per query vs 10.7 s and 13.3 s. Table 12, App. F

limits: The triple filter is a main error source: in 26% of 100 failed MuSiQue questions no supporting phrase survives filtering, and 18% end with no triple at all.
Graph search can still miss supporting passages when the right phrases are linked.
QA needs more GPU memory than the baselines (9.9 GB vs 1.7 GB for NV-Embed-v2) because of the fact embeddings.
Associative QA degrades as the corpus grows, at about the same rate as dense retrieval.
Episodic memory for long conversations is left for future work.
discussion.limits_src: paper App. E, App. F, §6.3, §7 (no separate limitations section)
reading: The reader always gets 5 verbatim passages; the graph only re-orders them, so HippoRAG 2 is best read as a graph-based reranker over a passage corpus rather than a store the model reads from.
Every passage is a PageRank seed with its dense score, so dense retrieval stays in the loop; Table 5 shows the result is sensitive to that weight (MuSiQue recall@5 77.9 to 80.5).

The abstract's 7% associativity gain matches recall@5 averaged over MuSiQue, 2Wiki and HotpotQA (87.1 vs 80.2); in QA F1 the average gain over NV-Embed-v2 on the four multi-hop sets is about 4 points, and on HotpotQA it is 0.2.
At the pinned commit a phrase's seed weight is the last kept triple's score divided by how many passages contain the phrase; the paper describes an average, and the division is not described.

GraphRAG and LightRAG answers are re-phrased with HippoRAG's QA prompt (App. G.2), and LightRAG averages 6.6 F1 with Llama (13.9 with GPT-4o-mini), so part of the gap to these baselines reflects how they were ported.
LV-Eval (124 questions) and NarrativeQA (293 questions over 10 documents) are small samples; the other five sets use 1,000 sampled questions each.
Continual learning is tested only by adding corpus segments (Fig. 3); no experiment updates or corrects stored facts.

abstract.text: HippoRAG 2 treats retrieval-augmented generation as non-parametric continual learning and asks whether structure-augmented RAG can match strong dense retrievers on simple factual questions while keeping its advantage on multi-hop and long-narrative ones. It keeps HippoRAG's LLM-built open knowledge graph and Personalized PageRank search, but adds the passages themselves as graph nodes, links the whole question to triples instead of to extracted entities, and lets an LLM filter those triples before they seed the search. On seven QA benchmarks it reports the best average F1 against large embedding models and graph- or summary-based RAG, with the largest gains on multi-hop sets.

stages.ingestion: A fixed corpus of passages (all candidate passages of 1,000 dev questions per dataset) is indexed offline in one batch.
stages.construction: An LLM first lists the named entities of each passage, then extracts open-IE triples that should contain those entities; the triples' subject and object phrases become KG nodes.
stages.organization: Nodes are joined by triple edges (weighted by how often the pair co-occurs in triples) and by synonymy edges between phrases whose encoder similarity is at least 0.8; each node keeps links to the passages it came from.
stages.update: The paper argues new passages can be added by adding nodes and edges, without re-summarising; the experiments index a fixed corpus once.
stages.retrieval: Query entities from a 1-shot LLM NER are linked to their closest nodes, seeded with weight 1/#passages, and Personalized PageRank (damping 0.5) spreads probability over the KG; passages are scored by the probability of their phrases.
stages.answer: The top-5 passages go to a 1-shot CoT reader (GPT-3.5-turbo-1106); in IRCoT mode each reasoning step's thought is used as the next query.

systems.summary: Retrieval memory modelled on hippocampal indexing: an LLM turns every passage into an open knowledge graph, and a question's entities seed Personalized PageRank over that graph so passages linked through shared entities are found in one step.

discussion.takeaway: Indexing a corpus as an LLM-built open knowledge graph and ranking passages with Personalized PageRank from the question's entities retrieves multi-hop evidence in a single step, beating dense retrievers on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA and matching iterative IRCoT at far lower online cost.

claims.claim: Single-step retrieval beats standard and LLM-augmented retrievers on multi-hop QA.
claims.evidence: R@5 2Wiki 89.1 vs 68.2 (ColBERTv2), MuSiQue 51.9 vs 50.1 (best baseline); HotpotQA slightly lower (77.7 vs 79.3). Table 2, §4.

claims.claim: HippoRAG and iterative retrieval are complementary.
claims.evidence: IRCoT + HippoRAG R@5 57.6 / 93.9 / 83.0 vs IRCoT + ColBERTv2 53.7 / 74.4 / 82.0. Table 3.

claims.claim: Better retrieval gives better QA.
claims.evidence: F1 with a GPT-3.5 reader: 2Wiki 59.5 vs 43.3 (ColBERTv2); IRCoT + HippoRAG best on all three (33.3 / 62.7 / 59.2). Table 4.

claims.claim: PPR is what makes the graph useful.
claims.evidence: Query nodes only: average R@5 56.2 vs 72.9 with PPR. Table 5.

claims.claim: Single-step multi-hop: all supporting passages retrieved more often.
claims.evidence: AR@5 75.7 vs 37.1 on 2Wiki, 22.4 vs 16.1 on MuSiQue. Table 6.

claims.claim: Much cheaper and faster than iterative retrieval online.
claims.evidence: $0.1 and 3 min per 1,000 queries vs $1-3 and 20-40 min for IRCoT. Table 17, App. G.

limits: All components are used off the shelf; most errors come from NER and OpenIE (48% and 28% of 100 MuSiQue errors), which fine-tuning could reduce.
PPR errors remain; letting relations guide the graph walk is left for future work.
OpenIE quality drops on longer passages.
Scalability to much larger indexes is not yet shown.
reading: The reader only ever sees raw passages; the KG changes which passages are chosen, not what is read.
Relation labels are not used anywhere in scoring (edges carry counts or similarity), which matches the authors' note that relations do not yet guide the walk.
Query NER keeps only entities, so non-entity cues in the question are lost; this is the largest error class (48%, Table 11).
Main results use corpora built from the candidate passages of 1,000 dev questions each (6k-12k passages), much smaller than open-domain settings.
QA is reported only for the ColBERTv2 variant and against ColBERTv2 and IRCoT, not the LLM-augmented baselines (RAPTOR, Propositionizer).

abstract.text: HippoRAG is a retrieval framework modelled on the hippocampal indexing theory of long-term memory. Offline, an LLM turns every passage into open knowledge-graph triples, and a retrieval encoder adds edges between similar phrases, forming an index over the corpus. Online, the question's named entities are linked to graph nodes and Personalized PageRank spreads relevance from them, so passages connected through shared entities are found in one retrieval step. On multi-hop QA (MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA) it beats standard retrievers by up to 20% and rivals iterative retrieval at a fraction of the cost and time.

paper.title: HyperGraphRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Hypergraph-Structured Knowledge Representation

construction.unit: n-ary fact: one hyperedge sentence plus the entities it connects
construction.kept_as: chunks verbatim; LLM-extracted hyperedge sentences and entity descriptions
construction.processing: documents cut into 1,200-token chunks (100 overlap); one LLM prompt splits each chunk into knowledge segments (hyperedges, completeness score 0-10) and lists each segment's entities (name, type, description, importance 0-100); up to 2 extra gleaning passes
construction.writer: GPT-4o-mini

organization.structure: knowledge hypergraph stored as a bipartite graph: entity nodes and hyperedge nodes, an edge for each membership
organization.stores: NetworkX graph + three NanoVectorDB stores (entities, hyperedges, chunks) + chunk text store
organization.index: text-embedding-3-small over entity name + description and over hyperedge sentences; chunk vectors are built but not queried

management.operations: new documents are chunked and extracted into the same graph; entities with the same (upper-cased) name are merged, their descriptions joined and LLM-summarised past 500 tokens; identical hyperedge sentences merge with summed scores

retrieval.query: the construction prompt is run on the question: its entity names form the entity query and its extracted sentences form the hyperedge query (code)
retrieval.candidates: top 60 entities and top 60 hyperedges by cosine similarity (> 0.2)
retrieval.selection: one-hop expansion in the bipartite graph (entities to their hyperedges, hyperedges to their entities) plus the source chunks of both; each list cut at 4,000 tokens
retrieval.budget: about 9.2k retrieved tokens at k = 60 (Medicine, Fig. 6a)

use.context: three CSV tables (entities, hyperedges, source chunks) merged from both routes, inside a unified prompt
use.reasoning: single GPT-4o-mini call: reasoning in <think>, answer in <answer>

classify.note: The hypergraph is stored as an ordinary bipartite graph. Candidates come from dense search; the graph only adds one-hop neighbours. Management is 'consolidate' because same-name entities are merged and long descriptions LLM-summarised (inherited LightRAG code); nothing is deleted or edited otherwise.

stages.ingestion: Domain documents (for example the 2024 ESC hypertension guideline, 179k tokens) are cut into 1,200-token chunks with 100 tokens of overlap.
stages.construction: An LLM rewrites each chunk as a list of knowledge segments, each one sentence with a completeness score, and names the entities in each segment with type, description and importance score.
stages.organization: Each segment becomes a hyperedge node linked to its entities in a bipartite graph; entities and hyperedges are embedded in separate vector stores.
stages.update: New documents are added to the same graph; entities with the same name are merged and their descriptions summarised when long.
stages.retrieval: Entities and hyperedges are matched to the question by vector similarity (top 60 each); retrieved entities pull in their hyperedges, retrieved hyperedges pull in their entities, and both pull in the chunks they came from.
stages.answer: The generator reads entity, hyperedge and chunk tables and answers after a reasoning block.

systems.summary: Replaces the binary triples of graph RAG with n-ary facts: each LLM-extracted sentence becomes a hyperedge over all its entities, and entities and hyperedges are retrieved by vector search and expanded to their neighbours and source chunks.

headline: A memory item is an LLM-written sentence (hyperedge) tied to every entity it mentions, not a (subject, relation, object) triple; the source chunk stays attached.
Retrieval is plain vector search over entities and over hyperedges (top 60 each), then one hop in the bipartite graph; there is no graph walk or reranker.
In the code the question is run through the same extraction prompt as the corpus, and the paper's score weighting, thresholds and separate chunk search are not implemented.

glance.a: A hyperedge: one LLM-written sentence stating a fact, linked to every entity it mentions (name, type, description), plus the chunk it came from.
The chunk is kept verbatim; hyperedges and entity descriptions are LLM rewrites, and long merged descriptions are summarised.
A bipartite graph of entity nodes and hyperedge nodes, with separate vector stores for entities and hyperedges.
No. Items are ordered by cosine similarity (scores only break ties) and cut at 4,000 tokens per list.

discussion.takeaway: Storing facts as sentences linked to all their entities, rather than as binary triples, and retrieving them together with their source chunks gives the best F1 on the authors' five domain QA sets, where binary graph RAG methods mostly fall below chunk RAG.

claims.claim: HyperGraphRAG beats every baseline in every domain.
claims.evidence: Overall F1 35.35 / 33.89 / 31.30 / 43.81 / 48.71 vs StandardRAG 27.90 / 27.43 / 28.93 / 37.34 / 43.20 (Medicine / Agriculture / CS / Legal / Mix); R-S and G-E also highest. Table 2, §5.2

claims.claim: Binary-relation graph RAG methods often do worse than chunk RAG.
claims.evidence: Medicine overall F1: GraphRAG 17.60, LightRAG 12.79, PathRAG 14.94, HippoRAG2 21.34 vs StandardRAG 27.90. Table 2

claims.claim: Entity retrieval, hyperedge retrieval and chunks each help.
claims.evidence: Medicine F1 35.4 full; 29.8 without entities, 26.4 without hyperedges, 29.2 without chunks, 12.9 with none. Fig. 4, §5.3

claims.claim: The hypergraph captures more knowledge than binary graphs.
claims.evidence: CS: 26,902 hyperedges vs 930 GraphRAG communities and 5,632 LightRAG relations. Fig. 5f, §5.4

claims.claim: Cost stays close to other graph RAG methods.
claims.evidence: 3.084 s and $0.0063 per 1k construction tokens (HippoRAG2 2.758 s / $0.0056); 0.256 s and $3.184 per 1k queries (LightRAG 0.359 s / $3.359). Table 3, §5.7

limits: Text only; images, tables and structured records are left for a multimodal version.
Retrieval uses fixed similarity metrics that may not match downstream usefulness; learning retrieval with RL is future work.
Assumes the knowledge can be centralised; a federated, privacy-preserving version is future work.
A hypergraph is built per task or domain; a pretrained hypergraph retrieval model is future work.
Not yet tested on harder tasks such as multi-hop QA or broader domains.
discussion.limits_src: paper App. I (Limitations and Future Work)
reading: The headline gains over StandardRAG (+7.45 F1, +7.62 R-S, +3.69 G-E) are exactly the Medicine differences in Table 2; averaged over the five domains the gaps are +5.65 F1, +13.1 R-S and +2.67 G-E. The N-ary claim (+5.3 F1) matches the five-domain average, but the Binary claim (+8.6) matches neither (average +5.99, Medicine +9.58).

In the released evaluation code the StandardRAG context is the 'Sources' part of HyperGraphRAG's own retrieval (chunks reached through retrieved entities and hyperedges), not an independent top-5 dense search as App. G states. Its Medicine row (27.90 / 62.57 / 55.66) equals the ablation 'w/o ER & HR' (27.9 / 62.6 / 55.7), consistent with that.

So the StandardRAG gap measures adding the entity and hyperedge tables on top of the same chunks, and the ablation 'without chunks' keeps entity and hyperedge tables whose selection still depends on the graph.
The paper's score weighting (similarity x score with thresholds 50 and 5) and chunk retrieval (k = 5, tau = 0.5) are not in the code; the code uses cosine > 0.2, top 60 and 4,000-token caps per list.
At query time the question is run through the corpus extraction prompt, so hyperedge search matches LLM-written sentences about the question rather than the question itself.

The evaluation sets are built by the authors (GPT-written questions from sampled knowledge fragments, human-checked; 512 per domain); no public QA benchmark is used, although App. I lists multi-hop QA as future work.

G-E averages the judge's seven 0-10 scores with the answer's F1 (App. E Eq. 45), so it is not independent of F1; R-S compares retrieved text with the gold fragments via SimCSE and is 0 for any method that retrieves nothing.

HippoRAG2 is run with 'top-60' units (Table 4) and scores far lower here than in its own paper's setting (for example R-S 18.58 on Agriculture); how its passages were limited to the shared token budget is not described.

abstract.text: HyperGraphRAG argues that graph-based RAG is held back by binary edges, which split facts involving several entities into disconnected triples. It instead has an LLM rewrite documents into short fact sentences, each a hyperedge joining all the entities it involves, stores them as a bipartite graph with vector indexes for entities and hyperedges, and retrieves both before expanding to neighbours and source chunks. On question sets the authors built over medicine, agriculture, computer science, law and a mixed corpus, it reports higher answer F1, retrieval similarity and judged generation quality than chunk RAG and four binary graph RAG methods, at similar cost.

systems.name: HyperMem

paper.title: HyperMem: Hypergraph Memory for Long-Term Conversations

construction.unit: episode (dialogue segment with title, summary and third-person narrative) + facts
construction.kept_as: LLM-rewritten episode narrative and summary; extracted fact sentences; raw turns kept
construction.processing: LLM boundary detector cuts the stream into episodes; LLM writes title, summary and narrative; facts extracted per topic
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4.1-mini in the released config)

organization.structure: three-level hypergraph: topics → episodes → facts; a topic is a weighted hyperedge over its episodes, an episode a weighted hyperedge over its facts
organization.stores: topic, episode and fact nodes with BM25 and dense indexes
organization.index: Qwen3-Embedding-4B dense (embeddings propagated through hyperedges, λ = 0.5) + BM25

management.operations: LLM matches each new episode against existing topics: joins and regenerates matched topics, or starts a new one

retrieval.query: question used as is
retrieval.candidates: BM25 + dense fused by RRF at each level: topics, then episodes of the chosen topics, then facts of the chosen episodes
retrieval.selection: top-10 topics, top-10 episodes, top-30 facts; paper adds Qwen3-Reranker-4B at each level (off by default in the released code)
retrieval.budget: 10 episodes + 30 facts (7.5x Mem0's tokens, Fig. 5)

use.context: episode narratives with timestamps + fact sentences with time and place
use.reasoning: single chain-of-thought answer call

classify.note: The paper reranks each level with Qwen3-Reranker-4B; the released code turns the reranker off by default, so the top-k of the RRF list decides.

stages.ingestion: Messages stream into a buffer; an LLM boundary detector decides after each new message whether the buffer forms a complete episode (topic change, time gap, closing signals).
stages.construction: Each episode gets an LLM-written title, 2-4 sentence summary and a detailed third-person narrative with absolute dates; the raw turns are kept. Facts (a sentence, the questions it could answer, keywords, an importance weight) are later extracted per topic and anchored to their source episodes.
stages.organization: Topics group episodes through weighted episode hyperedges; each episode groups its facts through a weighted fact hyperedge. Node embeddings are shifted towards their hyperedges' weighted means (h' = h + 0.5·Σ h_e).
stages.update: The LLM compares a new episode with all existing topics (10 per call); matched topics absorb it and get a regenerated title and summary, otherwise a new topic is created. An episode can join several topics.
stages.retrieval: Coarse to fine: BM25 + dense RRF over topics keeps 10, RRF over those topics' episodes keeps 10, RRF over those episodes' facts keeps 30. The paper reranks each level with Qwen3-Reranker-4B over 100 RRF candidates.
stages.answer: GPT-4.1-mini answers with a step-by-step prompt from the 10 episode narratives and 30 facts; topic text is not included.

systems.summary: Conversation memory as a three-level hypergraph (topics over episodes over facts) with hyperedge-smoothed embeddings, read top-down from topics to episodes to facts.
systems.notes: Venue: ACL 2026 long paper (aclanthology 2026.acl-long.1627), matching the arXiv comment 'ACL 2026 Main'. The paper says code is 'about to be released'; the official repo EverMind-AI/HyperMem (linked from EverOS's README) was checked at commit 15c70090 (2026-06-03). HyperMem shares its episode prompt design with EverMemOS (same group, EverMind AI).

sources.code_note: Repo created 2026-06-02, about two months after paper v2; 6 commits, head 15c70090. The run script defaults (reranker off, top-k 10/10/30) and the README (top-k 15/25/30) disagree with each other and with the paper (reranker on), so exact identity with the paper's runs is not guaranteed. Episode detection (stage 1) is not in the default run script, which starts from stage 2.

abstract.text: HyperMem argues that pairwise links in RAG and graph memories miss joint relations among several pieces of a long conversation. It stores memory as a hypergraph with three levels: topics, episodes (contiguous dialogue segments) and facts, where hyperedges group all episodes of a topic and all facts of an episode. Embeddings are smoothed along hyperedges and indexed with BM25, and retrieval narrows from topics to episodes to facts. On LoCoMo the authors report 92.73% LLM-judge accuracy, above RAG and memory-system baselines.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: The answer model reads LLM-written episode narratives plus extracted facts; topic text and raw turns are not included.
Topics only route: the answer comes from episodes and facts inside the 10 chosen topics, each level re-scored from the question alone.
Removing episode context costs the most (92.66 → 88.90); skipping topic retrieval costs 0.72 points.

discussion.takeaway: Grouping a conversation into topics, episodes and facts linked by hyperedges, and reading it top-down, gives the highest LoCoMo score in the paper (92.73), mostly thanks to returning whole episode narratives alongside facts.

claims.claim: State of the art on LoCoMo.
claims.evidence: 92.73 overall vs 86.49 HyperGraphRAG and 85.38 MIRIX. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Hyperedges bind scattered episodes for multi-hop questions.
claims.evidence: multi-hop 93.62 vs 84.04 LightRAG; facts-only retrieval loses 5.68 on multi-hop. Table 1, §4.3

claims.claim: Episode context is the most important component.
claims.evidence: without it 88.90 (−3.76), temporal −5.61. Table 2, Fig. 3

claims.claim: Enough topics must be opened.
claims.evidence: topic top-k 1 → 10 raises 76.88 → 92.66. §4.4, Fig. 4

claims.claim: More accurate and cheaper than graph RAG.
claims.evidence: 92.73 at 7.5x Mem0 tokens vs GraphRAG 67.60 at 35.3x and HyperGraphRAG 86.49 at 26.3x. Fig. 5

limits: Assumes a single user; multi-user or multi-agent memory raises access-control and isolation issues.
Open-domain questions stay hard because they need knowledge beyond the conversation.
reading: Memory-system baselines are copied from other papers (Mem0, MIRIX, MemOS) that used other answer models: the Mem0-sourced rows used GPT-4o-mini while HyperMem uses GPT-4.1-mini, and MIRIX's source judged with GPT-4.1, not the GPT-4o-mini the caption states.
The best result (92.73) and the ablation baseline (92.66) come from slightly different top-k settings; λ and top-k were tuned on LoCoMo itself, the only benchmark.

Topics only select which episodes are searched: their text never reaches the answer model, and episode and fact scores do not use the topic score or the hyperedge weights (code stage4 L680-L710, L795-L825).

Skipping topic retrieval costs 0.72 points, while dropping episode narratives costs 3.76, so most of the gain comes from giving the answer model rewritten episodes, much as in EverMemOS from the same group.
BM25 at the episode and fact levels scores the whole conversation and keeps only hits inside the chosen set (top 2k), so it can contribute few candidates.
The released code has no reranker by default and a question-type 'temporal enhancement' flag that is computed but unused; which settings produced Table 1 cannot be checked.
The repo README reprints Table 1 with a few different baseline cells (OpenAI open-domain 63.22 vs 62.29, LangMem 72.20 vs 71.12, MemU 50.56 vs 50.01).

systems.name: In-Context Autoencoder (ICAE)

paper.title: In-context Autoencoder for Context Compression in a Large Language Model

construction.unit: span of k memory slots (continuous vectors) encoding one context
construction.kept_as: compressed: k = 128 hidden-state vectors per ≤512-token context
construction.processing: LoRA-adapted copy of the LLM reads the context plus k learnable memory tokens; the final hidden states at the memory positions are the slots
construction.writer: ICAE encoder: target LLM + LoRA (query, value) + memory-token embeddings, trained by autoencoding, text continuation and instruction fine-tuning

organization.structure: one fixed-length span per context; long inputs are split into chunks whose spans are concatenated
organization.stores: none beyond the slots, which can be cached for reuse

management.operations: none; slots are produced once per context

retrieval.query: none; the prompt is appended after the slots
retrieval.candidates: all slots
retrieval.selection: none
retrieval.budget: k = 128 slots for up to 512 tokens (4x); k = 32, 64, 256 also tested

use.context: memory slots followed by the prompt; the original tokens are not given
use.reasoning: single generation by the frozen target LLM

classify.note: A context compressor rather than a searchable store: the decoder always reads every slot, and multi-span inputs only concatenate spans.

stages.ingestion: A context of up to 512 tokens (training maximum) is taken as is; longer inputs are cut into chunks that are compressed one by one (§3.3.3).
stages.construction: k learnable memory tokens are appended to the context and run through the LLM with a LoRA adapter on the query and value projections; the last-layer hidden states at those k positions are the memory slots (k = 128 by default).
stages.organization: One span of slots per context; for long inputs the chunk spans are concatenated in order.
stages.retrieval: No retrieval: the decoder receives every slot.
stages.answer: The untouched target LLM reads the slots followed by the prompt (wrapped in a fine-tuning marker token in the code) and generates the response.
stages.learning: The encoder (LoRA + memory-token embeddings, about 1% extra parameters) is pretrained on the Pile with autoencoding and text continuation, then fine-tuned on 240k PwC (context, prompt, response) triples; the decoder LLM stays frozen.

systems.summary: Compresses a context into 128 memory slots with a LoRA-tuned copy of the LLM, pretrained by autoencoding and continuation so the unchanged LLM can read the slots in place of the original 512 tokens (4x).

headline: The memory is 128 continuous vectors per 512-token context, written by a LoRA-tuned copy of the LLM; the LLM that reads them is left unchanged.
Nothing is searched: the decoder reads every slot, so ICAE is a context compressor, not a retrieval memory.
The main quality numbers are GPT-4 pairwise judgements on the authors' own PwC set, not accuracy on an external benchmark.
