discussion.takeaway: An LLM can be taught, with a small LoRA encoder, to squeeze a 512-token context into 128 vectors that the unchanged LLM reads almost as well as the text. Pretraining the encoder by autoencoding is what makes the slots faithful.

claims.claim: The slots keep almost all of the context at 4× compression.
claims.evidence: Autoencoding BLEU 99.1-99.8 and loss below 0.02 for 512 → 128 (Table 6); near-perfect restoration below 300 tokens (Fig. 4).

claims.claim: An LLM reading 128 slots can beat other 7B models reading the full context.
claims.evidence: Llama-7b + ICAE vs Alpaca: win 56.7 / lose 26.9; vs StableLM: 74.1 / 18.8 (Table 4).

claims.claim: Pretraining matters more than slot count.
claims.evidence: Pretrained k=64 roughly matches non-pretrained k=128 (33.1 vs 28.0 win/lose); pretrained vs not at k=128: 60.4 vs 9.5 (Table 5).

claims.claim: Slots are more informative than a natural-language summary of the same length.
claims.evidence: vs a 128-token GPT-4 summary: win 34.1, lose 17.6 (Table 5).

claims.claim: Stronger LLMs compress better.
claims.evidence: Continuation PPL gap +0.49 / +0.37 / +0.30 for Llama-7b / Llama-2-7b / Llama-2-13b (Table 6).

claims.claim: Compression speeds up inference.
claims.evidence: 2.2× to 3.6× lower total latency; over 7× suggested if slots are cached (Table 7, §3.3.2).

limits: Experiments stop at 13B-parameter Llama models because of compute.
Compression is lossy: the compressed model still trails its counterpart with the original context, and going beyond 4× is hard.
The GPT-4 judge favours longer answers, which the authors say understates ICAE's short fine-tuned outputs.
reading: ICAE is working memory for one context: nothing is stored across sessions, searched or updated, and the decoder always reads every slot.
The slots are computed without seeing the prompt, so one span can serve many questions; that is also why they must keep everything rather than what a question needs.
Against the same Llama-2-7b-chat reading the original context, ICAE at k = 128 wins 19.6% and loses 45.4% (Table 4); the large wins are against different models (Alpaca, StableLM).
PwC prompts, reference answers and the judge all come from GPT-4, and training and test contexts are about 512 tokens, so there is no external long-context benchmark in the paper.
The human-like memorisation argument rests on one restoration example (Table 2) and a three-row test on random text (Table 3).

abstract.text: ICAE compresses a long context into a short sequence of memory slots that an LLM can read in place of the original text. The encoder is the same LLM with a small LoRA adapter and a set of memory tokens whose final hidden states become the slots; the LLM that reads them is left unchanged. The encoder is pretrained on large text corpora to reconstruct and continue the input from the slots, then fine-tuned on context-prompt-response data. With Llama models it reaches 4x compression with small quality loss, faster inference and lower GPU memory, and the authors relate the slots to human working memory.

construction.unit: tree node: raw chunk, chunk/cluster summary, or surprising-information text
construction.kept_as: leaves verbatim; summaries and surprising facts written by the LLM
construction.processing: chunk (≤600 tokens), LLM writes a summary plus a list of surprising facts; GMM clusters the summaries and each cluster is summarized again, recursively (RAPTOR-style)

organization.structure: RAPTOR tree of recursive summaries, with surprising-information nodes beside each summary
organization.stores: one tree per document, searched as a flat table; Short-Term Memory (STM) text buffer at query time
organization.index: SBERT embeddings of all nodes

management.operations: STM overwritten with the answer model's new output each inner-loop round
management.forgetting: previous STM text is replaced

retrieval.query: user query plus current STM text
retrieval.candidates: collapsed tree: every node of every level in one table
retrieval.selection: nearest by vector distance (top-k not stated)
retrieval.budget: not stated; up to 5 inner-loop rounds

use.context: retrieved nodes + previous STM + question
use.reasoning: repeat retrieve-then-write until STM stops changing (LCS check) or 5 rounds; final STM is the answer

classify.note: The document tree is append-only; what is updated in place is the STM buffer, which the answer LLM rewrites each round and which is fed back into the next query.

stages.ingestion: The long input is split into contiguous chunks of at most 600 tokens; a sentence that would cross the limit moves to the next chunk.
stages.construction: The summary model writes, per chunk, a regular summary and a separate list of surprising facts that differ from the main text.
stages.organization: As in RAPTOR, summaries (not surprising facts) are embedded with SBERT, clustered with Gaussian mixtures and summarized again, recursively, into a multi-level tree.
stages.update: At query time a Short-Term Memory (STM) holds up to the answer model's output length; each inner-loop round overwrites it with the new answer text.
stages.retrieval: Collapsed-tree search: all nodes sit in one table and the closest by vector distance to the query (question plus current STM) are returned.
stages.answer: The answer model reads retrieved info, the previous STM and the question and writes a new STM; the loop stops when STM converges (LCS) or after 5 rounds, and the STM is returned as the answer.

systems.summary: RAPTOR-style summary tree whose nodes also keep 'surprising' facts, read by an inner loop that re-queries the tree with the LLM's own intermediate answer (Short-Term Memory) until it stops changing.
systems.notes:
Long-context QA paper (4-page NeurIPS 2024 AFM workshop paper); memory is a document tree plus a query-time scratch buffer, not a conversational store. Results are heatmaps on M-NIAH and BABILong with 10 test cases per cell; there is no official code link in the paper and no repository was found by name search.

sources.code_note: No code link in the paper; a GitHub search for ILM-TR and the full method name found no repository. Top-k, retrieved-token budget and the LCS convergence threshold are not stated (App. A.3 says unlisted parameters are defaults).

abstract.text: ILM-TR targets long inputs that exceed the model's context window. It builds a RAPTOR-like tree of chunk and cluster summaries, but asks the summarizer to also list surprising facts that do not fit the main content. At question time an inner loop retrieves from the tree, lets the LLM write an intermediate answer into a small Short-Term Memory, and uses that memory together with the question as the next query, until the memory stops changing. With Llama-3-70B the authors report finding all needles in a multi-needle test up to 500k tokens and gains over RAPTOR on BABILong.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Two changes to RAPTOR: summaries also list 'surprising' facts, and retrieval loops, feeding the LLM's own intermediate answer back into the query.
The Short-Term Memory is a single ≤200-token text that is overwritten each round and returned as the final answer.
Results are 10 test cases per heatmap cell with a 4-bit Llama-3-70B; no top-k or context budget is given.

The loop repeats until the STM stops changing or after 5 rounds, and the STM itself is returned as the answer.

discussion.takeaway: Letting the LLM's intermediate answer steer further retrieval, and keeping surprising facts in the summaries, helps a RAPTOR tree find several scattered needles in very long inputs.

claims.claim: Adding surprising information to summaries improves multi-needle retrieval.
claims.evidence: M-NIAH: RAPTOR finds no needle in any of the 40 cells, ILM-TR without the loop finds all three in 23 and two in 13 (150k-500k tokens). §4, Fig. 3

claims.claim: The inner loop finds all needles.
claims.evidence: M-NIAH: all 40 cells score 10 up to 500k tokens. Fig. 3(c)

claims.claim: ILM-TR beats the RAPTOR baseline on BABILong.
claims.evidence: e.g. qa1 at 128k: 60 vs 0; qa5 at 64k: 70 vs 20 (10 cases per cell). Fig. 4

claims.claim: No major loss as context grows to 500k tokens.
claims.evidence: §1 and Fig. 3(c)

limits: The inner loop needs several iterations, so answering takes longer.
Writing surprise summaries needs a model that follows complex instructions; 7-8B models failed the prompt, so a slower 70B model was used.
reading: Each heatmap cell has only 10 test cases (BABILong) and M-NIAH cells are shown by colour only, so small differences are within noise; our M-NIAH counts are read from colours.
The loop's gain on BABILong is mixed: ILM-TR is below its no-loop variant in some cells (qa2 at 8k 10 vs 20, qa4 at 64k 70 vs 80, qa5 at 32k 60 vs 70) and above in others.

The RAPTOR baseline uses a plain summary prompt and a plain answer prompt, while ILM-TR's no-loop variant changes only the summary prompt, so the no-loop variant isolates the surprise-summary change and the full system isolates the loop.
Retrieval top-k and token budget are not reported; the final answer is the STM text, which can still hold intermediate reasoning (App. A.2.2), and the BABILong scoring rule is not stated.
M-NIAH uses three needles on one topic (pizza ingredients) inserted into a haystack whose source text is not named.

discussion.takeaway: Rebuilding the agent's context each round around a self-written report, instead of appending every step, lets a 30B MoE deep-research agent keep improving with more turns; in the authors' tests it beats open-source agents on six benchmarks and helps frontier models as a prompt.

claims.claim: Best open-source deep-research agent on six benchmarks.
claims.evidence: Average +14.5pp over the best open-source agent: HLE 28.8, BC 37.3, BC-zh 45.2, GAIA 72.8, Xbench-DS 71.0, SEAL-0 39.6. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: The iterative workspace beats a growing context under the same training data.
claims.evidence: Average 49.1 vs 36.5 for Mono-Agent (which had 64K context vs 40K). Table 2, §4.3

claims.claim: Accuracy keeps rising with more allowed turns.
claims.evidence: BrowseComp-200: 3.5% at 2 turns to 42.5% at 2048, trained with Tmax 32. Fig. 3, App. B.3

claims.claim: Works as a prompting strategy without training.
claims.evidence: BrowseComp over ReAct: o3 49.7 → 62.4 (+12.7), DeepSeek-V3.1 30.0 → 49.2 (+19.2). Fig. 4

claims.claim: The discounted reward makes exploration shorter at similar accuracy.

discussion.limits_src: not stated: the paper has no limitations section
reading: Nothing bounds the report except the trained policy; the paper never reports report lengths, so the O(1) workspace claim is untested in numbers.

The text and Fig. 3 disagree: the text says 5.5% → 50.1% and 80.1 average turns at 2048, the figure and abstract say 3.5% → 42.5% and 129.5 turns; App. B.3 cites 15.2% at Tmax 32 where the figure shows 23.5.
App. C.3 says Table 1 baseline numbers were taken from the original papers, so tools, search back-ends and turn budgets differ from IterResearch's (which uses Tmax up to 256).
The Mono-Agent ablation changes paradigm and context length (64K vs 40K) together; it is the fairest comparison in the paper but not a single-variable one.
The 'last tool response' is often already a summary: Visit returns a helper LLM's goal-directed extract of the page, not the page.
The released code is a reproduction with different tools, so the reported numbers cannot be traced to code.

abstract.text: IterResearch targets long-horizon deep-research agents, which usually append every search result and thought to one growing context until it fills with noise. Instead, each round the agent works from a small rebuilt workspace: the question, a report it rewrites itself to hold all findings, and only the latest tool call and response. A 30B MoE model is trained for this with rejection-sampling SFT and an RL objective whose rewards are discounted by trajectory length. The authors report large gains over open-source agents on six benchmarks, accuracy that keeps rising up to 2048 turns, and gains for o3 and DeepSeek-V3.1 when the scheme is used only as a prompt.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: KnowledgeEditor

paper.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models

construction.unit: one revision (input x, old prediction y, new prediction a) written into the LM's weights
construction.kept_as: a weight shift Δθ predicted by a hyper-network; no text is stored
construction.processing: a BiLSTM encodes the revision; per weight matrix, small FFNN heads turn that code and the gradient of the loss on a into ΔW
construction.writer: trained hyper-network (54M parameters for BERT, 67M for BART)

organization.structure: none: the fact is spread over the LM's weight matrices
organization.stores: the LM's own parameters

management.operations: one additive update θ' = θ + Δθ per edit; the +loop variant re-applies it until the prediction flips
management.conflicts: editor trained under a KL limit so outputs on other inputs stay the same; edits are evaluated one at a time, never stacked

retrieval.query: any input to the LM
retrieval.candidates: none: the model reads its parameters

use.context: the input alone; the revised fact is read from the edited weights
use.reasoning: one forward pass; beam search (5 beams in code) for QA, sign of the logit for fact-checking

classify.note: Parametric memory: an edit changes the LM's weights and every later query reads them in one forward pass; there is no store to search.

stages.ingestion: An edit request names an input x, the model's current prediction y and the desired prediction a.
stages.construction: A hyper-network encodes the request with a BiLSTM and, for each weight matrix, combines that code with the gradient of the loss on a to predict a weight shift ΔW.
stages.update: The shift is added to the weights once (θ' = θ + Δθ); an optional test-time loop re-applies it until the prediction changes.
stages.answer: Every later query is answered by the edited model directly from its parameters.
stages.learning: The hyper-network is trained once per model by constrained optimization: raise the likelihood of a (and optionally of paraphrases of x) while keeping the KL divergence on other inputs below an annealed margin, solved with a Lagrange multiplier.

systems.summary: Learned knowledge editor: a hyper-network turns one fact revision and its gradient into a weight update for BERT or BART, trained to change that fact and its paraphrases while keeping all other predictions fixed.
systems.notes:
VENUE: EMNLP 2021 main (Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing; aclanthology 2021.emnlp-main.522). arXiv comment says 'Accepted at EMNLP2021' but then names the 2020 proceedings; the ACL Anthology page confirms 2021. Text read from arXiv v2 (2021-09-08).
SCOPE: memory here is the LM's parameters, not an external store. Each edit is evaluated on its own starting from the original model; the paper does not test sequences of edits.
RESULTS: all four metrics go in category with metric 'other' (they are accuracies except performance deterioration, a relative drop where lower is better). QA equivalence accuracy has two numbers (generated / human paraphrases), kept as two categories.

headline: The 'memory' being edited is the LM's weights; nothing is stored outside the model and nothing is retrieved.
One learned network writes each edit as a single weight update; a KL limit during its training is what keeps other predictions unchanged.
Every edit is scored alone on a fresh copy of the original model, so the results say nothing about many edits in a row.

abstract.text: Language models hold facts in their weights, and some of those facts are wrong or go out of date. KnowledgeEditor fixes a single fact without retraining: a hyper-network, given the fact to change and the model's gradient, predicts a weight update. It is trained with a constraint that keeps the model's output distribution on other inputs unchanged, and optionally with paraphrases so that equivalent questions change too. The authors test it on a BERT fact-checker (FEVER) and a BART closed-book QA model (zsRE) and find the updates concentrate in a few components.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

units.name: Edit
units.role: one fact revision applied to the model
units.made_by: KnowledgeEditor hyper-network

fields.name: condition text
fields.what: the revision written as 'y >> a || x' (old prediction, new prediction, input) and read by the BiLSTM

fields.name: gradient
fields.what: gradient of the loss of a on x for every weight matrix of the frozen LM

fields.name: weight shift Δθ
fields.what: σ(η)·(α̂∘∇W + β̂) per matrix, with α̂ and β̂ rank-one outer products; added to every matrix except biases, norms and embeddings
fields.src: paper §4 Eq. 3; code one_shot_learner.py L35-L69, bart_seq2seq_augmented_kilt.py L75-L100

write.how: BiLSTM (hidden 128 per direction) over 'y >> a || x', then an FFNN to a 1,024-dim vector h
write.src: paper App. B.5; code one_shot_learner.py L72-L105

write.how: backpropagate the loss of the new prediction a on x through the frozen LM
per weight matrix, an FFNN on h gives α, β, γ, δ, η; ΔW = σ(η)·(softmax outer product ∘ gradient + bias term)
θ' = θ + Δθ, once
write.out: success rate 98.80 (FC) / 94.65 (QA) with a single update

write.how: minimize the loss on a (and on paraphrases for +Px) plus α·(KL on the rest of the mini-batch - margin); α is updated by gradient ascent and clipped at 0; margin ×0.8 whenever > 90% of validation edits succeed
write.src: paper §4, App. A, B.6; code bart_seq2seq_augmented_kilt.py L245-L283, L411-L436

read.scores: nothing is matched; the query runs through the edited weights
read.how: QA: beam search, top-1 (5 beams in code); FC: positive logit means 'true'
if the prediction is still not a, add the same Δθ again; test time only
read.src: paper §6.1, Table 1 †; code bart_seq2seq_augmented_kilt.py L369-L404, eval_bart_seq2seq.py L255-L265

excludes: paraphrases (used only in training and scoring)

compression.basis: Not applicable in token terms: an edit is a dense shift over all weight matrices of a 110M (BERT) or 139M (BART) model, produced by a 54M / 67M-parameter editor (App. B.5).

numbers.value: BERT on FEVER 77.1%; BART on zsRE 22.1% exact match

numbers.label: Chance full KE beats all baselines

paper_vs_code.paper: Adam, lr 3e-4 (1e-1 for the multiplier)
paper_vs_code.code: centered RMSprop with the same learning rates

paper_vs_code.paper: stop on success or after at most 100 gradient steps
paper_vs_code.code: eval scripts loop until the prediction flips, with no step limit

paper_vs_code.paper: updates are applied in a loop until success (up to a maximum), affecting all metrics
paper_vs_code.code: the loop runs only when scoring paraphrases; success and retain use the single update (the looped Δθ is discarded), unlike the FEVER script

paper_vs_code.paper: five FFNNs [1024, tanh, d] per weight matrix
paper_vs_code.code: one FFNN per matrix (1,024 → 128, tanh → output) whose output is split into the five vectors

paper_vs_code.paper: 200k updates, batch 1,024 (FC) / 256 (QA)
paper_vs_code.code: FC script: batch 256, 50k steps on 1 GPU; QA script: batch 64 on 4 GPUs, 200k steps

open_questions: Edits are never accumulated, so whether retain accuracy holds after tens or thousands of edits is untested.
Retain accuracy compares against the model's own old predictions, not gold answers, so it rewards stability rather than correctness.
Alternative QA answers are other beam hypotheses of the same model, which may be easier targets than arbitrary new facts.

discussion.takeaway: A small learned editor can rewrite one fact in a fine-tuned LM with a single weight update, keeping about 98% of other predictions, whereas fine-tuning or norm-constrained fine-tuning trades success, stability and paraphrase consistency against each other.

claims.claim: KnowledgeEditor meets all three desiderata at once, unlike the baselines.
claims.evidence: FC 98.80 success / 98.14 retain / 82.69 equiv.; QA 94.65 / 98.73 / 86.50; probability of beating all baselines ≈97% (FC) and ≈88% (QA). Table 1, Fig. 6

claims.claim: A constraint in function space (KL) is needed; one in parameter space is not enough.
claims.evidence: With an L2 constraint retain accuracy falls to 45.10 (FC) and 46.66 (QA). Table 1, §6.2

claims.claim: Training with paraphrases improves consistency without hurting success or retain.
claims.evidence: FC equivalence 82.69 → 95.25, QA 86.50 → 91.20 (generated). Table 1, §6.3

claims.claim: Fine-tuning either forgets or does not generalize.
claims.evidence: All layers: retain 86.95 FC / 67.55 QA; 1st layer on FC: equivalence 42.24. Table 1, §6.1

claims.claim: Edits concentrate in a few components, unlike gradients or fine-tuning.
claims.evidence: Update magnitudes, Fig. 4, §6.4; low cosine similarity with fine-tuning updates, App. C Table 2

limits: The editor is trained for a single update; applying several in sequence is left to future work.
The same tool could be used to insert false facts into a model.
discussion.limits_src: paper §6.1 fn. 8, Ethical Considerations (no separate limitations section)
reading: Every edit starts from the original model and is scored alone, so the setting is one fact at a time, not a growing memory.
The edited models are small fine-tuned classifiers and QA models (BERT-base, BART-base with 22.1% zsRE accuracy), and the new QA answers are the model's own lower-ranked beam hypotheses.

Baselines stop only on success (fine-tuning) or after a hyperparameter search that includes retain accuracy (Zhu et al.); KnowledgeEditor without the loop gets one update, so success rates are not measured under equal budgets.
The paper states Adam and a 100-step cap for fine-tuning; the released code uses RMSprop for the editor and has no step cap, and its QA eval applies +loop only to paraphrases.

systems.name: LightMem

paper.title: LightMem: Lightweight and Efficient Memory-Augmented Generation

construction.unit: entry {topic, summary embedding, user turn, model turn}
construction.kept_as: LLMLingua-2-compressed turns + LLM topic summary
construction.processing: LLMLingua-2 token compression; attention+similarity topic segmentation; LLM summarizes each topic group
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4o-mini / Qwen3-30B-A3B / GLM-4.6); LLMLingua-2 compresses

organization.structure: flat LTM; sensory and STM are transient buffers
organization.stores: one LTM store (512-token sensory buffer, th-token STM buffer before it)
organization.index: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings of summaries

management.operations: test-time soft insert only; offline parallel LLM update (add/delete/update/merge)
management.conflicts: each entry's queue: top-k similar entries with later timestamps may update it

retrieval.query: user query as is
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity over all LTM entry embeddings
retrieval.selection: top-k; retriever and k shared with baselines (k value not stated)

use.context: retrieved entries appended to the query
use.reasoning: single answer call

classify.note: Offline add/update/delete/merge is treated as consolidation.

stages.ingestion: Turns are fed one at a time; LLMLingua-2 pre-compresses each turn (keep tokens above the r-th percentile of retention probability) into a 512-token sensory buffer.
stages.construction: When the sensory buffer fills, topic boundaries are the intersection of LLMLingua-2 attention local maxima and low adjacent-turn embedding similarity; topic groups enter an STM buffer and, at threshold th tokens, the backbone LLM summarizes each topic group into entries {topic, embedding(summary), user turn, model turn}.
stages.organization: Flat long-term store of topic-indexed entries (summary embedding plus compressed original turns).
stages.update: Test time: soft update (direct insertion only). Sleep time: for each entry an update queue of top-k similar, later-timestamped entries is built and backbone-LLM updates run offline in parallel.
stages.retrieval: Cosine-similarity vector retrieval (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), same retriever and number of retrieved entries as baselines.
stages.answer: Retrieved entries are appended to the query for the chat model (same backbone as memory model).

systems.summary: Atkinson-Shiffrin-inspired pipeline: token-level pre-compression and topic segmentation (sensory), topic-batched summarization (STM), and offline parallel 'sleep-time' LTM updates, cutting memory-construction tokens and API calls by 1-2 orders of magnitude.
systems.notes:
AXES CORRECTED from the paper; earlier taxonomy row was: MTM entry | compressed | SLM write, offline LTM graph | STM/MTM/LTM | vector 2K -> SLM filter K. AXES-CHECK: the paper disagrees with the seed taxonomy row in several places. (1) Stages are sensory memory -> STM -> LTM; there is no 'MTM'. (2) Entries are written by the backbone LLM (GPT-4o-mini / Qwen3-30B-A3B / GLM-4.6); the small model (LLMLingua-2) only compresses tokens and gives attention for topic segmentation, it does not write entries. (3) LTM is a flat store of entries with an offline parallel update; no graph (a KG is listed only as future work). (4) Retrieval is plain cosine top-k with all-MiniLM-L6-v2; the paper describes no '2K candidates -> SLM filter K' stage (that may come from a later code release; not verified). VENUE: the seed taxonomy listed an ACL version, but LightMem was accepted at ICLR 2026 (OpenReview dyJ0GWpjJB, ICLR 2026 poster; GitHub README). No ACL version found; the same group's StructMem was accepted at ACL 2026, and EverMemOS is ACL 2026 - possibly the source of the mix-up. Numbers taken from the latest arXiv HTML (which adds LoCoMo and GLM-4.6; the v1 abstract covered only LongMemEval).
DESIGN: Sec 3.1-3.3, 5.1, App. A.1 (Tables 4-5), C.1, D. Corrected prefill: 'offline LTM update' moved from construction.processing to management; structure clarified as flat LTM (sensory/STM are buffers, no MTM, no graph); unit made concrete. Nulls: forgetting (no deletion policy beyond LLM update ops), retrieval budget (number of retrieved entries not stated).

systems.name: MAGMA

paper.title: MAGMA: A Multi-Graph based Agentic Memory Architecture for AI Agents

construction.unit: event node: one dialogue turn (episode grouping optional, off by default)
construction.kept_as: verbatim turn + LLM summary, facts, relations, activities, entities and dates
construction.processing: two LLM calls per turn extract a summary, entities, facts, relations and dates (the prompt also sees the neighbouring turns); relative dates resolved by rules
construction.writer: gpt-4o-mini

organization.structure: multigraph over event nodes: temporal chain, semantic, shared-entity and reply/question links, plus session nodes
organization.stores: graph store + vector index (FAISS) + keyword index
organization.index: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding of the LLM summary + keywords; keyword index over extracted terms

management.operations: paper: fast path adds node and temporal edge, an async LLM pass infers causal and entity edges; code: all links built by rules in one batch after ingestion

retrieval.query: question; rule-based type (9 kinds) sets weights and depth
retrieval.candidates: vector top 20 + keyword top 20 + full scan top 25, fused by RRF (k 60); BFS from the top 15 seeds over graph edges (≤ 800 nodes)
retrieval.selection: weighted rule rerank (keyword, entity, time, phrase, similarity); keep 15, or 30 when the gold category is multi-hop
retrieval.budget: 15 or 30 nodes; no token budget in code

use.context: numbered list of nodes: date, speaker, verbatim turn and up to 2 facts, relations and activities each, plus key sentences
use.reasoning: one answer call with a category-specific prompt; code default runs it 3 times and keeps the answer the judge scores highest against the gold answer

classify.note: Anchors are found by hybrid vector + keyword search, but the candidate set comes from walking graph edges out of them; a weighted rule score picks the final nodes.

stages.ingestion: Each dialogue turn becomes one event node timestamped from its session date (episode segmentation exists but is off by default).
stages.construction: Two LLM calls per turn extract a summary, entities, topic, facts, relations, activities and dates; the verbatim turn is kept alongside. The summary plus keywords is embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
stages.organization: Nodes are linked into a multigraph: temporal chain and near-in-time links, semantic neighbours (top 3, similarity > 0.5; ±3 turns), shared-entity links, reply and question-to-next-turn links, and session nodes built from the dataset's session summaries.
stages.update: The paper describes an asynchronous LLM consolidation that adds causal and entity edges; in the released code it is switched off and links are built by rules in one batch after ingestion.
stages.retrieval: Vector, keyword and full-scan lists are fused by RRF (k 60); a similarity-thresholded BFS expands from the top 15 seeds, and a weighted rule score keeps 15 nodes (30 for multi-hop).
stages.answer: The answer model reads a numbered list of the kept turns with dates, speakers and extracted facts, under a prompt chosen by question category.

systems.summary: Conversation memory that stores each turn as an event node linked by temporal, semantic, causal and entity edges, and retrieves by fusing vector and keyword anchors and then walking the graph with query-type weights.

abstract.text: MAGMA stores an agent's conversation history as event nodes connected in four separate graphs: semantic, temporal, causal and entity. At question time it classifies the query, finds entry nodes by fusing vector, keyword and time signals, and walks the graphs with weights that depend on the query type. The retrieved nodes are ordered and serialized into a compact context for the answer model. The authors report better LoCoMo and LongMemEval scores than A-MEM, MemoryOS and Nemori, with lower query latency.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: In the released code the answer model reads the verbatim turns plus LLM-extracted facts; the paper's LLM causal edges, entity nodes and intent-weighted beam search are not on the executed path.
The default LoCoMo script uses gold labels at answer time: the category picks the prompt and node count, and best-of-3 keeps the answer the judge scores highest against the gold answer.
Scores come from the authors' own graded judge (0-1 rubric, gpt-4o-mini) over all 1,986 LoCoMo questions, adversarial included.

discussion.takeaway: Splitting memory links into temporal, causal, semantic and entity views and weighting them by query type gives MAGMA the best LoCoMo judge score in its own comparison (0.700), with the lowest query latency.

claims.claim: Best accuracy among agentic memory systems on LoCoMo.
claims.evidence: Judge 0.700 vs Nemori 0.590, A-MEM 0.580, MemoryOS 0.553, full context 0.481. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Robust on adversarial questions.
claims.evidence: Adversarial 0.742 vs 0.205-0.616 for baselines. Table 1

claims.claim: Generalizes to LongMemEval with far fewer tokens.
claims.evidence: 61.2% vs full context 55.0% and Nemori 56.2%, with 0.7-4.2K tokens per query vs 101K. Table 2, §4.3

claims.claim: Fastest queries.
claims.evidence: 1.47 s vs 2.26 s (A-MEM) and 32.68 s (MemoryOS); 3.37k tokens per query. Table 3, §4.4

claims.claim: Every relation view and the adaptive policy contribute.
claims.evidence: Full 0.700; w/o adaptive policy 0.637, causal 0.644, temporal 0.647, entity 0.666; no single graph above 0.60. Tables 4-5, §4.5

limits: Graph quality depends on the LLM used for consolidation, which can add wrong or miss relations.
Several graphs and two processing streams add storage and engineering cost over a vector-only store.
Evaluated only on conversational benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval); other settings such as multimodal agents may need adaptation.
reading: The default LoCoMo script uses gold labels at answer time: the category chooses the prompt, the node count and an adversarial-only post-filter, and best-of-3 keeps the answer the judge scores highest against the gold answer (at temperature 0 the three answers may often be identical). The paper says the instruction comes from the router with no oracle labels.
Session nodes are built from LoCoMo's own session summaries, and the query code hard-codes LoCoMo-specific keyword-to-session hints (query_engine.py L174-L188).
The LLM causal edges, entity nodes and intent-weighted beam search that define the method in §3 are not on the executed path; the ablations therefore remove rule-built links.
The judge is the authors' graded 0-1 rubric with gpt-4o-mini, and adversarial answers are scored by a refusal pattern in code; scores are not comparable with binary-judge LoCoMo results.
The LongMemEval script scores with a lenient string matcher rather than the LLM judge the paper describes, and routes prompts by the gold question type.
Hyperparameters were tuned on LoCoMo (App. B.1), the benchmark of the main table.
The code's default command tests categories 1-4 and 50 questions per conversation, while Table 1 reports all five categories over 1,986 questions; the exact command behind the tables is not given.

stages.ingestion: Inputs arrive as a sequence of chunks (dialogues, documents, labelled examples or book passages wrapped as user-assistant turns), processed one at a time.

stages.retrieval: At question time BM25 ranks semantic and episodic entries separately against the question and keeps the top 20 of each (fewer if the prompt would exceed 30K tokens).
stages.answer: A frozen Qwen3-32B answers from the core paragraph plus the retrieved entries in a fixed memory prompt.
stages.learning: The writer (Qwen3-4B) is trained with GRPO, without a KL term, on 562 instances of up to 30K tokens; reward = QA accuracy of the final memory + tool-call success + 0.05 × compression + 0.1 × a Qwen3-32B check that each write fits its memory type.

systems.summary: Trains a small model with RL to write a core/semantic/episodic memory through tool calls, rewarding the QA accuracy that a fixed BM25 reader achieves on the final memory; the learned writer generalises from 30K-token training inputs to 400K+.

headline: Only the memory writer is trained: a 4B model learns by RL which insert / update / delete calls to make; retrieval (BM25) and the answer model (Qwen3-32B) stay fixed.
The reward is the QA accuracy that fixed reader gets from the final memory, plus tool-call success, a compression term and an LLM check that each write fits its store.
While writing, the agent sees only the core paragraph and the 5 newest entries of each list, so it can edit only those.

abstract.text: Mem-α argues that memory agents fail less from missing tools than from not knowing what to store, where, and when to update, and proposes to learn this with reinforcement learning. An agent reads a stream of chunks and writes to a memory made of a core summary, a semantic fact list and an episodic event list through tool calls; after the stream ends, questions are answered from that memory by a fixed retriever and reader, and the accuracy becomes the reward, together with format, compression and content-validity terms. A Qwen3-4B trained this way on a purpose-built dataset beats long-context, BM25 RAG, MemAgent and MEM1 baselines, and although trained on inputs of at most 30K tokens it handles MemoryAgentBench inputs above 400K tokens.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

discussion.takeaway: Train the memory writer, not the reader: RL on end-task QA accuracy teaches a 4B model to fill a core/semantic/episodic memory well enough to beat long-context and RAG baselines, and the skill carries over to inputs more than 13× longer than any seen in training.

claims.claim: Mem-α beats all baselines on average, in and out of distribution.
claims.evidence: Validation avg 0.642 vs 0.588 (Long-Context) and 0.567 (RAG-Top2); MemoryAgentBench avg 0.592 vs 0.502 and 0.461. Tables 1-2, §4.2

claims.claim: The gain comes from RL, not the memory design.
claims.evidence: Same framework with an untrained Qwen3-4B writer 0.389, with gpt-4.1-mini 0.517, with Mem-α 0.642. Table 3, §4.3

claims.claim: Trained on ≤30K tokens, it generalises to 400K+.
claims.evidence: MemoryAgentBench Multi-Doc inputs reach 474K tokens; Mem-α 0.680 there vs 0.450 RAG-Top2. Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: The content-validity reward is essential.
claims.evidence: γ = 0 drops the validation average to 0.543 (0.445 on MemoryAgentBench). Table 4, Table 9

claims.claim: The compression reward trades memory size for accuracy.
claims.evidence: β 0.2 and 0.4 give 4.7K and 3.6K tokens at 0.525 and 0.509; β 0.05 shrinks BookSum memory from 4.5K to 2.2K at similar accuracy. Table 4, §4.4

claims.claim: Flat single-paragraph memories are not enough.
claims.evidence: MemAgent 0.198 and MEM1 0.071 on MemoryAgentBench. Table 2, §4.2

limits: The memory architecture is simple; richer systems such as MIRIX could help.
Training and evaluation run in simulated settings; real databases and production use raise latency, scalability and safety questions.
Conflict resolution is not trained or evaluated, for lack of realistic benchmarks (§3.4).
Qwen3-8B could not follow the tool format reliably and was dropped (App. C.1).
reading: The 'Mem.' columns count everything stored, not what the reader sees: on MemoryAgentBench Mem-α stores 129K tokens on average, but the reader gets at most core + 20 + 20 entries under 30K tokens (code), while RAG-Top2 reads only 2 raw chunks and Long-Context the last 32K tokens.

Mem-α does not win every set: on MemoryAgentBench it trails Long-Context on NLU (0.710 vs 0.740), Clinic (0.730 vs 0.860) and Banking77 (0.700 vs 0.770) and RAG-Top2 on LME(S*) (0.520 vs 0.581); on validation it trails on HotpotQA, NLU and PubMed.
Table 1 sets are the validation split of the training sources, so they are in-distribution; Table 2 is the out-of-distribution test.
MemAgent answers with its own 14B model, while every other method answers with Qwen3-32B.
When writing, the agent is shown only the 5 newest entries of each list, so updates and deletes can target only recent entries; older contradictions cannot be fixed.
Embeddings (text-embedding-3-small) are computed for every entry but the default reader ranks by BM25 only.
The averages mix different metrics (SubEM, EM, keyword hit, LLM judge), and the LME(S*) judge model is not named.
The paper gives γ = 1 in §4.1 and γ = 0.1 in §4.4; the code and README use 0.1.

paper.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory

construction.unit: fact (Mem0^g: entity nodes + relation triplets)
construction.kept_as: extracted
construction.processing: LLM extracts salient facts from message pair, summary, last 10 messages
construction.writer: GPT-4o-mini

organization.structure: flat (+ directed labeled entity graph in Mem0^g)
organization.stores: vector database (+ Neo4j graph for Mem0^g)
organization.index: dense embeddings (model not named)

management.operations: ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP chosen per candidate fact
management.conflicts: LLM compares each new fact with the 10 most similar memories
management.forgetting: DELETE of contradicted memories; Mem0^g marks relations invalid instead

retrieval.candidates: Mem0^g: entity-anchored subgraph plus query-triplet similarity; base Mem0 unstated
retrieval.selection: Mem0^g: triplets above relevance threshold, ranked by similarity

use.reasoning: single answer call, step-by-step prompt

classify.note: The graph variant Mem0^g adds an entity graph.

stages.ingestion: Processes each new message pair together with an asynchronously refreshed conversation summary and the last m=10 messages.
stages.construction: An LLM (GPT-4o-mini) extracts a set of salient candidate facts from the new exchange. Mem0^g additionally extracts entities and relationship triplets.
stages.organization: Flat store of natural-language memories in a vector database; the graph variant stores a directed labeled entity graph in Neo4j.
stages.update: Each candidate fact is compared with the top s=10 similar memories and an LLM tool call chooses ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP. Mem0^g marks conflicting relations invalid instead of deleting them.
stages.retrieval: Dense similarity search over memories; Mem0^g adds entity-anchored subgraph expansion plus dense matching over relationship triplets.
stages.answer: Retrieved timestamped memories of both speakers are placed in an answer prompt (App. A).

systems.summary: Extracts salient facts from each message pair and lets an LLM consolidate them against similar existing memories with ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP; an optional graph variant stores entity-relation triplets.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: the paper does not state a top-10 retrieval size at query time; s=10 is the number of similar memories used in the update phase (Sec 2.1). Embedding model for Mem0's own store is not named. Graph variant (Mem0^g) is recorded as system mem0, variant 'graph'. Venue from IOS Press FAIA vol. 413 (ECAI 2025); paper points to https://mem0.ai/research for code.
DESIGN: Sec 2.1-2.2, Sec 3.3, Sec 4.5, App. A. Corrected: 'add/update/delete' moved from construction.processing to management.operations; retrieval 'dense top-10' dropped (s=10 is update-phase, query-time k not stated).

systems.name: MemAgent

paper.title: MemAgent: Reshaping Long-Context LLM with Multi-Conv RL-based Memory Agent

construction.unit: one free-text memory of at most 1,024 tokens per question
construction.kept_as: LLM-written notes (copied sentences plus the model's comments), rewritten whole after every chunk
construction.processing: the model reads question + previous memory + next 5,000-token chunk and writes a new memory that replaces the old one
construction.writer: RL-trained Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct (RL-MemoryAgent), same model that answers

organization.structure: single text buffer inside the prompt
organization.stores: one memory string; no external store

management.operations: overwrite the whole memory after each chunk
management.conflicts: left to the model; no explicit rule
management.forgetting: implicit: whatever the new memory omits is gone; output beyond 1,024 tokens is cut

retrieval.query: the question is in every update prompt, so writing is question-conditioned
retrieval.candidates: no retrieval: every chunk is read once, in order
retrieval.selection: the RL-trained model decides what to keep while writing
retrieval.budget: memory 1,024 + chunk 5,000 + question 1,024 + output 1,024 tokens (8K window)

use.context: question + final memory only
use.reasoning: single answer call after K memory updates

classify.note: No store or search: the model streams the whole document and keeps one overwritten text memory; selection happens at write time by an RL-trained policy.

stages.ingestion: The document is tokenised and cut into consecutive 5,000-token chunks that are fed one per call; nothing is indexed.
stages.construction: At each chunk the model sees the question, the previous memory and the chunk, and generates a new memory (at most 1,024 tokens) through a fixed prompt.
stages.update: The new memory overwrites the old one, so keeping, merging and dropping are all implicit in what the model writes.
stages.answer: After the last chunk a second prompt gives the model only the question and the final memory and asks for the answer.
stages.learning: Multi-conv DAPO: all K update calls and the answer call of a rollout share one advantage computed from a rule-based exact-match reward on the final answer (group size 16), in two curriculum stages on synthetic HotpotQA and DocQA data.

systems.summary: An LLM reads a long document chunk by chunk and overwrites a fixed 1,024-token text memory after each chunk; RL on the final answer (Multi-conv DAPO) teaches it what to keep, so an 8K-window model is tested up to 3.5M tokens.
systems.notes:
Venue: arXiv comment and PDF footer both say ICLR 2026 (oral per the arXiv comment; OpenReview forum k5nIOvYGCL). PDF read: arXiv v2 (29 Jul 2026). Code: BytedTsinghua-SIA/MemAgent at ef4219b (2026-05-12, latest; evaluation files last changed 2025-07). Was a baseline-only entry in extra_systems.json under the same id.
DESIGN: §2.1-2.3, §3.1, App. A. There is no retrieval stage; control.retrieval=none. classify.structure=none because the memory is one buffer in the prompt, not a store.

The evaluation loop (taskutils/memory_eval) and the training agent (recurrent/impls/memory.py) were last changed in July 2025, after paper v1; whether they are exactly the runs behind v2's tables is not stated. headline: The only memory is one text string of at most 1,024 tokens that the model rewrites after every 5,000-token chunk; the answer call sees only this string and the question.
Nothing is retrieved or revisited: a 3.5M-token input means about 700 update calls in sequence.
What to keep is learned end to end: every update call gets the reward of the final answer (Multi-conv DAPO).

No run separates the RL-learned write policy from the chunked workflow at matched length except the w/o-RL rows; the no-RL agent is the untrained instruct model, not a prompted strong model.

key_numbers.value: stage I 32,768 × ~32K tokens; stage II 2,560 up to 60K

discussion.takeaway: A fixed-size, overwritten text memory trained with RL on the final answer lets a model with an 8K window handle inputs of millions of tokens with a small drop, where long-context models collapse past their windows.

claims.claim: Near-lossless extrapolation far beyond the training length.
claims.evidence: RL-MemAgent-14B 80.47 at 7K and 71.09 at 3.5M on RULER-HQA; 7B 81.25 → 71.88. Table 1

claims.claim: Long-context baselines degrade sharply.
claims.evidence: Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B-1M 60.16 at 7K, 0.00 at 896K; QwenLong-L1-32B 11.72 at 896K. Table 1

claims.claim: RL is what makes the workflow work.
claims.evidence: NIAH avg at 512K: 14B w/o RL 40.10 vs RL 98.18. Fig. 5; RULER-HQA and LongBench-QA plots, Fig. 6-7

claims.claim: The learned memory transfers to other tasks.
claims.evidence: LongBench-QA avg 51.0 (14B) vs 50.7 QwenLong-L1-32B, Table 3; best or second-best ROUGE recall on GovReport and QMSum, Table 2

claims.claim: Better than RAG over the same text.
claims.evidence: RULER-HQA at 3.5M: best RAG row 66.41 (Qwen2.5-14B, K=6) vs 71.09; LongBench-QA avg: best RAG 39.42 (14B, 2,048-token chunks, K=8) vs 51.00. Tables 10-11

claims.claim: The 1,024-token memory is a reasonable choice and results are stable across 256-4,096.

limits: No limitations section. The authors show failure cases: early distractors fill the memory and a key fact appended later is cut off; a multi-hop fact seen before its bridge is not kept; an early wrong reading of the question is reinforced (App. F).
reading: RULER-HQA is built the same way as the stage I training data (§3.1), so Table 1 is in-distribution in task type; only the length is out of distribution.
Baselines are run with 120K inputs (990K for the 1M models) and the code cuts the middle of longer inputs, so above those lengths they see only part of the document while MemAgent reads all of it.

Answers are sampled at temperature 0.7 with one sample per question in the released evaluation, and RULER-HQA has 128 questions per length, so differences of a few points are within one or two questions' worth of noise (1 question = 0.78 points).
Mem0 is described as a baseline in App. D.2 (GPT-5.1, top-30 memories) but no Mem0 number appears in any table or figure.
The LongBench-QA gain over the 32B reasoning baselines is small (51.0 vs 50.7 and 49.0 avg), and on NarrativeQA and Qasper MemAgent-14B is within 1-2 points of them.

abstract.text: MemAgent turns long-document question answering into a loop: the model reads the text in fixed chunks and after each one rewrites a short memory, then answers from that memory alone. Because the memory has a fixed size, cost grows linearly with length and the model's own window never has to grow. The authors train the memory updates with an extension of DAPO in which every update call shares the reward of the final answer. Models trained on 32K-60K inputs with an 8K window keep most of their accuracy up to 3.5M tokens and score above 95% on 512K needle tests.

abstract.text: MemGPT borrows virtual memory from operating systems to let a fixed-context LLM work with far more information than fits in its window. The prompt is split into read-only instructions, a small editable working context and a queue of recent messages; older messages are evicted into a recursive summary but stay searchable in recall storage, and an archival store holds arbitrary text. The LLM moves information between these tiers with its own function calls and can chain calls before replying. On multi-session chat and on document analysis tasks it outperforms fixed-context baselines.

discussion.takeaway: Treat the context window like an OS treats RAM: keep a small working set in the prompt and let the LLM page information in and out of external stores with function calls. With MemGPT the same base models answer questions about earlier sessions far more accurately than with a recursive summary.

claims.claim: Paging memory improves consistency in long conversations.
claims.evidence: DMR accuracy 92.5 vs 32.1 (GPT-4), 93.4 vs 35.3 (GPT-4 Turbo), 66.9 vs 38.7 (GPT-3.5 Turbo); ROUGE-L recall 0.814 vs 0.296 with GPT-4. Table 2

claims.claim: Memory makes conversation openers as engaging as human ones.
claims.evidence: SIM-1 0.830-0.868 vs 0.800 for the human opener; SIM-H 0.767-0.817. Table 3

claims.claim: Document QA no longer caps at what fits in the window.
claims.evidence: Accuracy stays flat as retrieved documents grow, while truncating baselines degrade. Fig. 5 (values plotted, not tabulated)

claims.claim: Function chaining enables multi-hop lookup.
claims.evidence: Nested KV: MemGPT with GPT-4 is unaffected by nesting level; GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo baselines reach 0% by 3 levels, GPT-3.5 at 1. Fig. 7, §3.2.2

limits: With GPT-3.5 MemGPT degrades markedly on document QA because of weaker function calling.
MemGPT often stops paging through retriever results before exhausting them.
With GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-3.5 it drops off at 2 nesting levels by making too few lookups.
Open directions: other unbounded-context domains, other memory tier technologies, and better control-flow and memory-management policies.
reading: In DMR the baselines read a lossy summary of sessions 1-5 while MemGPT searches the full history; no baseline is given the full five sessions, which the paper describes as about a dozen messages each.

There is no ablation of working context, recursive summary or recall search, so Table 2 does not show which tier carries the gain; the DMR persona tells the agent to use core memory and conversation search (App. 6.1.1).
DMR questions were written by an LLM and scored by an LLM judge whose model is not named; the conversation-opener table has no without-MemGPT row, only the human opener.
Code at tag 0.3.2 differs from the text: alert at 75% (not 70%), eviction of 75% of message tokens keeping the last 3 (not about 50%), and 5 results per page where Fig. 6 shows 10.
Recall storage search in the code is a case-insensitive substring match, not embedding search; the paper does not say how recall is searched.
The MSC task scripts are not in the repository, so how the five sessions were loaded into recall storage for DMR cannot be checked.

systems.name: MemLLM

paper.title: MemLLM: Finetuning LLMs to Use Explicit Read-Write Memory

construction.unit: relation triple (subject, relation, object) over 96 Wikidata relation types
construction.kept_as: extracted triples; entity and relation names as text plus Contriever vectors
construction.processing: finetuned write model reads each sentence with its preceding sentences and emits a MEM_WRITE call listing the triples in that sentence
construction.writer: memory-write model: Mistral-7B-v0.1 + LoRA

organization.structure: triple store: a Triples table of (subject id, relation id, object id) linked to Entities and Relations tables
organization.stores: Triple Memory; Entities (name, vector); Relations (name, vector)
organization.index: Contriever vectors of entity and relation names (HNSW in code); each (s, r, o) stored once

management.operations: insert; identical triples and names are stored once
management.conflicts: knowledge-editing runs only: a new triple with the same entity and relation replaces the old one (§4.3)

retrieval.query: the read model decides where to read and writes queries (s, r, ?) or (?, r, o) in a MEM_READ call
retrieval.candidates: entities and relations whose name vectors are close to the query's (cosine thresholds)
retrieval.selection: triples joining a candidate entity and relation whose mean similarity passes a threshold; the other entity's name is returned
retrieval.budget: at most 30 entity names per call (paper: drop the call above 30; code: keep 30 names taken from an unordered set, i.e. unranked)

use.context: returned entity names appended inline after the call; the call is deleted when the next one starts
use.reasoning: the model keeps decoding (language modeling, or a 5-shot QA answer in editing)

classify.note: Memory is an entity-relation triple store; the model writes the query, but the matching is a fixed similarity-threshold rule over name vectors (no graph walk, no reranker). Replacement of old triples happens only in the knowledge-editing experiment.

stages.ingestion: Text is split into sentences; each sentence is given to the write model as the focus sentence, bracketed by tags, after the preceding sentences (up to 24 in the Wikipedia indexing script).
stages.construction: A LoRA-finetuned Mistral-7B emits ({MEM_WRITE--> s»r»o; ...}) with the triples stated in the focus sentence, using late stopping so it does not close the list too early.
stages.organization: Triples go into a Triples table that points to separate Entities and Relations tables; names are stored once as text with a Contriever vector.
stages.update: Identical triples are stored once. In the knowledge-editing run a new triple with the same entity and relation as an old one replaces it.
stages.retrieval: While generating, the read model emits ({MEM_READ( with one to a few (s, r, ?) or (?, r, o) queries; candidate entities and relations are found by cosine similarity of name vectors, matching triples are joined, and up to 30 entity names are returned.
stages.answer: The returned names are appended after '-->' and the model continues; the call is removed when the model starts a new one, or right away if nothing came back.
stages.learning: Two LoRA adapters on Mistral-7B are finetuned with the language-modeling loss on API data built from Re-DocRED, distant-supervised DocRED (filtered with Mixtral) and counterfactual Re-DocRED variants; read data is built against a memory filled by the trained write model.

systems.summary: An LLM finetuned to call an explicit triple-store memory: a write model extracts (subject, relation, object) triples sentence by sentence, and a read model inserts MEM_READ queries mid-generation whose matched entity names are appended to the text.
systems.notes:
Venue: TMLR, published 04/2025 (PDF header 'Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (04/2025)'; reviewed on OpenReview id dghM7sOudh). The list guess 'TMLR 2025 journal' is confirmed from the arXiv v3 PDF; the OpenReview page itself sat behind a browser check and was not read. Code link from the paper abstract: github.com/amodaresi/MemLLM.
DESIGN: §3.1 (memory structure, query rule), §3.2 (API, inference), §3.3 (training data), §4.1 (setup), App. A (late stopping), App. B (ambiguous queries), App. D (hyperparameters). Trigger is 'other': writing runs once per sentence of any input text, not per dialogue turn. Retrieval control is learned-sft because the finetuned model decides where to read and what to ask; the match itself is a fixed rule.

sources.code_note: Commit f786ae30 (2024-08-13, 'Added codes') is the only commit with code; all later history is README edits before it, and the repo has not changed since, while paper v3 is from 2025-04. It is taken as the evaluation code. Released scripts have placeholder paths (model dirs, memory server URI), so exact run settings can only be read from the constants in the eval scripts.

headline: Memory is a database of (subject, relation, object) triples that the model itself writes and queries through special text calls it learned by finetuning.
What comes back is only a list of entity names, not the triples: the model must infer from its own query what each name answers.
In the perplexity evaluation, reads happen only at positions fixed by the evaluation data (before target entities); the model's choice enters as the probability of opening a call there.

read.how: HNSW search on Contriever vectors; keep entities within distance 0.15 (of the nearest 300) and relations within 0.15 (of the nearest 25)
read.src: paper §3.1, App. D; code memory_controller_v3.py L153-L157, evaluate_v4_mistral.py L54-L55

collect the other entity's name from every triple, dedupe with a Python set and keep 30 of them (set order, so no ranking); if none, drop the call and continue without memory

answer_context.sees: the text so far plus the latest call with up to 30 entity names
answer_context.format: …text ({MEM_READ(q1;q2)--> e1;e2;…}) continuation
excludes: the matched triples and their relations
the source sentences of the facts
includes: entity names returned by the latest read
answer_context.note: An empty result or a new '({' removes the call from the context.

open_questions: Rows 1-3 of Table 2 differ in both memory size and whether the memory holds facts from the evaluated documents themselves, so the small gap does not isolate scaling.

The editing comparison mixes protocols: baselines copied from WISE are scored after all 1000 edits with token-level accuracy, MemLLM by answer containment in a script that scores each edit right after writing it.

discussion.takeaway: Finetuning an LLM to write and query an explicit triple store through text API calls lowers perplexity on entities that memory can supply, and the same memory handles 1000 sequential knowledge edits better than the parametric editors it is compared with.

claims.claim: Memory reads improve language modeling, mostly on target entities.
claims.evidence: TARGET PPL 2.986 with a full-Wikipedia memory vs 3.510 with memory disabled and 3.550 for Mistral-7B (Table 2, §4.2).

claims.claim: The approach scales with memory size.
claims.evidence: 111M-triple Wikipedia memory is only slightly worse than a memory built from the evaluation documents alone (TARGET 2.986 vs 2.821, Table 2).

claims.claim: Better memory reads and writes would help further.
claims.evidence: Gold queries on gold triples reach TARGET 1.364; own writes with gold positions and queries 1.938 (Table 2 rows 4, 7).

claims.claim: Outperforms knowledge-editing methods on sequential edits.
claims.evidence: ZsRE, 1000 edits, Mistral-7B: AVG 0.84 vs WISE 0.79, GRACE 0.67, DEFER 0.24 (Table 3).

claims.claim: Structured storage is more compact than proposition-level RAG.
claims.evidence: Under 20% of records at 111M facts (§4.2, Fig. 4).

limits: Only the 96 relation types used in training can be extracted and queried.
Relations that follow from several stored triples are neither inferred nor used.
The model does not know what memory lacks: if a fact is missing it falls back on parametric knowledge or hallucinates.
RAG methods are not compared.
reading: The model only sees returned entity names, not the triples; the paper's own error analysis has cases where the right name came back under the wrong relation and was ignored (§4.3).

In the perplexity code the read positions come from the evaluation data (just before annotated target entities) and the with/without-read outputs are mixed by the probability of '({'; so 'MemLLM chooses where to read' is measured only at those positions (footnote 3; evaluate_v4_mistral.py L120-L176).
Much of the OVERALL gain over Mistral-7B comes from in-domain finetuning alone (5.823 → 4.997 with memory disabled); memory adds 4.997 → 4.905.

The ZsRE baselines are copied from WISE and scored with EasyEdit token accuracy after all 1000 edits; the released MemLLM script scores answer containment and evaluates each edit right after writing it, so Table 3 does not compare like with like.
Code thresholds differ from App. D in both experiments (see paper vs code).
The reliability error breakdown (45 write, 95 read, 63 not used) adds up to 203 of the 216 errors the paper counts; the remaining 13 are not explained (§4.3).

abstract.text: MemLLM gives an LLM an explicit, structured memory it can both write to and read from. Facts are kept as (subject, relation, object) triples in database tables, with entity and relation names embedded for fuzzy matching. Two LoRA adapters on Mistral-7B are finetuned on data built from relation-annotated Wikipedia text: one writes the triples found in each sentence, the other issues memory queries during generation and uses the returned entities. On Re-DocRED the memory lowers perplexity, especially on entities, and on ZsRE it handles 1000 sequential edits better than model-editing baselines.

systems.name: Memoria

paper.title: Memoria: Resolving Fateful Forgetting Problem through Human-Inspired Memory Architecture

construction.unit: engram: one hidden-size vector (no text)
construction.kept_as: learned compression of the previous segment's final hidden states
construction.processing: a trained attention abstractor with N_wm learnable queries turns segment t-1's last hidden states into N_wm engrams (working memory)
construction.writer: abstractor module inside the model, trained end to end with the task loss

organization.structure: three tiers (working, short-term queue, unbounded long-term) plus a directed weighted graph of co-retrieval counts over all engrams
organization.stores: working memory (this step's engrams), short-term memory (FIFO queue, fixed capacity), long-term memory (no size limit)
organization.index: squared L2 distance to working-memory engrams; co-retrieval count matrix as edge weights

management.operations: each step: co-retrieved pairs' counts +1; retrieved engrams gain lifespan in proportion to the memory attention they received; all engrams lose 1; WM moves to STM; STM overflow (oldest) moves to LTM
management.forgetting: lifespan decay: engrams whose lifespan reaches 0 are deleted permanently; only retrieval and use extend lifespan

retrieval.query: the current working-memory engrams (made from the previous segment)
retrieval.candidates: STM: top N_stm by mean exp(-L2^2) to WM; LTM: from each retrieved STM engram follow the strongest link into LTM, then walk the strongest unvisited links to depth 10
retrieval.selection: top N_ltm of the walked LTM engrams by similarity to WM
retrieval.budget: WM + STM + LTM engrams equal the segment length in sorting (1/8, 1/4, 5/8); 50/50/50 on Wikitext-103 and PG-19; 64/64/64 on Hyperpartisan

use.context: the model cross-attends to WM engrams and then to the retrieved STM/LTM engrams in every memory layer (same attention weights for both)
use.reasoning: one forward pass per segment; the memory attention weights are fed back as the lifespan increment

classify.note: STM candidates come from vector distance, but LTM is reached only by walking co-retrieval links from the retrieved STM engrams, which is the distinctive step.

stages.ingestion: The input is processed segment by segment (e.g. 150 tokens for Wikitext-103 and PG-19, 512 characters for enwik8, 256-1024 symbols for sorting).
stages.construction: A trained attention abstractor with N_wm learnable queries turns the previous segment's final hidden states (the current segment's layer-l states in the BERT variant) into N_wm engram vectors that form the working memory.
stages.organization: Engrams sit in working memory, a fixed-capacity short-term queue and an unbounded long-term store; every pair of engrams has a co-retrieval count, read as the directed edge weight Count_ij / Count_ii.
stages.update: After each step, co-retrieved engrams' pair counts rise by one (Hebbian), retrieved engrams gain lifespan proportional to the memory attention they received (scale α = 8), every engram loses 1, engrams at 0 are deleted, WM moves to STM and STM overflow moves to LTM.
stages.retrieval: Working memory is the cue: the N_stm STM engrams closest to it are retrieved; from each, the strongest link into LTM starts a greedy walk of depth 10 over unvisited LTM engrams, and the N_ltm walked engrams closest to WM are kept.
stages.answer: The model cross-attends to the WM engrams and then to the retrieved engrams inside its layers; the result is the next-token prediction (or class) for the current segment.
stages.learning: The abstractor and memory-attention layers are trained with the task loss (from scratch for language modeling and sorting, fine-tuned from BERT, RoBERTa or GPT-2 elsewhere); the memory rules themselves are fixed.

systems.summary: Neural memory module with working, short-term and long-term stores of engram vectors, where Hebbian co-retrieval links guide search into long-term memory and a use-driven lifespan decides what is forgotten.
systems.notes:
Architecture-level memory for Transformers, not an agent memory: engrams are latent vectors that the model attends to; there is no text store and no LLM prompting. Evaluated on synthetic sorting, language modeling (Wikitext-103, PG-19, enwik8) and Hyperpartisan classification.
VENUE: ICML 2024 (PMLR 235:39587-39615, proceedings.mlr.press/v235/park24a; OpenReview yTz0u4B8ug); the arXiv v3 PDF also carries the ICML 2024 footer.
DESIGN: §3.1-3.4, §4, App. D, E, G; code memoria.py and modeling_gpt2_with_memoria.py at v1.0.0 (the version the experiment requirements pin).

abstract.text: Memoria is a memory module for neural networks that tries to keep important old information instead of always favouring the most recent input. It stores engram vectors in working, short-term and long-term memory, links engrams that are retrieved together (a Hebbian rule), searches long-term memory by following those links, and forgets engrams whose use-driven lifespan runs out. Plugged into GPT-2-style decoders and BERT/RoBERTa encoders, it beats Transformer-XL, Compressive Transformer and ∞-former on long sorting sequences and on language modeling, and improves long-document classification. An analysis of the surviving engrams shows primacy, recency and temporal-contiguity effects like those in human memory.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Memory holds vectors, not text: each engram is the abstractor's summary of a past segment, read through cross-attention.
Long-term memory is never searched by similarity alone: candidates are reached by walking co-retrieval links from the STM engrams, then ranked by distance to working memory.
Forgetting is driven by use: an engram lives only as long as it keeps receiving attention.

open_questions: The Full LTM Search variant (65.84) beats link-guided search (63.26) on 48K sorting, so the links trade accuracy for compute; no run isolates how much each saves in time.
Language-modeling gains over ∞-former are small on PG-19 (29.149 vs 29.154) and Memoria ties Compressive Transformer on enwik8 (1.16), and no variance is reported for these single runs.

text: Working memory picks the nearest short-term engrams; their strongest links lead into long-term memory, which is walked 10 steps and ranked by distance to working memory (50 + 50 in the LM runs).
The model cross-attends to these engrams inside its layers, and the attention each receives becomes its new lifespan.

key_numbers.value: start 9 (LM), 5 (sorting), 12 (classification); gain scale α = 8; −1 per step

components.model: greedy walk over co-retrieval counts, depth 10
GPT-2-style decoder (12 layers, 768-d for LM) or BERT/RoBERTa-base with memory cross-attention

ablation.src: paper App. C, Tables 5-6 (sorting accuracy, segment length 1024)

discussion.takeaway: Giving memory a use-driven lifespan and associative links lets a segment-recurrent Transformer keep information from the start of a very long sequence. The effect is clearest on long sorting sequences; language-modeling and classification gains are smaller.

claims.claim: Memoria resists fateful forgetting as sequences grow.
claims.evidence: Sorting with 32 segments of 1024: 63.42 vs 39.71 (∞-former), 35.07 (Compressive), 33.87 (Transformer-XL). Table 7, Fig. 4

claims.claim: Better language modeling than other memory Transformers.
claims.evidence: Wikitext-103 PPL 23.471 vs 24.543 Transformer-XL; PG-19 29.149 vs 29.154 ∞-former; enwik8 1.16 BPC tied with Compressive. Table 1

claims.claim: Works when fine-tuning pre-trained models.
Helps long-document classification.
claims.evidence: Hyperpartisan test F1 96.51 (Memoria RoBERTa) vs 95.24 RoBERTa, 94.56 Longformer, 93.24 BigBird. Table 2

claims.claim: Hebbian links matter.
claims.evidence: LTM gain on 48K sorting falls from +8.39 to +1.26 with random wiring. Table 6

claims.claim: Memoria shows primacy, recency and temporal contiguity like human memory.
claims.evidence: Creation-time density of surviving engrams and link weight vs age difference on Wikitext-103. §6, Fig. 7

limits: The multi-store model it follows ignores the continuous levels-of-processing view of memory.
Interference, a main cause of forgetting in human long-term memory, is not modelled.
Memory built during inference may keep user data, which raises privacy concerns.
reading: Engrams are latent vectors read by cross-attention inside a trained model, so Memoria cannot be dropped into a frozen LLM or inspected as text; it is a different design point from agent memories.
The Hebbian search is a compute saving rather than an accuracy gain: exhaustive LTM search scores higher (65.84 vs 63.26, Table 6).
Wikitext-103, PG-19 and enwik8 numbers come from one run each; the PG-19 margin over ∞-former is 0.005 PPL.
Memoria BERT is below Longformer and BigBird on Hyperpartisan validation F1 (78.24 vs 78.33, 81.22); only the RoBERTa variant leads on both splits.
Hyperparameters differ by task (initial lifespan 5, 9 or 12; STM capacity 128 to 1,360), and Table 9 shows perplexity moving between 23.38 and 23.83 when they change.

stages.ingestion: Every user-AI exchange is appended verbatim to the user's log under today's date.
stages.construction: On request (at login in the demos) an LLM writes a daily event summary and a daily personality/emotion analysis for each unsummarised day, then a global event summary and a global personality portrait with a reply strategy.
stages.organization: Exchanges and daily summaries are embedded (MiniLM for English, Text2vec for Chinese) into a FAISS index, rebuilt whenever the user logs in.
stages.update: Paper: each memory has strength S (1 at first mention); recall adds 1 and resets elapsed time; memories fade by R = e^(-t/S). Code: when the optional path is enabled, each exchange is kept with probability e^(-t·S/5) at login and deleted otherwise.
stages.retrieval: The current user message is embedded and the top 2 pieces are retrieved (ChatGLM/BELLE demo default), grouped by date. The ChatGPT variant queries a LlamaIndex vector index over whole-day documents and gets an LLM-written answer back.
stages.answer: The meta prompt holds the retrieved memories and their dates, the global user portrait with the reply strategy, and the last 7 exchanges of the session.
stages.learning: No memory learning. Separately, the open-source SiliconFriend backbones (ChatGLM, BELLE) are LoRA-tuned on 38k psychological dialogues for empathy.

systems.summary: Early long-term memory for LLM chat companions: a dated log of exchanges with LLM-written daily and global summaries and a user portrait, dense retrieval of past exchanges, and an Ebbinghaus-style forgetting rule where recalled memories get stronger.

discussion.takeaway: An early, simple recipe for companion memory: keep the dated chat log, summarise days and the user's personality with an LLM, retrieve a few past exchanges by embedding, and decay unused memories. Its evaluation is a small human-scored probe of three SiliconFriend variants without baselines.

claims.claim: MemoryBank lets LLMs recall past interactions and adapt to the user's personality.
claims.evidence: Qualitative examples, Figs. 2-4, §4.1

claims.claim: It works with both open- and closed-source LLMs.
claims.evidence: Retrieval accuracy 0.763-0.856 for ChatGLM, BELLE and ChatGPT variants in English and Chinese. Table 2

claims.claim: The ChatGPT variant gives the best responses overall.
claims.evidence: English correctness 0.716, coherence 0.912, ranking 0.818 vs 0.438-0.479 correctness for ChatGLM/BELLE. Table 2

claims.claim: Psychology tuning gives more empathetic replies.
claims.evidence: Comparison with base ChatGLM on a real conversation. Fig. 2

limits: The memory updating model is exploratory and highly simplified; real forgetting depends on the person and the kind of information.
reading: The quantitative test has no baseline without memory or with plain retrieval, and only compares three variants of the paper's own system with human labels; the number of annotators is not stated.
The paper does not say whether the forgetting mechanism was on for the Table 2 runs; in the code it is off by default and cannot be switched on without a missing module.
Where forgetting is implemented, e^(-t·S/5) makes frequently recalled memories decay faster, the reverse of the paper's rule; daily summaries are never decayed.
The global event summary is computed but not placed in any prompt template.

ChatGLM/BELLE retrieve single exchanges from FAISS, while the ChatGPT variant retrieves whole-day documents through LlamaIndex and receives an LLM-written answer; its lower retrieval accuracy (0.763/0.711) comes from a different retriever, not only a different backbone.
The repository has 100 probing questions per language; the paper reports 97 per language.

abstract.text: MemoryBank adds long-term memory to LLM chatbots. It stores the dated conversation log, LLM-written daily and global event summaries, and an evolving portrait of the user's personality, and retrieves relevant past exchanges with a dense retriever. An update rule inspired by the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve lets memories fade with time and strengthen when recalled. The authors build SiliconFriend, a companion bot on ChatGPT, ChatGLM and BELLE (the latter two LoRA-tuned on psychological dialogues), and test memory recall with simulated 10-day conversations of 15 users and human-scored probing questions.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

stages.construction: Pages evicted FIFO from STM are grouped into MTM topic segments when cosine(embedding) + Jaccard(LLM keywords) similarity exceeds theta=0.6; segment content is summarized by an LLM.
stages.organization: Three tiers: STM (dialogue pages), MTM (segmented paging, max 200 segments), LPM (user profile, User KB, 90-dimension User Traits, agent profile/traits).
stages.update: Segment heat = visits + page count + recency decay; lowest-heat segments are evicted, segments with heat > 5 are promoted to LPM where an LLM extracts user traits/KB facts (User KB and Agent Traits are FIFO queues of 100).
stages.retrieval: All STM pages; MTM two-stage: top-m=5 segments by the cosine+Jaccard score, then top-k pages (10 on LoCoMo) by semantic similarity; LPM: top-10 User KB and Agent Traits entries plus full profiles/traits.
stages.answer: Retrieved STM, MTM and LPM content is assembled into one prompt with the query for the LLM.

systems.summary: OS-inspired three-tier memory (short-term pages, mid-term segment-paged topics, long-term persona) with FIFO and heat-based promotion/eviction between tiers.

The embedding model is not named in the paper. Venue: EMNLP 2025 main (aclanthology 2025.emnlp-main.1318).

paper.title: MemoTime: Memory-Augmented Temporal Knowledge Graph Enhanced Large Language Model Reasoning

retrieval.query: question or sub-question text
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity over records of the same kind (and temporal type)

classify.note: The memory is the experience pool of past reasoning traces. The facts come from a fixed temporal KG, which LLM-chosen toolkits search; that search is not the memory.

stages.ingestion: Test questions arrive one at a time. Question entities are linked to a fixed temporal knowledge graph (MultiTQ: ICEWS05-15; TimeQuestions: Wikidata).
stages.construction: Once the final LLM check accepts an answer, MemoTime writes the question's decomposition and, for each freshly retrieved step, the seed choice, the toolkit choice and the sub-question with its answer and evidence path.
stages.organization: Records form one flat pool typed by record kind and temporal question type, with a sentence-embedding index over the query text.
stages.update: A record with the same normalized text is overwritten, and hit counts grow on lookup. The paper's pruning, decay and cross-type labels are not in the released code.
stages.retrieval: Similar past records (top 10 for decomposition and toolkit choice, top 3 for seeds) become few-shot examples. Evidence itself comes from toolkit searches of the temporal KG, pruned to 80 paths and then to 3 by an LLM.
stages.answer: A final LLM call reads every step's sub-question, chosen answer, evidence path and top candidate paths.

systems.summary: Temporal KGQA agent that splits a question into a tree of time-constrained sub-questions, answers each with operator-specific KG toolkits, and keeps verified decompositions and tool choices as few-shot examples for later questions.
systems.notes: Venue: WWW 2026 (Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026, DOI 10.1145/3774904.3792581), as printed in the arXiv v3 PDF; arXiv comment agrees. The ACM DL page could not be fetched (HTTP 403). Track taken as main (21-page research paper); the PDF does not name a track. Code: SteveTANTAN/MemoTime, pinned at 84ed588 (2026-06-15); Python files last changed 2026-02-18, five days before arXiv v3. DESIGN: §4.1-4.4, App. A (Alg. 1-4), App. D. The experience pool is a store of reasoning traces, not of dialogue or documents; classified as procedural memory.
