abstract.text: MemoTime answers time-sensitive questions over a temporal knowledge graph with an LLM. It breaks a question into a tree of sub-questions whose time constraints must stay consistent, and answers each with toolkits built for specific temporal operators such as 'first after' or 'last before'. Retrieved paths are filtered by time, reranked and narrowed by the LLM. Verified decompositions and tool choices are kept in an experience memory and shown as examples on later questions. The authors report the best results on MultiTQ and TimeQuestions, and say small models such as Qwen3-4B come close to GPT-4-Turbo.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: The memory holds the system's own past reasoning (decompositions, seed and tool choices), not facts. Facts always come from the temporal KG.
In the released code, stored sub-question answers are never reused: every sub-question searches the KG again, and memory acts only as few-shot examples.
The pool is filled from test questions as the run goes. An LLM check, not the gold answer, decides what is written.

discussion.limits_src: The paper has no limitations section.
reading: Every baseline number is copied from earlier papers (App. D), mostly with GPT-3.5-Turbo backbones, while MemoTime runs GPT-4o-mini to GPT-4-Turbo; only Table 3's IO rows share a backbone with MemoTime.
Table 3 gives different MemoTime scores than Tables 1-2 for the same backbone (GPT-4-Turbo 76.3 vs 77.9 on MultiTQ, 68.1 vs 71.4 on TimeQuestions); the paper does not explain the gap.
On TimeQuestions the GPT-4o-mini (60.9) and Qwen3-32B (60.6) runs are below the fine-tuned TimeR4 (64.8), so the best result there needs DeepSeek-V3 or GPT-4-Turbo.
In the released code the experience pool only supplies few-shot examples: stored sub-question answers are never reused (stepwise.py L1097), and type classification uses rules, not memory.
The pool is written from test questions during evaluation, gated by an LLM check; results can depend on question order, which the paper does not report.
The code's answer string joins up to three candidate answers with ', or ' and is scored by a lenient matcher, while baselines' Hits@1 comes from their own papers' scoring.
The code skips questions already marked correct for the same configuration on reruns (main.py L252-L260); the paper does not say how many runs produced the tables.

paper.title: Memp: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory

construction.unit: procedural memory entry: task description (key) + LLM-distilled workflow script (+ full gold trajectory in the Trajectory / Proceduralization settings)
construction.kept_as: LLM-written workflow paragraph; gold trajectories verbatim (paper settings only)
construction.processing: LLM distils a successful trajectory into a workflow ('direct') or into state/action events and keeps the critical steps ('round')
construction.writer: backbone LLM (MODEL_NAME in the code; the paper does not name the builder model)

organization.structure: flat list of entries
organization.stores: one FAISS vector store keyed by task text
organization.index: dense embeddings of the task text (text-embedding-3-small in the code); per-keyword embeddings for AveFact

management.operations: after every t tasks: add distilled runs (Vanilla), add only solved runs (Validation), or add solved runs and LLM-revise the retrieved workflow on failure (Adjustment)
management.conflicts: Adjustment rewrites the workflow in place using the failed trajectory
management.forgetting: code: delete an entry used at least 3 times with success rate below 0.5 (not described in the paper)

retrieval.query: new task description (Query key) or LLM-extracted keywords of it (AveFact)
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity of task embeddings; AveFact averages similarity over matched keywords
retrieval.selection: top-k by similarity (k = 10 in the code; paper sweeps 0-20)
retrieval.budget: k = 10 entries in the code, FAISS score threshold 0.5

use.context: retrieved task names and workflows appended to the task as 'guidelines' (paper's best setting also adds the retrieved gold trajectories)
use.reasoning: ReAct loop in the environment, up to 30 steps (code default)

classify.note: The best update policy (Adjustment) rewrites a retrieved workflow in place after a failure; the code also deletes rarely successful entries.

stages.ingestion: Completed agent trajectories (gold training trajectories offline; the agent's own test runs online) together with the environment's 0/1 reward.
stages.construction: An LLM turns each trajectory into procedural memory: a script-like workflow paragraph, or (paper) the verbatim trajectory, or both (Proceduralization). The entry is keyed by the task description.
stages.organization: A flat store of entries keyed by task text and embedded for vector search; no links or hierarchy.
stages.update: After every t tasks the store is refreshed: Vanilla adds all runs, Validation only successful ones, Adjustment adds successes and has an LLM revise a retrieved workflow that led to failure. The code additionally deletes entries used at least 3 times with a success rate below 0.5.
stages.retrieval: The new task is embedded and the most similar stored tasks are returned by cosine similarity (Query key) or by averaged keyword similarity (AveFact); the code keeps the top 10.
stages.answer: Retrieved workflows are appended to the task prompt as guidelines and the agent acts ReAct-style in the environment.

systems.summary: Treats procedural memory as an object to optimise: agent trajectories are distilled into task-keyed workflow scripts (optionally with the raw trajectory), retrieved by task similarity, and revised after failures, compared across build, retrieve and update strategies on ALFWorld and TravelPlanner.
systems.notes:
Venue: ACL 2026 Findings (arXiv comment; ACL Anthology 2026.findings-acl.866, pages 17490-17502). PDF read: arXiv v4 (15 Apr 2026). Code: zjunlp/MemP at 3066a1b2 (2026-01-30), linked from the paper; it contains only the ALFWorld runner, memory class and prompts, not the TravelPlanner pipeline, the keyword extractor for AveFact, the config.yaml used by the online script, or the trajectory-in-context (Proceduralization) setting.
DESIGN: paper §3.1, §4.2-4.3, Fig. 2, App. C; code memory.py, run_memp_offline.py, run_memp_online.py, memory_adjust.py, prompt_generator.py, llm_api.py. The paper is an empirical study of strategies rather than one fixed system: design fields describe the best-scoring choices (Proceduralization build, AveFact or Query retrieval, Adjustment update) and note where the code differs. fidelity 'mixed' because the paper's best setting stores verbatim trajectories plus LLM scripts; the released code stores scripts only.

It covers ALFWorld only (offline and online runners over one Memory class); TravelPlanner code, the AveFact keyword extractor, ProcedureMem/config.yaml (read by the online runner) and the Proceduralization setting are not in the repository.

headline: One memory entry = a stored task description (the key) plus an LLM-written workflow for it; retrieval compares only task descriptions.
The best build setting (Proceduralization) puts both the retrieved script and the retrieved gold trajectory in the prompt; the released code passes scripts only.
Updates use the environment's success signal: keep successful runs, and on failure let an LLM rewrite the workflow that was retrieved.

discussion.takeaway: Giving an agent both an abstract script and a concrete solved trajectory of a similar past task raises success and cuts steps on ALFWorld and TravelPlanner, and revising scripts after failures keeps improving it over time.

claims.claim: All build strategies beat no memory; combining script and trajectory is best.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o ALFWorld dev/test 87.14/77.86 vs 39.28/42.14, steps 15.01 vs 23.76; TravelPlanner #CS 79.94 vs 71.93. Table 1

claims.claim: Scripts generalise better to unseen tasks, trajectories fit similar tasks.
claims.evidence: Script relatively better on the ALFWorld test split, Trajectory on dev. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Similarity-based keys beat random sampling.
claims.evidence: Key=AveFact best #CS for all three models (76.02, 65.76, 63.41). Table 2

claims.claim: Error-driven revision (Adjustment) is the best update policy.
claims.evidence: Highest reward gain (about 0.7) and largest step reduction (about 14) by the fifth task group. Fig. 3, §4.3

claims.claim: Memory built by a strong model helps a weaker one.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o memory lifts Qwen2.5-14B on TravelPlanner: delivery 91.4 to 96.6, commonsense 59.3 to 65.5, steps 16.9 to 15.3. Fig. 5(a)

claims.claim: More retrieved memories help up to a point.
claims.evidence: ALFWorld score 40.7 (k=0) rising to 82.5 (k=10), then 79.3 (k=20). Fig. 5(b)

limits: Retrieval is vector similarity over hand-designed keys; BM25 and other methods were not tried.
Updates depend on the benchmark's explicit reward, so the method cannot yet judge success where rewards are missing.
reading: Memory is keyed and matched only by the task description; environment state, room layout and the agent's progress play no part in retrieval.
Key=AveFact in Table 2 has exactly the numbers of Trajectory in Table 1, so the retrieval comparison is run on trajectory memory, not on the best (Proceduralization) setting.

Figure 4 (ReAct, ExpeL, AWM, Memp on ALFWorld) gives bars without values or settings; the Memp and ReAct bars match Table 1's Proceduralization and No Memory rows, so the baselines are presumably also GPT-4o, but the paper does not say how ExpeL and AWM were run.

The text says Adjustment beats the second-best policy by '+0.7 points'; Fig. 3 shows a reward gain of about 0.7 for Adjustment against about 0.55-0.6 for the others, so the margin is smaller than the phrase suggests.
The transfer experiment is described as Fig. 5(b) in the text but is Fig. 5(a); its ALFWorld gains are stated without numbers.
Figure 5(b)'s k = 0 score (40.7) sits between Table 1's no-memory dev (39.28) and test (42.14) values; the split is not stated.

The released code covers ALFWorld with scripts only: no TravelPlanner runner, no trajectory-in-context path, and no config for the online runs, so Table 1's best rows cannot be reproduced from it as released.

abstract.text: Memp studies how an LLM agent can keep procedural memory, knowledge of how to carry out tasks, outside its weights. Past trajectories are distilled into step-level instructions and higher-level scripts, stored under the task description and retrieved for similar new tasks. The paper compares strategies for building, retrieving and updating this memory, including revising entries after failures. On TravelPlanner and ALFWorld, agents succeed more often and use fewer steps as memory is refined, and memory built with GPT-4o also helps a smaller model.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: MemSearcher

paper.title: MemSearcher: Training LLMs to Reason, Search and Manage Memory via End-to-End Reinforcement Learning

construction.unit: one natural-language memory passage per question
construction.kept_as: LLM rewrite of the previous memory plus the new search results
construction.processing: after each search, the same LLM reads question, memory, its thought, the call and the passages, and writes a new memory
construction.writer: the policy LLM itself (Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B-Instruct, RL-trained)

organization.structure: single text buffer
organization.stores: one memory string, overwritten every turn

management.operations: overwrite the whole memory each turn (keep relevant details, add new ones)
management.forgetting: thoughts, calls and passages leave the context after each turn; only what the model writes into memory survives

retrieval.candidates: none: the whole memory is in every turn's prompt (the search tool retrieves Wikipedia passages, not memory)
retrieval.budget: memory up to 1,024 tokens (paper); each memory write is capped at 512 new tokens in the code

use.context: system prompt + question + memory; no earlier turns
use.reasoning: multi-turn: think, then answer in \boxed{} or search; one memory update per search

classify.note: A single rewritten memory string replaces the growing ReAct history; what to keep is learned by RL, and the memory is always read whole.

stages.ingestion: Each turn the search tool returns Wikipedia passages (2018 dump, E5 retriever) for the model's query.
stages.construction: In a second generation call the same LLM reads the question, previous memory, its thought, the call and the passages, and writes an updated memory inside <memory> tags.
stages.organization: One plain-text memory; no structure or index.
stages.update: The new memory overwrites the old one; the prompt asks to keep relevant earlier details and add new ones. The paper caps memory at 1,024 tokens; in training a trajectory ends if the cap is exceeded.
stages.retrieval: None for memory: the next turn's prompt is the system prompt, the question and the whole memory.
stages.answer: When the memory suffices, the model answers in \boxed{}; otherwise it searches again, up to the turn limit.
stages.learning: Multi-context GRPO: each trajectory's reward (format check plus answer F1) gives one group-normalised advantage that is copied to every turn, and each turn is optimised as a separate sample. Trained on NQ + HotpotQA, 5 rollouts per question.

systems.summary: A search agent that keeps a compact, LLM-rewritten memory instead of the growing ReAct history, so each turn sees only the question and the memory; the policy learns what to keep through multi-context GRPO.
systems.notes: Venue checked on the ACL Anthology: Findings of ACL 2026, 2026.findings-acl.736, under the title 'MemSearcher: Iterative Memory Integration for Search Agent via End-to-End Reinforcement Learning'. The arXiv comment says 'Accepted to ACL 2026', but the proceedings list it in Findings. Main-table numbers in the Anthology PDF match arXiv v2 (8 May 2026), which was read in full. Memory is per question (a working buffer), not kept across questions.

discussion.takeaway: Replacing the growing ReAct history with one memory the model rewrites every turn keeps the context small and, after RL training, gives higher EM than ReAct-style search agents of the same or larger size.

claims.claim: MemSearcher beats search-agent baselines at every size.
Smaller MemSearcher models beat larger baselines.
claims.evidence: 7B at 48.9 above ReSearch 32B at 48.3 (Table 2).

claims.claim: Context stays nearly constant across turns.
claims.evidence: Under 4K tokens vs a linear rise for ReSearch (Fig. 4, §4.2.2).

claims.claim: RL is needed, and beats SFT.
claims.evidence: 3B: 14.4 without RL, 28.5 with SFT, 43.8 with RL (Tables 3-4).

claims.claim: A middle memory size is best.
claims.evidence: 256 to 2,048 tokens; gains up to 1,024 on Musique, saturated at 256 on Bamboogle (Fig. 6, §4.3.3).

limits: Only a simple memory design is studied; RAG-like or structured memories for RL search agents are left open.
Multi-context GRPO may carry length bias, and more RL techniques remain to be explored.
reading: The memory is per question and lives for at most a handful of turns; it is context compression for multi-hop QA, not long-term memory.
Caps of 1,024 and 2,048 give the same scores on all eight curves of Fig. 6, which fits the code writing each memory with at most 512 new tokens.

Baselines are listed with sizes but no statement of who ran them or with which retriever; the paper notes ZeroSearch and R1-Searcher used Google search in their own evaluation, so those rows at least are not under the same retrieval setup.
The case study (Table 6) writes 'Sylvester comes from Latin' into memory after a passage about a singer, so the rewrite can add unsourced facts.
Table 3's 'without training' baseline is the untrained model inside the MemSearcher loop, not a ReAct agent, so it measures RL rather than memory.

abstract.text: Search agents in the ReAct style append every thought, call and retrieved passage to their context, which grows long and noisy. MemSearcher instead keeps one compact memory: each turn the model sees the question and the memory, searches, and then rewrites the memory from the new passages, so context length stays nearly flat. Because each turn has its own context, the authors train it with multi-context GRPO, which gives every turn the trajectory's advantage. On seven QA datasets MemSearcher models from 3B to 14B beat RL-trained ReAct-style search agents while keeping contexts under 4K tokens.

stages.ingestion: The input is a user's time-ordered list of past documents (e.g. paper titles and abstracts, reviews, headlines) from the LaMP profiles.
stages.construction: Each document is embedded with BGE-M3 and clustered with K-means (K = 5 in the paper); a graph links consecutive documents (temporal edges) and documents in the same cluster (semantic edges).
stages.organization: Two memories: the behavior graph over raw documents and a cognitive memory, a short text built by summarizing groups of documents and then merging those summaries (paper: time phases; code: K-means clusters).
stages.update: The paper describes incremental updates (append and link new documents, cluster the new batch alone, re-merge summaries), which track a full rebuild at lower cost in a simulation (Fig. 5); the released code rebuilds instead.
stages.retrieval: A random walk starts at the document most similar to the query and moves to neighbours with probability tied to query similarity, time gap and recency (alpha 1.5, lambda1 0.01, lambda2 0.02), for at most 10 steps; the code reranks the visited documents and keeps 5.
stages.answer: The LLM is prompted with the user summary, the selected past documents and the task query.
stages.learning: Training-free; ROPG and CFRAG baselines are trained on the LaMP training split, MemWeaver only uses the test split.

systems.summary: Personalized generation from a user's past texts: the history becomes a graph (temporal and same-cluster semantic edges) that is sampled by a query-guided random walk, plus a two-stage LLM summary of the user's preferences, and both go into the prompt.

abstract.text: MemWeaver personalizes LLM outputs from the texts a user has written or interacted with. It keeps two memories: a behavioral memory, sampled per query by a random walk over a graph whose edges join time-adjacent and topically similar past documents, and a cognitive memory, an LLM summary of the user's preferences built from summaries of parts of the history. Both are placed in the prompt of an 8B model. On six LaMP tasks it beats plain retrievers and trained personalization retrievers (ROPG, CFRAG) on every metric.

headline: The answer model reads 5 raw past documents plus one LLM-written user summary; the graph only decides which 5.
In the released code the walked documents are reranked by dense similarity, so the walk acts as a candidate filter before plain dense top-5.
The paper builds the summary from time phases; the code (and App. D.1) builds it from K-means clusters.

text: The walk starts at the past document most similar to the query and repeatedly steps to one of the three best-scoring unvisited neighbours, for at most 10 nodes.
The visited documents are reranked by dense similarity and the top 5 go into the prompt together with the user summary.

key_numbers.label: Cluster kept for a summary if

discussion.takeaway: Choosing past documents by a walk that mixes query similarity with time structure, and adding an LLM summary of the user, beat plain and trained retrievers on all six LaMP tasks with 8B models; the concrete documents matter more than the summary.

claims.claim: MemWeaver is best on all twelve LaMP metrics with both backbones.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B LaMP-1 Acc 0.6733 vs 0.6566 (CFRAG), LaMP-3 MAE 0.2800 vs 0.3266, LaMP-5 R-1 0.4757 vs 0.4698; t-test p < 0.05. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Both memories are needed, with behavioral memory as the base.
claims.evidence: Without behavioral memory LaMP-4 R-1 falls from 0.1724 to 0.1069; without cognitive memory to 0.1651. Table 2, §4.3.1

claims.claim: Edge weighting and semantic edges matter more than temporal edges, although temporal edges are traversed more.
claims.evidence: w/o edge weighting LaMP-1 0.5708, w/o semantic 0.6324, w/o temporal 0.6233 (full 0.6733); temporal edges are the majority of traversals on every task. Table 2, Fig. 3

claims.claim: Incremental updates approach a full rebuild at a fraction of the cost.
claims.evidence: Fig. 5 (accuracy and tasks/s vs history share); no table of numbers.

claims.claim: It also beats memory systems.
claims.evidence: LaMP-1 Acc 0.673 vs 0.652 (Mem0), 0.650 (MemoRAG), 0.579 (Memory-R1). Table 5, App. C.2

limits: The paper has no limitations section; §4.6 notes that the best recency and continuity weights depend on the task.
reading: The prompt holds 5 original documents plus a summary; in the released code the walk only narrows the pool before a dense top-5, so the gap to the BGE baseline (also top-k dense) comes from which documents the walk reaches and from the summary.

In the code, a node with more than 3 unvisited neighbours makes the sampling call raise, and the walk falls back to plain retrieval; with semantic edges on, dense clusters make this common. The example script turns K-means off, leaving a pure temporal chain.
In Table 1 every LaMP-1 F1 is exactly half of the accuracy, and LaMP-2 F1 (0.025-0.031) is about a fifteenth of the accuracy; the paper does not explain these F1 values.
Without behavioral memory (summary only) LaMP-3 MAE is 0.64, worse than no personalization at all (0.52), so the summary alone hurts rating prediction.
Without edge weighting LaMP-1 accuracy (0.5708) is below the Random baseline (0.58).
The appendix memory baselines (Mem0, MemoRAG, Memory-R1, Table 5) come without setup details (backbone, what is stored), so how they were run cannot be checked.
Baselines' top-k is not stated in the paper; the code default is 5.

systems.name: MindMemOS

paper.title: MindMemOS: A Portable and Self-Evolving Memory Operating Layer for AI Agents

construction.unit: entity-property-time record (MindSchema); flat typed record (MindVanilla)
construction.kept_as: extracted, with source references
construction.processing: LLM segments episodes, extracts schema entities/properties, fuses entities
construction.writer: LLM extractor guided by scenario schema (schema evolved by MindMemEvolve)

organization.structure: 3D entity-property-time graph with relation and timeline links
organization.stores: memory graph + archive; separate skill registry
organization.index: BM25 + dense embeddings

management.operations: Add/Reinforce/Update/Merge/Skip; dreaming merges/archives; feedback add/update/delete
management.conflicts: entity fusion expires outdated values; dreaming resolves conflicts with two LLM calls
management.forgetting: dreaming archives obsolete or redundant records

retrieval.query: LLM controller sets temporal scope, memory types, search queries
retrieval.candidates: BM25 + dense RRF with forward/reverse entity-property traversal
retrieval.selection: iterative plan; sufficiency check; temporal/relational expansion
retrieval.budget: top-k=50 in MemoryAgentBench runs

use.context: entity-centred memories with property timelines

stages.ingestion: MindVanilla groups messages into turns and token-bounded chunks with source references; MindSchema uses an LLM segmenter to cut the message stream into topic episodes.
stages.construction: MindVanilla extracts flat typed records (profile, fact, episodic, tool trace, experience, skill candidate) with recall-aware extraction; MindSchema maps each episode to schema-defined entities and first/higher-order properties with absolute timestamps, plus an episodic entity as fallback.
stages.organization: 3D entity-property-time memory graph: entities with relations, property timelines per entity-property pair; schema is scenario-adaptive.
stages.update: Deterministic gate maps candidates to Add/Reinforce/Update/Merge/Skip; entity fusion merges property timelines and expires outdated values; offline 'dreaming' clusters records per entity and uses two LLM calls to merge, resolve conflicts and archive; explicit/implicit user feedback triggers add/update/delete.
stages.retrieval: Compact search: an LLM controller plans iterative queries (temporal scope, memory types, sufficiency check) over an inner engine of BM25 + dense RRF with forward/reverse entity-property traversal and optional temporal/relational expansion.
stages.answer: Retrieved entity-centred memories are passed to the answer model (gpt-4.1-mini in the LoCoMo/PersonaMem evaluation).
stages.learning: MindMemEvolve: LLM-guided evolutionary search over memory schemas using judge-scored validation QA (no weight updates); MindSkillEvolve refines skills from execution trajectories.

systems.summary: Memory layer built on an entity-property-time graph with schema-guided extraction, offline 'dreaming' consolidation, feedback-driven correction and evolutionary search over the memory schema itself.
systems.notes:
AXES CORRECTED from the paper; earlier taxonomy row was: schema entry | rewritten | schema learning, dreaming | typed schema | feedback-driven (vector). Authors: Kaichao Liang et al. (MindMemOS Team, Noah's Ark Lab, Huawei). Two add policies: MindVanilla (schema-free) and MindSchema (schema-guided). GitHub README reports LoCoMo overall 93.64 for MindMemOS-schema, whereas the paper's Table 1 reports 94.03. AXES-CHECK: the seed taxonomy's selection 'feedback-driven (vector)' disagrees with the paper: selection is an LLM agentic planner over hybrid BM25+dense RRF with bidirectional graph traversal; feedback is a memory-maintenance (update) mechanism, not a selection mechanism. The seed taxonomy's 'schema learning' corresponds to MindMemEvolve (offline, validation-driven), which is only used for MindSchema.
DESIGN: Sec 2.2, 3.1-3.6, 4.1-4.2. Corrected: construction.processing was 'schema learning, dreaming' (dreaming is management; schema learning is offline MindMemEvolve). trigger 'other' = per memory-add request (async mode buffers until topic shift). use.reasoning null: answer procedure not described.

systems.name: MIRIX

paper.title: MIRIX: Multi-Agent Memory System for LLM-Based Agents

construction.unit: typed entry (e.g. episodic: event_type, summary, details, actor, timestamp)
construction.kept_as: LLM-written summaries/details; Resource and Knowledge Vault keep verbatim content
construction.processing: Meta Memory Manager routes input to per-type Memory Managers, which write in parallel
construction.writer: multi-agent LLMs (gpt-4.1-mini on LoCoMo; Gemini 2.5 Flash on ScreenshotVQA)

organization.structure: six typed stores
organization.stores: Core, Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, Knowledge Vault
organization.index: sqlite; embedding, BM25 and string-match search

management.operations: Memory Managers update own store avoiding redundancy; Core rewritten above 90% capacity

retrieval.query: LLM-generated topic from current context
retrieval.candidates: top-10 entries from each of the six stores (active retrieval)
retrieval.selection: Chat Agent picks stores and method (embedding_match, bm25_match, string_match)
retrieval.budget: top-10 per store

use.context: source-tagged retrieved memories injected into the system prompt
use.reasoning: Chat Agent runs targeted tool searches, consolidates, then answers

stages.ingestion: New input (text or screenshots) triggers a search over the memory base; input plus retrieved context go to a Meta Memory Manager.
stages.construction: The Meta Memory Manager routes content to per-type Memory Managers that write structured entries (e.g., episodic: event_type/summary/details/actor/timestamp; semantic: name/summary/details/source) in parallel, avoiding redundancy.
stages.organization: Six typed stores: Core (persona + human blocks), Episodic, Semantic, Procedural, Resource, Knowledge Vault (verbatim sensitive values with access control).
stages.update: Memory Managers update their own stores; Core Memory is rewritten when above 90% capacity; the Chat Agent can directly request precise updates.
stages.retrieval: Active Retrieval: the agent generates a topic from context and retrieves the top-10 entries from each of the six stores into the system prompt; the Chat Agent can additionally call embedding_match, bm25_match or string_match on chosen stores.
stages.answer: Chat Agent consolidates retrieved, source-tagged memories and synthesizes the response.

systems.summary: Multi-agent memory with six typed stores (core, episodic, semantic, procedural, resource, knowledge vault) coordinated by a meta memory manager, with topic-based active retrieval.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: consistent with the paper; retrieval is 'topic search per store' (top-10 per store) plus agent-chosen embedding/BM25/string-match tool calls. Some stores keep verbatim content (Resource Memory, Knowledge Vault), so fidelity tagged mixed. No peer-reviewed venue found (arXiv preprint as of 2026-09). Also evaluated on the multimodal ScreenshotVQA (not recorded as it is not a conversational-memory benchmark).
DESIGN: Sec 3.1-3.3, 4.1.2. Corrected prefill: 'meta-manager routing' kept in construction.processing but made concrete; kept_as changed from 'rewritten' because Resource Memory and Knowledge Vault store verbatim content. conflicts/forgetting null: no contradiction handling or deletion policy described (only Core Memory compaction).

sources.code_note: Branch public_evaluation, which the paper names as its evaluation code (§4.1.2, footnote 3). Commit 7b143c50 (2025-07-12, 'finish public_evaluations') is the first commit on that branch after paper v1 (2025-07-10). Later commits on the branch (to 33e4bde5, 2025-08-20) change the run scripts and a sqlite fix, not the memory or retrieval code read here.

abstract.text: MIRIX splits an agent's long-term memory into six typed stores: core facts about the user and agent, time-stamped episodes, semantic knowledge, procedures, resources such as documents, and a vault for exact sensitive values. A meta memory manager decides which stores new input concerns, and one LLM manager per store writes and edits its entries in parallel. Before answering, the chat agent writes a short topic, retrieves the best matches from each store into its prompt, and can search further with tools. The authors report 85.38 on LoCoMo with gpt-4.1-mini and higher accuracy than retrieval and long-context baselines on ScreenshotVQA, a new benchmark of one to four weeks of screenshots.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

units.name: Core memory
units.role: short always-visible profile of the user and the agent
units.made_by: Core Memory Manager (LLM) via append, replace and rewrite calls

fields.name: human block
fields.what: enduring facts about the user; rewritten to about half when a block passes 90% of its 5,000-character limit
fields.src: paper §3.1; code core_memory_agent.txt L10, constants.py L156-L158

fields.name: persona block
fields.what: the agent's identity and tone; the evaluation overwrites it with a be-concise persona before questions

units.name: Episodic event
units.role: one time-stamped event, the main store for LoCoMo
units.made_by: Episodic Memory Manager (LLM), one insert, merge or replace call per write

fields.name: summary
fields.what: one-line LLM summary of the event

fields.name: details
fields.what: longer LLM description of the event; prompt asks to record as much as possible
fields.src: code episodic_memory_agent.txt L16; details embedding searched in agent.py L1190; text returned only by search_in_memory (base.py L104-L115)

fields.name: occurred_at
fields.what: event time; the 10 most recent events are always shown

fields.name: tree_path
fields.what: LLM category path such as personal > travel
fields.src: code episodic_memory_agent.txt L18; shown as Path in agent.py L1182

fields.name: event_type, actor
fields.what: category of the event and who produced it
fields.src: paper §3.1; returned only by search_in_memory (base.py L113)

units.name: Semantic item
units.role: knowledge about a person, place or concept
units.made_by: Semantic Memory Manager (LLM)

fields.name: name, summary
fields.what: entity name and a one-sentence description

fields.name: details
fields.what: longer LLM description; its embedding is matched against the topic

units.name: Procedural, resource and vault entries
units.role: how-to steps, documents and exact values; little used on LoCoMo text
units.made_by: their own managers (LLM)

fields.name: procedure summary, steps
fields.what: goal description and a list of steps

fields.name: resource title, summary
fields.what: name and overview of a shared document or file

fields.name: resource content
fields.what: full or excerpted text; not embedding-searchable, only BM25 or string match via the tool

fields.name: vault caption, secret_value
fields.what: exact values such as addresses or keys; high-sensitivity entries excluded from automatic retrieval. Retrieved each turn but left out of the prompt template
fields.src: paper §3.1; code agent.py L1164-L1174, L1263-L1301; base.py L141-L151

units.name: Source conversation
units.role: the LoCoMo session as sent to the memory managers
units.made_by: evaluation script, one session per write call

fields.name: session text
fields.what: raw turns with the session date, plus instructions to turn relative dates into absolute ones; kept only in the memory agents' message logs

discussion.takeaway: Route memory into typed stores, each kept by its own LLM manager, and put topic-matched summaries from every store into the prompt before answering. With gpt-4.1-mini this reaches 85.38 on LoCoMo, close to full context (87.52).

claims.claim: State of the art on LoCoMo among memory systems.
claims.evidence: 85.38 overall vs Zep 79.09, LangMem 78.05, Mem0 62.47 and RAG-500 51.62, all with gpt-4.1-mini; full context 87.52. Table 2

claims.claim: Largest gains on multi-hop questions, because events are stored already consolidated.
claims.evidence: Multi-hop 83.70 vs full context 77.70 and Zep 69.16. Table 2, §4.3

claims.claim: Much better and far smaller than retrieval and long-context baselines on screenshots.
claims.evidence: ScreenshotVQA accuracy 0.5950 vs SigLIP@50 0.4410 (+35%) and Gemini 0.1166 (+410%); storage 15.89 MB vs 15.07 GB and 236.70 MB. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Runs are stable enough that MIRIX stays best across repeats.
claims.evidence: Three runs 83.98, 87.34, 84.82 overall. Table 3, App. A

limits: Open-domain questions gain least; the authors attribute this to relying on retrieval, which lacks a global view of the conversation.
Some single-hop misses come from ambiguous questions where the stored consolidated event replaces an earlier plan.
Harder real-world benchmarks are left for future work.
reading: There is no ablation: the six-store split, the meta router and topic retrieval are never removed, so the gain over baselines cannot be assigned to any one of them.

In the evaluation code the prompt holds only one-line summaries (10 recent and 10 topic-matched episodes, 10 each from semantic, resource and procedural memory); details reach the answer only through a search tool call. The paper does not report how often the agent calls it.
The knowledge vault is retrieved every turn but the prompt template has no slot for it, so 'top-10 from each of the six components' (§3.2) holds for five stores in the code.
Memory is written one whole LoCoMo session at a time, with instructions to convert relative dates to absolute ones before storing; baselines were run with their own pipelines.
The paper names GPT-4.1 as judge, while the released llm_judge.py at this commit calls gpt-4o-mini with Mem0's prompt.
MIRIX and full context are averaged over 3 runs, the baselines run once; the LangMem gpt-4.1-mini row differs between Table 2 (78.05) and Table 3 (79.22).

The text says MIRIX beats all baselines on multi-hop by over 24 points, but Table 2 shows +14.5 over Zep (69.16) and +6.0 over full context; it also gives 26,000 tokens per LoCoMo conversation (§4.1.1) where the Table 2 caption says 9k.

systems.name: PASK

paper.title: PASK: Toward Intent-Aware Proactive Agents with Long-Term Memory

construction.unit: three tiers: user profile, session workspace, global tree with episode leaves ⟨fine tag, content⟩
construction.kept_as: profile traits (summarized); session history in the context window; episodes extracted from finished sessions
construction.processing: workspace state tracked every step; after a session, candidate traits are extracted for the profile and new episodes are inserted as raw leaves under a buffer node
construction.writer: not stated (a 'memory agent'; model unnamed)

organization.structure: cache / main memory / external storage; the global memory is a bounded-depth rooted tree of tag nodes over episode leaves
organization.stores: user memory (system prompt), workspace memory (context window), global memory (tree + RAG; Redis-style hot state and object/vector-store persistence per §5)
organization.index: RAG over leaf content under the anchor node (retriever not named)

management.operations: time-decayed profile update with conflict resolution; lazy CompressAndMerge of a node's children once their count exceeds η_merge; depth capped at D_max
management.conflicts: ResolveConflict reinforces matching traits, overwrites decayed contradictions and discards low-confidence anomalies
management.forgetting: confidence decay of outdated preferences; obsolete information pruned during merges

retrieval.query: q_t built from the latest segment, the history, an LLM observation summary and salient entities
retrieval.candidates: coarse: tag of the anchor node reused from the previous step; fine: RAG over leaves under that anchor
retrieval.selection: MemLoader (trained Qwen3-4B) distills the evidence; the Demand Detector then replies or stays silent

use.context: user profile + workspace state + anchor tag + distilled RAG evidence
use.reasoning: memory is read only when the detector emits <full_assistance>; otherwise silence or a fast reply from context

classify.note: Index and candidate type are read from 'RAG' and the vector-store backend in §5; the retriever itself is not described. A trained detector decides whether to retrieve and a trained MemLoader distills what is kept.

stages.ingestion: A frontend (glasses, computer, phone) turns speech and vision into a stream of text segments; the detector reads one segment per step.
stages.construction: Within a session the workspace memory keeps the history and a tracked state; after the session, traits are extracted for the user profile and episodes become new leaves under a buffer node of the global tree.
stages.organization: User memory sits in the system prompt (reused via KV cache), workspace memory in the context window, and global memory in a rooted tree whose internal nodes hold semantic tags and whose leaves hold a fine tag and episodic content.
stages.update: Offline only: profile traits decay over time and conflicts are resolved; a node's children are compressed and merged once they exceed η_merge, and depth is capped at D_max.
stages.retrieval: Only on a <full_assistance> token: an LLM summarizes the recent context and entities into a query, the anchor node from the previous step supplies a coarse tag, and RAG searches only that node's leaves; MemLoader distills the result.
stages.answer: The Demand Detector (Qwen3-30B-A3B, SFT + RL) writes the proactive reply or stays silent, using the profile, workspace and distilled evidence.
stages.learning: Demand Detector and MemLoader are fine-tuned separately on 100k synthetic samples, then jointly with DAPO RL on 2K real sessions (rule + LLM-judge rewards). The memory store itself is not trained.

systems.summary: Proactive assistant whose trained detector decides each turn whether to stay silent, answer from context, or load memory from a three-tier store (profile cache, session workspace, lazily merged global tree).
systems.notes:
Memory is one of three parts (DD-MM-PAS); most of the paper is the IntentFlow demand detector and the LatentNeeds benchmark. The released code (eval/, bench/) covers the benchmark only: no Pask-MM tree, RAG or MemLoader. In the benchmark every model, IntentFlow included in the released results, sees the same precomputed session 'memory' summary. Paper lists no η_merge, D_max, top-k or retriever.
DESIGN: §3.1, §4.1-4.3, §5, §6.1; code eval/prompts.py, bench/02_build_turns.py.

sources.code_note: The official repo (latest commit d54646c5, 2026-04-18) releases the LatentNeeds-Bench pipeline, evaluation prompts and per-model result/score files, but no code for Pask-MM (tree, RAG, merge, MemLoader) or IntentFlow training. The memory figures therefore follow the paper only; the benchmark facts follow the code.

headline: Memory is read only when the trained detector asks for it; most turns are silence or a fast reply from context.
Global retrieval does not search the whole tree: it reuses the previous step's anchor node and runs RAG only under it.
The benchmark gives every model the same precomputed memory summary, so none of the reported numbers isolates Pask-MM.

open_questions: No run removes or swaps the memory module, so the benchmark cannot show what Pask-MM adds; the stability claim rests on IntentFlow vs other models, all given the same summary.
IntentFlow is the fine-tuned model; its gain over its base (58.9 → 84.2) mixes intent training with anything memory-related.

glance.a: Three kinds: profile traits in the system prompt, the session history in the context window, and leaves in a global tree holding a fine tag and an episode.
As a cache / main memory / external storage hierarchy; the global tier is a rooted tree of semantic tags with a capped depth.
The workspace is updated every step; profile and tree are updated only after the session ends.
Only when the detector emits <full_assistance>; retrieval then searches the leaves under the previous step's anchor node.
Not in isolation. The benchmark gives every model one precomputed summary of earlier parts; long-term memory is shown only through case studies.

text: The detector emits one token per segment: stay silent, reply from context, or load memory.
Loading memory reuses the last anchor node's tag and runs RAG only under it; a small trained model distills the evidence before the detector replies.

discussion.takeaway: A proactive agent needs a fast gate that decides when to speak and when to load memory. PASK trains that gate (IntentFlow) and pairs it with a tiered memory, and reports the best balanced accuracy on its own LatentNeeds-Bench at the lowest latency.

claims.claim: A trained open model matches fast frontier models on latent-need detection.
claims.evidence: Balanced accuracy 84.2 vs 80.8 (Gemini-3-Flash), 77.2 (GPT-5-Mini); demand accuracy 83.1 vs 83.3 (Gemini-3-Flash). Table 1, §6.2

claims.claim: Training, not the base model, gives the gain.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-30B-A3B base 58.9 → IntentFlow 84.2. Table 1

claims.claim: Performance stays stable over long sessions with Pask-MM.
claims.evidence: 86.1 → 81.8 from turns 1-4 to 57-60 (−5.0%), vs −17.3% Gemini-3-Flash and −19.0% GPT-5-Mini. Table 3, §6.4

claims.claim: Lowest latency.
claims.evidence: 1.3-1.5 s per turn vs 3.2-4.4 s for Gemini-3-Flash. Table 4, §6.5.1

claims.claim: Long-term memory helps with background, knowledge and preferences.
claims.evidence: Case studies only, no metric. Fig. 9, §6.5.2

limits: The benefits of long-term memory are hard to measure in open-ended settings, so they are shown by case studies.
IntentFlow does not set a new ceiling; it trails Gemini-3-Flash on demand accuracy (83.1 vs 83.3) and in Work scenarios (84.8 vs 91.5).
Daily-life assistance is the hardest in the user study; deep intent understanding remains unsolved.
reading: The benchmark input gives all models the same scene description, a precomputed summary of earlier parts and the full 60-turn part history; none of the scored runs uses the global tree, RAG or MemLoader, so Table 1 and Table 3 measure the detector, not Pask-MM.
No memory ablation is reported; the multi-turn stability claim compares different models, not IntentFlow with and without memory.
The released code sets the judge to gpt-4.1-mini while the paper names GPT-5.2.
Each baseline is reported at its best of three prompt levels, while the released IntentFlow scores are from the neutral level only.
A reply on a no-demand turn counts as correct if the judge accepts it (score files label it fp_accepted), so No-Dem. accuracy is not simply staying silent.
Key memory settings (η_merge, D_max, top-k, retriever, what extracts traits and episodes) are not given anywhere.

abstract.text: PASK studies proactive assistants that listen to a live stream and must decide, turn by turn, whether and how to help without being asked. It proposes a three-part design: demand detection, memory modelling and an always-on agent system. Demand detection is done by IntentFlow, a Qwen3-30B-A3B model trained with SFT and RL that emits a silence, fast-reply or memory-backed token; memory is split into a user profile, a session workspace and a lazily merged global tree searched by RAG. On a new real-world benchmark, LatentNeeds-Bench, IntentFlow reaches the best balanced accuracy among the tested models at the lowest latency.

construction.unit: memory fragment (key, value, date, message id) typed factual / experiential / subjective; plus reasoning fragments
construction.kept_as: LLM-extracted present-tense phrases; LLM-inferred cross-session insights
construction.processing: LLM extracts typed fragments per session with normalised dates; fragments are clustered per session and matched to earlier clusters; an LLM writes insights for each matched pair under five evolution patterns
construction.writer: same LLM family as the answer model, largest size (Qwen2.5-72B, Gemma3-27B or GPT-4.1)

organization.structure: two flat stores: fragments M and reasoning fragments R; session clusters exist only while building
organization.stores: M (extracted fragments), R (reasoning fragments)
organization.index: Stella_en_400M_v5 dense embeddings of 'key: value'

management.operations: append new fragments; append reasoning fragments for each earlier cluster that matches a new cluster (cos > 0.6); a matched earlier cluster leaves the persistent pool
management.conflicts: not resolved in place; a 'transformation' insight can record a change, both old and new fragments stay

retrieval.query: question used as is (Stella s2p query prompt)
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity over M ∪ R
retrieval.selection: top 102 (token budget / 20), added in rank order until 2,048 tokens, then sorted by session date
retrieval.budget: 2,048 tokens in the main tables (1,024 and 4,096 also tested)

use.context: retrieved fragments as '[key, date]: value' lines, oldest first; no original messages
use.reasoning: single answer call with a short-phrase prompt

classify.note: Session clusters and the persistent pool only decide which fragment groups the LLM reasons over at write time; the read side is one flat dense search over fragments and derived insights. 'consolidate' because new cross-session insight items are written; nothing is edited or deleted.

stages.ingestion: Each session is processed after it ends; in LoCoMo each speaker's messages are sent to the extractor separately, in LongMemEval the whole session at once (code).
stages.construction: An LLM pulls out every personal statement as a fragment with a key, a present-tense value, the source message id and a date written as the message date, an absolute date, 'Before [date]' or 'After [date]', typed as factual, experiential or subjective.
stages.organization: Fragments go to a flat store M. For building only, each session's fragments are k-means clustered (k chosen by silhouette) and compared with a pool of earlier clusters.
stages.update: For every earlier cluster whose centroid similarity with a new cluster exceeds 0.6, the LLM reads both groups and writes short insights (extension, accumulation, specification, transformation, connection) into store R; matched earlier clusters leave the pool.
stages.retrieval: The question is embedded with Stella_en_400M_v5 and compared by cosine with every item in M and R; the top items are added until 2,048 tokens and then ordered by date.
stages.answer: One answer call reads the '[key, date]: value' lines and the question and returns a short phrase.

systems.summary: Moves cross-session reasoning to write time: an LLM extracts typed, dated fragments per session and writes explicit insights (extension, accumulation, specification, transformation, connection) for clusters that match earlier ones, so a plain dense search over fragments and insights serves the answer model.

Baselines are compared at the same nominal 2,048-token budget, but Table 6 reports 3.7-4.0k context tokens for HippoRAG-2 and 5.9-6.3k for A-Mem.

abstract.text: PREMem argues that long-term conversational memory should do its cross-session reasoning when memories are written, not when a question is answered. For each session an LLM extracts short, dated fragments sorted into factual, experiential and subjective information. Fragment clusters that resemble clusters from earlier sessions are handed to an LLM, which writes explicit insights about how the information evolved (extension, accumulation, specification, transformation, connection). At question time a plain dense search over fragments and insights fills a small context, and the authors report gains on LongMemEval and LoCoMo across model sizes, with small answer models approaching larger baselines.

discussion.takeaway: Doing the cross-session synthesis when memory is written lets a plain dense retriever and a small answer model do well; in the paper's own runs PREMem leads on overall LLM-judge score on both benchmarks for every model family.

claims.claim: Shifting reasoning to storage time improves long-term dialogue QA across model sizes.
claims.evidence: GPT-4.1: 71.4 vs 55.9 (A-Mem) on LongMemEval, 67.7 vs 57.3 (HippoRAG-2) on LoCoMo. Table 2

claims.claim: Gains are largest on cross-session questions.
claims.evidence: LongMemEval multi-hop 83.5 vs 41.4 and knowledge update 93.7 vs 64.7 (A-Mem, GPT-4.1). Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: Small answer models with PREMem match larger models with baselines.
claims.evidence: GPT-4.1-nano 58.7 / 58.8 vs the best GPT-4.1 baseline 55.9 (LongMemEval) and 57.3 (LoCoMo). Table 3

claims.claim: Extraction is essential and pre-storage reasoning helps.
claims.evidence: Without Step 1 scores drop 32.7-61.0%; without Step 2 LoCoMo drops 3.2-5.4%. Table 4, §4.4

claims.claim: PREMem holds up at small token budgets.
claims.evidence: At 1,024 tokens: 70.2 LongMemEval, 67.3 LoCoMo (GPT-4.1) vs 71.4 / 67.7 at 2,048. Table 5

claims.claim: BM25 and smaller construction models are workable substitutes.
claims.evidence: GPT-4.1: BM25 67.4 vs 71.4 (LongMemEval); PREMem_S 68.1. Fig. 2, Table 6

limits: Single-hop questions score lower than with direct retrieval of messages.
Original messages are not kept, so conversational style and wording are lost.
No forgetting or memory-size limit.
The contribution is empirical rather than theoretical.
reading: On LongMemEval, removing Step 2 raises the score for Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen2.5-72B and GPT-4.1-mini (Table 4); the consistent Step-2 gain is on LoCoMo (3-5 points).

The LoCoMo category names follow the code's id map (1 single-hop, 2 multi-hop, 3 temporal, 4 open-domain merged into single-hop; data/preprocess/locomo.py L178-L182). In the released outputs 'When did Caroline go to the LGBTQ support group?' is scored as multi-hop, so the LoCoMo per-category labels are not those most other papers use.

Totals include the adversarial questions scored by the LLM judge (LoCoMo 1,986 questions: the released GPT-4.1 run gives 67.73, matching Table 2), while the 'Adv Acc' column is a separate safe-refusal rate.
Baselines are said to run at the same 2,048-token budget, but Table 6 reports 3.7-4.0k context tokens for HippoRAG-2 and 5.9-6.3k for A-Mem.
The Full-history baseline uses about 18.7k tokens on LongMemEval-S (Table 6), far below the ~115k-token histories (§4.1), so it is a truncated history.
Every construction step (extraction, reasoning) uses the largest model of the answer model's family, while baselines such as A-Mem and HippoRAG-2 build memory with settings the paper does not state.
Table 3 lists Gemma3-27B Session at 33.3 on LoCoMo, where Tables 2 and 6 give 43.3.

systems.name: PRIME

paper.title: PRIME: Large Language Model Personalization with Cognitive Dual-Memory and Personalized Thought Process

construction.unit: per-user LoRA adapter (semantic memory); raw past threads (episodic memory, variants only)
construction.kept_as: parametric: the user's history is trained into LoRA weights; episodic threads stored verbatim
construction.processing: LoRA task fine-tuning on the user's past CMV threads (query -> delta-awarded reply), then self-distilled personalized thinking (profile, replay, rejection sampling, proxy-written thoughts, 1-epoch fine-tune)
construction.writer: LoRA training of the base model (Llama, Qwen, Ministral or Phi, 3B-14B)

organization.structure: one LoRA adapter per user (+ raw thread list in EM variants)
organization.stores: semantic memory: LoRA weights ΔH(a); episodic memory: past engagements (dropped in final PRIME)

management.operations: none after instantiation: both memories are frozen

retrieval.query: the new query (OP and candidate replies)
retrieval.candidates: final PRIME: none, the user's LoRA is merged into the model; EM variants: 3 most recent threads (CMV) or 4 (LaMP)
retrieval.selection: recency in EM variants; relevance retrieval tested in §4 (retriever not named)
retrieval.budget: 3 threads (CMV) / 4 (LaMP) in EM variants

use.context: the query only; the model with the user's LoRA writes a thinking trace that restates the user profile before answering
use.reasoning: one generation of up to 2,048 tokens: user experience, OP summary, outline, per-candidate analysis, reflection, answer

classify.note: Final PRIME keeps each user's history only as LoRA weights: no stored text is searched, and the memory is trained once and frozen (placed under append-only as the nearest value: nothing is edited or deleted). The episodic store of raw threads exists only in the EM, DUAL and EM-included variants.

stages.ingestion: A user's history is their past engagements: for CMV, single-turn Reddit threads (OP plus direct replies, one marked by the OP's delta); for LaMP, the benchmark's user profiles.
stages.construction: Semantic memory: a LoRA adapter per user trained with task-oriented fine-tuning (query with candidates -> the delta-awarded reply's option ID) for 3 epochs (2 on LaMP). Episodic memory: the raw engagements, stored as is.
stages.retrieval: At test time the user's LoRA is merged into the base model. EM variants also prepend the 3 (CMV) or 4 (LaMP) most recent engagements; the final PRIME drops this because it lowered scores.
stages.answer: The model generates a personalized thinking trace (user-experience summary, OP summary, outline, analysis of each candidate, reflection) and then the ranked top-3 option IDs, up to 2,048 tokens.
stages.learning: Personalized thinking is self-distilled: the LoRA model writes a user profile, replays the user's past threads as queries and keeps those it gets right; a proxy model (base model + profile text) writes structured thoughts given query and gold answer; thoughts reaching the gold answer are kept and the LoRA model is fine-tuned on them for one epoch.

systems.summary: Cognitive dual-memory framing of LLM personalization: episodic memory as recalled past engagements and semantic memory as a per-user LoRA, plus self-distilled personalized thinking; the final system keeps only the LoRA and the thinking, evaluated on a new Reddit ChangeMyView ranking dataset and LaMP.
systems.notes: Venue verified on ACL Anthology: EMNLP 2025 main, pages 33707-33736 (2025.emnlp-main.1711). PDF read: arXiv v3 (26 Sep 2025). The linked repository (launchnlp/LM_Personalization, HEAD 14e4adbd80b75148bcb23e3080256e5b769a7e8b, 2025-06-25) contains only the CMV data and a README saying the code is still being refactored, so nothing here comes from code. New benchmark ids proposed in .cache/annot/new_benchmarks_prime.json ('cmv-persuasion', 'lamp'); new baselines in .cache/annot/new_extra_prime.json ('r1-distill', 'oppu'). Final PRIME excludes episodic memory (§6 Implementation Details, Table A3), so 'dual memory' applies to the DUAL and EM-included PRIME variants. The paper uses 'episodic memory' in two ways: recalled raw engagements (§4) and, in the profile-replacement study, the textual profile summary (App. D). Footnote 18 gives the Qwen2.5-14B model card as Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, apparently a typo.

sources.paper: arXiv 2507.04607v3 (PDF read 2026-09-30); ACL Anthology 2025.emnlp-main.1711 checked for venue
sources.code_note: The paper links https://github.com/launchnlp/LM_Personalization; at commit 14e4adbd80b75148bcb23e3080256e5b769a7e8b (latest, 2025-06-25) it holds only the CMV dataset (history, evaluation, target authors) and states that the code is still being refactored. No method code, so everything below is from the paper.

abstract.text: PRIME frames LLM personalization with the cognitive split between episodic memory (specific past engagements of a user) and semantic memory (lasting beliefs and preferences). The authors first compare many ways to build each memory, finding that recency beats relevance for recall and that per-user LoRA fine-tuning on the task is the strongest semantic memory. PRIME combines these and adds personalized thinking, learned by self-distilling reasoning traces from the user's own history. They also release a Reddit ChangeMyView dataset where the model must rank the reply that changed a user's view, and report gains over non-personalized and generic-reasoning baselines on it and on LaMP.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: In the final PRIME a user's history lives only in a per-user LoRA adapter; no stored text is retrieved at test time.
The episodic part (recent past threads in the prompt) was dropped from the final system because it lowered scores; the dual memory survives only in the DUAL and EM-included variants.
The model restates a user profile at the start of its own thinking, a behaviour learned by self-distillation on the user's past threads.

units.name: Semantic memory
units.role: the user's preferences and beliefs, trained into weights
units.made_by: LoRA task fine-tuning on the user's history, then fine-tuning on self-distilled thoughts

fields.name: LoRA weights ΔH(a)

fields.name: profile summary
fields.what: text summary of the user written by the LoRA model (Parametric Knowledge Reification); used to build the proxy model for thought synthesis, and regenerated by PRIME inside its thinking

units.name: Episodic memory
units.role: specific past engagements of the user
units.made_by: none: raw threads stored as is

fields.name: past threads
fields.what: the user's single-turn CMV threads (OP and replies) or LaMP profile items; 3 (CMV) or 4 (LaMP) most recent are prepended in EM and DUAL variants; not used by final PRIME

write.how: task-oriented fine-tuning per user: input is a past OP with candidate replies, target is the delta-awarded reply's option ID
the LoRA model summarises the user (PKR)
each past engagement is turned into a query; keep those the LoRA model answers correctly
a proxy model (base model + profile text) is given the query and its answer and writes structured thoughts that restate the profile; keep those whose answer matches
train the LoRA model 1 epoch with cross-entropy: plain query in, thinking trace + answer out

read.how: merge the user's LoRA into the base model
prepend the 3 most recent engagements (CMV) before the new OP; not in final PRIME
one generation: user experience, OP summary, outline, per-candidate analysis, reflection, ranked answer

answer_context.sees: the query only (author name, OP title and body, candidate replies as JSON); personalization comes from the merged LoRA weights
answer_context.format: standard CMV template (Fig. A7) followed by the personalized-thinking output instructions (Fig. A10)

compression.what: user history vs what the answer model reads
compression.basis: Not comparable in tokens: final PRIME reads no history text; the history (183.2 engagements per CMV user on average, Table A1) is held in LoRA weights whose rank and size are not reported.

open_questions: The LoRA rank, learning rate and adapter size are not reported, so the memory capacity per user is unknown.
PRIME vs SM mixes two changes (thought fine-tuning and a longer generation with a structured prompt); a SM + thinking-prompt-without-training variant is not reported for the trained models.
Only 133 CMV queries from 41 users; results average 10 runs but no variance is given.

discussion.takeaway: For personalization, a per-user LoRA trained on the task beats recalling past engagements, and teaching that adapter to reason from a recalled profile adds more; the recalled engagements themselves were left out of the final system.

claims.claim: Semantic memory beats episodic memory.
claims.evidence: SM vs EM Avg on CMV: 31.24 vs 26.88 (Llama-3.1-8B), 37.22 vs 30.65 (Qwen2.5-14B); same trend on LaMP (Tables 3-4, A3).

claims.claim: Recency recall beats relevance retrieval for episodic memory.
Personalized thinking is crucial and PRIME is model-agnostic.
claims.evidence: PRIME best Avg for all 6 base models on CMV, e.g. 34.13 vs 32.24 DUAL on Llama-3.1-8B (Table 3).

claims.claim: Generic reasoning hurts personalization.
claims.evidence: R1-distilled models below non-personalized base on CMV for Llama-8B (25.18 vs 26.58) and Qwen-7B (23.36 vs 27.89) (Table A3).

claims.claim: PRIME uses the specific user's history rather than popularity.
claims.evidence: Swapping in another user's LoRA and profile lowers scores, most for the most similar users (Fig. 2, App. D).

limits: Two benchmarks cannot cover the range of personalization tasks, e.g. long-form personalization.
Models only up to 14B parameters, for budget reasons.
Inference is costly: 10-20 hours per model on one A40 or L40 GPU.
reading: Combining both memories is not consistently better: DUAL is below SM alone for Qwen2.5-7B (28.71 vs 30.20) and Llama-3.2-3B (28.87 vs 30.25), which is why the final PRIME drops episodic memory (§6, §7.1).

On LaMP, PRIME is below DUAL on LaMP-3 (MAE .223 vs .188) and LaMP-5 (ROUGE-1 47.3 vs 52.2), and all non-OPPU methods trail OPPU, which trains on other users' data and uses Llama-2-7B, so that comparison differs in both data and base model.

The CMV test set was filtered to queries the base Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B get wrong without history (Hit@1 ≤ 0.3, Hit@3 ≤ 0.5), which removes 194 queries and lowers the non-personalized baseline for those two models by construction.
Every trained variant fits one adapter per user on the same task format it is tested on (task-oriented FT), so SM is closer to per-user supervised training than to a memory read at test time.
The main text reports Hit@3 and Avg; Table A3 shows Ministral-8B PRIME's Hit@3 (40.75) slightly below SM and DUAL (40.83).

systems.name: PRINCIPLES

paper.title: PRINCIPLES: Synthetic Strategy Memory for Proactive Dialogue Agents

construction.unit: principle: 'When [situation], you should [strategy], rather than [failed strategy], because [reason]'
construction.kept_as: LLM-derived lesson in a fixed template; the When clause is also stored separately
construction.processing: offline self-play; a turn whose critic reward rises yields a principle; a turn that does not rise is revised and re-simulated (up to 3 tries) and a success after revision yields a contrastive principle
construction.writer: LLM prompted with the dialogue, the successful turn and any failed tries

organization.structure: flat set of principles per domain
organization.stores: one FAISS index per dataset
organization.index: embedding of the When clause (text-embedding-ada-002, L2 distance)

management.operations: none after construction (append-only while building)

retrieval.query: the dialogue so far (state s_t)
retrieval.candidates: L2 nearest When clauses (FAISS)
retrieval.selection: top-k = 3; each retrieved principle is rewritten by an LLM to fit the current dialogue
retrieval.budget: 3 principles per turn

use.context: the reinterpreted principles replace the strategy slot of the agent's response prompt
use.reasoning: one reply per turn; no separate strategy-planning call at inference

classify.note: The LLM reinterpretation rewrites the 3 retrieved principles but does not choose among them.

stages.ingestion: Offline self-play on training dialogues: an agent, a user simulator and a critic LLM play out conversations started from the first turn of a training dialogue (50 simulations per dataset, up to 10 turns).
stages.construction: After each turn the critic's averaged reward is compared with the previous turn. If it rose, an LLM writes a When/should/because principle from the turn. If not, the strategy is revised from the failed tries, the turn is replayed from the same state (up to 3 tries), and a success yields a When/should/rather than/because principle.
stages.organization: About 100 principles per domain in one flat set; the When clause is embedded for search.
stages.retrieval: At each turn the dialogue so far is embedded and the 3 principles whose When clauses are closest (L2, FAISS) are retrieved; an LLM rewrites each to fit the current dialogue.
stages.answer: The reinterpreted principles serve as the dialogue strategy in the agent's reply prompt (one short sentence per turn).
stages.learning: No parameter updates; memory is built from simulated experience only.

systems.summary: A strategy memory for proactive dialogue built by offline self-play: turns that raise the critic's reward, or that succeed after backtracking and revision, are turned into When / should / rather than / because principles, retrieved by situation and reinterpreted to guide each reply.

headline: Memory is a set of ~100 strategy rules written by an LLM during offline self-play, not records of the user or the conversation.
Only the When clause is matched; the whole rule is then rewritten by an LLM for the current dialogue and handed to the agent as its strategy.
Failed turns are replayed from the same state with revised strategies, so many rules carry a 'rather than' contrast with what failed.

components.role: Plans and revises strategies in self-play

components.model: GPT-4o by default (Table 7 also tries Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Llama-3.1-8B)

discussion.takeaway: Strategy rules mined from an LLM's own simulated successes and repaired failures, stored as situation-indexed principles, beat prompted and trained strategy planners on emotional-support and persuasion self-play without any training.

claims.claim: Principles widen strategy coverage.
claims.evidence: SR 73.85 ESConv, 86.15 ExTES, 59.17 P4G+ vs best baselines 58.46, 71.54, 53.33; P4G 95.00 vs PPDPP 96.67. Table 1

claims.claim: Principles reduce strategy preference bias.
claims.evidence: Highest macro F1, weighted F1 and entropy on ESConv (10.52 / 17.67 / 1.21) and P4G (14.96 / 24.30 / 2.67). Table 2

claims.claim: No training is needed and cost stays low.
claims.evidence: PPDPP training costs about 11.5x more (Fig. 3); DPDP 18.07x training and 3.07x inference cost for 79.23 vs 73.85 SR on ESConv. Table 4

claims.claim: Lessons from both success and failure are needed.
claims.evidence: Both sources together beat either alone on ExTES and ESConv. Fig. 8

claims.claim: All four parts of the template matter.
claims.evidence: ESConv SR 73.85 full, 62.31 without 'rather than', 64.00 without 'because'. Table 5

claims.claim: Principles can also be built online.
claims.evidence: ESConv SR 66.15 online (success only) vs 73.85 offline. Table 6

limits: Retrieval uses L2 embedding distance between the dialogue and the When clause, which can miss fine contextual differences; reinterpretation may not fix very specific or ambiguous situations.
Planning is turn by turn with no explicit long-term goal, so the agent may chase short-term reward in tasks such as negotiation.
Principles are not reviewed by experts; no clinical claims are made for emotional-support use.
reading: All scores come from self-play with an LLM user simulator and an LLM critic (gpt-4o); the same kind of critic reward also decides which turns become principles, so the memory is shaped by the evaluator.
The paper states that user simulator and critic are gpt-4o but does not state the agent backbone for PRINCIPLES and the baselines in Table 1; the released script uses gpt-4o-mini for all roles.
Figure 10 shows ESConv SR 80.0 at k = 9 against 73.9 at the default k = 3, and P4G 95.0 at k = 3; results are sensitive to k and the main table uses one fixed value.
Figure 9 shows P4G+ SR 60.0 at 25 simulations and 59.2 at 50, so '50 is optimal' holds for ExTES (86.2) but not clearly for P4G+.
In Table 3, the 'w/o Structured' and 'w/o Reinterpretation' rows are identical on both datasets (83.85 / 56.67).
Table 7: principles built with Llama-3.1-8B score higher on ESConv (86.15) than those built with GPT-4o (73.85).
The paper cites Ask-an-Expert as Zhang et al. 2024b in the text but lists it as 2023 in the references and Fig. 28 caption.

abstract.text: PRINCIPLES targets strategy planning in proactive dialogue such as emotional support and persuasion, where fixed strategy sets cover too little, LLMs favour a few strategies, and trained planners are costly. The method runs offline self-play on training dialogues and converts turns that improved the critic's score, or that succeeded after backtracking and revision, into structured principles. At inference, principles matching the current situation are retrieved, adapted to the dialogue and used to guide the agent, with no training. It outperforms prompted and trained baselines on ESConv, ExTES, P4G and an extended P4G+.

headline: All the novelty is at write time: five extra steps check and repair what one extraction pass wrote, and reading is a plain top-20 dense lookup.
