discussion.takeaway: Extracting details, events and relations separately and checking the result against the dialogue gives more complete and more accurate memory than one summary pass, at roughly the token cost of Mem0.

claims.claim: One-pass extraction loses information and cannot be fixed by extracting more.
claims.evidence: Naive RAG QA drops from 74.13 (raw, 157K tokens) to 50.66 (one-off memory, 12.79K); larger memories give limited F1 gains. §3.1, Fig. 3

claims.claim: Best memory quality on HaluMem.
claims.evidence: Memory accuracy 94.68 and F1 87.52, both highest in Table 1; QA 63.43 is second to MemOS (67.23). §4.2

claims.claim: The gain comes from the method, not from spending more tokens.
claims.evidence: 11.59K tokens vs 10.56K for full LightMem, which scores 55.81 QA and 71.19 F1. §4.2, Table 1

claims.claim: Each check helps.
claims.evidence: Without completeness check integrity falls 81.37→69.48; without hallucination check QA hallucination rises to 21.40; without detail anchoring QA falls to 57.80. Table 2

claims.claim: Works with small models.
claims.evidence: With Llama3.1-8B for extraction and QA: integrity 43.09 vs 30.59 and QA 49.15 vs 38.41 for Mem0. Table 3

claims.claim: Transfers to other benchmarks and systems.
claims.evidence: LongMemEval-S 72.12 and LoCoMo 77.56 vs LightMem 68.64 / 72.99 (Fig. 5); swapping ProMem memory into MemOS raises HaluMem QA 67.23→68.46 (Fig. 6c).

limits: Verification and recovery add tokens and latency over one-pass summarization, which may matter for real-time or low-resource use.
The checks depend on the backbone's reasoning; a weak model may write poor probe questions, and the smallest workable model is unknown.
reading: Baseline rows in Table 1 match HaluMem-Medium Table 3 of the HaluMem paper exactly (e.g. Memobase 14.55/92.24/25.13/35.33), where answers come from GPT-4o. ProMem does not say they were copied or which HaluMem split it uses.

MemOS's memory integrity 84.81 is HaluMem's weighted recall, while the other baselines use plain recall (MemOS plain recall is 74.07); MemOS's F1 79.70 matches plain recall, so the integrity column mixes two measures.
Naive RAG over the raw dialogue scores 74.13 QA on HaluMem (Fig. 3), above every Table 1 system including ProMem (63.43).
On LongMemEval-S single-session-assistant, ProMem gets 42.67 against 98.21 for Naive RAG (Table 7): the draft prompt extracts facts about the user only.
The paper says detail anchoring uses turn ids without embedding work, yet Table 6 lists it as the largest verification cost (3.055K tokens, 26%).
No construction code is released, and the answer model for QA is not named; the main run also compresses the dialogue with LLMLingua-2 at an unstated ratio.

abstract.text: ProMem argues that memory systems for LLM agents lose most of their information at the extraction step, because a single summary prompt runs before future questions are known and is never checked. It splits extraction into turn-level details, topic-level events and event relations, and then verifies the result: missed events are recovered by matching them against a first draft, entries are checked with NLI against their source turn and repaired at the level of atomic facts, and relation edges are kept only when needed. On HaluMem it reports the best memory accuracy and F1 at a token cost close to Mem0, and it also improves QA on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: QUMem

paper.title: QUMem: Personalized Memory for Query-Conditioned User-State Inference in LLM Agents

construction.unit: atomic typed memory, linked to a variable-length episode
construction.kept_as: episode retained; atomic memories extracted
construction.processing: LLM decomposes each episode into factual, preference, insight memories (3 calls)
construction.writer: LLM decomposer; Qwen3.5-4B SFT continuity classifier sets episode boundaries

organization.structure: three typed stores linked to source episodes
organization.stores: factual, preference, transferable-insight stores

retrieval.query: A1 identifies information needs; A2 rewrites them into multiple queries
retrieval.candidates: A2 routes each query to chosen typed stores; merge and deduplicate
retrieval.selection: A3 selects task-relevant evidence into a user state
retrieval.budget: top-k=5 per retrieval

use.context: query-conditioned user state: chronological facts, preference evolution, insights
use.reasoning: three sequential agents, then downstream response model

classify.note: The main text does not name the retrieval method inside each store.

stages.ingestion: A lightweight continuity classifier (fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-4B on LoCoMo-derived data) decides for each pair of adjacent user utterances whether they belong to the same event, producing variable-length dialogue episodes.
stages.construction: Each finished episode is decomposed by an LLM, called three times (once per type), into atomic factual, preference and transferable-insight memories, each with its temporal position and source turns; the episode itself is retained as context.
stages.organization: Three typed memory stores (F, P, I) linked back to source episodes.
stages.retrieval: Information-Need Agent identifies what must be verified; Retrieval Planning Agent rewrites needs into queries and routes each to one or more typed stores (top-k=5 per retrieval); results are merged and deduplicated.
stages.answer: User-State Inference Agent composes a query-conditioned user state (chronological facts, preference evolution, applicable insights) that is given with the query to the response model.
stages.learning: Only the episode-boundary classifier is fine-tuned (SFT); the rest is prompt-based.

systems.summary: Semantic-continuity episodes decomposed into typed fact/preference/insight memories, with a three-agent query-conditioned pipeline that infers a temporally valid user state for personalization.
systems.notes:
Authors: Heng Wang, Yifei Li, Lingling Zhang, Pengyu Li, Xinyu Che, Xinyu Zhang, Zesheng Yang. 9 pages; no code link found. Evaluated on PersonaMem (32K/128K/1M) and KnowU-Bench (mobile-agent personalization; not recorded here as it is a GUI-agent benchmark with SR/Score metrics). AXES-CHECK: seed taxonomy row consistent; the main text does not say the per-store retrieval is vector/dense (retrieval method details deferred to an appendix not available in the fetched text), so '(vector)' is unverified.
DESIGN: Sec 3.2-3.4, 4.1. trigger 'other' = when the classifier closes an episode. index and all management fields null: main text does not describe the retrieval index or any update/forgetting; appendix not available.

systems.name: RAPTOR

paper.title: RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval

construction.unit: 100-token chunk (leaf) or cluster summary node
construction.kept_as: leaves verbatim; parents LLM summaries
construction.processing: SBERT embed, UMAP+GMM soft clustering (BIC), gpt-3.5-turbo summaries, recursively
construction.writer: gpt-3.5-turbo (summaries); SBERT multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1 (embeddings)

organization.structure: tree of recursive summaries
organization.stores: one tree per corpus
organization.index: SBERT embeddings of all nodes

management.operations: none
management.conflicts: none
management.forgetting: none

retrieval.query: query embedded with SBERT
retrieval.candidates: collapsed tree: all nodes of all layers (or layer-wise traversal)
retrieval.selection: cosine top-k
retrieval.budget: token budget (collapsed tree), top-k per layer (traversal)

use.context: concatenated retrieved node texts
use.reasoning: single reader call

stages.ingestion: The corpus is split into ~100-token chunks without cutting sentences.
stages.construction: Chunks are embedded with SBERT (multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1); GMM soft clustering over UMAP-reduced embeddings (BIC chooses cluster count) groups them and gpt-3.5-turbo summarises each cluster, recursively.
stages.organization: Multi-layer tree: raw chunks as leaves, cluster summaries as parent nodes.
stages.retrieval: Collapsed-tree retrieval (cosine top-k over all nodes of all layers up to a token budget) or tree traversal (top-k per layer from root down); collapsed tree performed better.
stages.answer: Retrieved node texts are concatenated as context for the reader LLM.

systems.summary: Builds a tree of recursive cluster summaries over document chunks and retrieves across all abstraction levels.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: leaf nodes are the original 100-token chunks kept verbatim and are retrievable alongside summaries, so 'text kept as: rewritten' understates it (fidelity tag set to verbatim+derived). Evaluated on NarrativeQA, QASPER, QuALITY (document QA); no conversational-memory benchmark, so no results file was written. Code URL not read in the paper text (known official repo).
DESIGN: Sec 3 (overview, clustering, summarization, querying). Corrected: kept_as 'rewritten' -> leaves verbatim + summaries.

systems.name: ReadAgent

paper.title: A Human-Inspired Reading Agent with Gist Memory of Very Long Contexts

construction.unit: page (episode) + its gist
construction.kept_as: raw page kept + LLM gist ('shorten')
construction.processing: LLM chooses pause points (min/max words), then shortens each page into gist
construction.writer: backbone LLM (PaLM 2-L; GPT-3.5 in App. B)

organization.structure: flat ordered list of page-tagged gists
organization.stores: gist memory + original pages
organization.index: page numbers (no vector index)

management.operations: none
management.conflicts: none
management.forgetting: none

retrieval.query: task/question as is
retrieval.candidates: all gists in context
retrieval.selection: LLM picks raw pages to look up (parallel -P or sequential -S)
retrieval.budget: max look-up pages per task (e.g. 1-2, up to 5-6)

use.context: gists with looked-up raw pages substituted in place
use.reasoning: look-up call(s) then answer call

classify.note: All gists are read; the LLM then picks raw pages to look up.

stages.ingestion: Reads the long text sequentially; the LLM picks a natural pause point between min_words and max_words (episode pagination).
stages.construction: Each page is shortened by the LLM into a gist, tagged with its page number; gists are concatenated into the gist memory.
stages.organization: Ordered flat list of page gists; raw pages are kept for look-up.
stages.retrieval: The LLM reads all gists and chooses which raw pages to look up, either all at once (ReadAgent-P) or one at a time (ReadAgent-S); looked-up pages replace their gists.
stages.answer: The LLM answers from the gist memory with expanded raw pages.

systems.summary: Prompting-only reading agent that paginates long text, keeps short gists of every page, and interactively looks up raw pages when answering.
systems.notes:
AXES-CHECK: selection is not only reading gists - the model then retrieves raw pages (interactive look-up); '3.5-20x' in the paper is the effective context-length extension, not strictly a gist compression ratio. The paper evaluates on QuALITY, NarrativeQA, QMSum (long-document QA) and Mind2Web (web navigation) with PaLM 2-L (GPT-3.5 in App. B); no conversational-memory benchmark, so no results file was written. Code/prompts: project site read-agent.github.io.
DESIGN: Sec 3.1-3.4, Sec 4 intro. Corrected: selection is not only reading gists - LLM then retrieves raw pages; '3.5-20x' is effective context extension.

systems.name: RoG (Reasoning on Graphs)

paper.title: Reasoning on Graphs: Faithful and Interpretable Large Language Model Reasoning

construction.unit: KG triple (head, relation, tail) of an existing Freebase subgraph; relation-path knowledge tuned into the LLM
construction.kept_as: verbatim KG triples; which relation sequences exist is learned into LLaMA2-Chat-7B weights
construction.processing: offline only: shortest paths between question and answer entities of training questions give relation-path labels; one LLM is instruction-tuned on planning and on answering from retrieved paths
construction.writer: instruction tuning of LLaMA2-Chat-7B (3 epochs, 2 A100-80G, 38 h)

organization.structure: knowledge graph of entities and relations (Freebase subgraph; one subgraph per question in the released data)
organization.stores: KG triples; fine-tuned LLM weights
organization.index: none beyond the graph: exact relation-name match starting from labelled question entities

management.operations: none; the KG is fixed and nothing is written at question time

retrieval.query: the fine-tuned LLM writes 3 relation paths for the question (beam search)
retrieval.candidates: breadth-first search from each labelled question entity that follows each relation path hop by hop
retrieval.selection: none: every complete matching path goes to the reasoner (shuffled and cut only if the prompt would exceed ~4k tokens)
retrieval.budget: K = 3 relation paths; no cap on reasoning paths; prompt limit 3,996 tokens in code

use.context: reasoning paths as 'e0 -> r1 -> e1 -> ...' lines, then the question
use.reasoning: single call to the same fine-tuned LLM returning all answers as a list; any other LLM can read the same paths

classify.note: The KG is given and never changed, so there is no management to place. The walk is planned by the fine-tuned LLM's relation paths, and the same LLM then picks answers from all matched paths; no score or top-k cut sits in between.

stages.ingestion: Questions arrive with their topic entities already linked to Freebase; the KG is a Freebase subgraph of triples within the maximum hop count of the question entities (2.57M entities, 8.31M triples).
stages.construction: Nothing is written at run time. Offline, the shortest paths between question and answer entities of WebQSP and CWQ training questions give relation-path labels, and LLaMA2-Chat-7B is instruction-tuned for 3 epochs to generate such paths and to answer from retrieved paths.
stages.organization: The KG stays a plain set of triples; the tuned model holds which relation sequences lead from question to answer.
stages.retrieval: The tuned LLM writes the top-3 relation paths by beam search; a breadth-first search from each question entity follows each path's relations in order and keeps every complete match.
stages.answer: All matched reasoning paths are written as 'entity -> relation -> entity' lines before the question, and the same LLM lists the answers; ChatGPT, Alpaca, LLaMA2-Chat or Flan-T5 can read the same paths instead.
stages.learning: Joint instruction tuning on planning (216,006 examples), retrieval-reasoning (30,465) and explanation data (2,000 answers written by ChatGPT).

systems.summary: Treats a knowledge graph as the memory and teaches an LLM its relation vocabulary: the model writes relation paths as plans, the plans are executed on the KG, and the same model answers from the entity paths they retrieve.
systems.notes:
Venue: ICLR 2024 main conference, verified on proceedings.iclr.cc (hash 3e2aeb66481dd63a32421bf032b70384, listed under 'ICLR 2024 Conference') and the PDF header 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024'; arXiv 2310.01061 (v2, comment 'Accepted by ICLR 2024') was confirmed with the arXiv API. The OpenReview PDF sits behind a bot challenge, so the proceedings PDF was read. data/extra_systems.json already has the id 'rog' for this same system (used in rrp-2506.10508 results); this file uses the id given for the task, so the two should be merged.
DESIGN: §3-4 (framework, planning, retrieval-reasoning), §5.1 and App. A.4-A.6 (data, training, K=3), App. A.3 (Algorithm 1), App. A.10 (prompts). Memory here is the KG itself plus relation-path knowledge distilled into the LLM; write_time 'learned' and structure 'parametric' refer to that tuning, since no memory is written per question. Question entities are assumed labelled and linked (§3), so retrieval starts from gold entities.

sources.code_note: Latest commit ccf8ec84 (2025-03-05) only edits scripts/plug-and-play.sh. The planning, retrieval, prompt and evaluation code (src/qa_prediction, src/utils, prompts) last changed on 2023-11-20 (fdc5939), before the camera-ready, so it is taken as the paper's code. The graphs come from the released Hugging Face datasets rmanluo/RoG-webqsp and rmanluo/RoG-cwq (one subgraph per question), which were not downloaded here.

headline: The memory is an existing KG and RoG writes nothing to it; what it learns is which relation sequences to follow, stored in the LLM's weights.
Retrieval starts from question entities the dataset already labels and matches relation names exactly; there is no embedding search.
Every path matching one of the 3 planned relation paths reaches the reasoner, so precision rests on the reasoning LLM (without it, WebQSP precision falls from 74.77 to 46.90).

No run feeds the reasoner random paths of the same number, so how much of the gain is precise paths versus simply more KG text is not isolated (random plans retrieve different paths and also change their number).

discussion.takeaway: Use relation paths as plans: an LLM tuned to write paths that exist in the KG retrieves exact entity chains, and reading them lifts a 7B model above earlier KGQA systems on WebQSP and CWQ.

claims.claim: State of the art on KGQA.
claims.evidence: Hits@1 85.7 on WebQSP vs 82.1 for DECAF (+4.4%); 62.6 on CWQ vs 51.2 for UniKGQA (+22.3%), CWQ F1 56.2 vs 49.1. Table 1, §5.2.

claims.claim: Both planning and reasoning are needed.
claims.evidence: F1 without planning 49.69 / 33.76, without reasoning 49.56 / 22.26, random plans 35.24 / 37.64, vs 70.81 / 56.17 for RoG. Table 2.

claims.claim: The planning module plugs into other LLMs without retraining them.
claims.evidence: WebQSP Hits@1: ChatGPT 66.77 → 81.51, LLaMA2-Chat-7B 64.37 → 74.20, Flan-T5-xl 30.95 → 67.87. Table 3.

claims.claim: Generated relation paths are faithful: more of them cover more answers.
claims.evidence: Answer coverage of retrieved paths rises with K = 1…5 while reasoning F1 levels off; K = 3 chosen. Fig. 3, §5.4.

claims.claim: RoG transfers to another KG cheaply.
claims.evidence: MetaQA-3hop 88.98 Hits@1 after tuning from the Freebase model vs 84.81 from scratch; 2 h vs 38 h. Tables 12-13.

limits: The paper has no limitations section; it notes only that larger K brings more noise and retrieval time (§5.4, App. A.7.4) and that more Freebase QA data could help further (App. A.7.2).
reading: Question and answer entities are assumed labelled and linked to the KG (§3), so retrieval starts from gold entities; systems that must find entities themselves face a harder task.
The non-LLM baselines are copied from UniKGQA and DECAF (App. A.6) and the LLM baselines are zero-shot without KG access; fine-tuned LLMs without paths (Table 16) reach 73.89 / 53.49, closer to RoG.

The text reports Hits@1 gains of 8.5%, 15.3% and 119.3% for four LLMs, but Table 3 gives +22% for ChatGPT; in Table 3 the WebQSP cells of Alpaca + RoG (56.16 / 74.20) and LLaMA2 + RoG (74.20 / 56.16) look swapped.
RoG is tuned on WebQSP and CWQ together; trained on one dataset it scores 81.5 and 59.1 Hits@1 (Tables 14-15).
In the code the KG is an undirected simple graph, so a path can run against a relation's direction and parallel relations between two entities collapse to one.
Hits@1 in the code is a substring hit over the whole answer list, not the top-1 answer, which favours long answer lists.

abstract.text: RoG targets LLM question answering over knowledge graphs, where models lack current facts and invent reasoning steps. It plans with relation paths: a fine-tuned LLM writes sequences of KG relations that could lead from the question to the answer, the paths are executed on the KG to retrieve concrete entity chains, and the LLM reasons over those chains to answer and explain. The model is trained on two instruction tasks distilled from the KG, planning and reasoning over retrieved paths, and its planner can also feed other LLMs. It reports state-of-the-art results on WebQSP and CWQ with interpretable answers.

stages.ingestion: After each test task the agent's trajectory (think/action steps; code uses the agent's thinking as a stand-in for page observations) and final answer are collected; no ground truth is used.
stages.construction: The backbone LLM, prompted as a judge (temperature 0), labels the trajectory success or failure; a success-specific or failure-specific prompt then distils at most 3 memory items (title, description, content) at temperature 1.0.
stages.organization: Each task becomes one entry (query, trajectory, label, items) appended to a flat JSON bank; the query's embedding is cached separately. The code keeps one bank per WebArena website subset.
stages.update: Plain append after every task, including failures; no merging, pruning or deduplication. MaTTS instead extracts up to 5 items by contrasting k rollouts of the same task (parallel) or uses self-refinement notes (sequential).
stages.retrieval: The new query is embedded (gemini-embedding-001) and compared by cosine with past task queries; the memory items of the top-1 most similar past task are returned.
stages.answer: The items are appended to the agent's system prompt with an instruction to state at each step whether it uses each item; the ReAct agent then acts for up to 30 steps.

systems.summary: Distils each finished agent task, judged by the agent itself as success or failure, into up to three short strategy or lesson items, retrieves the items of the most similar past task by query embedding, and adds memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS) that contrasts several rollouts of one task to write better items.

discussion.takeaway: Storing short, self-judged lessons from both successful and failed runs, instead of raw trajectories or success-only workflows, gives a web or coding agent a few points more success with fewer steps, and extra rollouts per task help more when they feed this memory.

claims.claim: Beats memory-free and trajectory/workflow memory on every backbone.
claims.evidence: WebArena overall SR +8.3 / +7.2 / +4.6 over No Memory for Gemini-2.5-flash / -pro / Claude-3.7 (48.8, 53.9, 46.3). Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Also helps on Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified.
claims.evidence: Mind2Web cross-domain step SR 36.6 vs 31.9 (flash); SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate 38.8 vs 34.2 (flash), 57.4 vs 54.0 (pro). Tables 2-3

claims.claim: Learning from failures matters.
claims.evidence: WebArena-Shopping 46.5 with successes only, 49.7 with failures; AWM drops 44.4 → 42.2 when failures are added. Fig. 7, §5

claims.claim: Memory-aware scaling beats plain scaling.
claims.evidence: At k = 5 parallel MaTTS 55.1 vs 52.4 for vanilla TTS and 42.2 without memory (Best-of-N, Shopping). Fig. 4, §4.3

claims.claim: Cheaper per task despite the extra LLM calls.
claims.evidence: 53.1k vs 50.8k tokens per task (+4.3%) for +20.5% relative SR; fewer steps, most on solved tasks (up to 2.1). Table 5, Table 4

limits: Only memory content is studied; episodic or hierarchical memory designs are not compared.
Retrieval (embedding similarity) and consolidation (append) are deliberately simple.
Success and failure labels come from an LLM judge and can be wrong on ambiguous tasks.
reading: The key used for lookup is the past task's query, not the stored strategy text, so the method retrieves by task similarity exactly like the trajectory baseline Synapse; only what is shown differs (App. B.1 says all methods share retrieval and consolidation).
More retrieved tasks hurt: k = 1 gives 49.7 on Shopping and k = 4 gives 44.4 (Fig. 13), so each prompt carries at most three items.
Memory is written from the test stream itself with self-judged labels; the code runs tasks in task-id order and keeps a separate bank for each WebArena site, including the 29-task Multi subset.
The judge agreed with gold labels 72.7% of the time; Fig. 8 simulates noisier and cleaner labels and reports small changes, with gold labels best.
+MaTTS rows in Table 1 use 5 rollouts per task and Best-of-N selection in Fig. 4; baselines use one rollout.
The released code covers WebArena and SWE-Bench only; the MaTTS scripts read a single trial folder, so the parallel self-contrast numbers cannot be reproduced from them as released.

abstract.text: ReasoningBank is a memory for LLM agents that face a stream of tasks and have no ground truth at test time. After each task the agent judges its own run, and an LLM distils short, reusable strategies from successes and cautionary lessons from failures; for a new task, the lessons of the most similar past task are placed in the prompt. The authors also propose memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS), which spends extra rollouts on each task and contrasts them to write better memory. On WebArena, Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified it beats memory-free agents and trajectory or workflow memories in success rate and step count.

construction.kept_as: verbatim turn until a topic recurs; then LLM-written episodes and extracted facts

management.conflicts: the fact refiner is told to drop facts already known and to record changes as time-anchored updates; answer prompt prefers the most recent memory
management.forgetting: turns that are consolidated are deleted from the subconscious store (code only; the paper says they stay)

retrieval.candidates: dense top-k from each of the three stores

classify.note: Tiers because turns are promoted from the subconscious store to episodes and facts; within each tier storage is flat.

stages.ingestion: Each user-assistant exchange becomes one unit, prefixed with its (session) timestamp and embedded with text-embedding-3-small; no LLM is called at this point.
stages.construction: A turn that finds enough similar turns in the subconscious store (cosine above θsim, count reaching θcount) triggers an LLM that writes 1-3 time-ordered episodes from the cluster; semantic refinement then extracts under 10 new facts that the episode left out.
stages.organization: Three flat vector stores per conversation: unconsolidated raw turns, episode narratives and atomic facts.
stages.update: Before gating, a turn is compared with its nearest episode; above the threshold an LLM decides whether it continues that topic and rewrites the episode, followed by fact refinement on that turn. In the code, consolidated or merged turns are removed from (or never enter) the subconscious store.
stages.retrieval: The question embedding pulls 10 raw turns, 5 episodes and 10 facts by cosine similarity.
stages.answer: One LLM call reads the three lists (episodes, raw turns, facts) under a prompt that explains their roles and asks to avoid double counting.

systems.summary: Defers LLM consolidation: turns sit as embedded raw text until a topic recurs enough times, then an LLM writes episodes and refines facts, cutting memory-building tokens by up to 87% versus Mem0 and A-Mem.

Venue: ACL 2026 Findings, verified on ACL Anthology (2026.findings-acl.1619); the arXiv comment and repo README say the same. Text from arXiv v1 PDF (pdftotext). Code read at commit a84252f6 (2026-05-15, the only commit, 'Initial open-source release').

abstract.text: RecMem argues that memory systems waste tokens by running an LLM over every incoming turn. It keeps each exchange as an embedded raw record in a cheap 'subconscious' store and calls the LLM only when a topic recurs: once enough similar turns accumulate, they are turned into episode narratives, and a refinement step extracts the specific facts the narrative dropped. At question time it reads a fixed number of raw turns, episodes and facts by embedding similarity. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S the authors report higher accuracy than Mem0, A-Mem and MemoryOS with far fewer memory-building tokens.

headline: No LLM runs on a turn until its topic has come up about five times (θcount 5, θsim 0.7 on LoCoMo); until then the turn is only embedded.
The answer model reads 10 raw turns next to 5 episodes and 10 facts; removing the raw-turn store costs the most (81.10 to 51.88 on LoCoMo).
In the released code, turns that get consolidated are deleted from the raw store, so only never-consolidated turns remain verbatim.

open_questions: Because consolidated turns are deleted, the 'no subconscious' ablation (51.88) removes only never-consolidated turns; the paper does not report how many turns that is, so it is unclear how much evidence exists only in raw form.
On LoCoMo each baseline keeps its own answer prompt (App. E.3) while RecMem's prompt explains its three memory types, so accuracy gaps mix memory design and prompting.
The ablation keeps each module's budget fixed rather than total context fixed, so removing a store also shrinks the context.

glance.a: Three kinds: a raw exchange with its timestamp, an LLM-written episode narrative, and a one-sentence fact.

glance.q: When is the LLM called while building memory?
glance.a: Only when a turn is close to an existing episode (merge) or when about five similar turns have accumulated (consolidation). Other turns are just embedded.
Recurring topics are rewritten into 3-6 sentence episodes and extracted facts; the raw turns of those topics are then deleted in the code.
No. Each store returns its top-k by cosine similarity to the question.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: 5 episodes, 10 raw turns and 10 facts in one prompt.

key_numbers.value: ≥ 5 similar turns (sim > 0.7) on LoCoMo · ≥ 4 (sim > 0.6) on LongMemEval-S

components.role: Embeds turns, episodes, facts and questions
Writes and merges episodes, refines facts

discussion.takeaway: An LLM does not need to process every turn: consolidating only recurring topics, while keeping the rest as embedded raw text, keeps accuracy at or above the tested memory systems at a fraction of their memory-building tokens.

claims.claim: Eager per-turn consolidation is the main cost driver of current memory systems.
claims.evidence: Construction tokens per LoCoMo conversation: Mem0 1520.8K, A-Mem 1459.9K vs RecMem 193.2K (-87.3%, -86.8%), GPT-4.1-mini. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Cheaper construction does not cost accuracy.
claims.evidence: Best overall among memory systems: LoCoMo 81.10 vs A-Mem 68.83; LongMemEval-S 76.80, best of all methods including full context (66.20). Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Recurrence-based clustering helps temporal reasoning.
claims.evidence: LongMemEval-S temporal 68.42 vs 62.41 for Mem0 (GPT-4.1-mini). Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: All three stores contribute; the raw store most.
claims.evidence: 81.10 full; 79.94 without episodes; 70.58 without facts; 51.88 without raw turns. Fig. 2, §4.3

claims.claim: Episodes make fact extraction better.
claims.evidence: Direct extraction without episode reference 74.22 vs 79.94 for the refinement variant, both without episodic retrieval. Fig. 2, §4.3

limits: θsim and θcount are set by hand per dataset and may need recalibration for other interaction densities.
Recurrence is a proxy for importance; one-off but critical details get no episode or fact and rely on the raw store.
Evaluated only offline on public benchmarks.
reading: In the released code, turns that were consolidated or merged are removed from the raw store, so the Limitations claim that every turn stays retrievable does not hold for the code; for recurring topics the answer model sees only LLM text.
Full context still beats RecMem on LoCoMo (84.18 vs 81.10 with GPT-4.1-mini; 76.43 vs 72.47 with GPT-4o-mini); the lead over all methods is on LongMemEval-S only.
Thresholds differ per dataset (0.7/5 vs 0.6/4); the sensitivity sweeps that show a peak at the LoCoMo defaults are run on the LoCoMo test questions themselves (App. C).

On LoCoMo each baseline answers with its own prompt, while on LongMemEval-S all use RecMem's prompt body (App. E.3); RecMem's A-Mem LoCoMo score is 68.83 in Table 1 but 69.7 in Table 3, and full context 84.18 vs 84.8.
Construction savings come partly from the merge path: every turn close to an existing episode still triggers an LLM merge and a fact refinement, so the cost depends on how often topics repeat.

systems.name: Reflexion

paper.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

construction.unit: self-reflection: a few sentences of text written after a failed trial
construction.kept_as: LLM-written diagnosis of the failure and a plan for the next attempt
construction.processing: after a failed trial the reflection LLM reads the trajectory (and, in ALFWorld, earlier reflections) and writes what went wrong and what to do instead
construction.writer: reflection LLM, prompted with 2 few-shot reflections (same model family as the actor)

organization.structure: per-task list of reflections (long-term) next to the current trajectory (short-term)
organization.stores: one reflection list per task; the running trajectory

management.operations: append each new reflection; keep only the most recent Ω
management.forgetting: sliding window: reflections older than the last Ω drop out (Ω = 3 ALFWorld and HotPotQA, 1 programming)

retrieval.candidates: every kept reflection of the current task
retrieval.selection: the last Ω by recency; no search or ranking
retrieval.budget: Ω = 1-3 reflections (§3)

use.context: few-shot examples + reflections + task + current trajectory in the actor prompt
use.reasoning: ReAct or CoT actor; the task is retried until solved or the trial budget runs out

classify.note: Memory is a short list per task; all kept reflections go into the prompt. The only management is the sliding window of Ω entries.

stages.ingestion: Each trial produces a trajectory of actions and observations (short-term memory); an evaluator turns it into a reward: exact match on HotPotQA, a hand-written heuristic or an LLM classifier on ALFWorld, self-written unit tests for code.
stages.construction: After a failed trial a reflection LLM, prompted with two example reflections, writes a few sentences diagnosing the failure and proposing a new plan.
stages.organization: Reflections are appended to a list kept for that task only; there is no index and no sharing across tasks.
stages.update: The list is bounded to the last Ω reflections (Ω = 3 for ALFWorld and HotPotQA, 1 for programming).
stages.retrieval: No search: every kept reflection of the task is placed in the actor prompt of the next trial.
stages.answer: The actor (ReAct or CoT; for code, an implementation generator) reads few-shot examples, the reflections, the task and its current trajectory.
stages.learning: Called 'verbal reinforcement learning': behaviour changes across trials only through the reflection text; no weights are updated.

systems.summary: An agent retries a task and, after each failure, writes a short self-reflection that is kept in a per-task sliding-window memory (last 1-3 reflections) and prepended to the next attempt's prompt.
systems.notes:
Venue: NeurIPS 2023 main track, verified on proceedings.neurips.cc (hash 1b44b878bb782e6954cd888628510e90) and the neurips.cc poster page. The arXiv v4 PDF still carries a 'Preprint. Under review.' footer. Code link in the paper is github.com/noahshinn024/reflexion, which now resolves to github.com/noahshinn/reflexion.
DESIGN: §3 (Actor, Evaluator, Self-reflection, Memory), §4.1-4.3, Alg. 1. Memory is per task: the paper frames it as trial-and-error on the same task, not cross-task transfer. Retrieval fields describe that the whole bounded buffer is read; there is no query.

sources.code_note: Commit 612e6166 (2023-10-11) is the first commit after arXiv v4 (2023-10-10); the only later commits are a user change, formatting and a README link. The repo has separate runners per task: alfworld_runs, hotpotqa_runs, programming_runs, webshop_runs.

headline: Memory is a handful of LLM-written reflections about one task; it is never searched and never shared with other tasks.
The benefit shows up across repeated attempts at the same task, and each retry is triggered by an evaluator (on HotPotQA, exact match against the gold answer).

discussion.takeaway: Turning a pass/fail signal into a short written lesson, and showing the last few lessons on the next attempt, lets an LLM agent improve on the same task over trials without any weight updates.

claims.claim: Reflection improves sequential decision-making.
claims.evidence: ALFWorld: 130 of 134 tasks solved with the heuristic evaluator over 12 trials; ReAct alone plateaus after trial 6-7 (§4.1, Fig. 3).

claims.claim: Reflection improves reasoning over retries.
claims.evidence: HotPotQA (100 q): ReAct 0.30 → 0.55 and CoT (GT) 0.60 → 0.77 with text-davinci-003 (Table 5); baselines solve no new question after trial 1 (§4.2).

claims.claim: Verbal reflection beats just showing the last trajectory.
claims.evidence: About 8 points above the episodic-memory (last trajectory) baseline on CoT (GT) (§4.2, Fig. 4c).

claims.claim: State of the art on code generation.
claims.evidence: HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs 80.1 for GPT-4 (Table 1); MBPP Python is the exception (77.1 vs 80.1), linked to a 16.3% false-positive rate of self-generated tests (Table 2).

claims.claim: Both test generation and self-reflection are needed.
claims.evidence: HumanEval Rust hardest 50: 68 full vs 52 without tests and 60 without reflection (Table 3).

limits: Policy optimisation in language can still get stuck in local minima; on WebShop it did not improve after 4 trials (App. B.1).
Long-term memory is only a sliding window with a maximum size.
Test-driven code feedback struggles with non-deterministic, impure, hardware-dependent or concurrent functions.
Self-correction appears only with stronger models: starchat-beta gains nothing (App. A, Table 4).
reading: Memory never leaves the task: each environment or question keeps its own list, so the results measure improvement on repeated attempts, not transfer to new tasks.
On HotPotQA the between-trial signal is exact match against the gold answer, so the agent knows when it is wrong; accuracy after several trials is not comparable with single-attempt QA.
The HotPotQA code does not enforce the 3-reflection bound stated in the paper, and the ALFWorld code stops trials on a different rule than the one described (see paper vs code).
Table 1 does not name the model behind the Reflexion column; only Table 3 states GPT-4 as the base model (HumanEval Rust).
Most ALFWorld and HotPotQA numbers are shown only as curves (Fig. 3-4); the text gives 130/134 and the 22%/20% improvements.

abstract.text: Reflexion lets a language agent learn from trial and error without fine-tuning. After each attempt an evaluator gives a scalar or binary signal, and a second LLM turns a failure into a short written self-reflection. These reflections are kept in a small episodic buffer and added to the prompt of the next attempt at the same task. The authors report gains on ALFWorld, HotPotQA and code generation, including 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, and analyse which kinds of feedback and components matter.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

stages.ingestion: The agent is run N=8 times per training task (temperature 0.9); per task the highest- and lowest-reward trajectories are kept for summarization.
stages.construction: An LLM extracts keypoint-level experiences from successful runs, from failed runs and by comparing the higher- and lower-scoring run; each has a when-to-use scenario, content, keywords, confidence and tools used, and an LLM judge keeps those scoring at least 0.5.
stages.organization: Experiences sit in one flat vector store, keyed by the embedding of the when-to-use text.
stages.update: Near-duplicates (cosine > 0.5 in the code) are dropped. In the dynamic setting experiences are added only from solved tasks, a failed task triggers a retry with lessons from the failure, recall and success counters are updated, and experiences recalled at least 5 times with utility/freq below 0.5 are deleted.
stages.retrieval: At the start of a task its query is embedded and matched against when-to-use embeddings; the top 5 are reranked by an LLM and rewritten by an LLM into one task-specific guidance.
stages.answer: The guidance is appended to the task text and the agent solves the task with tool calls.

systems.summary: Procedural memory of LLM-extracted keypoint experiences keyed by a written usage scenario, reused through retrieve-rerank-rewrite and kept small by success-only addition and deletion of often-recalled but rarely helpful entries.

open_questions: Does retrying failed tasks with reflections count toward Avg@4 and Pass@4? The dynamic setting both adds memory and allows retries, and the paper does not say how trials and retries relate.

discussion.takeaway: Procedural memory helps tool-using agents most when it is fine-grained and kept up to date while working: success-only addition, retries after failure and deletion of unhelpful entries lift Qwen3-8B above a memoryless Qwen3-14B.

claims.claim: ReMe beats No Memory, A-Mem and LangMem at every model size.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B average 34.94 Avg@4 / 55.03 Pass@4 vs 27.65 / 46.20 without memory; A-Mem and LangMem fall below no memory on AppWorld Avg@4 for Qwen3-8B and 14B. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Memory can stand in for model scale.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B + ReMe (dynamic) Pass@4 55.03 vs Qwen3-14B without memory 54.65; Qwen3-14B + ReMe 44.66/63.71 vs Qwen3-32B without memory 40.89/61.52. Table 1

claims.claim: Keypoint-level experiences beat whole-trajectory workflows.
Selective addition, reflection and deletion each help.
claims.evidence: 40.83 → 44.33 → 45.00 → 45.17 Avg@4; Pass@4 68.00 with deletion. Table 3

claims.claim: The LLM-written usage scenario is the best retrieval key.
claims.evidence: 44.50 vs 44.00 (task query) on Qwen3-8B; the ranking varies by model. Table 9, Fig. 4

claims.claim: A stronger summarizer helps.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B agent with Qwen3-32B summarizer: 47.83 vs 44.50 Avg@4. Table 5

limits: Experiences are retrieved once, at the start of each task; retrieval during the task is left for future work.
Validation relies on an LLM judge, which may miss finer aspects of experience quality.
Gains depend on the summarizer; better summarization with small models is open.
reading: Only the when-to-use sentence is embedded, so retrieval quality depends on how the LLM phrased that scenario, not on the advice text.

In the released pipeline recall and rerank both use k = 5; the LLM reranker reorders five items that are then all rewritten into one paragraph, so its effect on content is limited to emphasis (Table 4 still reports +1.7 Avg@4 for rerank alone).
Most of the benefit on AppWorld comes from the dynamic setting (Qwen3-8B 17.06 fixed vs 24.70 dynamic Avg@4), which learns from the test tasks themselves while evaluating and also allows retries.
Table 4 is run with thinking off (No Memory 24.41) while Table 1 uses thinking on for BFCL-V3 (No Memory 40.33), so its numbers are not comparable with the main table.
The paper names two embedders (text-embedding-v4 in §4.1, Qwen3-Embedding in App. B.4.2); the code defaults to text-embedding-v4.
A-Mem and LangMem were adapted to procedural memory with prompt changes by the authors; both fall below no memory on AppWorld Avg@4 for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B.

abstract.text: ReMe is a procedural memory for tool-using LLM agents that treats the memory as something to refine, not only to accumulate. From past runs, an LLM distils short experiences about key steps: what made successes work, what triggered failures, and what separated better from worse attempts. For a new task, experiences whose usage scenario matches are retrieved, reranked and rewritten into guidance tailored to the task. While the agent works, only successful runs add experiences, failures prompt a reflective retry, and experiences that are often recalled but rarely help are deleted. On BFCL-V3 and AppWorld with Qwen3 models the authors report the best results among the memory systems they compare, with Qwen3-8B plus ReMe beating a memoryless Qwen3-14B.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: REMem

paper.title: REMem: Reasoning with Episodic Memory in Language Agent

construction.unit: gist (one time-stamped event sentence) + fact (triple with time qualifiers)
construction.kept_as: LLM-restated event sentences with resolved dates + extracted triples; raw messages kept as nodes
construction.processing: per session (LoCoMo) one LLM call writes gists, a second writes time-qualified triples from the text and the gists
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4.1-mini)

organization.structure: hybrid graph: gist nodes, phrase nodes (fact subjects/objects), relation, context and gist synonymy edges
organization.stores: one graph with embedding stores for messages, gists, facts and phrases
organization.index: NV-Embed-v2 dense over gists and facts + BM25

management.operations: append only; synonymy edges between gists with similarity >= 0.8
management.conflicts: contradictory gists and facts are all kept as a history

retrieval.query: question on the first step; afterwards sub-queries and tool arguments written by the agent
retrieval.candidates: agent calls semantic (dense) or lexical (BM25) search, gist-context and entity-context graph tools with time filters
retrieval.selection: each call returns top-10 gists + top-10 facts; the agent decides when to stop
retrieval.budget: 3 steps (LoCoMo, REALTALK), 5 steps (Complex-TR, Test of Time); ~9k input tokens per LoCoMo query

use.context: question + whole agent history (thoughts, tool calls, retrieved gists and facts, draft answer)
use.reasoning: ReAct loop of tool calls, then one answer call

classify.note: REMem-S (single step) is a plain top-10 dense read; the headline REMem-I lets the agent choose tools and when to stop.

stages.ingestion: Conversations are fed one session at a time (LoCoMo, REALTALK) or one passage per event statement; each message is also stored as its own node.
stages.construction: An LLM restates each session as a list of single-event gists prefixed with the session timestamp and with relative dates resolved; a second call extracts (subject, predicate, object) facts with point-in-time or start/end qualifiers.
stages.organization: Gists and phrase nodes (fact subjects and objects) form one graph: facts link subject to object, each gist links to the phrases and facts from the same chunk, and gists with embedding similarity >= 0.8 get synonymy edges.
stages.update: Nothing is overwritten: new and contradictory items are added alongside old ones.
stages.retrieval: A ReAct agent (GPT-4.1-mini) calls semantic_retrieve, lexical_retrieve, find_gist_contexts or find_entity_contexts, each returning up to 10 gists and 10 facts, optionally filtered by time; at most 3 steps on conversation sets and 5 on reasoning sets.
stages.answer: When the agent calls output_answer, an answer LLM reads the question, the agent's draft answer and the full step history with every retrieved gist and fact.

systems.summary: Episodic memory as a graph of time-stamped event gists and time-qualified triples, read by a tool-using agent that can filter by dates and walk the graph.

abstract.text: REMem targets episodic memory for language agents: recalling what happened when, and reasoning across several events on a timeline. It indexes experiences into a graph that mixes short time-stamped event gists with subject-predicate-object facts carrying time qualifiers. A ReAct-style agent then answers questions by calling retrieval and graph-exploration tools that can filter by time, over several steps. On LoCoMo, REALTALK, Complex-TR and Test of Time the authors report gains over Mem0, Graphiti and HippoRAG 2, largest on the reasoning sets, and better refusal on unanswerable questions.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: The answer model reads LLM-written gists and triples plus the agent's own step history and draft answer; raw messages are stored but not shown.
REMem-S (one dense search, 10 gists + 10 facts) is best on LoCoMo LLM-J (77.5 vs 76.2); the multi-step agent wins on the reasoning sets (Test of Time EM 93.1 vs 72.5).
Gists are longer than the dialogue they come from: 21.7k gist tokens vs 16.0k input tokens per LoCoMo conversation (Table 22).

units.name: Gist node
units.role: one event from a session, as a standalone sentence
units.made_by: LLM gist prompt, one call per session

fields.name: gist text
fields.what: '[date, time] who did what …' with relative dates followed by the absolute date in parentheses

fields.name: gist embedding
fields.what: NV-Embed-v2 vector of the gist text

units.name: Fact
units.role: time-scoped triple; its subject and object become phrase nodes
units.made_by: LLM fact prompt, reads the session and its gists

fields.name: subject, predicate, object
fields.what: schemaless short phrases, e.g. (Alice, purchased, 3 cows)

fields.name: qualifiers
fields.what: record_time plus point_in_time or start_time / end_time

units.name: Message node

fields.name: verbatim message
fields.what: the raw turn with speaker and date
fields.src: code episodic_gist_strategy.py L94-L114; answer_generator.py L182, L280-L309 (verbatim context off by default)

write.how: one chunk per session with its date on top; messages also split into separate nodes
LLM restates every fact or event as one sentence prefixed with the session timestamp and resolves relative dates
LLM extracts triples with time qualifiers from the session text and its gists
subject → object edge per fact; each gist → the phrases and facts of its chunk; each message → its gists and phrases
gist-to-gist edges when embedding similarity ≥ 0.8 (at most ~100 per gist)
write.out: 1,082 synonymy edges per LoCoMo conversation

read.input: the full question (the tool's query argument is overridden)
read.scores: gist text and fact text + qualifiers
read.how: agent must start with semantic or lexical retrieve
ReAct: the agent picks one of five tools per step from the question and the history so far
start/end time with lt/le/ge/gt/eq filters facts by their qualifiers; gists are not filtered
a separate answer call over the step history

answer_context.sees: question, the agent's draft answer, and every step's thought, tool call, observation and up to 10 gists and 10 facts (each cut at 1,500 characters)
answer_context.format: 'Question: …' + 'Preliminary Answer (for reference)' + 'Agent Interaction History: Step n: {reasoning, function, parameters} - Truncated top gists / facts'

compression.what: per-query input tokens, REMem-I vs full context on LoCoMo
compression.basis: §5.1: Full-Context uses 26k input tokens per LoCoMo query, REMem-I 9k and REMem-S 0.9k at inference

compression.what: gist text vs source text, one LoCoMo conversation
compression.basis: Not a reduction: Table 22 reports 21,743.8 gist-node tokens vs 15,965.8 input tokens per graph, so gists are about 1.36x longer than the input

paper_vs_code.paper: two node types: gists and phrases (App. B)
paper_vs_code.code: also message (verbatim) nodes and fact nodes linked to gists

paper_vs_code.paper: the tool explores gists linked by synonymy edges
paper_vs_code.code: graph edges are added with only a weight attribute, while the tool keeps neighbours whose edge predicate contains 'synonym'; as released it seems to return linked facts but no synonym gists (not run by us)

paper_vs_code.paper: retrieval tools filter memory by temporal conditions
paper_vs_code.code: semantic and lexical retrieve filter only facts; gists are ranked without the filter

open_questions: REMem-S beats REMem-I on LoCoMo LLM-J, so on conversational recollection the gain over baselines comes from the gist index rather than from agentic retrieval.
Baselines retrieve 10 raw messages; REMem sees 10 gists + 10 facts per step for up to 3-5 steps, so context size is not matched.

discussion.takeaway: Storing conversations as time-stamped event gists plus time-scoped triples, and letting an agent query them with date filters, helps most when questions need reasoning across several events on a timeline.

claims.claim: REMem beats state-of-the-art memory systems on episodic recollection.
claims.evidence: LoCoMo LLM-J 77.5 (REMem-S) / 76.2 (REMem-I) vs 74.0 HippoRAG 2 and 73.0 NV-Embed-v2; REALTALK 65.3 vs 59.5. Table 3

claims.claim: The gain is larger on episodic reasoning.
claims.evidence: Complex-TR LLM-J 89.6 vs 81.5 (HippoRAG 2); Test of Time EM 93.1, the only method above 90. Table 4, Table 13

claims.claim: Multi-step tool use matters for reasoning.
claims.evidence: REMem-I over REMem-S: LLM-J +7.0 on Complex-TR, EM +20.6 on Test of Time. §5.2

claims.claim: Gists carry most of the signal; facts help multi-hop.
claims.evidence: without gists LoCoMo LLM-J 76.2 → 48.9; without facts Complex-TR 89.6 → 87.2 and LoCoMo multi-hop −7.1. Table 5, App. C.6

claims.claim: REMem refuses unanswerable questions more reliably.
claims.evidence: refusal F1 64.0 vs 53.1 Graphiti and 13.5 Mem0 on 446 LoCoMo adversarial questions. Table 6

limits: Tested on conversation and temporal reading benchmarks, not on agents acting in complex environments.
Memory is built by offline batch indexing; building it as a stream is left open.
Error analysis: wrong value on the right slot (46%), temporal or numeric slips (19%) and abstaining despite retrieved evidence (18%) on LoCoMo.
reading: On LoCoMo the single-step REMem-S has the higher LLM-J (77.5 vs 76.2), and the paper notes most questions need one session; the agent pays 10x the inference tokens (18.1M vs 1.83M input) for no gain there.
Baselines retrieve 10 raw messages (HippoRAG 2: 3 sessions), while REMem reads 10 gists + 10 facts per step for up to 3-5 steps, so context sizes differ.

The paper's LoCoMo category names follow a different id mapping from Mem0's: its 'Single-Hop' (321) and 'Temporal' (96) are ids 2 and 3, which Mem0-style papers call temporal and open-domain. Per-category numbers cannot be compared across papers by name.
LoCoMo scores include the 446 adversarial questions in the average (1,986 questions), unlike papers that report 1,540.
The judge is the run's own LLM (GPT-4.1-mini in the code) with Mem0's prompt; the paper does not name the judge model.
Gist text per conversation (21.7k tokens) exceeds the source (16.0k), so this is re-expression, not compression.

At the released commit, find_gist_contexts looks for edges labelled 'synonym' but synonymy edges carry no label, so the tool may never return similar gists; yet removing synonymy edges changes scores (Table 5), which suggests the paper's runs used different code or the edges act elsewhere.

systems.name: RF-Mem

paper.title: Evoking User Memory: Personalizing LLM via Recollection-Familiarity Adaptive Retrieval

construction.unit: raw chunk: one user query + one assistant reply (PersonaMem) or one session (PersonaBench, LongMemEval)
construction.kept_as: verbatim dialogue text
construction.processing: none; chunks are embedded as they are

organization.structure: flat list of chunks
organization.stores: one FAISS inner-product index per user history
organization.index: sentence-embedding vectors (multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1 in the main runs; MPNet and BGE also tested)

retrieval.query: question embedding; in recollection rounds, the query is mixed with cluster centroids (α-mix plus the original query)
retrieval.candidates: probe top-10 by cosine; the mean score and softmax entropy decide between one-shot top-K (familiarity) and iterative retrieve-cluster-mix (recollection)
retrieval.selection: familiarity: top-K; recollection: KMeans into B clusters per round, keep B best branches, collect new chunks until K
retrieval.budget: K = 10 chunks on PersonaMem (≈3.6k tokens at 32K)

use.context: retrieved raw chunks joined before the question, instruction and options
use.reasoning: single answer call (multiple choice)

classify.note: A retrieval-only method over an unchanged embedding index; the gate and the recollection loop are fixed rules on similarity scores, with no LLM or reranker.

stages.ingestion: User history is cut into chunks: a user query plus the assistant reply for PersonaMem, one session for PersonaBench and LongMemEval.
stages.organization: Chunks are embedded with a sentence encoder into one flat inner-product index; nothing is summarized, linked or updated.
stages.retrieval: A top-10 probe gives a mean cosine and a softmax entropy; a high mean or low entropy takes the one-shot top-K path, otherwise a recollection loop retrieves (B+r)·F chunks, clusters them with KMeans, mixes each centroid into the query and searches again until K new chunks are gathered.
stages.answer: The retrieved raw chunks are placed before the question, a fixed multiple-choice instruction and the options, and the LLM picks one option.

systems.summary: A retriever-only memory method: a probe's mean score and entropy route each question either to plain top-K search or to an embedding-space loop that clusters hits and mixes centroids into the query, with no LLM in retrieval.

headline: Nothing is written or rewritten: memory is the raw dialogue, cut into chunks and embedded. The method is only the retriever.
The gate and the recollection loop use embeddings only (cosine, entropy, KMeans, vector mixing); no LLM or reranker runs before the answer.
Baselines are the same index read other ways (dense top-K, recollection always on, full context, no memory); no other memory system is compared.

discussion.takeaway: Deciding per question whether to do a plain top-K search or a few embedding-space expansion rounds gives small but consistent gains over always doing either, at near dense-retrieval latency.

claims.claim: Best overall accuracy at every corpus size with compact inputs.
claims.evidence: PersonaMem 0.6350 / 0.5394 / 0.4589 at 32K / 128K / 1M vs dense 0.5908 / 0.5259 / 0.4518; full context 0.6129 at 32K with 24.7k tokens vs 3.6k. Table 1

claims.claim: Gating is cheaper than always recollecting and at least as accurate.
Familiarity suits fact lookups, recollection suits context-heavy questions.
claims.evidence: PersonaBench Pref-Hard Recall@10 0.6267 (recollection) vs 0.5561 (familiarity) under MiniLM. Table 2, §3.3

claims.claim: Robust retrieval across encoders.
claims.evidence: RF-Mem matches or beats both modes in overall Recall@5/10 on PersonaBench and LongMemEval-S/M for MiniLM, MPNet and BGE. Tables 2-3

claims.claim: Works as a layer over other memory designs.
claims.evidence: Best overall with a MemoryBank summary index (0.5314), HyDE expansion (Recall@10 0.5194) and Search-o1 (0.6146). Tables 4-6

limits: Evaluated only on text dialogue memory.
List entropy and similarity scores are rough proxies for task difficulty and semantic ambiguity.
The index is static: no temporal updates or conflicts across sessions are modeled.
Better surfacing of old history may expose sensitive information.
reading: Gains over dense retrieval shrink with corpus size: +0.044 at 32K, +0.0135 at 128K, +0.0071 at 1M overall accuracy (Table 1).
The code's entropy is the paper's H divided by K (mean instead of sum), and its recollection output is the first 10 chunks collected rather than the top 10 by score.
App. B lists all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as a PersonaBench encoder while Tables 2, 17 name all-mpnet-base-v2; §3.2 gives 7.12 ms for 1M recollection while Table 1 says 8.12 ms.
The released PersonaMem script calls gpt-4.1-mini, which the paper never names; α and τ are swept in the scripts and the reported choice is not stated.
Only the question is embedded, with no LLM query rewriting, so the comparison is against dense top-K on the same index rather than against other memory systems.

abstract.text: RF-Mem borrows the recollection-familiarity idea from memory research to decide how hard a personalized LLM should search its user history. A quick probe search yields a mean similarity and an entropy over the scores; if the question looks familiar the system returns the top-K chunks at once, and otherwise it runs a few rounds that cluster the hits, blend each cluster centroid into the query and search again. Everything happens in embedding space over raw dialogue chunks, with no LLM in the loop. On PersonaMem, PersonaBench and LongMemEval the authors report higher accuracy or recall than plain dense retrieval and full-context prompting at close to one-shot latency.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

construction.unit: memory entry: (topic summary, raw dialogue turns it came from)
construction.kept_as: LLM topic summary as search key + verbatim turns
construction.processing: at session end an LLM splits the session into topics, writing one personal summary per topic with its turn ids, for each speaker
construction.writer: prompted LLM (model not named for this step; the generator is Gemini-1.5-Flash)

organization.structure: flat memory bank of topic entries
organization.stores: one memory bank per user/conversation
organization.index: dense embeddings of topic summaries (Contriever default; Stella, GTE tested)

management.operations: each new topic memory is compared with its Top-K most similar entries; LLM chooses Add() or Merge(index, merged_summary)
management.conflicts: handled by merge: the LLM rewrites the old summary with the new information

retrieval.query: current user query
retrieval.candidates: dense retriever Top-K=20 over topic summaries
retrieval.selection: learned reranker (residual linear adapters on query and memory embeddings, dot product) with Gumbel-softmax sampling keeps Top-M=5; reranker trained online by REINFORCE from the LLM's citations
retrieval.budget: Top-M = 5 entries (10 with Top-K = 50 in Table 5)

use.context: the 5 memories, each as personal summary plus its original turns, with the current session
use.reasoning: one LLM call writes the response and cites the memories it used

classify.note: The reranker is a small learned model on embeddings, not a cross-encoder; it is updated online by REINFORCE from the answer LLM's citations.

stages.ingestion: Memory is written once per finished session; the session's turns are passed whole to the extraction prompt.
stages.construction: Prospective Reflection: an LLM decomposes the session into topics and writes a concise personal summary for each, with references to the turn ids it came from; this is done separately for each speaker.
stages.organization: A flat memory bank of (topic summary, raw dialogue) entries; the summary is the retrieval key.
stages.update: Each new topic memory is compared with the Top-K most similar existing entries, and an LLM either adds it or merges it into one of them with a rewritten summary.
stages.retrieval: A frozen dense retriever returns Top-K=20 entries; a lightweight reranker (residual linear maps on query and memory embeddings, dot-product scores) samples Top-M=5 with the Gumbel trick at τ = 0.5.
stages.answer: The LLM sees the current session and the 5 memories (summary plus original turns), writes the reply and cites the memories it used in the same call.
stages.learning: Retrospective Reflection: each retrieved memory gets +1 if cited and −1 if not, and REINFORCE (baseline 0.5, lr 1e-3, batch 4) updates only the reranker, online during the conversation.

systems.summary: Topic-level memories (LLM summary as key, original turns as content) are written and merged at session end, and a small reranker over retriever embeddings is trained online with REINFORCE using the answer LLM's own citations as reward.
systems.notes: arXiv v2 (2025-07-28) read from the PDF; arXiv comment and ACL Anthology (2025.acl-long.413, pp. 8416-8439) give ACL 2025 main. No official code was found (paper gives no link; only an unofficial third-party plugin exists on GitHub). Baselines MemoryBank and LD-Agent were re-implemented with the LongMemEval codebase (App. A.4). The LLM for memory extraction/merge is not named; Gemini-1.5-Flash is the generator. LongMemEval variant (S/M/oracle) is not stated.

headline: A memory entry pairs an LLM topic summary (the search key) with the original turns, and the answer model reads both.
The only learned part is a small reranker on top of a frozen retriever; its reward is whether the answer LLM cited each memory (+1) or not (−1).
The reranker is updated after every response, so it learns during the conversation itself; the paper does not separate this from the evaluation questions.

discussion.takeaway: Organise memory by topic rather than by turn or session, and let the answer model's own citations train a small reranker online. On LongMemEval with GTE this lifts accuracy from 63.6 (turn-level RAG) to 70.4.

claims.claim: RMM beats all baselines on MSC and LongMemEval.
claims.evidence: GTE: MSC METEOR 33.4 vs 27.5, BERT 57.1 vs 52.1; LongMemEval Recall@5 69.8 vs 62.4, Acc 70.4 vs 63.6 over RAG. Table 1, §8.1

claims.claim: Both reflections help, and the reranker is needed for the RL signal.
claims.evidence: Contriever: RAG 58.8 → +PR 59.6, +RR 60.2, both 61.2 Acc; fine-tuning the retriever instead drops to 31.0. Table 2, §8.2

claims.claim: Citations are a reliable reward.
claims.evidence: Overall precision 87.6, recall 85.8, F1 86.7 against a Gemini-1.5-Pro judge. Table 3, §8.3

claims.claim: Topic granularity approaches the best per-instance fixed granularity.
claims.evidence: On 100 LongMemEval samples (GTE): Recall@5 78 (PR) vs 47 turn, 69 session, 86 best; Acc 49 vs 29, 34, 58. Fig. 4, §8.5

claims.claim: More retrieved and kept memories help.

limits: RL reranking can be computationally expensive for large-scale or real-time use.
Text-only; multimodal dialogue is not handled.
The memory update mechanism may need further work for dynamically evolving long-term interactions.
reading: The reranker is updated after every response (Algorithm 1), and no separate training stream is described for the main tables, so the reported scores include learning on the evaluation conversations themselves.
The gain from the full system over plain RAG with Contriever is small on LongMemEval accuracy (58.8 → 61.2) and larger on MSC METEOR (24.8 → 30.8); the headline 70.4 needs the GTE-7B retriever.
MemoryBank and LD-Agent are listed with 'specific' retrievers in Table 1, but App. A.4 says they were re-implemented in the LongMemEval codebase with Contriever as default retriever.
The answer model reads the original turns as well as the summaries, so the Prospective Reflection gain mixes a better search key with different context boundaries; no run separates the two.
The granularity study (Fig. 4) uses 100 samples and reports PR at 49 accuracy, well below the 70.4 of Table 1 with the same retriever and generator; the paper does not explain the gap.
No token, latency or LLM-call costs are reported, although extraction and merging add LLM calls at every session end.

abstract.text: RMM is a memory design for personalized dialogue agents that addresses two problems: memory cut at fixed turn or session boundaries, and retrievers that never adapt. Looking forward, it summarises each finished session into topic-level memories (a summary plus the turns it came from) and merges them with related existing ones. Looking back, it trains a small reranker on top of a frozen retriever with online reinforcement learning, rewarding memories the answer model cites. With Gemini-1.5-Flash it beats RAG, MemoryBank and LD-Agent baselines on MSC and LongMemEval, reaching 70.4% LongMemEval accuracy with the GTE retriever.

systems.name: RRP

paper.title: Reliable Reasoning Path: Distilling Effective Guidance for LLM Reasoning With Knowledge Graphs

construction.unit: reasoning path: chain of KG triples from a question entity (e0 -r1-> e1 ... -rn-> en)
construction.kept_as: KG triples as given (Freebase); paths generated per question, not stored
construction.processing: no per-question writing; offline, an LLM is fine-tuned on shortest question-answer paths and a GNN path model is trained with bidirectional distribution losses

organization.structure: knowledge graph (Freebase subgraph; Wiki-Movie for MetaQA)
organization.stores: one KG

retrieval.query: question; GloVe+LSTM encoding decoded into n reasoning instructions for the GNN
retrieval.candidates: union of LLM-generated semantic paths and GNN structural paths
retrieval.selection: score λ1·cos(LLM question, path) + λ2·cos(GNN question, mean path entity), drop below θ, sort descending
retrieval.budget: threshold θ (best 0.6 on WebQSP); number of paths not stated

use.context: question + surviving paths listed in order of importance
use.reasoning: single answer call (fine-tuned LLaMA2-Chat-7B, or any LLM plug-and-play)

classify.note: A KGQA method, not an agent memory: the store is a fixed knowledge graph that is never written. Candidates come from a fine-tuned LLM and a trained GNN; a fixed weighted score with a threshold (not a reranker model) decides what the answer model reads. How entities in the question are linked to the KG is not stated.

stages.organization: Knowledge lives in an existing KG (a Freebase subgraph for WebQSP/CWQ, Wiki-Movie for MetaQA-3); the method adds nothing to it.
stages.retrieval: A fine-tuned LLM generates semantically relevant reasoning paths, and a GNN that propagates over relation embeddings for n steps generates structurally related paths; each path is scored by a weighted sum of LLM-embedding and GNN-embedding cosine similarity with the question, paths below θ are dropped and the rest sorted.
stages.answer: The question and the kept paths, listed most important first, go to the answer LLM with a prompt asking for all possible answers as a list.
stages.learning: Offline: the path-generating LLM (LLaMA2-Chat-7B) is fine-tuned to maximise the likelihood of shortest question-to-answer paths (KL to a uniform posterior over them); the GNN is trained with KL losses to gold forward/backward entity distributions plus a Jensen-Shannon term tying forward and backward steps.

systems.summary: KG question answering that merges LLM-generated and GNN-mined reasoning paths and keeps only those whose combined semantic and structural similarity to the question passes a threshold, ordered by that score in the answer prompt.

headline: The 'memory' is a fixed knowledge graph; RRP decides which reasoning paths through it reach the answer model.
Two generators propose paths (a fine-tuned LLM and a trained GNN); a weighted similarity score with a threshold keeps and orders them.
Paths are handed to the answer LLM most important first, which is the point of the paper's case study.

open_questions: Table I compares against baseline numbers whose source (rerun or copied) the paper does not state.
How generated semantic paths are checked against or grounded in the KG is not described, so it is unclear whether they can contain hallucinated relations.
The ablation is on WebQSP only; the CWQ setting (λ2 = 0.9, mostly structural) is not ablated.

abstract.text: RRP targets knowledge-graph question answering, arguing that LLMs need not only facts from a KG but well-ordered reasoning paths through it. It produces candidate paths two ways: a fine-tuned LLM proposes paths that match the question's meaning, and a graph model trained with relation embeddings and forward/backward consistency proposes paths that match its structure. A rethinking step scores every path on both views, discards weak ones and sorts the rest before they are given to the answer model. The authors report state-of-the-art Hits@1 on WebQSP and CWQ with a 7B model, and large gains when the paths are given to other LLMs without fine-tuning.

discussion.takeaway: For KG question answering, which reasoning paths the LLM sees and in what order matters: combining LLM-proposed and graph-mined paths and ranking them lifts a 7B model above prior KG+LLM methods on WebQSP and CWQ.

claims.claim: State of the art among KG-enhanced LLM methods with a 7B model.
claims.evidence: WebQSP Hits@1 90.0 vs RoG 85.7 and SubgraphRAG+LLaMA3-8B 86.6; CWQ 64.5 vs RoG 62.6. Table I, §V-D

claims.claim: The paths help other LLMs without fine-tuning.
claims.evidence: WebQSP Hits@1: GPT-4o-mini 67.08 → 91.10, Flan-T5-xl 30.95 → 69.66; CWQ GPT-4o-mini 41.43 → 71.68. Table II

claims.claim: Semantic and structural paths complement each other, and Rethinking adds on top.
claims.evidence: WebQSP Hits@1 90.0 full, 86.7 without structural, 77.4 without semantic, 88.3 without Rethinking. Table V

claims.claim: Robust across KG sizes.
claims.evidence: MetaQA-3 (Wiki-Movie) 99.5 vs RoG 89.0; inference 2.9 s vs 2.6 s. Tables III-IV

limits: The paper has no limitations section; §V-F notes that a high θ discards valid paths and that the best λ differs by dataset.
reading: This is KG question answering with trained retrievers, not conversational or agent memory: nothing is written or updated per interaction.

Semantic paths with Rethinking reach 86.7, one point above RoG's 85.7; adding the GNN's structural paths gives 90.0. Without semantic paths the score falls to 77.4, so the fine-tuned LLM generator carries most of the performance.
λ is set per dataset (0.5/0.5 on WebQSP, 0.1/0.9 on CWQ); θ and λ1 are chosen from sweeps reported on WebQSP (Figs. 3-4), and the paper does not say whether a validation split was used.
Table I baselines include numbers with ChatGPT and LLaMA2-70B; the paper does not say whether they were rerun or copied, and several cells are blank.
The best result in Table II (GPT-4o-mini + RRP, 91.10 on WebQSP) uses the paths generated by the fine-tuned 7B pipeline with a stronger answer model.
Case study (Table VI) labels each path semantic or structural, but the answer prompt in Fig. 6 does not show whether these labels are given to the model.

stages.ingestion: Each executed GUI step is recorded as (observation, action, next observation) in the episodic store of the current task.
stages.construction: After a task, the trajectory is stored in experiential memory with an agent-written reflective summary, a text key and a visual key. Semantic memory holds general interaction rules; the paper does not say how they are written.
stages.organization: Three separate stores: episodic (current task), semantic (rules), experiential (past trajectories).
stages.update: Append-only: new trajectories keep accumulating during inference; nothing is merged or deleted.
stages.retrieval: Per step: the last H episodic steps; the top-K rules by cosine to the instruction; the top-K experiences by a λ-weighted mix of instruction-to-intent and screenshot-to-task similarity, keeping only their summaries.
stages.answer: The retrieved memory, instruction and screenshot go to the policy VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B based), which reasons and outputs one action.
stages.learning: MASE turns collected trajectories into training data: hindsight goal-shifting relabels failed trajectories with the sub-goal they reached; the policy gets grounding SFT and then GRPO with token-level ratios, an adaptive upper clip and a format/type/parameter reward.

systems.summary: GUI agent with three memories (recent steps, general rules, past trajectories retrieved by text plus screenshot similarity) whose collected trajectories are relabelled by hindsight goal-shifting and distilled into the policy with SFT and GRPO.

abstract.text: SE-GA targets GUI agents that lose track of long tasks and cannot learn from their own runs. At test time it keeps three memories: the recent steps of the current task, general interaction rules, and past trajectories with reflective summaries that are retrieved by instruction and screenshot similarity. The trajectories it collects are then used to retrain the policy: failed runs are relabelled with the sub-goal they did reach, and the model goes through grounding SFT followed by a modified GRPO. With a 7B Qwen2.5-VL base, the authors report 89.0 on ScreenSpot, 75.8 success on AndroidControl-High and 39.0 on AndroidWorld.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Memory feeds the agent at each step (recent steps, rules, experience summaries) and also becomes training data for the policy.
The paper gives no window size, top-K, λ or encoders; the code defaults are H = 10, 3 rules, 3 experiences, λ = 0.7, text-embedding-3-small and CLIP ViT-B/32.
Only the ablation separates memory from training: removing TTME drops AndroidControl-High success from 73.8 to 61.4.

open_questions: The ablation removes TTME as a whole, so the separate value of episodic steps, rules and experiences is not measured; a recency window of 10 steps alone may account for much of the gain.
No run compares the same trained policy with and without experiential memory on AndroidWorld, where the paper credits both memory and self-evolution.

Baseline numbers are largely copied from another paper while SE-GA is trained on AITW, AMEX and GUIOdyssey trajectories; overlap between training sources and GUIOdyssey test episodes is not discussed.

glance.a: A step record for the current task, a rule text, or a past trajectory with an agent-written summary.
By a weighted mix of instruction-to-intent text similarity and screenshot-to-task image similarity (λ 0.7 in the code); the top 3 summaries are shown.

glance.q: Is there reranking or an LLM in retrieval?
glance.a: No. Episodic memory is a recency window; the other two are cosine top-k.
Yes, indirectly: collected trajectories are relabelled and used for SFT and GRPO (MASE).
