ablation.src: paper Table 4 (7B); AC-High SR of the full model is 73.8 here but 75.8 in Table 2

discussion.takeaway: A GUI agent gains most on long, multi-step tasks when it both carries structured memory at test time and is retrained on its own relabelled trajectories.

claims.claim: State of the art among 7B GUI agents.
claims.evidence: ScreenSpot 89.0 (above UI-TARS-72B 88.4); AndroidControl-High SR 75.8; GUIOdyssey 83.9; AndroidWorld 39.0 vs UI-TARS-7B 33.0. Tables 1-3

claims.claim: TTME matters most on long-horizon tasks.
claims.evidence: Without TTME: AC-Low SR 88.6 → 83.0, AC-High SR 73.8 → 61.4. Table 4, App. C.3

claims.claim: MASE builds the base capability.
claims.evidence: Without MASE: AC-High SR 59.7, GUIOdyssey SR 60.4 (full 73.8, 83.9). Table 4

claims.claim: Repeated self-evolution keeps improving.
claims.evidence: Rounds 1-3: GUIOdyssey 52.3 → 75.1 → 83.9; AndroidWorld 28.6 → 34.5 → 39.0. Table 8

claims.claim: Failed trajectories are useful memory.
claims.evidence: Success-only retrieval 70.0 / 72.5 vs top-k 75.8 / 83.9 (AC-High / GUIOdyssey). Table 9

limits: Retrieval cost grows as experiential memory accumulates and may slow real-time use.
Training data is limited to about 4K trajectories.
No explicit sub-goal decomposition for very long workflows; cross-platform transfer untested.
reading: Table 4 reports 73.8 for the full model on AndroidControl-High SR while Table 2 reports 75.8 for the same setting; Table 7 labels its columns AndroidControl-High and GUIOdyssey but repeats Table 4's AndroidControl-Low and -High values.

Most baseline rows are copied from another paper (App. A.5), so they may differ from SE-GA in prompts and evaluation scripts; the paper does not say where the Qwen2.5-VL, OS-Atlas, OS-Genesis and GUI-Critic-R1 numbers come from.
The paper gives no memory hyperparameters and the released code has no evaluation pipeline, so the TTME settings behind the reported numbers cannot be confirmed.
The memory described for training (Eq. 7) and the released training prompts differ: the prompts carry only a short history of up to 10 steps.
ScreenSpot is single-screen grounding, so its gain cannot come from memory; the paper attributes it to the reward design.

systems.name: SeCom

paper.title: On Memory Construction and Retrieval for Personalized Conversational Agents

construction.unit: topical segment of consecutive turns within a session
construction.kept_as: verbatim segments; LLMLingua-2-compressed copy used for retrieval
construction.processing: LLM conversation segmentation; LLMLingua-2 denoising at 75% compression
construction.writer: GPT-4 zero-shot segmenter (Mistral-7B, RoBERTa alternatives); LLMLingua-2 xlm-roberta-large

organization.structure: flat segment-level memory bank
organization.stores: single memory bank
organization.index: BM25 or MPNet (multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1) with FAISS

management.operations: none (memory bank only built, never edited)
management.conflicts: none

retrieval.query: user request used as is
retrieval.candidates: BM25 or MPNet similarity over denoised units
retrieval.selection: top-N units within context budget
retrieval.budget: 4k tokens LOCOMO (~10 segments); 1k tokens Long-MT-Bench+

use.context: retrieved units in time order
use.reasoning: single response call (GPT-35-Turbo; Mistral-7B also)

classify.note: Evaluated with both BM25 and MPNet; BM25 gives its best LoCoMo result.

stages.ingestion: Each session is split into topically coherent segments by a conversation segmentation model (zero-shot GPT-4 for QA benchmarks; Mistral-7B and a RoBERTa model fine-tuned on SuperDialSeg also tested).
stages.construction: Segments become the memory units; LLMLingua-2 (xlm-roberta-large, 75% compression rate) is applied to memory units as compression-based denoising before retrieval.
stages.organization: Flat segment-level memory bank.
stages.retrieval: BM25 or MPNet (multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1) with FAISS retrieves units under a context budget (4k tokens on LOCOMO, 1k on Long-MT-Bench+).
stages.answer: Retrieved units are placed in time order as context for the response model (GPT-35-Turbo main; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 also tested).
stages.learning: Optional: the segmentation prompt is refined by LLM self-reflection on hard annotated examples (used for segmentation benchmarks, not for the QA runs).

systems.summary: Builds conversational memory at topical-segment granularity and denoises memory units with LLMLingua-2 compression to improve retrieval.
systems.notes:
Venue ICLR 2025 confirmed via iclr.cc poster page and Microsoft Research page (not stated in the arXiv text itself). Code URL from the Hugging Face paper page (auto-linked); project page https://aka.ms/secom. AXES-CHECK: the paper evaluates both BM25 (lexical) and MPNet (dense) retrievers, and its best LOCOMO result uses BM25, so 'dense (vector)' is only one of the two configurations. It is not fully clear from Eq. 2 whether the LLM receives the compressed or the original segment text.

systems.name: SEDM

paper.title: SEDM: Scalable Self-Evolving Distributed Memory for Agents

construction.unit: memory item: one short injectable snippet extracted from a task run, with a utility weight and provenance
construction.kept_as: extracted snippet (decisive reasoning or corrective step), deduplicated and canonicalized
construction.processing: package the run as an SCEC; extract one candidate; A/B replay with and without it; admit if S = ΔR − λL·ΔL − λT·ΔT ≥ η
construction.writer: not stated (extraction model and prompt are not described)

organization.structure: flat pool of weighted items, each paired with an abstracted general form; trajectory, query and insight graphs keep provenance
organization.stores: one repository of specific and general items
organization.index: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 dense embeddings (stated for FEVER/HotpotQA)

management.operations: weight update w ← w + α·Ū − β·f_use; promote stable items; merge near-duplicates; abstract recurring items into insights
management.conflicts: items whose injections repeatedly lower reward, or that contradict other rules, are demoted and removed below a threshold
management.forgetting: decay of rarely used or unhelpful items; removal or soft-delete below a weight threshold

retrieval.query: task query as is
retrieval.candidates: dense similarity over specific and general items
retrieval.selection: rank by s(q,m) = sim(q,m) × w(m); no reranker
retrieval.budget: same memory budget as baselines (size not stated); top-k not stated

use.context: selected items injected into the agent prompt
use.reasoning: the agent's own task loop (ReAct-style Search/Finish trace in the SCEC example)

classify.note: Admission and weights come from measured task feedback, but at read time the rule is fixed: similarity times weight. Merging and abstraction make management 'consolidate' rather than 'update in place'.

stages.ingestion: Each task run is packaged as a Self-Contained Execution Context (SCEC): inputs, outputs, summarised tool calls, seeds and config hashes, so it can be replayed without the original environment.
stages.construction: One candidate snippet is extracted per SCEC and tested by paired A/B replay (prompt with and without it); it is admitted only if the reward gain minus latency and token costs clears a threshold, and that score becomes its initial weight.
stages.organization: Admitted items sit in one weighted pool; right after admission each gets a general form with entities replaced by typed placeholders and a scaled-down weight.
stages.update: Weights move with realised utility and usage frequency; near-duplicates are merged, stable items promoted and abstracted, and items that keep hurting reward are demoted or removed.
stages.retrieval: Items are scored by embedding similarity to the query multiplied by their weight; specific and general forms compete in the same ranking, with no reranker.
stages.answer: Selected items are injected into the agent's prompt.
stages.learning: No model is trained; only per-item scalar weights change from observed outcomes.

systems.summary: Memory items enter only after an A/B replay shows they raise reward net of latency and token cost; that measured gain becomes a weight that multiplies similarity at retrieval and keeps being updated, merged and abstracted for cross-task transfer.
systems.notes: Paper v3 (2025-09-26) read from the arXiv PDF. No code: the abstract says code will be released on acceptance, and no official repository was found. Hyper-parameters λL, λT, η, α, β, top-k and the memory budget are not given. How SCEC replay and extraction are applied to LoCoMo dialogues is not described. The LoCoMo Table 1 rows for LoCoMo, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT and A-Mem equal A-Mem's (2502.12110) GPT-4o-mini Table 1 values rounded to one decimal, under different category labels; see results notes.

sources.code_note: No official code: the paper says code will be released upon acceptance, and a GitHub search found no repository. Everything here follows the paper text, Eqs. 1-10 and Figure 2.

headline: A memory item is admitted only if replaying the same run with it beats replaying without it, net of latency and token cost; the net score is its starting weight.
Retrieval is plain similarity times that weight: no reranker and no LLM at read time.
The paper gives no values for the thresholds, trade-off weights, top-k or memory budget, and does not say how the replay test is run on LoCoMo dialogues.

accept if S ≥ η; initial weight w₀ = max(0, S); otherwise discard

LoCoMo temporal F1: SEDM vs G-Memory

open_questions: How is an A/B replay with a task reward run on LoCoMo dialogue QA, and what is extracted from a conversation? The paper describes the pipeline only for agent task runs.
Gains over G-Memory on FEVER and HotpotQA (4 and 1 points) come without the number of test items, variance or the size of the shared memory budget.
The ablation adds the admission gate and the scheduler together with their weights; there is no run of weighting without the gate, or the gate without weighted retrieval.

glance.a: A short snippet taken from one task run (a decisive or corrective step), stored with a utility weight, provenance and a generalised copy.

glance.q: What decides whether it is stored?
glance.a: A paired replay of the same run with and without the snippet; it is kept only if the reward gain minus latency and token costs reaches a threshold.
Embedding similarity to the query times the item's weight; no reranker and no LLM step.

glance.q: Does memory change after it is written?
glance.a: Yes: weights follow observed utility and usage, similar items are merged, and harmful ones are demoted or removed.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: Its task prompt plus the selected items; the exact template and count are not given.

discussion.takeaway: Gate memory writes with a replay test that measures whether an item actually helps, and reuse that measured gain as a weight at retrieval. On FEVER and HotpotQA this beats G-Memory with fewer tokens, but beats no memory at a token cost.

claims.claim: SEDM improves accuracy while using fewer tokens than a strong memory baseline.
claims.evidence: FEVER 66 vs 62 (G-Memory) with 2.47M vs 3.62M prompt tokens; HotpotQA 39 vs 38 with 3.88M vs 4.63M. Table 2, §4.3

claims.claim: Both the admission gate and the scheduler contribute.
claims.evidence: HotpotQA 34 → 37 → 39, FEVER 57 → 64 → 66 as SCEC then self-scheduling are added. Table 3, §4.4

claims.claim: Best on LoCoMo temporal and open-domain questions.
claims.evidence: Temporal F1 47.5 vs 32.4 for G-Memory. Table 1, §4.2 (open-domain: see reading)

claims.claim: Memory learned on one task transfers to another.
claims.evidence: FEVER-collected memory gives 41 on HotpotQA vs 39 in-domain; HotpotQA memory gives 64 on FEVER. Table 4, §4.5

limits: The paper has no limitations section.
It notes that dialogue memory from LoCoMo transfers poorly to the other two tasks (HotpotQA 34, the no-memory level).
reading: The text says SEDM has the best open-domain F1 and BLEU-1 on LoCoMo, but Table 1 shows G-Memory higher (53.5 vs 51.7 F1, 44.0 vs 37.0 BLEU-1); SEDM is best only on temporal.

The LoCoMo, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT and A-Mem rows equal A-Mem's GPT-4o-mini Table 1 rounded to one decimal, but under different category names, and the paper does not say they were copied. §4.1 lists four question types while the table has five, including adversarial.
SEDM's LoCoMo run has no ablation, token count, embedder or description of how the replay reward is defined for dialogue QA.

The scheduler raises token use relative to the gate alone (FEVER 2.19M → 2.47M, HotpotQA 3.52M → 3.88M); the saving is only relative to G-Memory, and both memory methods use more tokens than no memory.
Every trade-off parameter (λL, λT, η, α, β), top-k and the shared memory budget are unreported, and there is no code, so the results cannot be reproduced from the paper.
α names both the utility step in Eq. 7 and the general-form weight scale in §3.4.

abstract.text: SEDM targets memory for long-running (multi-)agent systems, where stored trajectories pile up noise and cost. Each task run is packed into a self-contained, replayable context; a candidate memory item is kept only if replaying the run with it beats replaying without it, after charging for extra latency and tokens. The measured gain becomes a weight that multiplies embedding similarity at retrieval and keeps being revised, merged and generalised into placeholder forms that can move across tasks. On FEVER and HotpotQA with GPT-4o-mini it scores above G-Memory with fewer tokens, and it reports competitive LoCoMo scores and cross-task transfer.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: SelfMem

paper.title: SelfMem: Self-Optimizing Memory for AI Agents

construction.unit: agent-written workspace items over an immutable raw transcript
construction.kept_as: raw transcript verbatim; workspace agent-written
construction.processing: agent reads transcript via SQL, writes, reviews and revises memory operations
construction.writer: memory agent (GPT-5.4-nano) via tool calls

organization.structure: free-form workspace; structure chosen by the agent
organization.stores: read-only SQLite turns table + memory workspace
organization.index: SQLite turns table queried by read-only SQL

management.operations: add, replace, merge, archive, delete, pin, reorganize (Table 2)
management.conflicts: review tools flag contradictions/stale facts; agent revises

retrieval.candidates: relevant transcript turns/snippets; zero embedding requests reported

classify.note: Agent adds, merges, archives and reorganises its workspace; answer-time retrieval is fixed (App. B).

stages.ingestion: The raw transcript is stored unchanged as a read-only SQLite 'turns' table (turn index, role, time anchor, content).
stages.construction: An LLM agent runs an inspect-write-review-revise tool loop: it reads the transcript via manifest / read-only SQL / entity search, and writes auditable memory operations (add, replace, merge, archive, exact facts, timelines, retrieval hints) into a free-form workspace.
stages.organization: A free-form memory workspace whose structure (profile, preference list, timeline, project state, policy notes) is chosen by the agent.
stages.update: Memory-review tools flag missing source support, stale facts, contradictions and over-broad summaries; the agent revises the workspace accordingly.
stages.retrieval: At query time relevant transcript turns/snippets are retrieved using the workspace as a guide (targeted RAG / SQL / semantic search chosen by the model); no embedding requests in the reported runs.
stages.answer: The answer model receives the query, the final workspace and retrieved transcript evidence; the prompt treats retrieved evidence as authoritative over memory.
stages.learning: Optional iterative strategy refinement: the model rewrites its own memory-strategy notes from aggregate training-conversation scores and tool diagnostics (no weight updates).

systems.summary: Keeps the raw transcript immutable and lets an LLM agent decide, via memory tools and feedback diagnostics, what to write, revise and later retrieve, optionally refining its own memory strategy from aggregate feedback.
systems.notes:
Authors: Shu Yang, Junchao Wu, Derek F. Wong, Di Wang (KAUST PRADA Lab; University of Macau). An OpenReview forum entry exists (id fXHmKW9H8r) but no acceptance venue was confirmed. No code URL found. Only benchmark is BEAM (100K/500K/1M); no LoCoMo/LongMemEval results. AXES-CHECK: seed taxonomy row consistent with the paper.
DESIGN: Sec 3.3-3.7, 4.1, App. A Table 2, App. B, App. C Prompts 2-3. Table 2 describes SelfMem as conditionally retrieving, but App. B says answer-time retrieval is fixed; control.retrieval follows App. B. Optional strategy refinement from aggregate feedback (Sec 5) revises the construction policy. query/budget null: not specified.

systems.name: SimGRAG

paper.title: SimGRAG: Leveraging Similar Subgraphs for Knowledge Graphs Driven Retrieval-Augmented Generation

construction.unit: KG triple of an existing knowledge graph; one embedding per entity name, relation name and (DBpedia) entity type
construction.kept_as: verbatim triples; 768-d Nomic embeddings of the names
construction.processing: no LLM: names embedded with nomic-embed-text-v1 into Milvus HNSW indexes; triples stored as an adjacency list in both directions
construction.writer: Nomic embedding model (nomic-embed-text-v1)

organization.structure: existing KG (MetaQA, PathQuestions, WorldCup2014 KGs; DBpedia for FactKG)
organization.stores: adjacency list; vector indexes of entities, relations and (DBpedia) types
organization.index: Milvus HNSW over name embeddings, L2 distance (M 64, efConstruction 512)

management.operations: none; the KG is fixed

retrieval.query: an LLM (12-shot) rewrites the query as a small pattern graph of triples, with UNKNOWN placeholders for missing entities or relations
retrieval.candidates: nearest KG entities per pattern node and nearest relations per pattern relation (16 / 16 on MetaQA; 16,384 / 512 on DBpedia), then DFS matching of subgraphs with the pattern's shape
retrieval.selection: top-k subgraphs by Graph Semantic Distance (sum of L2 distances of matched nodes and relations), with lower-bound pruning
retrieval.budget: k = 3 subgraphs

use.context: the k subgraphs as triple lists labelled graph [1..k], after 12 worked examples
use.reasoning: single LLM call (Llama 3 70B, 4-bit, Ollama)

classify.note: Dense search only shortlists candidate entities and relations; subgraphs are then found by structural matching over the KG, and the 3 with the smallest summed distance are kept. The KG itself is never changed.

stages.ingestion: An existing KG is loaded as it is: MetaQA's movie KG (43k entities, 269k edges), PathQuestions, WorldCup2014, or DBpedia (9.9M entities, 42.9M edges) for FactKG.
stages.construction: Every entity name and relation name, and for DBpedia every entity type, is embedded with the 768-d Nomic model and indexed in Milvus HNSW; no LLM is involved.
stages.organization: Triples are held as an adjacency list in both directions, so edge direction is ignored when matching; DBpedia entities are also grouped by type.
stages.retrieval: An LLM turns the query into a pattern graph; each known pattern node and relation gets its nearest KG entities and relations by L2 distance; a DFS finds KG subgraphs with the pattern's shape and keeps the 3 with the smallest Graph Semantic Distance, pruning branches whose lower bound is already worse.
stages.answer: The 3 subgraphs are pasted as triple lists after the query with 12 examples, and the LLM answers (KGQA) or says True or False (FactKG).

systems.summary: Aligns a query with a knowledge graph through a pattern: an LLM drafts the query as a small graph, and the retriever returns the KG subgraphs of the same shape whose entity and relation names are closest in embedding distance.

headline: The memory is an existing KG that is never changed; SimGRAG adds only name embeddings for entities, relations and (DBpedia) types.
The LLM does not pick facts: it drafts the query as a small graph, and a rule-based matcher finds KG subgraphs of that shape ranked by summed embedding distance.
The answer model reads 3 small subgraphs as triple lists, never the pattern or the distances.

open_questions: No ablation removes the shape constraint or the distance ranking, so against KAPING (single triples by query similarity) the pattern step, the structure and the GSD are changed together.
The few-shot examples are hand-written per KG; 4 instead of 12 shots costs 5.0 points on MetaQA 3-hop and 2.8 on FactKG (Table 2), and the paper does not test other example sets.
Where the supervised baseline numbers (EmbedKGQA, NSM, UniKGQA, TransferNet, GEAR) come from is not stated.

discussion.takeaway: Let the LLM draw the query as a small graph and let a distance-ranked subgraph matcher find where that shape occurs in the KG; without training this nears supervised scores on MetaQA and beats other training-free KG-RAG methods, most clearly on multi-hop questions.

claims.claim: Best among training-free KG-driven RAG methods.
claims.evidence: MetaQA 3-hop 97.8 vs 88.2 (KG-GPT) and 43.0 (KAPING); PQ 3-hop 78.6 vs 52.1; FactKG 86.8 vs 75.5. Table 1, §6.3.

claims.claim: Close to supervised task-specific models without any training.
claims.evidence: MetaQA 98.0 / 98.4 / 97.8 vs 97.1-97.5 / 98.8-100 / 94.8-100; FactKG 86.8 beats supervised GEAR (77.7). Table 1.

claims.claim: Scales to a 10-million-node KG.
claims.evidence: 0.74 s retrieval per query on DBpedia (9.9M entities, 42.9M edges), 0.15 s of it matching. Table 5, §6.6.

claims.claim: Pruning keeps results exact and makes search faster.
claims.evidence: The optimized search returns the same top-k as the plain one (§5.2); Fig. 5 shows lower retrieval time at high retrieval Hits@1.

claims.claim: Works across LLMs.
claims.evidence: FactKG 86.1 with Phi4-14B and 83.6 with Qwen2.5-72B vs 86.8 with Llama 3 70B. Table 2.

limits: Quality depends on the LLM following the instructions in both prompts; weaker LLMs and complex queries suffer.
It assumes a KG whose schema matches human intuition; specialised industrial KGs may need fine-tuned LLMs or the schema in the prompt.
Linking query entities to domain-specific KG entities with an off-the-shelf embedding model may fail; fine-tuned embeddings or other entity linkers are left for future work.
reading: Most errors happen before retrieval: drafting the pattern causes 89% of MetaQA 1-hop errors and 49% on FactKG, and matching never fails on MetaQA (Table 4).
KG-GPT, KELP and G-Retriever are given oracle entities, so their numbers are upper bounds (Table 1 note), while KAPING and SimGRAG get none.
Edge direction is ignored in the definition and in the code (adjacency stored both ways), so a pattern can match a reversed relation.
The FactKG candidate sizes (16,384 / 512 / 16 types) equal the grid-search setting that reached retrieval Hits@1 of 1.0 on 100 hand-labelled FactKG queries (App. G).
In code an answer counts as correct if any gold string appears in the output, which rewards listing several answers; the prompt asks for all answers from all 3 subgraphs.

abstract.text: SimGRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation method for question answering and fact checking over knowledge graphs. It aligns a text query with KG structure in two steps: an LLM rewrites the query as a small pattern graph, and a retriever finds KG subgraphs with the same shape whose nodes and relations are closest in embedding distance, a score the authors call graph semantic distance. A pruned search returns the top subgraphs in under a second on a 10-million-node KG, and needs neither training nor user-supplied entity IDs. It outperforms other KG-driven RAG methods on question answering and fact verification.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on the ACL Anthology page.

systems.name: SimpleMem

paper.title: SimpleMem: Efficient Lifelong Memory for LLM Agents

construction.unit: atomic memory unit: self-contained factual statement with metadata
construction.kept_as: compressed (LLM-rewritten atomic statements)
construction.processing: LLM gate drops low-info windows; coreference and ISO-8601 time normalisation; atomisation
construction.writer: gpt-4.1-mini, temperature 0 (Table 7); 20-turn windows, stride 5

organization.structure: flat
organization.stores: one LanceDB store with three index views
organization.index: Qwen3-embedding-0.6b dense + BM25 sparse + metadata (time, entities, topic, salience)

management.operations: online semantic synthesis merges related units within session before commit
management.conflicts: answer prompt prioritises most recent memory unit

retrieval.query: LLM planner writes semantic, lexical and temporal queries plus complexity/depth
retrieval.candidates: top-n per view: cosine, BM25, metadata constraint filter
retrieval.selection: set union of the three views, deduplicated
retrieval.budget: n proportional to inferred depth, range 3-20 (Table 7)

use.context: abstract representations plus detailed units, ordered by relevance
use.reasoning: single answer call; recency-first conflict rule; abstain if missing

classify.note: Planner sets per-view k; the final set is the deduplicated union.

stages.ingestion: Dialogue is cut into overlapping sliding windows (20 turns, stride 5); an LLM-based implicit semantic-density gate emits nothing for low-information windows (e.g. phatic chit-chat).
stages.construction: For informative windows a single LLM pass (gpt-4.1-mini) extracts context-independent atomic memory units with coreference resolved and relative times converted to absolute ISO-8601 timestamps.
stages.organization: Each unit is indexed in three views in LanceDB: dense embedding (Qwen3-embedding-0.6b), BM25 sparse lexical index, and symbolic metadata (timestamp, entities, topic, salience) for SQL-style filtering; flat store.
stages.update: Online Semantic Synthesis consolidates related fragments within the current session into unified higher-density entries before they are written (v1 described this as asynchronous recursive consolidation).
stages.retrieval: An LLM planner infers search intent and emits semantic, lexical and symbolic queries plus a depth d; each view returns top-n (n proportional to d, range 3-20) and results are merged by set union.
stages.answer: The merged, deduplicated context is passed to the backbone LLM for answer generation.

systems.summary: Compresses dialogue at write time into atomic, time-normalised memory units indexed in dense, BM25 and metadata views, and uses an LLM planner to set per-query retrieval depth, cutting query tokens to about 530-580.
systems.notes:
Annotated from the current arXiv HTML (fetched 2026-09-28); v1 used the stage names Recursive Memory Consolidation / Adaptive Query-Aware Retrieval and had no LongMemEval table; LoCoMo tables are numerically identical across v1 and the current version. Paper uses the ICML template but no acceptance is stated. AXES-CHECK: 'semantic + lexical + symbolic' in the seed taxonomy's write-time column is really the indexing (organisation) step; the write-time processing in the paper is LLM gating/filtering + atomic extraction with coreference and timestamp normalisation + intra-session synthesis (consolidation).
DESIGN: Sec 2.1-2.3, Sec 3.1, App. A.1-A.3, App. B.2 (Table 7).

systems.name: Skill-Pro (ProcMEM)

paper.title: Skill-Pro: Learning Reusable Skills from Experience via Non-Parametric PPO for LLM Agents

construction.unit: Skill: name, activation (initiation) condition, 3-5 natural-language steps, termination condition, plus usage statistics
construction.kept_as: LLM-written procedure distilled from diagnosed trajectories; no trajectory text is stored with the skill
construction.processing: per-trajectory LLM diagnosis (semantic gradient) -> one LLM call merges them and rewrites the skill -> 3 candidates -> PPO Gate on action log-probs; best candidate added if J > 0
construction.writer: evolver LLM (--ge_model_name; default llama-3.3-70b-instruct in the code); the paper says skills are learned with Gemma-2-9B on TextArena and Qwen3-32B on ALFWorld

organization.structure: flat pool of at most K = 10 skills; refined versions keep a parent id and version number
organization.stores: one skill pool; per-skill buffer of trajectories that used it
organization.index: none for the default selection; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings of the activation condition are used for de-duplication and the similarity fallback

management.operations: refine a skill into a new version or synthesise a new skill; accept only if the PPO Gate score is positive; prune by score when the pool exceeds capacity
management.conflicts: versions of one skill coexist and compete on score; near-duplicates (cosine >= 0.95) keep the best
management.forgetting: score-based pruning (code: lower confidence bound of mean gain) and removal of duplicates

retrieval.query: current environment state
retrieval.candidates: whole pool listed to the LLM as name + activation condition (paper: similarity to the activation condition, optionally top-k then highest value)
retrieval.selection: the acting LLM picks one skill or NONE; with probability epsilon a random skill or none is used instead
retrieval.budget: one active skill at a time, kept until an LLM termination check says DONE or 8 steps pass

use.context: current state (plus admissible commands on ALFWorld) and the active skill's text with usage instructions
use.reasoning: one LLM call per step: match, apply the steps, output one action

classify.note: The code's default selector (llm_model) shows the LLM the whole pool of at most 10 skills; the paper describes similarity selection. Refinement adds new versions next to the parent, and score-based pruning removes the losers, so the net management effect is eviction.

stages.ingestion: Episodes are run with the current pool; each finished trajectory (state/action transitions, reward, names of the skills it used) is added to the buffer of every skill it used.
stages.construction: When a skill has at least 6 buffered trajectories, 3 lowest- and 3 highest-reward ones are diagnosed one by one by an LLM into structured fixes for the activation, steps and termination (semantic gradients); one more LLM call merges them and rewrites the skill. This is sampled 3 times to get candidates.
stages.organization: A flat pool capped at 10 skills. Refined skills are named <base>_v<n> and record their parent; the six hand-written seed skills are the starting pool.
stages.update: The PPO Gate re-scores the buffered actions under each candidate versus the old skill (clipped probability ratio times advantage); the best candidate is added if its score is positive, and the parent stays. After each iteration every used skill's gain is updated and the pool is pruned by score and de-duplicated.
stages.retrieval: Whenever no skill is active, the acting LLM reads the list of skill names and activation conditions and picks one or NONE (epsilon-greedy random picks during training and test).
stages.answer: The active skill's text is placed in the decision prompt; the LLM outputs one action per step. An LLM meta-controller checks each step whether the skill should stop.
stages.learning: No weights change. Skills improve through LLM-written rewrites that are accepted or rejected by the PPO-style gate and kept or pruned by their online gain.

systems.summary: Procedural memory as a small pool of natural-language skills (trigger, steps, stop condition) that an LLM rewrites from diagnosed trajectories, with a PPO-style log-probability gate deciding which rewrites enter the pool and score-based pruning keeping it at 10.

The code hint github.com/Miracle1207/ProcMEM redirects to Miracle1207/Skill-Pro. headline: Memory is at most 10 short skills (the paper reports 816 stored tokens in total, 102 per skill), not past trajectories.
A rewrite enters the pool only if re-scoring past actions under it gives a positive clipped advantage (the PPO Gate); in the code the log-probabilities come from the evolver model.
In the released code the acting LLM picks the skill from the whole list; the paper's similarity/value selection is not the default.

write.how: run 5 episodes per environment per iteration; each trajectory goes to the buffer of every skill it used
write.src: code run.py L211-L235; skill_evolution.py L386-L391; main.py L30

write.how: skills with >= 6 buffered runs are ranked by a priority that favours frequently used skills whose gain is below the best; up to 2 are evolved per iteration
for each of 6 runs (3 lowest and 3 highest reward) an LLM writes a diagnosis and fixes for trigger, steps and stop condition, or marks the run unrelated
write.src: paper §4.1, App. E; code skill_evolution.py L17-L56, L171-L245

write.how: one LLM call aggregates the fixes and rewrites the skill; if fewer than half the runs were related, it writes a new skill instead
score each candidate by the clipped ratio of old actions' log-probabilities (candidate vs old skill) times the run's advantage per step; add the best if its score > 0
write.out: 59.49% of candidates pass on Mastermind-v0 (Table 3)

write.how: each used skill gets an equal share of (return - task baseline) per call; when the pool exceeds 10, drop duplicates and skills with low lower-confidence-bound gain
write.src: paper §4.3; code data_structures.py L30-L66, skill_pool.py L457-L601

paper_vs_code.code: default --select_type llm_model: the acting LLM picks from all skills; similarity (MiniLM, threshold 0.5) only as fallback; ε-greedy random picks

paper_vs_code.code: trajectory advantage spread evenly over its steps; mean per-token log-prob from the evolver model, which is the acting model only when --ge_model_name equals --agent_name (defaults differ)

paper_vs_code.paper: Nc candidates from one aggregated semantic gradient
paper_vs_code.code: 3 candidates, each from a fresh round of per-run diagnoses; a 'new skill' mode when under half the runs are related

open_questions: Reuse rate counts the fraction of stored units used at least once, so a pool of about 8 skills and stores of hundreds of trajectories or insights are not on equal footing; Table 1 cannot separate better skills from a smaller store.

The six seed skills are hand-written and one (StrategicPlanning) already targets Mastermind openings, so how much of the Mastermind gain comes from the seeds versus NP-PPO is only partly shown by 'w/o NP-PPO' (0.563 vs 0.606).

discussion.takeaway: Store experience as a few executable skills rather than episodes, and admit a rewritten skill only when a PPO-style check on past actions says it helps. On TextArena Mastermind and ALFWorld this gives the highest reuse and mostly the best returns with under 1k stored tokens.

claims.claim: Learned skills are reused far more than episodic memories.
claims.evidence: In-domain reuse 0.925 vs at most 0.349 (RAG) on Mastermind-v0; cross-agent 0.850-0.875. Table 1

claims.claim: Procedural memory is much smaller and cheaper to use.
claims.evidence: 816 stored tokens vs 40,510-391,706; 273 added prompt tokens per step; retrieval at 59% of steps. Table 1

claims.claim: Performance improves despite the small memory.
claims.evidence: ALFWorld 0.900 train / 0.909 OOD success vs AWM 0.700 / 0.900; Mastermind-v0 0.606 vs 0.577 (G-Memory). Table 2

claims.claim: Semantic gradients, the PPO Gate and score pruning are all needed.
claims.evidence: Return drops to 0.530 / 0.453 / 0.439 without each; reuse to 0.306 / 0.222 / 0.131. Table 3

claims.claim: Skills transfer to function calling.
claims.evidence: BFCL v4 accuracy 0.433 vs 0.383 (ReAct). App. C.2, Table 5

limits: Skills are explicit text, unlike implicit human procedural memory; moving to implicit or directly executable skills is left for future work.
The PPO Gate needs output-token log-probabilities, which some closed APIs do not expose.
reading: Standard deviations are large (e.g. ALFWorld OOD 0.909±0.287 vs AWM 0.900±0.042; Mastermind-v0 0.606±0.234), and results average 50 episodes per setting; several gaps are within one standard deviation.
On Mastermind-v0-Extreme G-Memory (0.356) is above Skill-Pro (0.333) in Table 2.
The ablation and training curves are on Mastermind-v0 only.
The code's test mode still explores with ε = 0.3, so about 30% of skill picks at evaluation are random if the released defaults were used; the paper does not state ε at test.
The PPO Gate re-scores ALFWorld actions with a prompt holding only the last observation (the stored transition state) and no admissible commands, while the acting prompt had the full history.
ExperiencePool and GoldenExperiencePool are created but never filled; evolution uses only the per-skill buffers.

abstract.text: Skill-Pro lets an LLM agent learn procedural memory without changing weights. Memory is a pool of natural-language skills, each with an activation condition, a short procedure and a termination condition, used as temporally extended options in a Skill-MDP. Skills evolve by Non-Parametric PPO: an LLM turns batches of trajectories into structured fixes (semantic gradients) and rewrites the skill, and a clipped importance-ratio check on past actions (the PPO Gate) admits only candidates expected to improve return, while online scores prune weak skills. On TextArena Mastermind, ALFWorld and BFCL v4 the authors report higher reuse, better returns and far smaller memory than episodic-memory baselines.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

stages.ingestion: Raw, unstructured conversation history is stored as passages with no LLM structuring at ingestion.
stages.retrieval: Query parsed with SpaCy into NER/POS-weighted terms (PROPN 3.0 > NOUN 2.0 > VERB 1.0, +1.0 for entities); exact substring matching (grep) for recall with rule-based entity discovery for multi-hop and pseudo-relevance feedback; ColBERT dense fallback (~1% of queries). Candidates reranked by mxbai-rerank-large-v1 CrossEncoder + ColBERT fused by weighted RRF (0.7/0.3), then truncated by fixed word budget or score-adaptive threshold (alpha * max CE score).
stages.answer: Top passages within the token budget are given to the answer LLM (gpt-4o-mini or gpt-4.1-mini depending on protocol).

systems.summary: Fully deterministic retrieve-then-rank pipeline over raw conversation text (NER-weighted grep + CrossEncoder/ColBERT RRF + score-adaptive truncation), arguing ranking, not ingestion-time structure, is the bottleneck.

organization.index: text-embedding-ada-002 dense vectors, Euclidean distance

retrieval.candidates: dense top-3 nearest keys

classify.note: The store is built once from demonstrations and never changes at test time; 'append-only' is the closest level. On MiniWoB++ a majority vote over the top 3 picks one task whose exemplars are all used.

stages.ingestion: Demonstrations are collected before evaluation: hand-made MiniWoB++ trajectories for 48 tasks (observations cleaned by humans, parsing code sampled from GPT-4 and checked) and the 1,009 Mind2Web training tasks.
stages.construction: Each exemplar keeps a complete trajectory (task, clean observation, action, ..., observation, action); on Mind2Web the observations are the element ranker's top 3 elements. The key is task metadata embedded with text-embedding-ada-002.
stages.organization: Keys go into one FAISS index per benchmark; each key points to its exemplar (MiniWoB++: 5 keys per task from 5 random seeds).
stages.retrieval: At the start of a task its metadata is embedded and the 3 nearest keys (Euclidean) are found. MiniWoB++ takes the most common task among them and loads all its exemplars; Mind2Web uses the 3 trajectories.
stages.answer: At every step the LLM first abstracts the raw state into a short observation, then reads the exemplar trajectories plus the current task history and writes the next action(s), possibly several before asking for a new state.

systems.summary: Computer-control agent that prompts with whole trajectories of abstracted states and actions, picked from a FAISS memory of demonstrations by similarity of task metadata instead of a hard-coded task-to-exemplar map.
systems.notes: Venue: ICLR 2024 poster (PDF header 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024'; iclr.cc/virtual/2024/poster/18701; README links openreview Pc8AU1aF5e). Text read from arXiv v3 (19 Jan 2024). Code: github.com/ltzheng/Synapse at HEAD 08c3a25 (2026-01-07); the last .py change is 89dbbf8 (2024-03-05), so the code at HEAD is the code after the camera-ready. The memory is a read-only exemplar library, not a record of the agent's own experience: management fields are null and timing none. control.construction=none because demonstrations are prepared by humans / the dataset, not by the system.

sources.code_note: Official repository linked from the paper's project page. HEAD 08c3a25 (2026-01-07) is used; commits after 2024-03-05 only touch figures and the licence, so the Python code is the post-camera-ready release. Memory contents for MiniWoB++ (specifiers.json, exemplars.json) are in the repo; the Mind2Web memory is built by build_memory.py from the dataset.

headline: The memory holds demonstrations prepared before evaluation, not the agent's own experience; nothing is written back during or after a task.
Retrieval runs once per task, on task metadata; the retrieved trajectories stay fixed for every step of the episode.
On MiniWoB++ the 3 nearest keys only vote for a task name; the agent then gets every exemplar of that task, as a hard-coded map would.

discussion.takeaway: Cleaning states so that whole trajectories fit in context, and choosing those trajectories by task similarity, lets an in-context agent reach 99.2% on MiniWoB++ without self-correction; memory is the smallest of the three gains on Mind2Web.

claims.claim: First ICL method at human level on MiniWoB++.
claims.evidence: 99.2% mean over 64 tasks vs human 93.5%, RCI 90.6% (54 tasks), AdaPlanner 92.9% (53). Table 3, Fig. 3

claims.claim: State abstraction makes long pages solvable and leaves room for more exemplars.
claims.evidence: book-flight solved (1.00); email-inbox-nl-turk 52% to 100%. Fig. 5, §4.5

claims.claim: Trajectory exemplars cut error build-up on long tasks.
claims.evidence: guess-number / use-spinner / use-autocomplete 100 / 100 / 98% vs RCI 20 / 88 / 58%; Mind2Web Step SR +19% over abstraction only. §4.5, Table 1

claims.claim: Exemplar memory generalises to unseen tasks.
claims.evidence: 16 unseen MiniWoB++ tasks solved at almost 100%; Mind2Web Step SR +1.4 / +1.5 / +0.2 (GPT-3.5). §4.5, Table 2

claims.claim: 56% relative Step SR gain over MindAct on Mind2Web.
claims.evidence: GPT-3.5 average; 2.5x with CodeLlama-7B. §4.4, Table 1

limits: High inference latency from LLM calls.
Depends on the quality of the exemplars.
Memory structure and retrieval are left for further study.
Text-only; no multimodal or pixel-based control.
reading: The memory is a curated demonstration library built before evaluation; the agent does not store its own successes, so 'memory' here means exemplar selection.

On MiniWoB++ retrieval is a vote for a task name; with a clear task split this reproduces a task-to-exemplar map automatically. There is no MiniWoB++ run that swaps memory for a hand map, so its effect is shown only on the 16 unseen tasks.
On Mind2Web the memory gain is small (Step SR +0.2 to +1.5 with GPT-3.5; -0.2 cross-domain with CodeLlama), and the no-memory variant uses 3 random training trajectories.

In code, Mind2Web history observations always include the gold element and history actions are gold, so each step is scored with a teacher-forced history; this is how the static dataset is used, not an online run.
State abstraction runs only on 20 MiniWoB++ tasks in the code; the rest act on raw HTML.
Baseline MiniWoB++ averages cover different task sets (64 vs 104 vs 54 tasks), so the averages are not directly comparable.

abstract.text: Synapse is an in-context computer-control agent built from three parts. State abstraction shrinks raw HTML to the parts a task needs, so several complete demonstrations fit in the prompt. Trajectory-as-exemplar prompting shows the LLM whole successful trajectories of observations and actions and lets it continue the current one. An exemplar memory embeds task metadata and retrieves the closest demonstrations, so tasks without their own demonstrations can borrow from similar ones. The authors report 99.2% mean success on 64 MiniWoB++ tasks with demonstrations for 48, and a 56% relative step-success gain over MindAct on Mind2Web.

construction.unit: event summary per dialogue round + one sentence per character per round
construction.kept_as: LLM summaries (20-100 characters per round) and per-character extractions; raw turns kept alongside but not read
construction.processing: per round (a turn and its reply, with the 3 earlier rounds as context) the LLM writes an event summary and one sentence for each of the two characters; event summaries are batched, matched to near-duplicates, clustered and deduplicated by the LLM
construction.writer: Qwen3-8B (no-think)

organization.structure: event store linked into a DAG (edges between similar events, oriented by time) + two per-character stores
organization.stores: per conversation: FAISS indexes for events, character A and character B; a graph JSON over events
organization.index: dense (Qwen3-8B embedding, FAISS inner product on normalised vectors)

management.operations: paper: add / update / delete / no-op per cluster, Insert and ReInsert of edges, tombstone deletes; code: the LLM keeps or drops new event summaries per cluster and the kept ones are appended
management.conflicts: LLM consolidation over clusters of summaries with cosine ≥ 0.95

retrieval.query: question as is
retrieval.candidates: top-10 events by embedding (seeds) and top-10 from each character store
retrieval.selection: closure: every earlier event linked to a seed (up to 100 steps), sorted by timestamp and deduplicated; no reranker
retrieval.budget: 10 seeds + all their ancestors (no count cap) + 10 + 10 character sentences

use.context: event summaries in time order, then character sentences, pasted as one 'material' block before the question
use.reasoning: single answer call for text; a ReAct loop (retrieval, rag, clip QA) for video

classify.note: Dense top-10 seeds, then every earlier event linked to them is added; nothing reranks or filters the closure. Character sentences come from a separate dense top-10.

stages.ingestion: The dialogue is split into rounds (a turn and the reply); each round is processed with the three earlier rounds as context, 16 rounds in parallel.
stages.construction: Per round the LLM writes an event summary of 20-100 characters and one sentence about each of the two characters (relations, events, traits, objects); each is embedded.
stages.organization: Events go to a per-conversation FAISS index and are later linked into a graph: an edge joins events with cosine ≥ 0.9 (at most 5 per node), directed from later to earlier, and a shortcut a→c is dropped when a→b→c exists. Character sentences go to two separate FAISS stores.
stages.update: Each new event pulls stored events with cosine ≥ 0.95 (top 10); after 64 buffered events the pool is clustered (≥ 0.95) and an LLM keeps or drops the new summaries per cluster. The paper's online ReInsert and tombstone deletion are not in the code.
stages.retrieval: The question's top-10 events are seeds; every earlier event reachable through graph edges (≤ 100 steps) joins, sorted by timestamp and deduplicated; top-10 sentences from each character store are appended.
stages.answer: Qwen3-8B (no-think, temperature 0) reads the joined text as material and outputs one option letter on ZH-4O.

systems.summary: Per-round event summaries and per-character notes are batch-deduplicated by an LLM, linked into a time-ordered graph of similar events, and read by taking the question's best-matching events together with every earlier event they link to.

discussion.takeaway: Summarise every round into short event and character notes, deduplicate them in batches, and at question time add every earlier event linked to the best matches. It is best on the Chinese role-play benchmark ZH-4O but trails full context on LoCoMo.

claims.claim: TeleMem is the most accurate method on ZH-4O.
It beats Mem0 by 19% in accuracy with 43% fewer tokens and a 2.1× speedup.
claims.evidence: Abstract. The accuracy gap is 16.13 points (86.33 vs 70.20); no table or setup is given for tokens or speed.

claims.claim: Both the write and the read model matter, and they should be scaled together.
claims.evidence: Accuracy 52.72 with 0.6B writer and reader, 86.33 with 8B/8B, best 87.55 with 14B/14B. Table 2

claims.claim: On LoCoMo it is strong on single-hop and temporal questions but weak on multi-hop.
claims.evidence: Single-hop 64.53, temporal 78.47, multi-hop 20.56; overall 61.49 vs 70.71 for long context and 57.59 for Memobase. Table 3, §4.2

limits: Weaker on multi-hop questions over stored memories (LoCoMo).
The closure can grow large; the paper suggests bounding depth or budgeted expansion.
reading: There is no ablation: no run removes the graph closure or the character stores, so what the DAG adds to 86.33 is untested.
The graph comes from embedding similarity (cos ≥ 0.9) and processing order, not from causal links in the dialogue; edges point from later to earlier by timestamp.

Timestamps are the wall-clock time a summary was written or consolidated, and rounds are summarised on 16 threads, so 'chronological' order in the answer context follows processing rather than the dialogue.
The code never updates or deletes a stored entry: consolidation only keeps or drops new summaries, and the online Insert / ReInsert / tombstone steps of §3.2.3 are absent.
The answer context mixes the graph closure with a plain dense top-10 from each character store; the ZH-4O score cannot separate the two.
The LoCoMo run has no code in the repo, the extraction prompts are Chinese, and TeleMem's multi-hop score (20.56) is below RAG (32.39); the LoCoMo setup (judge prompt, answer prompt) is not given.
The '19%' matches (86.33 − 70.20) / 86.33, i.e. relative to TeleMem's own score; relative to Mem0 the gain is 23%.
Table 2 is not monotonic in the reader as the text says: a 32B reader scores below 8B and 14B readers for 8B, 14B and 32B writers.
ZH-4O is multiple choice, so chance level is above zero; LoCoMo drops the adversarial category (1,540 questions).

abstract.text: TeleMem builds long-term memory for agents as threads of events rather than isolated snippets. Dialogue rounds are summarised into event notes and per-character notes; new notes are batched, matched to similar stored ones, clustered and consolidated by an LLM before storage. Events are linked into a time-ordered graph, and a question retrieves its closest events together with the earlier events they depend on. A multimodal module turns video into event and object memories read by a ReAct-style agent. The authors report higher accuracy than Mem0 on the ZH-4O role-play benchmark with fewer tokens and faster processing.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

management.operations: append and link only; no memory is updated or deleted
management.conflicts: kept on purpose: outdated memories stay and are linked (e.g. by 'Changed')

retrieval.query: current dialogue context (all turns of the session so far)
retrieval.candidates: top-3 memories by embedding similarity, each expanded to its connected component
retrieval.selection: one linear timeline through each hit (sampled at random, n=1); an LLM then rewrites each timeline for the current dialogue
retrieval.budget: k=3 hits, so at most 3 refined timelines

use.context: refined timelines (numbered) + current dialogue
use.reasoning: one refinement call per timeline, then one response-generation call

classify.note: Dense top-3 seeds a walk over the memory graph; which path is used is random, and the LLM refinement rewrites rather than filters, so no learned or LLM selector fixes the set.

stages.ingestion: Nothing happens during a session; memory is written once the session ends.
stages.construction: An LLM summarizes the finished session into numbered fact sentences about the speakers; each becomes a memory (event, session).
stages.organization: Each new memory is compared with its top-3 most similar past memories; an LLM labels each pair with one of 7 cause-effect relations or None, and the new memory is linked to the most recent related memory in each connected component.
stages.update: No update or deletion: old and contradicting memories remain in the graph, joined by edges such as 'Changed'.
stages.retrieval: The dialogue so far retrieves the top-3 memories; for each, the linear paths from the oldest memory of its component through it to an end are listed and one is picked at random; an LLM rewrites each timeline to suit the current dialogue.
stages.answer: The response model reads the refined timelines and the current dialogue and writes the next utterance.

systems.summary: Keeps every past memory and links them into a graph by temporal order and LLM-labelled cause-effect relations; at response time it retrieves whole timelines around the best matches and has an LLM tailor them to the conversation.

discussion.takeaway: Instead of updating or deleting stale memories, keep them all and link them by time and cause; retrieving whole timelines and letting an LLM tailor them gives better responses on MSC and CC than retrieval or update baselines.

claims.claim: THEANINE generates better responses than the baselines.
claims.evidence: MAUVE 18.62 vs 13.71 best baseline on MSC, 64.41 vs 38.16 on CC; BERTScore highest on both. Table 1

claims.claim: Methods without memory update generally score higher, supporting removal-free memory.
claims.evidence: e.g. Memory Retrieval 15.49 vs 15.30 ROUGE-L with update on MSC. Table 1, §4

claims.claim: Every phase helps; relation-aware linking helps most, then whole-timeline retrieval, then refinement.
claims.evidence: MAUVE 41.52 full vs 39.69 / 38.49 / 41.34. Table 2

claims.claim: Retrieved memories are more helpful and more often correct.
claims.evidence: golden memory retrieved 72% vs 68% Memory Retrieval (50 instances, human). Table 3, Fig. 5

claims.claim: Responses entail past conversations more often.
claims.evidence: 68% entail, 4% contradict (100 turns, human). Fig. 6

claims.claim: Harder to fool with counterfactual questions.
claims.evidence: TeaFarm success rate 0.21 avg vs 0.18 Memory Retrieval. Table 4

limits: Only five sessions per conversation, for lack of longer English open-domain datasets.
No comparison with MemoryBank, whose forgetting curve needs day-level time gaps the datasets lack.
API-based LLMs raise privacy concerns; distilling into small local models is left open.
reading: Automatic metrics compare to the reference next utterance; on MSC Memory Retrieval has higher BLEU-4 (1.92 vs 1.80) and ROUGE-L (15.49 vs 15.37), so the headline gain rests mostly on MAUVE.
THEANINE costs about 5.9× the Memory Retrieval baseline per episode ($0.0135 vs $0.0023), mainly from linking and one refinement call per timeline.
Each response uses one randomly chosen timeline per hit; the paper does not report variance across runs.
Automatic results use 50 sampled episodes per dataset and sessions 3-5; TeaFarm uses 200 questions graded by GPT-4, and all success rates are low (at most 0.24).
The released code links a new memory to every related top-3 memory, whereas the paper links only the latest per component (footnote 5 says the two gave similar responses).
Session numbers order the graph but are never shown to the LLM; the timeline's order is the only time signal the response model gets.

abstract.text: THEANINE is a memory framework for dialogue agents that talk to a user over many sessions. Rather than updating or deleting outdated memories, it keeps all of them and links each new memory to related older ones with a temporal order and a cause-effect relation chosen by an LLM. When responding, it retrieves the timelines of linked memories around the best matches and has an LLM refine them for the current conversation before generation. The paper also introduces TeaFarm, which tests memory by asking the agent counterfactual questions about past sessions.

paper.title: Think-on-Graph: Deep and Responsible Reasoning of Large Language Model on Knowledge Graph

construction.unit: knowledge-graph triple (head entity, relation, tail entity) reached during the search
construction.kept_as: verbatim KG triples: entity names and raw relation ids
construction.processing: nothing is written ahead of time; per question, the top 3 triples of each search depth are appended to a working list
construction.writer: none: the KG (Freebase or Wikidata) is pre-built and read-only

organization.structure: external knowledge graph, plus a flat per-question list of kept triples
organization.stores: Freebase behind a SPARQL endpoint, or Wikidata behind nine API calls; the triple list lives only in the prompt
organization.index: entity ids (Freebase mid, Wikidata qid) looked up by fixed SPARQL/API queries

management.operations: append up to 3 triples per depth; their tail entities become the next frontier; the KG itself is never changed by the system

retrieval.query: the question, starting from topic entities supplied with the dataset (paper: extracted by the LLM)
retrieval.candidates: all relations of each frontier entity (minus type/common/freebase/sameAs), then the tail entities of the chosen relations (5 sampled at random if 20 or more)
retrieval.selection: LLM picks and scores 3 relations per entity, LLM scores the tail entities; a triple scores relation × entity and the top 3 overall are kept; an LLM check after each depth decides whether to stop
retrieval.budget: width N=3, depth D=3: at most 9 triples; at most 2ND+D+1 = 22 LLM calls per question (paper)

use.context: the question and all kept triples as "head, relation, tail" lines, with 5 in-context examples
use.reasoning: the sufficiency reply also states the answer when it says Yes; if depth 3 ends without Yes, a CoT prompt answers without any triples

classify.note: Memory here is an existing knowledge graph that the system only reads. The per-question triple list only grows; the LLM scores decide which neighbours are kept, and a fixed rule keeps the top 3.

stages.organization: Knowledge lives in an existing KG (Freebase for CWQ, WebQSP, GrailQA, SimpleQuestions and WebQuestions; Wikidata for the other four sets); ToG only reads it.
stages.update: During one question, each search depth appends its top 3 triples to a working list whose tail entities seed the next depth.
stages.retrieval: From the topic entities, fixed SPARQL queries list neighbouring relations; the LLM keeps 3 per entity with scores, the tails of those relations are fetched and scored by the LLM, and the 3 triples with the highest relation × entity score are kept. An LLM check after each depth (at most 3) decides whether the triples suffice.
stages.answer: When the check says Yes, its reply (with the answer in braces) is the output; if 3 depths pass without Yes the LLM answers by chain-of-thought with no triples.

systems.summary: An LLM walks a knowledge graph by beam search, choosing relations and entities at each hop and stopping when it judges the collected triples sufficient; it needs no training and works with Freebase or Wikidata.
systems.notes: VENUE: ICLR 2024 poster (listed at iclr.cc/virtual/2024/poster/17844; arXiv v6 carries the header 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024' and the comment 'Accepted by ICLR 2024'). abstract.text: Think-on-Graph (ToG) lets an LLM take part in reasoning over a knowledge graph instead of only translating a question into a query. Starting from the question's topic entities, the LLM repeatedly picks promising relations and neighbouring entities, keeping the best few paths in a beam, until it judges the gathered triples enough to answer. The method needs no training and can be paired with different LLMs and graphs. Across nine knowledge-intensive datasets it sets a new best result on six with GPT-4, and the explicit paths let people trace and correct faulty facts.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Nothing is written: memory is an existing KG, and the LLM only decides which neighbouring relations and entities to follow.
The answer model sees at most 9 triples (3 per depth, 3 depths) as a flat list; if it never says the list is enough, it answers from its own knowledge with no triples.
In the released code the start entities come from the dataset (gold-linked ids), not from LLM extraction as the paper says.

open_questions: Topic entities in the released data are gold-linked ids, so the reported scores do not include entity-linking errors that a system extracting entities itself would face.
About 20% of correct answers come from the LLM's own knowledge alone (App. B.2), and every run that ends at depth 3 answers without triples; the paper does not report how often that fallback fires.

No run compares ToG with a plain retriever that feeds the same number of KG triples to the LLM, so the value of LLM-guided pruning over retrieval is shown only against BM25/SentenceBERT pruning inside ToG (Table 5).

discussion.takeaway: Letting the LLM choose each hop on a knowledge graph, and stop when it judges the evidence enough, beats both LLM-only prompting and fixed KG retrieval without training; with GPT-4 it matches or beats fine-tuned systems on most of nine sets.

claims.claim: Tight LLM-KG coupling (the LLM reasons on the graph) beats using the LLM only to write queries.
claims.evidence: §1, Fig. 1; no direct head-to-head with a query-generation system beyond KB-BINDER numbers (Table 1).

claims.claim: Best result on 6 of 9 datasets without training.
claims.evidence: With GPT-4: WebQSP 82.6, GrailQA 81.4, QALD10-en 54.7 (ToG-R), WebQuestions 57.9, Zero-Shot RE 88.3, Creak 95.6, each above the cited prior SOTA. Table 1, §3.2.1

claims.claim: Larger gains over the LLM alone on multi-hop questions.
claims.evidence: GrailQA +51.8 and Zero-Shot RE +42.9 over prompting without KG; gains over CoT grow with question depth (App. B.2, Fig. 13). §3.2.1

claims.claim: A small LLM with ToG can beat a large LLM alone.
claims.evidence: Llama-2-70B ToG-R 57.6 CWQ vs GPT-4 CoT 46.0. Table 2, §3.2.2

claims.claim: The LLM is the best pruner.
claims.evidence: BM25 or SentenceBERT pruning drops CWQ by 8.4 and WebQSP by 15.1 points on average. Table 5

claims.claim: Explicit paths make answers traceable and let users correct KG errors.
claims.evidence: one worked example (Fig. 4, §3.3); not measured.

limits: Computation grows with depth and width; the paper keeps both at 3 and lists ways to cut LLM calls (App. B.2.1).
Accuracy depends on KG quality and coverage; Wikidata search and pruning are harder than Freebase for these sets (§3.2.3).
Single-hop sets gain less than multi-hop ones (§3.2.1).
Remaining errors are hallucinations and refusals; longer paths add a few format errors (App. B.2).
discussion.limits_src: paper §3.2, App. B.2 (no separate limitations section)
reading: The released code starts from topic entities stored in the data files; for CWQ these are the ids in the gold SPARQL, which removes entity linking from the task.

Table 1 and Table 2 disagree on which of ToG and ToG-R scored what: on CWQ with ChatGPT Table 1 gives ToG 57.1 / ToG-R 58.9 but Table 2 gives ToG 58.9 / ToG-R 57.1 (same swap with GPT-4, 67.6 / 69.5). Table 10 follows Table 1; our results file uses Table 1.
Llama-2 WebQSP numbers differ between Table 2 (ToG-R 68.9, ToG 63.7) and Table 11 (69.4, 64.1).
The Table 1 footnote credits CWQ's prior FT SOTA 70.4 to Das et al. (2021), but Tables 2 and 10 give that 70.4 to DecAF and 67.1 to CBR-KBQA (Das et al.).
Ablations (Tables 3-6) use 1,000-question subsets, so their full-system numbers (58.8 CWQ) differ from Table 1.

The released eval script matches by substring and takes the text in the first braces, which for replies from the sufficiency check is 'Yes'; the paper's numbers therefore cannot have come from that script unchanged.
IO, CoT and SC baselines use 6 examples; ToG reasoning prompts use 5.

systems.name: TiMem

paper.title: TiMem: Temporal-Hierarchical Memory Consolidation for Long-Horizon Conversational Agents

construction.unit: node of a five-level Temporal Memory Tree: L1 fragment, L2 session, L3 day, L4 week, L5 monthly profile
construction.kept_as: L1: third-person LLM rewrite of one exchange (new facts only); L2-L5: LLM summaries, pattern reports and profiles
construction.processing: L1 written after every user-assistant exchange; each higher node is written by an LLM from its children in a closed time window plus the last 3 memories at its own level, with a level-specific prompt
construction.writer: backbone LLM (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, temperature 0.7)

organization.structure: temporal tree with explicit parent-child links; each node covers a time interval inside its parent's
organization.stores: PostgreSQL tables per level + parent-child relation table; Qdrant vectors
organization.index: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B dense over content; BM25 over title + content, computed at query time

management.operations: scheduled consolidation: session, day, week and month nodes written when their window closes; the profile is refined from the previous profiles
management.conflicts: none at storage; the recall gate is said to drop redundant or conflicting memories at read time

retrieval.query: question for dense search; an LLM planner labels complexity (simple / hybrid / complex) and extracts 1-3 keywords (no names) for BM25
retrieval.candidates: L1 only: dense top 40 + BM25 over all L1 of the conversation, fused 0.9 / 0.1, top 20; then ancestors of those leaves at the levels the complexity label opens
retrieval.selection: one LLM gate call keeps or drops each candidate
retrieval.budget: 20 L1 + up to L2 4, L3 2, L4 2, L5 1 (code, LoCoMo); ~511 tokens after gating on LoCoMo, ~1,271 on LongMemEval-S

use.context: kept memories grouped by level (L1 to L5), each prefixed with its date; Mem0 QA prompt on LoCoMo, LongMemEval non-CoT prompt
use.reasoning: single answer call

classify.note: Hybrid dense + BM25 picks the L1 leaves; higher levels arrive by fixed parent links; an LLM gate makes the final keep/drop call, so 'LLM decides' rather than 'top-k rule'.

stages.ingestion: The dialogue is cut into fixed windows of one user-assistant exchange (w_d = 1); no semantic segmentation.
stages.construction: An LLM rewrites each exchange into a third-person L1 fragment that keeps only facts not already in the last 3 fragments; relative times are left as written.
stages.organization: Fragments are the leaves of a Temporal Memory Tree: L2 session, L3 day, L4 week and L5 monthly profile nodes, each with a time interval that contains its children's, linked parent to child.
stages.update: When a session, day, week or month closes, an LLM writes the parent node from its children plus the last 3 nodes at that level, with a level-specific prompt (facts, events, patterns, profile). Nothing is deleted or edited afterwards.
stages.retrieval: An LLM planner labels the question simple, hybrid or complex and extracts keywords; dense + BM25 over L1 picks 20 leaves; their ancestors at the levels opened by the label are added through parent links; an LLM gate keeps or drops each candidate.
stages.answer: The answer model reads the kept memories grouped by level, each with its date, under level headers.

systems.summary: Dialogue is rewritten exchange by exchange into leaf memories and consolidated on a calendar schedule into session, day, week and monthly-profile nodes of a temporal tree; recall searches only the leaves, climbs parent links to levels chosen by a query-complexity planner, and filters with an LLM gate.

Code: github.com/TiMEM-AI/timem pinned at 6d279a5 (HEAD, 2026-05-27); retrieval, config and experiment code are identical to the initial commit f369184 (2026-02-08) except one import line. TAXONOMY CHECK (not edited here): consolidation-trigger 'scheduled-periodic' is right for L2-L5 (written when a session/day/week/month window closes, §3.2.2, App. B.1; code 01_memory_generation.py simulates a 02:00 daily backfill). retrieval-traversal 'top-down-routing' is wrong: recall is bottom-up (search L1 leaves by dense + BM25, then follow parent links upward; the code class is BottomUpRetrieverBase), which fits 'similarity-plus-aggregation'. DESIGN: trigger=every-exchange is the L1 write; higher levels are scheduled, hence management.timing=both. control.management=fixed-rule because the calendar decides when to consolidate (the writing itself is a prompted LLM). Baselines: the paper says it ran all five with their recommended configurations under one LLM/embedding setup (§4.1, App. B.2), so run_by=rerun.

sources.code_note: Official repository linked from the paper. It has 7 commits; the first (f369184, 2026-02-08) is after paper v1 and already contains the retrieval, config and experiment scripts. Later commits change README, licence, CLI and restore two model/schema modules; retrieval code differs by one import line. Pinned at HEAD 6d279a5 (2026-05-27). Whether this is exactly the code behind the v2 tables is not stated.

headline: Only L1 fragments are searched. Session, day, week and profile memories reach the answer only as ancestors of the 20 best-matching fragments, found by parent links, never by their own similarity to the question.
An LLM gate then cuts the candidates from about 4.4k to 0.5k tokens on LoCoMo (Table 3), and the answer model reads what survives, grouped by level.
In the released code the complexity-specific gate prompts are not wired in: the dataset config names templates the prompt file does not contain, so a generic keep/drop prompt runs.

open_questions: Table 4's 'L1 only, hierarchical recall' (73.18 / 72.40) beats flat recall over the full tree; with no higher levels it is unclear what the hierarchical path adds beyond the gate and fewer tokens, and the paper does not define flat recall precisely.

No run gives the higher levels their own similarity search, so the tests cannot tell whether session/day/week summaries help because of their content or because they widen context around the chosen leaves.
On LoCoMo L2 and L3 counts are equal (272 each): with one session per day, the day level mostly restates the session level.

glance.a: A node of a time tree: an L1 fragment is an LLM rewrite of one exchange; above it sit session, day, week and monthly-profile nodes, each written by an LLM from its children.
Each exchange is rewritten in third person keeping only new facts; the higher levels are summaries of 200-600 words. The raw turns are stored but never read.
glance.src: paper App. E.3; code postgres_store.py L134-L156

glance.a: By the calendar, not by topic: a parent node covers the time window of its children (session, day, week, month), linked explicitly parent to child.
No cross-encoder. One LLM call reads all candidates and returns the ids to keep.

glance.q: Is memory reconstructed at question time?
glance.a: No second search. The planner only chooses which levels to collect; an answer-time reflection loop exists in the code but the evaluation prompts never trigger it.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: Up to 20 fragments plus a few session/day/week summaries and the profile, whatever the gate kept, each with a date: about 511 tokens on LoCoMo.

steps.what: L1 fragments scored (dense top 40, BM25 over all)
kept by the LLM gate (LoCoMo average)

funnel.src: code bottom_up_retriever_base.py L125-L531, retrieval_config.yaml L56-L110; paper Table 6

flow.title: Label the question
flow.sees: The question only. Questions about preferences, prediction or reasoning go to complex; multi-fact questions to hybrid; single facts to simple. Personal names are banned from the keywords.
flow.src: paper App. E.3.7; code llm_retrieval_planner.py L185-L255

flow.title: Search the fragments
flow.out: every L1 with a fused score
flow.sees: Dense: the question against each fragment's content, top 40. BM25: the keywords against title + content of every fragment of the conversation pair. Scores are divided by their maximum and summed 0.9 / 0.1; fragments outside the dense top 40 get only the BM25 part.

flow.title: Keep 20 leaves
flow.method: rule: top 20 by fused score, then sorted by time
flow.sees: Scores only. The 20 are then put in time order, which also sets the order of the next step.

flow.title: Collect ancestors
flow.method: rule: follow parent links from each leaf
flow.sees: No text is compared. For each leaf (oldest first) the code walks L2→L3→L4→L5 and keeps a parent at each level the label opened until that level's quota is full; a session is taken once.

flow.title: Gate
flow.method: LLM judgement over the whole list, temperature 0.3
flow.sees: Each candidate as "[n-level] title", its content, time and session id, with the question. If it keeps nothing, the first 5 are used.

flow.title: Answer
flow.sees: Kept memories grouped by level with headers, each as "[date] content", oldest first within a level. No original turns.

discussion.takeaway: Organise conversational memory by the calendar (exchange, session, day, week, month) and let an LLM consolidate each closed window; at question time search only the finest level, pull in the ancestors, and let an LLM prune. In its own tests this is the best of six systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S with the shortest context on LoCoMo.

claims.evidence: LoCoMo LLJ 75.30 vs MemOS 69.24; LongMemEval-S 76.88 vs MemOS 68.68 (gpt-4o-mini), 78.96 vs 73.07 (gpt-4o). Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Much shorter recalled context.
claims.evidence: 511 tokens per LoCoMo question, 52.2% below Mem0's 1,070. Table 6, §4.5

limits: Consolidation and recall rely on general-purpose LLMs through prompts; smaller fine-tuned models might be cheaper.
Higher levels are free text without categories or knowledge graphs.
There is no storage-time forgetting.
Time boundaries are fixed (session, day, week, month) rather than detected.
reading: Higher levels are never searched by the question; they only arrive as parents of the 20 leaves, so the tree adds context around what dense + BM25 already found rather than finding new evidence.
In the code the leaves are put in time order before the parent walk, so the level quotas (e.g. 4 sessions) are filled from the earliest matching leaves, not the most relevant ones.
The released config does not load the complexity-specific gate prompts shown in App. E.3.6; if the reported runs used this config, the gate was a generic keep/drop prompt.
Complex-query budgets in Table 7 (L2 8, L3 4) are twice the LoCoMo config values (L2 4, L3 2).

Baselines were rerun by the authors with gpt-4o-mini, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and k = 20 for all; each baseline's own retrieval settings may differ from its paper, and the number of runs behind the ± values is not stated.
LoCoMo numbers use Mem0's lenient judge prompt over 1,540 questions (adversarial excluded), so they are comparable only with rows using the same judge.

abstract.text: TiMem stores a long conversation as a time-ordered tree: each exchange becomes a short LLM-written fragment, and fragments are consolidated on a schedule into session, day, week and monthly-profile memories, each covering the time span of its children. No model is fine-tuned; each level has its own prompt. At question time an LLM judges how complex the question is, fragments are found by dense and keyword search, their ancestors at the matching levels are added, and an LLM gate keeps only what is needed. The authors report the best accuracy among evaluated systems on LoCoMo (75.30) and LongMemEval-S (76.88) with about half Mem0's recalled context on LoCoMo.

stages.ingestion: Before each model call, rule passes rewrite the prompt prefix (placeholders for agent id, working directory, timestamps; tool definitions moved to the end) and shrink tool results (deduplicate repeated reads, truncate long outputs to a 600+400-char preview, slim HTML, downsample images).
stages.construction: Trimmed outputs keep a preview and an archive key; the full payload is saved on disk under its content hash.
stages.organization: The context is a byte-stable prefix followed by turns grouped into task segments tracked in a registry with lifecycle states.
stages.update: Every B turns (B = 3) a Qwen3.5-35B-A3B estimator reads a compressed view of recent turns and the registry and moves tasks active → completed → evictable; evictable tasks are archived and removed in one pass.
stages.retrieval: No search: the agent reads the whole kept context. It can call a recovery tool with an archive key to get a trimmed payload back in full.
stages.answer: The host agent (OpenClaw, GPT-5.4-mini) answers from the managed context as usual.

systems.summary: Context manager for tool-using agents that keeps the prompt prefix byte-stable for provider KV caching, trims tool outputs at ingestion with a recovery tool, and evicts whole finished tasks in batches when an LLM estimator judges them no longer useful.

headline: The aim is cost, not recall: keep the prompt prefix byte-identical so the provider's cache discounts it, and cut tokens only where that does not break the cache.
Nothing is searched; the agent reads its whole kept context and can fetch a trimmed payload back by key.
Whole tasks leave the context only after an LLM estimator marks them evictable, checked in batches of 3 turns.
