discussion.takeaway: For API-served agents, cutting context text can cost more than it saves if it breaks the provider's prefix cache. TokenPilot keeps the prefix stable, trims tool output only at ingestion and evicts whole finished tasks in batches, lowering cost 56-87% at similar scores.

claims.claim: Lowest cost of 11 methods in every setting.
claims.evidence: PinchBench $3.22 isolated / $2.79 continuous; Claw-Eval $2.27 / $10.58, vs Vanilla $8.31 / $7.24 / $5.16 / $81.52. Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Task scores stay competitive.
claims.evidence: PinchBench 81.0 / 81.3 vs Vanilla 80.5 / 79.2; Claw-Eval 63.1 / 60.8 vs 64.5 / 63.4. Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Stable placeholders turn cold starts into cache hits.
claims.evidence: Cache hit rate 38.7% → 79.2% (PinchBench), 67.2% → 83.1% (Claw-Eval); cost $8.31 → $4.35. Fig. 4, Table 4

claims.claim: The recovery tool is needed.
claims.evidence: Without it score 80.9 → 77.1 and cost $2.87 → $4.03. Table 4, §4.4

claims.claim: Model-judged residual utility is the cheapest retention signal.
claims.evidence: $4.69 vs $5.17-$6.82 (category-grouped) and $5.25 vs $5.79-$7.04 (mixed streams), similar scores. Table 7

limits: The estimator can mislabel segments when interactions are ambiguous or sparse.
The frequency threshold τ and batch size B may need tuning per deployment.
Prefix stabilization helps only when the provider supports prefix caching.
Continuous mode groups same-category tasks; heterogeneous streams may reuse prefixes less.
reading: The contribution is a cost optimization for prefix-cached APIs; recall of past information is never tested apart from task scores.
On Claw-Eval TokenPilot scores below Vanilla in both modes (63.1 vs 64.5, 60.8 vs 63.4); the 'competitive' claim rests mostly on PinchBench.
In isolated mode the global layer alone (Table 4: 80.92, $2.87) is cheaper than the full system in Table 1 (81.0, $3.22), so eviction pays off only in continuous sessions.
The main continuous results group same-category tasks, which favours cross-task reuse; on shuffled streams (Table 9) TokenPilot scores 69.10 at $4.83, still the cheapest.
Savings depend on the price ratio: the cost model uses GPT-5.4-mini's 10× discount for cached input.
τ for the ingestion gate is never given, and the code's closest mechanism blocks repeated reads instead of restoring full content.
In code an evicted task leaves a one-line stub whose text names no archive key, so the agent has no stated way to recover it.

abstract.text: TokenPilot targets the cost of long agent sessions, where context grows with every tool call. The authors argue that pruning or summarizing history changes the prompt layout and so defeats the provider's prefix cache, which can erase the savings. TokenPilot instead fixes the prompt prefix byte for byte, trims noisy tool output before it enters the history (keeping a recoverable archive), and has a small LLM mark finished tasks for eviction only in periodic batches. On PinchBench and Claw-Eval it reports 56-87% lower cost than an unmanaged OpenClaw agent with similar task scores.

paper.title: TraceMem: Weaving Narrative Memory Schemata from User Conversational Traces

construction.unit: episode summary (shared) + per-user experience trace; traces clustered into memory-card threads
construction.kept_as: rewritten dated episode narrative + extracted per-user experience traces
construction.processing: one LLM pass per session labels each turn as topic change or development and writes a fact line per turn; LLM summarises each episode; LLM distils each speaker's own experiences from summary + fact lines
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4o-mini or GPT-4.1-mini)

organization.structure: per-user memory card: theme > topics > threads, over experience traces; flat episode store beside it
organization.stores: ChromaDB collections per conversation: episodes, semantics, experiences, threads; card JSON files per user
organization.index: text-embedding-3-small dense vectors (ChromaDB)

management.operations: PCA + UMAP + HDBSCAN clusters a user's traces into topics (min 5), then each topic into threads (min 2); LLM titles themes, topics and threads
management.forgetting: experience distillation returns N/A for episodes with no personal facts; these are dropped (13-25% of episodes, Table 3)

retrieval.query: question used as is
retrieval.candidates: dense search over episode summaries; separately an LLM reads the chosen user card(s) in full
retrieval.selection: top-K episodes by similarity; LLM returns up to 10 thread ids per user, threads fetched by id
retrieval.budget: K=10 episodes (paper) / 20 (code) + up to 10 threads per chosen user

use.context: episode summaries + joined experience traces of the selected threads
use.reasoning: single answer call with a step-by-step prompt

classify.note: Two paths are merged: episodes come from dense top-K; threads are chosen by an LLM reading the whole card. The card path is the paper's contribution, so it sets the placement.

stages.ingestion: Each session is formatted with numbered turns (image captions inlined) and one LLM call labels every turn as topic change or topic development; the session is cut before each topic change into episodes.
stages.construction: The same call writes a fact line per turn (the 'semantic' representation). An LLM rewrites each episode into an exhaustive dated summary, then, per speaker, distils that speaker's own experiences from the summary and their fact lines into one experience trace (or N/A).
stages.organization: Per user, experience-trace embeddings are clustered twice (PCA, UMAP, HDBSCAN; noise reassigned) into topics and then threads; an LLM titles each topic and the whole theme and writes a title and summary per thread, giving a JSON memory card (theme > topics > threads with ids).
stages.update: Cards are built in a separate pass after all sessions are added; the paper describes no incremental update or conflict handling.
stages.retrieval: An LLM picks which user card(s) the question is about, reads the full card(s) and returns thread ids (10 per user in the code); in parallel the question retrieves the top episode summaries by embedding similarity (K=10 in the paper, 20 in the code).
stages.answer: The answer LLM reads the episode summaries plus, per user, the concatenated experience traces of each selected thread, with rules for resolving relative dates.

systems.summary: Consolidates dialogue into per-user narrative memory cards: episodes are summarised, each speaker's own experiences are distilled, and these traces are clustered into topics and threads that an LLM browses at question time alongside dense-retrieved episodes.
systems.notes: Paper v1 (10 Feb 2026) read from the arXiv PDF; ACM template with placeholder header ('Trovato et al.'), no venue stated, so recorded as a preprint. Appendix prompt figures are images; prompts were read from the code instead. Code checked at commit 1b681ed9 (19 Feb 2026, latest on main). Table 2 backbone labels: the paper's text ties the 0.9019 block to GPT-4o-mini and the 0.9227 block to GPT-4.1-mini; the table itself lists them in that order.

glance.a: Two kinds: an episode summary (an LLM rewrite of one topic segment, dated) and, per speaker, an experience trace of that speaker's own facts from the episode.
Yes. Episodes are stored only as LLM summaries told to omit nothing; the raw turns are not kept in memory.
Each user's traces are clustered into topics (HDBSCAN, min 5) and threads (min 2), written up as a JSON memory card: theme > topics > threads with titles, summaries and ids.
No. Episodes are taken in embedding order; threads are picked by an LLM that reads the whole card.

glance.q: Is memory reconstructed at question time?
glance.a: No second round: three LLM calls (pick card, pick threads, answer) and one embedding search per question.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: The episode summaries (20 in the code) and, for each chosen user, the joined experience traces of the selected threads. No original turns, fact lines or card summaries.

discussion.takeaway: Turn dialogue into per-user narratives: summarise episodes, keep each speaker's own experiences, and cluster them into topic and thread cards that an LLM browses at question time. claims.evidence: Overall 90.19 (GPT-4o-mini) and 92.27 (GPT-4.1-mini) vs best baseline Nemori 74.03 and 80.52. Table 2, §4.2

limits: The paper has no limitations section. Its open discussion names memory rewriting on recall, regulated forgetting, and deciding when to use memory at all as unaddressed.
Only LoCoMo is evaluated (the repo's LongMemEval folder holds only an empty readme).
reading: Full context scores 73.05 and 87.40 here while TraceMem scores 90.19 and 92.27, so the memory beats giving the model the whole conversation; the answer prompts differ, and the paper does not say which prompt the baselines used.
Fact lines (semantic memory) are stored in ChromaDB but read by no retrieval or answer code; they only feed trace distillation.
Thread summaries in the card carry no dates (the prompt forbids them), but the fetched thread text is the raw traces, which begin with 'As of <date>'.
The released code retrieves 20 episodes; the paper and its episodic-only ablation use 10.
No token, latency or cost figures are reported, although building cards adds per-user clustering and LLM titling after ingestion and each question needs three LLM calls.
Table 4 does not name its backbone; its full row matches the GPT-4o-mini numbers.

abstract.text: TraceMem builds long-term memory for dialogue agents by imitating memory consolidation. Each session is cut into topic episodes by an LLM that labels every turn, the episodes are summarised, and each speaker's own experiences are distilled from them. These experience traces are clustered per user into topics and threads and packaged as a structured memory card. At question time an LLM chooses cards and threads while dense search supplies episode summaries, and the authors report the best LoCoMo scores among their baselines with two GPT backbones.

construction.unit: memory piece: summary + time + start/end line numbers
construction.kept_as: LLM summaries of the session and of each mentioned event, dated by inferred event time; raw lines linked by line numbers
construction.processing: one LLM call per session (timeline summarization): session summary at the session date plus one summary per mentioned event at its inferred date or date range
construction.writer: backbone LLM (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini or GPT-3.5-Turbo)

organization.structure: timeline: pieces grouped by inferred date
organization.stores: one memorization pool per conversation
organization.index: inferred date (no embedding index described)

management.operations: new pieces added to the pool and organised on the timeline (f_org in Alg. 1)

retrieval.query: the temporal question
retrieval.candidates: all memory pieces, shown to an LLM as numbered options
retrieval.selection: LLM selects one or more option numbers (prompt inherited from MemoChat)

use.context: selected pieces (summary, time, related dialogue lines) + question + options + generated Python code and its output
use.reasoning: LLM writes Python (datetime, dateutil, weekRange helpers), code is executed (regenerated on error), then a final LLM call picks the option

classify.note: The timeline groups pieces by date, but retrieval does not use the dates as an index: an LLM reads every piece as a numbered option and picks some. Structure kept as flat because the paper describes no levels or links beyond the date grouping.

stages.ingestion: Each dialogue session is given to the LLM as a numbered-line conversation with its session timestamp.
stages.construction: Timeline summarization: the LLM writes a summary of the session at the session date and, for every event the speakers place at another time, a separate summary linked to the inferred date (or a date range for vague expressions such as 'last week'), each with the start and end line numbers it covers.
stages.organization: Memory pieces are arranged as a timeline: events at the same inferred time are grouped and indexed by that time.
stages.retrieval: For a question, an LLM is shown the question and all memory pieces as numbered options and returns the numbers of the relevant ones.
stages.answer: The LLM translates the question, options and retrieved evidence into Python code using datetime/dateutil and provided helpers (weekRange, lastWeekendRange); the code is executed (and regenerated if it fails), and a final LLM call reads the evidence, code and output and picks one option (A-E, including 'Unanswerable').

systems.summary: Temporal QA over multi-session dialogue with time-aware memory (per-session summaries plus one summary per mentioned event at its inferred date) and neuro-symbolic reasoning, where the LLM writes and runs Python date code before choosing the answer; also contributes a 600-question LoCoMo-based temporal benchmark.

abstract.text: TReMu targets temporal questions about long multi-session conversations, where people refer to events with relative times and across sessions. The authors build a 600-question multiple-choice benchmark by augmenting LoCoMo dialogues with GPT-4o and manual checking, covering when an event happened, which of two happened first, and how far apart they were, plus unanswerable questions. Their method writes memory as a timeline: each session is summarised and every mentioned event gets its own summary dated by when it happened. At question time an LLM picks relevant memory, writes Python date code that is executed, and then chooses the answer; with GPT-4o accuracy rises from 29.83 (standard prompting) to 77.67.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Memory separates when an event was mentioned from when it happened: each mentioned event is stored at its inferred date, not the session date.
There is no embedding search: an LLM reads all memory pieces as numbered options and picks the relevant ones.
The answer is chosen after the LLM writes and runs Python date arithmetic; the benchmark is multiple choice, so the method is not tested on free-form answers.

units.name: Memory piece
units.role: one summarised event (or the whole session) tied to a date
units.made_by: backbone LLM with the time-aware memorization prompt (Fig. 11), once per session

fields.name: time
fields.what: session date for the session summary; inferred date (mm/dd/yyyy) or range ('During 07/24/2022 to 07/30/2022') for mentioned events

fields.name: summary
fields.what: paragraph summary of the session, or a short summary of one mentioned event from the perspective of its own date

fields.name: start / end line
fields.what: line numbers of the conversation the summary covers

fields.name: related dialogue
fields.what: the original turns in that line range, each marked with its timestamp; shown with the retrieved piece

write.how: LLM reads one session (numbered lines, session timestamp) and writes a paragraph summary at the session date
write.out: JSON list of {time, summary, start, end}

write.how: for each event the speakers place at another time, the same call writes a separate summary linked to the inferred date; vague times become a date range
write.out: e.g. 5 dated pieces from one LoCoMo session (Table 4)

write.how: group events that happen at the same time and index them by inferred time
write.note: the paper gives no prompt or rule for this step

read.scores: question vs every memory piece, read together by the LLM
read.how: LLM gets the question and all memory pieces as numbered options and returns the chosen numbers ('N#M')

few-shot prompt; the LLM writes Python with datetime/dateutil and helpers weekRange and lastWeekendRange, defining separate variables for when an event was mentioned and when it happened; an event with no inferable time is set to None
run the code; if it fails, regenerate it
LLM reads evidence, question, options and the code with its output, and returns one letter A-E

answer_context.sees: selected memory pieces (summary, time and the related dialogue turns with timestamps), the question, the answer options, and the generated code with its printed output
answer_context.format: 'Related Evidence: <MEMORY> Query Question: <QUERY> Answer Options: <OPTIONS> Rationales: <CODE>', output JSON {"final answer": letter}

compression.what: retrieved evidence vs one LoCoMo conversation
compression.basis: Not reported: the paper gives no memory size, number of pieces per session or context length. LoCoMo conversations average 9,209.2 tokens (Table 1).

open_questions: The retrieval step is never ablated on its own: Timeline + CoT changes both the stored memory and keeps LLM selection, so how much of the gain comes from dated event pieces versus the linked raw dialogue lines is not separated.
SP and CoT read the whole dialogue while memory methods read selected pieces; GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini fit LoCoMo in context, and there memory alone (MemoChat) scores below CoT.
The paper does not report how many memory pieces are produced or retrieved, or the token cost of the three LLM calls per question.

components.model: Python interpreter with datetime, dateutil and helper functions

discussion.takeaway: Storing each mentioned event at the date it happened, then doing the date arithmetic in executed Python, lifts GPT-4o from 29.83 to 77.67 accuracy on a new LoCoMo-based temporal multiple-choice benchmark.

claims.claim: Temporal reasoning across sessions is hard for current LLMs.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o 29.83 with SP and 61.67 with CoT; GPT-3.5-Turbo 23.83 and 25.83 (Tables 5, 7, §4.2).

claims.claim: TReMu beats all baselines on accuracy and unanswerable F1 with all three LLMs.
Time-aware memorization beats standard session summaries.
claims.evidence: Timeline + CoT vs MemoChat + CoT: 71.50 vs 41.67 (GPT-4o), 49.67 vs 28.00, 30.67 vs 28.50 (§4.3).

claims.claim: Executed code helps beyond CoT on the same memory.
claims.evidence: TReMu vs Timeline + CoT: +6.17 (GPT-4o), +1.50 (4o-mini), +3.00 (3.5) (§4.3).

claims.claim: Code generation is reliable.
claims.evidence: Execution failures 1.80% to 14.16% (Fig. 2, §4.4).

limits: Evaluation is multiple choice rather than open-ended dialogue, because free-form temporal answers are hard to score.
Only closed models are tested; most open models could not fit LoCoMo dialogues (about 10% fit Llama-3-70B) or follow the output format.
reading: The benchmark was built by the same authors with GPT-4o (event extraction, linking, QA writing) plus manual review, and TReMu's memory is also written by an LLM prompted to date events; no other memory system except MemoChat is tested on it.

Gains shrink with weaker models: over Timeline + CoT, TReMu adds 6.17 points with GPT-4o but 1.50 with GPT-4o-mini; it loses on precedence with GPT-4o-mini (46.08 vs 59.80) and GPT-3.5-Turbo (37.25 vs 44.12), and on interval with GPT-3.5-Turbo (22.22 vs 22.65).
With GPT-4o-mini TReMu's unanswerable recall is 92.86 but precision 29.21, so part of its accuracy may come from answering 'Unanswerable' often; the paper does not discuss this.
Memory methods (MemoChat, MemoChat + CoT) score below full-dialogue CoT for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini (§4.2); the memory advantage appears only once dated event pieces are added.
For GPT-3.5-Turbo, dialogues longer than its window are cut by dropping earlier turns for SP and CoT, so those baselines see less text than memory methods.

systems.name: True Memory

paper.title: Storage Is Not Memory: A Retrieval-Centered Architecture for Agent Recall

construction.unit: event (one verbatim message row)
construction.kept_as: verbatim
construction.processing: write message row + FTS5 and 256-d vector rows; encoding gate disabled in benchmarks
construction.writer: L1 writer (no LLM); gate uses gzip novelty, salience, prediction error

organization.structure: flat event table plus derived side tables
organization.stores: single SQLite file: messages, summaries, timelines, entity profiles, surprise scores
organization.index: FTS5 BM25 + sqlite-vec 256-d dense (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B or Model2Vec)

management.operations: L4 consolidator writes cluster summaries, contradiction records, timeline rows
management.conflicts: contradiction records by entity/predicate; superseded-by timeline links

retrieval.query: question; HyDE expansion in Pro tier
retrieval.candidates: FTS5 BM25 top-k + dense top-k, weighted RRF (k=60)
retrieval.selection: temporal/engram/surprise reweighting, cross-encoder rerank of top 100
retrieval.budget: top-k=10 to answer model

use.context: top-10 reranked events
use.reasoning: single gpt-4.1-mini answer call, max 200 tokens

stages.ingestion: An encoding gate (gzip-based novelty, salience, embedding prediction error) admits or rejects each event; it is disabled (every event admitted) in all reported benchmark numbers. Admitted events are written verbatim to a SQLite messages table with FTS5 and 256-d sqlite-vec indices.
stages.construction: Post-ingestion batch jobs build an L5 per-event surprise score and an L0 speaker engram (preference attribute map + char-n-gram style vector).
stages.organization: Single SQLite file: verbatim messages plus side tables (summaries, contradiction records, timelines, entity profiles, surprise scores, episodes).
stages.update: L4 consolidator produces cluster summaries, contradiction records and timeline rows with superseded-by links, kept alongside the verbatim events.
stages.retrieval: FTS5 BM25 and dense top-k fused by weighted RRF (k=60), reweighted by conditional temporal boost, speaker-engram prior and surprise boost, then cross-encoder rerank (pre-rerank window 100) with modality factor; top-k (default 10) to the answer model. Pro tier adds HyDE query expansion.
stages.answer: gpt-4.1-mini answers from the retrieved top-k (temperature 0, max 200 tokens).

systems.summary: Retrieval-centered memory over verbatim events in a single SQLite file (BM25+dense RRF, salience/engram reweighting, cross-encoder rerank), arguing extraction at ingestion is the wrong primitive.
systems.notes:
Authors: Joshua Adler, Guy Zehavi (Sauron Labs). Three tiers: Edge (Model2Vec potion-base-8M + ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2), Base (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B@256d + gte-reranker-modernbert-base), Pro (= Base + HyDE query expansion). All scores use a semantic-match judge that the authors say is more lenient than strict-match; absolute numbers not comparable to strict-match baselines. AXES-CHECK: seed taxonomy row consistent; paper adds an ingestion gate (disabled in benchmarks), L3 salience/L0 speaker-prior reweighting and HyDE (Pro) at selection time.
DESIGN: Sec 4.1 (Stages 1-10), 5, 5.2, 6 (Table 1). forgetting null: no deletion described; control.management null: consolidator mechanism (LLM or rule) not stated.

systems.name: WebWeaver

paper.title: WebWeaver: Structuring Web-Scale Evidence with Dynamic Outlines for Open-Ended Deep Research

construction.unit: evidence-bank entry per visited URL (goal, summary, evidence) + an outline whose sections cite entry ids
construction.kept_as: LLM-extracted evidence passages (asked to keep original wording) + LLM summary
construction.processing: web search → LLM picks URLs → page read (≤24k tokens) → LLM extracts summary and evidence; planner rewrites the cited outline
construction.writer: gpt-oss-120b (URL selection, summary, evidence); planner LLM (outline)

organization.structure: flat id-keyed evidence bank + hierarchical outline citing ids
organization.stores: memory bank (url → goal, summary, evidence); outline
organization.index: sequential ids <id_n> per URL; no embeddings

management.operations: append entries for new URLs (seen URLs reused); outline rewritten in each cycle

retrieval.query: writer names the ids cited under the current section
retrieval.candidates: bank entries with those ids (exact lookup)
retrieval.selection: writer LLM, guided by the outline citations
retrieval.budget: retrieved evidence cut at 20,000 characters per call; writer context cap 100k tokens

use.context: outline + goal and summary of every page + the current section's evidence; earlier evidence masked
use.reasoning: section-by-section ReAct writing (~25 steps per report)

classify.note: The bank itself is a flat append-only list keyed by id; the structure is the agent-written outline, which is rewritten each cycle and routes the writer to ids.

stages.ingestion: The planner issues batches of web queries; a search API returns the top 10 results per query, an LLM picks relevant URLs from titles and snippets, and each page is read and cut to 24k tokens.
stages.construction: An LLM (gpt-oss-120b) turns each page into a short query-focused summary and longer evidence (quotes, data, tables); summary and evidence are stored under a new <id_n> in the memory bank.
stages.organization: The bank is a flat list keyed by id. The planner keeps a hierarchical outline and cites bank ids under each subsection; only summaries enter the planner's own context.
stages.update: After new evidence arrives the planner rewrites the whole outline (expand, restructure, add citations); on average 2.2 outline rounds per task.
stages.retrieval: The writer walks the outline section by section, calling retrieve with the cited ids to pull those entries' evidence from the bank.
stages.answer: The writer reads the outline, every page's summary and the current section's evidence, writes the section, and the evidence is masked before the next section.
stages.learning: WebWeaver-3k (3.3k planning and 3.1k writing trajectories from a teacher) is used for full fine-tuning of Qwen3-30B-A3B.

systems.summary: Deep-research agent whose memory is an id-keyed evidence bank plus a dynamic outline that cites it: the planner interleaves search with outline rewriting, and the writer composes section by section from only the evidence each section cites.
systems.notes: DESIGN: paper §2 (actions, memory bank), §3.2-3.3, §4.1, Tables 3-4; code DeepResearch repo WebAgent/WebWeaver at f72f75d8 (2026-02-27). Venue: only arXiv v1-v3 known (v3 2025-10-07); arXiv comment 'An agent system for open-ended deep research'. Not a conversational memory system: the 'memory' is per-task working memory for one report. learning=mixed because the framework is prompt-only but the paper also SFTs a 30B model on WebWeaver-3k.

sources.code_note: The WebWeaver folder was added to the Alibaba-NLP/DeepResearch repo on 2026-02-26 (commit 330a5bf2) and patched the next day (f72f75d8, pinned here), about five months after arXiv v3. Its scripts default to qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507 for planner and writer, while the paper's default is Claude-sonnet-4; the summary model is any local vLLM model. Exact identity with the paper's runs is not guaranteed.

headline: The bank stores LLM-extracted evidence per URL, not the raw page; the planner only ever sees the short summaries.
The writer is not limited to cited evidence: its first prompt already holds every page's goal and summary; the retrieve call adds full evidence for the ids a section cites.
After each written section its evidence is masked from the context, so the writer's context stays near one section's evidence.

discussion.takeaway: For long web-research reports, keep gathered evidence out of the model's context in an id-keyed bank, let an outline that is rewritten as evidence arrives decide which ids each section needs, and write one section at a time. This gives the paper's best DeepResearch Bench, DeepConsult and DeepResearchGym scores, notably 93.37% citation accuracy.

claims.claim: State of the art on open-ended deep research.
claims.evidence: DRB RACE 50.62 (Qwen3-235B) and 50.58 (Claude-sonnet-4) vs 49.71 Gemini-2.5-pro deep research; DeepConsult win 66.86%; DRGym avg 96.77 vs 96.02. Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Outline-guided, per-section retrieval raises citation accuracy.
claims.evidence: C. acc. 93.37 vs 78.30 (Gemini) and 75.01 (OpenAI); 86.73 with the brute-force writer. Table 1, Fig. 10

claims.claim: Iterative outline optimization improves reports and outlines.
claims.evidence: DRB overall 48.15 → 49.55 over three rounds; outline judge score 81.9 → 92.3 (DRB), 77.2 → 88.2 (DRGym). Figs. 6-9

claims.claim: Section-wise writing beats writing from the whole bank.
claims.evidence: Insight 42.72 → 50.02, readability 43.82 → 49.79 on DRB. Fig. 10, §4.3

claims.claim: WebWeaver-3k SFT teaches a small model the workflow.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-30B-A3B citation accuracy 25.00 → 85.90, DRGym 77.27 → 90.89, DeepConsult 4.57 → 6.09. Fig. 14

discussion.limits_src: The paper has no limitations section.
reading: The 'memory' is per-task working memory for one report, filled from the web; there is no long-term or cross-task memory, so it is not comparable with conversational memory systems.
The writer's first prompt contains every page's summary (about 15k tokens on DRB), so each section is written with the whole summary set in view, not only its cited evidence.
The brute-force ablation removes both focused context and id-based retrieval at once.
In the outline-round study readability drops slightly on DRB (48.73 → 48.58) and clarity on DRGym (91.36 → 90.42) at round 3; the gains are in comprehensiveness, insight and support.
The text reports DRGym support 90.95 → 98.73 for brute-force vs hierarchical, while Fig. 11 labels the brute-force bar 91.82.
Proprietary baselines on DRB are copied from the leaderboard; whether the DeepConsult and DRGym baseline rows were rerun is not stated.
Released code (Feb 2026) defaults to Qwen3-235B for planner and writer, not the paper's Claude-sonnet-4.

abstract.text: WebWeaver targets open-ended deep research, where an agent must turn hundreds of web pages into a long, cited report. A planner alternates between web search and rewriting an outline, and every visited page is reduced to a summary and extracted evidence stored under an id in a memory bank that the outline cites. A writer then composes the report section by section, retrieving only the evidence cited for each section and dropping it afterwards. The system reports state-of-the-art results on DeepResearch Bench, DeepConsult and DeepResearchGym, and a 3k-trajectory SFT set lets a 30B model learn the workflow.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

systems.name: WISE

paper.title: WISE: Rethinking the Knowledge Memory for Lifelong Model Editing of Large Language Models

construction.unit: one edit (prompt, target) written as weight changes in a copy of one FFN value matrix
construction.kept_as: parametric: gradient updates to a random 20% of the copy's entries
construction.processing: each edit plus 10 model-written prefix variants is trained by SGD into the current shard's masked subspace, with an LM loss and a margin loss on the routing score
construction.writer: SGD on the side-memory copy (no LLM writes text)

organization.structure: main memory (original FFN value matrix) + one side memory (edited copy of layer 27's down_proj for LLaMA-2-7B); WISE-Retrieve keeps several side memories
organization.stores: side memory weights; per-shard random masks; routing threshold ε
organization.index: none; routing by an activation score computed inside the layer

management.operations: edits split into shards of 500 (k = 2) with different random masks; every 1,000 edits the shard copies are merged into one side memory by Ties-Merge
management.conflicts: random masks keep shards nearly disjoint; Ties sign election and disjoint mean resolve the overlapping entries

retrieval.query: the input's activations at the side-memory layer
retrieval.candidates: main memory vs side memory (vs each stored side memory in WISE-Retrieve)
retrieval.selection: side memory if its activation score exceeds ε (smallest edit score; × 0.88 in code), else main memory; WISE-Retrieve takes the highest-scoring side memory
retrieval.budget: one FFN matrix per forward pass

use.context: no retrieved text; the routed matrix computes layer 27's FFN output
use.reasoning: ordinary forward pass / generation

classify.note: Parametric memory: a main (pretrained) and a side (edited) weight matrix. Every query is scored against the side memory and a threshold rule (top-1 for WISE-Retrieve) picks which matrix computes the layer; the threshold's separation is trained in by a margin loss.

stages.ingestion: Edits arrive one at a time as (prompt, target) pairs; each is expanded with 10 short prefixes that the unedited model generates.
stages.construction: Each edit is trained by SGD into a copy of one FFN value matrix (layer 27 down_proj for LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B), with gradients masked to a random 20% of entries and a margin loss that pushes the routing score up for the edit and down for an unrelated prompt.
stages.organization: The original matrix is the main memory and the edited copy the side memory. Edits are grouped into shards (500 edits in the released config), each with its own random mask; WISE-Retrieve keeps several side memories.
stages.update: After every 1,000 edits the shard copies' weight changes are merged into one side memory with Ties-Merge (trim, sign election, disjoint mean).
stages.retrieval: At inference the layer measures how much the side memory changes its output; above threshold ε the side memory's output is used, otherwise the original one. WISE-Retrieve scores each stored side memory and uses the highest.
stages.answer: The model generates as usual with the routed FFN output; nothing textual is retrieved.

systems.summary: Lifelong model editing in a side copy of one FFN matrix: edits are trained into random parameter subspaces, merged with Ties-Merge, and an activation-score router picks the side or the original matrix for each query.
systems.notes: VENUE: NeurIPS 2024 main track; the camera-ready PDF (arXiv v3) carries the NeurIPS 2024 footer and the paper is listed in the NeurIPS 2024 proceedings (proceedings.neurips.cc hash 60960ad78868fce5c165295fbd895060). CODE: the paper's footnote points to EasyEdit; pinned to commit f8c59dac (2024-10-31), the last change to easyeditor/models/wise before arXiv v3 (2024-12-19). This is a model-editing paper: the memory is weights, so retrieval-side fields describe the router, not a search. TAGS: learning=sft because every edit is written by supervised gradient steps (LM loss + margin loss); fidelity=compressed because edits exist only as weight changes; control.retrieval=learned-sft because the router's separation is trained by the margin loss at edit time (the threshold itself is a fixed rule). Pre-edit accuracy (Table 3): ZsRE 0.36 (LLaMA) / 0.39 (Mistral); Hallucination PPL 27.4 / 19.4; Temporal 0.56 (GPT-J).

Settings quoted are from hparams/WISE/llama-7b.yaml and examples/run_wise_editing.py at that commit.

headline: The memory is weights: edits are trained into a copy of one FFN matrix and no text is stored or searched.
A threshold on how much the side matrix changes the layer's output decides, per query, whether the edits apply; a margin loss during editing makes that separation.
Main tables use WISE-Merge (one side memory); the released llama-7b config defaults to WISE-Retrieve (retrieve: True).

ablation.src: paper Tables 2, 6, 7, 11 (ZsRE, LLaMA-2-7B). Table 11 is a separate 100-edit run merging 2 MLPs of 50 edits each, so its Ties row differs from Table 2. Without random prefixes Rel./Gen. fall by 0.15/0.17 at T=1000 (Fig. 12).

discussion.takeaway: Keep edits in a separate, mergeable copy of one mid-to-late FFN matrix and route to it by activation. In its own experiments this holds reliability, generalization and locality together over 1,000 sequential ZsRE edits, where earlier editors give up one of the three.

claims.claim: Editing weights directly or retrieving activations cannot give reliability, generalization and locality together in lifelong editing (an 'impossible triangle').
claims.evidence: Fig. 1; Table 2 at T=1000 (LLaMA): ROME/MEMIT locality 0.00/0.02, GRACE generalization 0.08.

claims.claim: WISE leads after long edit sequences.
claims.evidence: ZsRE T=1000 average 0.83 (LLaMA) and 0.79 (Mistral) vs 0.67 and 0.68 for the next best (GRACE; MEMIT-MASS). Table 2, §3.2.

claims.claim: It also corrects hallucinations best.
claims.evidence: SelfCheckGPT T=600: perplexity 3.12 (LLaMA) and 5.21 (Mistral) with Loc. ≥ 0.93. The closest method that keeps locality is MEMIT-MASS (13.47 / 7.28); FT-EWC reaches 4.56 / 5.46 but with Loc. 0.24 / 0.25. Table 4.

claims.claim: Edits generalise out of distribution.
claims.evidence: Temporal, GPT-J, T=75: OOD Gen. 0.37 vs 0.28 for GRACE; average 0.78. Table 5.

claims.claim: The router is what keeps locality.
claims.evidence: Without the routing loss Loc. drops from 1.00 to 0.72 at T=1000. Table 7.

claims.claim: Mid-to-late layers are the right place for the side memory.
claims.evidence: Layer 26 gives ~0.80 Rel./Gen. with Loc. 1.00; layers 0, 1 and 31 fail (Loc. as low as 0.096). Fig. 4, §3.3.

claims.claim: It scales to 3,000 edits at small cost.
claims.evidence: WISE-Retrieve average 0.73 vs 0.66 GRACE and 0.53 MEMIT-MASS (Table 6); +0.64% parameters, +3% inference time for Merge (App. B.7, Fig. 6).

limits: Routing among several side memories falls short of an oracle (0.73 vs 0.82 average at 3K edits).
WISE-Retrieve's inference time grows with the number of edits (about 7% after 3K).
Editing can be misused to insert harmful content; the side memory can be discarded to undo edits.
reading: Locality is tested on NQ questions, and the released script trains the router's 'unrelated' side on NQ questions from the ZsRE train split, so test-time unrelated prompts come from the distribution the router learned to ignore (examples/run_wise_editing.py L50-L51).
Scores are EasyEdit's default 'token em': the share of target tokens predicted correctly with the gold prefix given (evaluate_utils.py L80-L152), not exact match of a generated answer as Eq. 9 reads.
The code's routing score and threshold differ from the paper (σ of the layer output, token mean, ε × 0.88); the figures follow the code.

Random-prefix augmentation is applied to every baseline (§3.1) and several baselines were re-tuned for LLaMA/Mistral (App. A.3), so baseline numbers are this paper's runs, not those papers' own settings.
The Hallucination set was cut to prompts of at most 254 tokens (906 of GRACE's 1,392; 600 test), and it has no generalization metric.
Table 11's Ties row (0.87 at 100 edits) comes from a different merge schedule (every 50 edits) than the main runs.

abstract.text: WISE targets lifelong model editing, where an LLM receives thousands of factual corrections one after another. The authors argue that editing the weights directly breaks unrelated knowledge while retrieval-style activation patches fail to generalise to paraphrases. WISE keeps edits in a side copy of one FFN matrix, trains a router that sends a query to the side or the original matrix, writes groups of edits into random parameter subspaces and merges them with Ties-Merge. On ZsRE, hallucination correction and an out-of-distribution temporal set with LLaMA-2, Mistral and GPT-J it reports the best balance of reliability, generalization and locality.

systems.name: XMem

paper.title: XMem: Long-Term Video Object Segmentation with an Atkinson-Shiffrin Memory Model

construction.unit: one feature element per pixel at stride 16: a 64-d key with a shrinkage scalar and a 512-d value per object
construction.kept_as: learned features of past frames and their predicted masks (no pixels kept)
construction.processing: every 5th frame the query key is copied as a memory key and a value encoder turns image + predicted mask into the value; the GRU state is updated every frame
construction.writer: trained networks: ResNet-50 query encoder, ResNet-18 value encoder, GRU

organization.structure: three tiers after Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory (GRU state), working (recent memory frames), long-term (compact prototypes)
organization.stores: sensory h (64 channels); working memory: first frame + latest frames, 5 to 10 frames; long-term memory: up to 10,000 prototype elements
organization.index: memory keys compared with query keys by an anisotropic L2 similarity (shrinkage per memory key, selection per query channel)

management.operations: when working memory reaches 10 frames, the 5 oldest frames other than the first become candidates: the 128 most-used elements are kept as prototypes and their values are rebuilt as a similarity-weighted average of all candidate values (potentiation)
management.forgetting: least-frequently-used eviction of long-term prototypes once 10,000 elements are reached; usage = accumulated top-k attention / time in memory

retrieval.query: the current frame's key at every pixel, with its selection weights
retrieval.candidates: all working and long-term memory keys
retrieval.selection: top 30 by similarity per query pixel, softmax, weighted sum of the values
retrieval.budget: top-k 30 per query pixel; the memory holds T·HW + L elements (T ≤ 10 frames, L ≤ 10,000)

use.context: readout feature F (512 channels per pixel) together with the sensory state h and the encoder's skip features
use.reasoning: one decoder pass per frame gives the mask; objects are merged by soft aggregation

classify.note: Reading is attention over every stored key; the similarity is learned, and the top-30 cut per query pixel is a fixed rule.

stages.ingestion: Given the first frame and its object mask, XMem processes the video frame by frame and predicts a mask for each new frame.
stages.construction: Every 5th frame the frame's key (copied from the query encoder) and a value (image + predicted mask through the value encoder) are added to working memory; the GRU sensory state is refreshed every frame, with a deep update from the value encoder on memory frames.
stages.organization: Three stores: a sensory GRU state, a working memory of the first frame plus recent memory frames (5-10), and a long-term memory of compact prototypes (up to 10,000 elements).
stages.update: When working memory reaches 10 frames, the 5 oldest non-first frames are consolidated: the 128 most-used elements become prototypes whose values average all candidate values by key similarity; least-used prototypes are evicted when long-term memory is full.
stages.retrieval: Each pixel of the query frame compares its key with every working and long-term key by anisotropic L2 similarity, keeps the top 30, and reads a softmax-weighted sum of their values.
stages.answer: The decoder combines the readout, the sensory state and skip features into a mask per object.
stages.learning: All networks are trained end to end on static-image pretraining, then YouTubeVOS and DAVIS (optionally BL30K), with 8-frame sequences so the sensory memory learns.

systems.summary: Video object segmentation with three feature memories (sensory, working, long-term); working-memory frames are consolidated into a small set of usage-selected prototypes so GPU memory stays bounded on very long videos.

Not an LLM memory: keys/values are CNN features, 'answer' is the segmentation mask. Result rows use answer_model 'none (end-to-end VOS network)' so rows of one table stay comparable. abstract.text: XMem segments a target object through long videos with three feature memories modelled on the Atkinson-Shiffrin theory: a sensory memory updated every frame, a high-resolution working memory of recent frames, and a compact long-term memory. When working memory fills up, its most-used elements are consolidated into long-term prototypes, which keeps GPU memory bounded without compressing new features right away. A new similarity function with per-key confidence and per-channel selection governs how the query reads memory. XMem clearly beats earlier methods on long videos while matching the best methods on standard short-video benchmarks.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: New frames enter working memory at full resolution; only when it holds 10 frames are the 5 oldest (never the first) squeezed into 128 prototypes, a 6328% compression.
Which elements survive is decided by usage: how much attention each element received while in working memory.
Reading is plain attention with a top-30 cut per pixel over working and long-term memory together; the sensory GRU state goes straight to the decoder.

units.name: Working-memory element
units.role: one pixel (stride 16) of a memory frame
units.made_by: query encoder (key) and value encoder (value), every 5th frame

fields.name: key
fields.what: 64-d feature of the frame, copied from the query encoder

fields.name: shrinkage s
fields.what: per-key confidence ≥ 1 that sharpens or widens the key's influence

fields.name: selection e
fields.what: per-channel weights of the frame; used only when the element is chosen as a prototype, to weight the potentiation similarity

fields.name: value
fields.what: 512-d feature per object from the image and the predicted mask

fields.name: usage
fields.what: accumulated top-k attention divided by the number of reads since insertion; ranks elements for consolidation (and, in long-term memory, eviction)

units.name: Long-term prototype
units.role: a consolidated element kept for the rest of the video unless evicted
units.made_by: consolidation rule (top usage) + potentiation (similarity-weighted average)

fields.name: key
fields.what: key of a high-usage candidate element, kept as is

fields.name: value
fields.what: softmax-weighted average of all candidate values by key similarity to the prototype

fields.name: shrinkage
fields.what: averaged the same way as the value

units.name: Sensory memory
units.role: short-term state that tracks position and motion
units.made_by: GRU on decoder features every frame; a second GRU on value-encoder features on memory frames (deep update)

fields.name: h
fields.what: 64-channel hidden state per object at stride 16, zero at the start

write.how: GRU refreshes h from multi-scale decoder features every frame; on memory frames a separate GRU uses value-encoder features instead (deep update)
every r-th frame (and any frame with a given mask) the key and a new value are appended to working memory
when working memory holds 10 frames, the first frame and the latest 4 stay; the 5 frames in between are candidates and the 128 elements with the highest usage become prototype keys
write.out: compression 6328% from working to long-term memory

write.how: each prototype's value becomes a softmax average of all candidate values, weighted by key similarity to the prototype (no top-k here); candidates are then deleted from working memory
before adding prototypes, if long-term memory is within 128 of its limit, the least-used prototypes are removed
write.out: about 3,900 frames' worth of information at r = 10 (App. D)
write.src: paper §3.3, App. D; code memory_manager.py L186-L187, kv_memory_store.py L135-L156

read.how: ResNet-50 features at stride 16; 3×3 convolutions give the key q and the selection e (sigmoid)

read.scores: query key vs every working and long-term key
read.how: anisotropic L2: negative squared distance weighted per channel by e and scaled per key by s
read.src: paper §3.2, Eq. 2, App. I; code memory_util.py L7-L39

read.how: for each query pixel keep the 30 highest similarities, softmax them, zero the rest; the attention mass is added to each element's usage
read.src: paper §4; code memory_util.py L41-L65, memory_manager.py L70-L119

read.how: weighted sum of the selected values gives F (512 channels per pixel)
decoder fuses F with the sensory state h and the query encoder's skip features, upsamples to stride 4 and outputs a logit per object; objects are merged by soft aggregation

answer_context.sees: readout F from working + long-term memory, sensory state h, and the query frame's own features
answer_context.format: feature maps concatenated in the decoder; no text
excludes: memory elements outside each pixel's top 30
includes: first-frame features (always kept in working memory)

compression.what: long-term prototypes vs working-memory candidates per consolidation
compression.basis: §4 states a 6328% compression ratio for T min 5, T max 10, P 128 (Table 6: 12625% at P 64, 3164% at P 256).

compression.what: maximum GPU memory, Long-time Video 3× (LT max 10,000)
compression.basis: 1,515 MB for XMem (App. D, Table S1); the paper does not give a no-consolidation baseline in the same units, so no ratio.

paper_vs_code.paper: Eq. 2 without a temperature
paper_vs_code.code: similarity is also divided by √64 before the softmax

paper_vs_code.paper: long-term usage (for eviction) is always tracked
paper_vs_code.code: tracked only when the video is long enough to fill long-term memory (frames / 5 × 128 ≥ 10,000); shorter videos never evict anyway

paper_vs_code.topic: Memory insertion rate on Long-time Video
paper_vs_code.paper: r = 10 on Long-time Video, 5 elsewhere
paper_vs_code.code: eval.py defaults to 5; the r = 10 run is a command-line flag given in docs/INFERENCE.md

open_questions: Without long-term memory the model scores slightly higher on the short sets (85.9 vs 85.7 on YouTubeVOS 2018, Table 4), so consolidation buys bounded memory and speed, not accuracy, on short videos.
Long-time Video has only three videos; the 3× variant plays them back and forth, so it tests memory size rather than new content.
Usage-based and random prototype selection differ by 0.3 J&F at P = 128 (Table 6), within the reported spread; potentiation (87.9 → 90.0) matters more than the selection rule.

ablation.src: paper Tables 4-8 (Long-time rows are means of 5 insertion offsets)

discussion.takeaway: Keeping several memories at different time scales, and consolidating working memory into a few heavily used prototypes only when it fills, lets video segmentation run on long videos with bounded GPU memory and no loss on short ones.

claims.claim: A single feature memory ties accuracy to memory cost; separate stores break that link.
claims.evidence: Fig. 1: methods with growing memory must insert sparsely and drop on long videos. §1

claims.claim: Clearly better than prior work on long videos.
claims.evidence: Long-time Video 3×: 90.0 J&F vs 84.6 STCN and 83.8 AFB-URR; 1×→3× change +0.2. Table 1

claims.claim: On par with the best short-video methods, and faster.
claims.evidence: YouTubeVOS 2018 85.7 vs AOT 85.5; DAVIS 2017 val 86.2 vs STCN 85.4; 22.6 FPS on DAVIS 2017 vs 20.2 STCN and 18.0 AOT. Table 2

claims.claim: Consolidation beats other long-video strategies.
claims.evidence: Long-time 3×: 90.0 vs 87.3 eager compression, 87.3 sparse insertion, 85.5 local window. Table 7

claims.claim: Potentiation matters.
claims.evidence: 87.9 → 90.0 on Long-time 3×. Table 6

claims.claim: Both similarity scaling terms help together.
claims.evidence: 86.2 with both vs 85.1 with neither on DAVIS 2017. Table 5

limits: Fails on very fast objects or heavy motion blur, where even the per-frame sensory memory cannot keep up (§4.4, App. C).
A stronger sensory memory with a larger receptive field might help (§4.4).
reading: Removing long-term memory slightly raises short-video scores (85.9 G, 86.3 J&F); the long-term store pays off only on long videos, where the ablation cannot run it without memory limits (n/a).

Table 1 baselines were re-run with reduced memory insertion to fit in memory, with 5 offsets; baseline numbers on the short sets (Table 2-3) are not said to be re-run except AOT on YouTubeVOS and the re-timed FPS.
r differs by dataset (10 on Long-time Video, 5 on the short sets; 3 in the multi-scale runs of App. H).
The selection term is stored with working-memory elements but only used to potentiate prototypes; long-term prototypes keep no selection term.
Default long-term size (10,000) is far above what Long-time Video needs: 1,000 elements already give 89.5 vs 90.0 (Table S1).
